lessons.title: Introduction: Blocks of the Periodic Table
lessons.notes_html:
The periodic table can be divided into four blocks: s, p, d and f. The classification of elements into blocks is based upon the valence orbital of the element involved in bond formation, that is, the sub-shell into which the last electron enters.

The Four Blocks

BlockGroupsLast electron entersElements per periodGeneral configuration
s-blockGroup 1, Group 2 and Period 1s-subshell2ns1-2
p-blockGroups 13 to 18 (except helium)p-subshell6ns2 np1-6
d-blockGroups 3 to 12d-subshell10(n-1)d1-10 ns1-2
f-blockLanthanides and actinidesf-subshell14(n-2)f1-14 (n-1)d0 or 1 ns2

The number of elements in each block per period is fixed by the capacity of the sub-shell: s holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14. The d-block elements are also known as transition elements. The specific d-subshell is one less (n-1) than the period number, and the specific f-subshell is two less (n-2) than the period number. In most periodic tables the f-block elements are placed below the table to save space.

Key Points

  • Elements are divided into s, p, d and f blocks according to the sub-shell that receives the last electron.
  • s-block: Groups 1 and 2, general configuration ns1-2, two elements per period.
  • p-block: Groups 13 to 18 except helium, general configuration ns2 np1-6, six elements per period.
  • d-block: Groups 3 to 12, general configuration (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2; these are the transition elements.
  • f-block: lanthanides and actinides, general configuration (n-2)f1-14 (n-1)d0 or 1 ns2, placed below the table.

lessons.title: Groups and Periods of Elements in the Periodic Table
lessons.notes_html:
The vertical columns of elements in the periodic table are called groups or families. There are two systems for numbering the groups: the older system and the newer IUPAC system. According to the latest IUPAC system, the modern periodic table has 18 groups. Elements in the same group show similar properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.

The horizontal rows of elements in the periodic table are called periods. The modern periodic table has seven periods.

Periods of the Periodic Table

PeriodNumber of elementsDescription
1st2 (hydrogen and helium)Shortest period
2nd and 3rd8 eachShort periods
4th and 5th18 eachLong periods
6th and 7th32 eachLongest periods

Key Points

  • Groups are the vertical columns; the modern table has 18 groups (IUPAC system).
  • Elements in the same group have similar properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.
  • Periods are the horizontal rows; there are seven periods.
  • Period lengths are 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements.
  • The 1st period is the shortest; the 6th and 7th periods are the longest.

lessons.title: Period 3 Elements (Na to Ar): Electronic Structure
lessons.notes_html:
Period 3 consists of eight elements: sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), aluminium (Al), silicon (Si), phosphorus (P), sulphur (S), chlorine (Cl) and argon (Ar). The properties of elements change from left to right across a period and from top to bottom down a group. The properties that change with the rise of atomic number are called periodic properties or atomic properties. They are based on the electronic configurations of the atoms. Some atomic properties are atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity, electrical conductivity, and melting and boiling points.

Across Period 3, from Na to Ar, each element has one more proton and one more electron than the one before it.

Electronic Configurations of Period 3 Elements

ElementSymbolAtomic NumberComplete Electronic ConfigurationValence Shell Configuration
SodiumNa111s2 2s2 2p6 3s13s1
MagnesiumMg121s2 2s2 2p6 3s23s2
AluminiumAl131s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p13s2 3p1
SiliconSi141s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p23s2 3p2
PhosphorusP151s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p33s2 3p3
SulphurS161s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p43s2 3p4
ChlorineCl171s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p53s2 3p5
ArgonAr181s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p63s2 3p6

The electronic configurations of atoms play an important role in knowing the physical and chemical properties of the elements and their compounds.

Key Points

  • Period 3 has eight elements: Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl and Ar.
  • Periodic properties change regularly with atomic number and depend on electronic configuration.
  • Across the period each element gains one proton and one electron.
  • The valence shell fills from 3s1 (Na) to 3s2 3p6 (Ar).
  • Argon has a complete octet, 3s2 3p6, so it is very stable and unreactive.

lessons.title: Trends in Atomic Radius in Period 3
lessons.notes_html:
The average distance between the centre of the nucleus and the outermost electronic shell of an atom is called atomic radius. The units used to measure atomic radius are nanometre (1 nm = 10^-9 m), angstrom (1 A° = 10^-10 m) and picometre (1 pm = 10^-12 m).

Atomic Radii of Period 3 Elements

ElementNaMgAlSiPSClAr
Atomic Radius (pm)19014511811198887971

The atomic radius generally decreases from Na to Ar across the period. This is due to the increase in the nuclear charge, which pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus. The number of core electrons remains the same across the period, so the shielding effect remains almost constant.

Key Points

  • Atomic radius is the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell.
  • Atomic radius decreases across Period 3, from 190 pm (Na) to 71 pm (Ar).
  • Reason: nuclear charge increases across the period and pulls the electron cloud inward.
  • The shielding effect stays almost constant because the number of core electrons does not change.

lessons.title: Trends in Ionization Energy in Period 3
lessons.notes_html:
Ionization energy is the minimum amount of energy required to remove an electron from the isolated gaseous atom or ion in its ground state. It shows how tightly the electron is bound to the nucleus. The higher the value of ionization energy, the more difficult it is to remove the electron. For example: Na → Na+ + 1e-, IE = 496 kJ/mol.

The minimum energy needed to remove the first electron is the first ionization energy (for Mg: Mg → Mg+ + 1e-, IE1 = 738 kJ/mol). The energy needed to remove the second electron is the second ionization energy (Mg+ → Mg2+ + 1e-, IE2 = 1451 kJ/mol), and the third is the third ionization energy (IE3 = 7730 kJ/mol for Mg). Ionization energy values increase with the removal of each electron, because the repulsion among the remaining electrons decreases and the attraction between the nucleus and the valence electron increases: 1st IE < 2nd IE < 3rd IE.

Ionization energy depends upon: (i) atomic radius, (ii) nuclear charge, (iii) shielding effect, and (iv) electronic configuration of the elements.

First Ionization Energies of Period 3 Elements

ElementNaMgAlSiPSClAr
IE (kJ/mol)4967385787861012100012511520

Ionization energy generally increases from sodium to argon across the period, due to the increase in nuclear charge and the decrease in atomic radius. The metals (Na, Mg and Al) have small values of ionization energies, while the non-metals (P, S, Cl and Ar) have high values because of their smaller size. The high ionization energy of argon is due to its stable electronic configuration.

Key Points

  • Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
  • Successive ionization energies increase: 1st IE < 2nd IE < 3rd IE.
  • Ionization energy depends on atomic radius, nuclear charge, shielding effect and electronic configuration.
  • First ionization energy generally increases across Period 3, from 496 kJ/mol (Na) to 1520 kJ/mol (Ar).
  • Metals have low ionization energies; non-metals have high values.
  • Argon's value is especially high because of its stable complete octet.

lessons.title: Trends in Electronegativity in Period 3
lessons.notes_html:
Electronegativity is the relative tendency (ability or power) of an atom in a molecule to attract a shared pair (bond pair) of electrons towards itself. Electronegativity has no unit. Elements with low electronegativity values are metals and have a tendency to lose electrons. Elements with high electronegativity values are non-metals and have a tendency to gain electrons.

Electronegativity Values of Period 3 Elements

ElementNaMgAlSiPSClAr
Electronegativity0.931.311.812.022.192.583.16-

The electronegativity of argon is not included in the table because the compounds of argon are rare. Electronegativity increases from sodium to chlorine due to the increase in nuclear charge. The shielding effect remains constant along the period.

Key Points

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons; it has no unit.
  • It increases across Period 3, from 0.93 (Na) to 3.16 (Cl).
  • Reason: nuclear charge increases while the shielding effect stays constant.
  • Low electronegativity means a metal that loses electrons; high electronegativity means a non-metal that gains electrons.
  • Argon is not assigned a value because its compounds are rare.

lessons.title: Trends in Electrical Conductivity in Period 3
lessons.notes_html:
Electrical conductivity is the ability of a material to carry an electric current. It is due to loose (free) electrons in a material. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are good conductors, silicon is a semiconductor, while the rest of the elements of Period 3 are non-conductors.

Electrical Conductivity of Period 3 Elements

ElementNaMgAlSiPSClAr
Electrical ConductivityGoodGoodGoodPoorNoneNoneNoneNone

Electrical conductivity increases from sodium to aluminium. This rise is due to the increasing number of delocalized electrons in the metallic solid: sodium provides one, magnesium two and aluminium three electrons for metallic bonding. Silicon has a giant covalent structure similar to that of diamond and has few delocalized electrons, so it is a semiconductor. The elements from phosphorus to argon are non-conductors because their electrons are tightly bound to the nucleus and are not free to move.

Key Points

  • Electrical conductivity is due to free, delocalized electrons.
  • Conductivity increases from Na to Al as the number of delocalized electrons rises from 1 to 3.
  • Silicon is a semiconductor because its giant covalent structure has few delocalized electrons.
  • P, S, Cl and Ar do not conduct: their electrons are tightly bound and cannot move.

lessons.title: Trends in Melting and Boiling Points in Period 3
lessons.notes_html:
The melting and boiling points of Period 3 elements increase from left to right up to silicon and then gradually decrease.

Melting and Boiling Points of Period 3 Elements

ElementNaMgAlSiPSClAr
Melting Point (°C)986506601420600119-102-189
Boiling Point (°C)8831100240024801000444-34-186

Melting and boiling points depend upon the number of valence electrons and bond strength. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium have strong metallic bonds; they contain one, two and three valence electrons respectively, so sodium provides one, magnesium two and aluminium three electrons for metallic bonds. Silicon, a semimetal, has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds with other silicon atoms in a giant structure, so it has the highest melting and boiling points of the period.

The other elements of Period 3 (P, S, Cl and Ar) are non-metals and have low melting and boiling points. They form simple molecules held together by weak London dispersion forces, so only a small amount of energy is required to overcome these forces. The melting and boiling points of sulphur are higher than those of the other three non-metals because the sulphur (S8) molecule is larger than P4, Cl2 and Ar, and the strength of London forces increases with the size of the molecules. The order is: S8 > P4 > Cl2 > Ar.

Key Points

  • Melting and boiling points rise from Na to Si, then fall to Ar.
  • Na, Mg and Al are held by metallic bonds that strengthen with more delocalized electrons.
  • Silicon has the highest values because of its giant covalent structure.
  • P, S, Cl and Ar form simple molecules with weak London dispersion forces, so their melting and boiling points are low.
  • Among the molecular elements the order is S8 > P4 > Cl2 > Ar, because larger molecules have stronger London forces.

lessons.title: Reactions of Period 3 Elements with Water
lessons.notes_html:
The Period 3 elements behave very differently with water: reactivity falls across the period.

Reaction of Sodium with Water

Sodium reacts with cold water violently to produce hydrogen gas and a colourless solution of sodium hydroxide. The reaction is exothermic.

2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2

Reaction of Magnesium with Water

Magnesium reacts with cold water gently to produce magnesium hydroxide.

Mg + 2H2O → Mg(OH)2 + H2

Magnesium burns in steam with a white flame to produce magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas.

Mg + H2O → MgO + H2

Reaction of Aluminium with Water

Finely divided aluminium reacts with steam to give aluminium oxide and hydrogen gas. The reaction is relatively slow due to the formation of an aluminium oxide layer on the surface of the metal.

2Al + 3H2O → Al2O3 + 3H2

Reaction of Silicon with Water

Silicon does not react with water in its elemental form at room temperature. It reacts with water at extremely high temperature, producing silicon dioxide and hydrogen gas. The inertness of silicon is due to a protective layer of silicon dioxide on its surface.

Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2

Reactions of Phosphorus, Sulphur and Argon with Water

Phosphorus, sulphur and argon do not react with water: P4 + H2O → No Reaction; S + H2O → No Reaction; Ar + H2O → No Reaction.

Reaction of Chlorine with Water

Chlorine reacts with water to produce a mixture of hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid. The reaction is reversible.

Cl2 + H2O ⇌ HCl + HOCl

The HOCl, in the presence of sunlight, is slowly decomposed into hydrochloric acid and oxygen gas: 2HOCl → 2HCl + O2. The overall change is: 2Cl2 + 2H2O ⇌ 4HCl + O2.

Key Reactions

ElementReaction with water
Na2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2 (violent, exothermic)
MgMg + 2H2O → Mg(OH)2 + H2 (gentle with cold water); Mg + H2O → MgO + H2 (with steam)
Al2Al + 3H2O → Al2O3 + 3H2 (with steam, slow)
SiSi + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2 (only at extremely high temperature)
P, S, ArNo reaction
ClCl2 + H2O ⇌ HCl + HOCl

Key Points

  • Reactivity with water decreases across Period 3.
  • Sodium reacts violently with cold water, giving NaOH and H2.
  • Magnesium reacts gently with cold water and burns in steam.
  • Aluminium reacts only with steam, slowly, because of its protective oxide layer.
  • Silicon is protected by a surface layer of SiO2; P, S and Ar do not react at all.
  • Chlorine gives HCl and HOCl with water; HOCl decomposes in sunlight to HCl and O2.

lessons.title: Reactions of Period 3 Elements with Oxygen
lessons.notes_html:
All Period 3 elements except chlorine and argon react directly with oxygen, forming oxides.

Reaction of Sodium with Oxygen

Sodium burns with a yellow flame to give a mixture of sodium oxide and sodium peroxide.

4Na + O2 → 2Na2O

2Na + O2 → Na2O2

Reaction of Magnesium with Oxygen

Magnesium burns in oxygen with a brilliant white flame to form magnesium oxide.

2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

Reaction of Aluminium with Oxygen

Finely divided aluminium burns in oxygen with a brilliant white flame to produce white alumina (aluminium oxide).

4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3

Reaction of Silicon with Oxygen

Silicon burns in oxygen with a bright yellow flame at high temperature and produces silicon dioxide.

Si + O2 → SiO2 (400-1000°C)

Reaction of Phosphorus with Oxygen

Phosphorus burns in oxygen with a white flame and produces white smoke. The smoke contains phosphorus (III) oxide and phosphorus (V) oxide.

P4 + 3O2 → P4O6

P4 + 5O2 → P4O10

Reaction of Sulphur with Oxygen

Sulphur burns in oxygen with a brilliant blue flame and gives sulphur dioxide gas.

S + O2 → SO2

Chlorine and Argon

Chlorine does not react with oxygen directly (Cl2 + O2 → No Reaction), and argon does not react with oxygen (Ar + O2 → No Reaction).

Key Reactions

ElementOxide formed
NaNa2O and Na2O2 (yellow flame)
MgMgO (brilliant white flame)
AlAl2O3 (brilliant white flame)
SiSiO2 (bright yellow flame, at high temperature)
PP4O6 and P4O10 (white flame, white smoke)
SSO2 (brilliant blue flame)
Cl, ArNo reaction

Key Points

  • Sodium gives a mixture of the oxide Na2O and the peroxide Na2O2.
  • Magnesium and aluminium burn with brilliant white flames to MgO and Al2O3.
  • Silicon needs a high temperature (400-1000°C) to form SiO2.
  • Phosphorus forms two oxides, P4O6 and P4O10; sulphur forms SO2.
  • Chlorine and argon do not react with oxygen directly.

lessons.title: Reactions of Period 3 Elements with Chlorine
lessons.notes_html:
All Period 3 elements except argon combine with chlorine to form chlorides.

Reaction of Sodium with Chlorine

Sodium burns in the presence of chlorine with a bright yellow or orange flame and forms sodium chloride.

2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl

Reaction of Magnesium with Chlorine

Magnesium burns in chlorine with an intense white flame and forms magnesium chloride.

Mg + Cl2 → MgCl2

Reaction of Aluminium with Chlorine

Aluminium readily combines with chlorine on heating to form aluminium chloride.

2Al + 3Cl2 → 2AlCl3

Reaction of Silicon with Chlorine

Silicon reacts with chlorine on heating to form liquid silicon tetrachloride.

Si + 2Cl2 → SiCl4

Reaction of Phosphorus with Chlorine

When dry chlorine gas is passed over molten white phosphorus, a mixture of two chlorides is obtained. Phosphorus gives phosphorus trichloride with a limited supply of chlorine and phosphorus pentachloride with excess chlorine.

P4 + 6Cl2 → 4PCl3 (limited chlorine)

P4 + 10Cl2 → 4PCl5 (excess chlorine)

Reaction of Sulphur with Chlorine

Sulphur reacts with chlorine on heating to form disulphur dichloride liquid.

2S + Cl2 → S2Cl2

Reaction of Argon with Chlorine

Argon does not react with chlorine: Ar + Cl2 → No Reaction.

Key Reactions

ElementChloride formed
NaNaCl
MgMgCl2
AlAlCl3
SiSiCl4 (liquid)
PPCl3 (limited Cl2); PCl5 (excess Cl2)
SS2Cl2 (liquid)
ArNo reaction

Key Points

  • Every Period 3 element except argon forms a chloride with chlorine.
  • Na and Mg burn in chlorine; Al and Si react on heating.
  • Phosphorus gives PCl3 with limited chlorine and PCl5 with excess chlorine.
  • Sulphur gives liquid S2Cl2 on heating with chlorine.
  • Argon forms no chloride because of its complete octet.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of the Oxides of Period 3 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Oxides are the binary compounds (compounds composed of only two elements) of oxygen with other elements. There may be oxides of all the elements except fluorine. Argon does not form an oxide because it has a complete outermost shell.

Structure of Oxides

The oxides of sodium, magnesium and aluminium consist of giant structures of metal ions and oxide ions. Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure. The oxides of phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine consist of molecules.

Na2OMgOAl2O3SiO2P4O6 / P4O10SO3 / SO2Cl2O / Cl2O7
Giant ionicGiant ionicGiant ionic with covalent characterGiant covalentMolecular covalentMolecular covalentMolecular covalent

Na2O, MgO, Al2O3 and SiO2 have strong attractive forces in all directions, so their particles are arranged regularly and the arrangement is repeated many times throughout the substance: these are giant structures. The oxides of the non-metals (phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine) consist of molecules held by weak intermolecular forces (London forces), so they have simple structures.

Nature of Oxides

Sodium and magnesium oxides are ionic. Aluminium oxide is mostly ionic and has a significant covalent character. Silicon dioxide and the oxides of phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine have covalent character. The ionic character of the oxides decreases while covalent character increases along the period, due to the decrease in the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) between the element and oxygen: Na2O 2.51, MgO 2.13, Al2O3 1.83, SiO2 1.54, P4O10 1.25, SO3/SO2 0.86, Cl2O/Cl2O7 0.44. Elements form ionic bonds when the electronegativity difference is large and covalent bonds when it is small.

Melting and Boiling Points of Oxides

OxideNa2OMgOAl2O3SiO2P4O10P4O6SO3SO2Cl2O7Cl2O
Melting Point (°C)12752852204016103402417-72-92-120.6
Boiling Point (°C)195036002977223036017345-10822.2

The oxides of sodium, magnesium and aluminium have high melting and boiling points because they are ionic and a lot of energy is required to break the strong attractive forces between the ions. The melting and boiling points of silicon dioxide are also high because a large amount of energy is required to break the very strong silicon-oxygen covalent bonds. The oxides of phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine are simple molecular covalent compounds, so their melting and boiling points are much lower: they consist of molecules with weak intermolecular forces (dipole-dipole forces or London dispersion forces).

Electrical Conductivity of Oxides

The oxides of metals (Na2O, MgO and Al2O3) do not conduct electricity in the solid state due to the absence of mobile electrons or free ions. They conduct electricity in the molten state because of the movement of ions. Silicon dioxide does not conduct electricity either as a liquid or as a solid, because there are no mobile electrons or ions in SiO2 (in the molten state its conductivity is very low). The oxides of non-metals do not conduct electricity as gas, liquid or solid, because they consist of molecules with no free electrons or ions.

Key Points

  • Oxides are binary compounds of oxygen; argon forms no oxide.
  • Na2O and MgO are giant ionic; Al2O3 is giant ionic with covalent character; SiO2 is giant covalent; the P, S and Cl oxides are simple molecules.
  • Ionic character decreases across the period as the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) falls from 2.51 to 0.44.
  • Giant-structure oxides have very high melting and boiling points; molecular oxides have low ones.
  • Metal oxides conduct only when molten (moving ions); SiO2 and the molecular oxides do not conduct.

lessons.title: Acid-Base Behaviour of the Oxides of Period 3 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Sodium and magnesium oxides are ionic and contain the oxide ion, O2-. The oxide ion is a strongly basic ion that reacts with water to form hydroxide ions:

O2- + H2O → 2OH-

Al2O3 has both ionic and covalent character and is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases to form salts. SiO2 has a covalent character, does not contain the oxide ion, and is weakly acidic: it reacts with strong bases to form salts. The oxides of non-metals have covalent character and are acidic in nature; they form acidic solutions when dissolved in water.

Acid-Base Behaviour of the Oxides

OxideNa2OMgOAl2O3SiO2P4O10SO3Cl2O7
CharacterStrongly BasicWeakly BasicAmphotericWeakly AcidicAcidicStrongly AcidicVery Strongly Acidic
ΔEN2.512.131.831.541.250.860.44

Trends in Acid-Base Behaviour

The basic character of the oxides of Period 3 elements decreases while the acidic character increases along the period, due to the decrease in the electronegativity difference (ΔEN). Basic oxides react with acidic oxides to form salts.

Key Points

  • Na2O is strongly basic and MgO is weakly basic; both contain the O2- ion, which forms OH- with water.
  • Al2O3 is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and bases.
  • SiO2 is weakly acidic; the non-metal oxides are acidic, and Cl2O7 is very strongly acidic.
  • Across the period the oxides change from basic, through amphoteric, to acidic as ΔEN decreases.

lessons.title: Reactions of Oxides with Water, Acids and Bases
lessons.notes_html:
Reactions of Oxides with Water

Sodium oxide reacts readily with water to form a basic solution; the pH of the solution is around 14.

Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH

Magnesium oxide reacts with water to form a basic solution. The reaction is slow and some magnesium hydroxide is formed; the pH of the solution is around 9.

MgO + H2O → Mg(OH)2

Aluminium oxide is insoluble in water and does not react with water (Al2O3 + H2O → No Reaction). Silicon dioxide does not react with water because it has a giant covalent structure and is completely insoluble in water (SiO2 + H2O → No Reaction). The oxides of non-metals (phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine) react with water to form acidic solutions:

Oxide + WaterAcid formed
P4O6 + 6H2O → 4H3PO3Phosphorous acid
P4O10 + 6H2O → 4H3PO4Phosphoric acid
SO2 + H2O → H2SO3Sulphurous acid
SO3 + H2O → H2SO4Sulphuric acid
Cl2O + H2O → 2HClOHypochlorous acid
Cl2O7 + H2O → 2HClO4Perchloric acid

Reactions of Oxides with Acids

Sodium oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form an aqueous solution of sodium chloride:

Na2O + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O

Magnesium oxide reacts with warm dilute hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride solution:

MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O

Aluminium oxide reacts with hot dilute hydrochloric acid to form aluminium chloride solution; in this reaction aluminium oxide acts as a base:

Al2O3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2O

Silicon dioxide is a stable compound and does not react with most acids at normal conditions. It reacts only with hydrofluoric acid (HF):

SiO2 + 4HF → SiF4 + 2H2O

The tetrafluorosilane (SiF4) reacts further with HF to produce hexafluorosilicic acid: SiF4 + 2HF → H2[SiF6].

Reactions of Oxides with Bases

Aluminium oxide reacts with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution of sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate; in this reaction aluminium oxide acts as an acid:

Al2O3 + 2NaOH + 3H2O → 2Na[Al(OH)4]

Silicon dioxide slowly reacts with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to form a colourless solution of sodium silicate and water:

SiO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O

Phosphorus trioxide reacts directly with sodium hydroxide to produce two series of salts (sodium dihydrogenphosphite and sodium hydrogenphosphite):

4NaOH + P4O6 + 2H2O → 4NaH2PO3

8NaOH + P4O6 → 4Na2HPO3 + 2H2O

Phosphorus pentaoxide reacts directly with sodium hydroxide to produce three series of salts (sodium dihydrogen phosphate, sodium hydrogen phosphate and sodium phosphate):

4NaOH + P4O10 + 2H2O → 4NaH2PO4

8NaOH + P4O10 → 4Na2HPO4 + 2H2O

12NaOH + P4O10 → 4Na3PO4 + 6H2O

Sulphur dioxide reacts directly with sodium hydroxide solution to produce sodium sulphite; when SO2 is in excess, sodium bisulphite is formed:

SO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SO3 + H2O

SO2 + NaOH → NaHSO3

Sulphur trioxide reacts directly with sodium hydroxide solution to produce sodium sulphate:

SO3 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + H2O

The chlorine oxides also react with sodium hydroxide:

Cl2O + 2NaOH → 2NaClO + H2O

Cl2O7 + 2NaOH → 2NaClO4 + H2O

Key Points

  • Na2O gives a strongly alkaline solution (pH about 14); MgO reacts slowly (pH about 9).
  • Al2O3 and SiO2 do not react with water; the non-metal oxides give acids with water.
  • Basic and amphoteric oxides react with acids to form salts and water.
  • SiO2 reacts only with HF among the acids.
  • Al2O3 acts as a base with acids and as an acid with hot concentrated NaOH: this proves it is amphoteric.
  • Acidic oxides react with bases to form salts and water.

lessons.title: Chlorides of the Period 3 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Nature and Structure of Chlorides

The chlorides of sodium and magnesium consist of metal ions (Na+ and Mg2+) and chloride ions (Cl-), which are strongly attracted to each other to form giant ionic structures. Aluminium chloride has a layer structure with significant covalent character; on heating it is converted into a molecular form and exists as a dimer, Al2Cl6, at about 180°C. Silicon tetrachloride (SiCl4) and phosphorus trichloride (PCl3) are liquids, while phosphorus pentachloride (PCl5) is a solid. At ordinary temperature PCl5 is ionic, made up of [PCl4]+ and [PCl6]- ions, while in the gaseous state it exists as molecules. Disulphur dichloride (S2Cl2) has a simple molecular structure.

ChlorideNaClMgCl2AlCl3SiCl4PCl3PCl5S2Cl2
StructureIonic latticeIonic latticeIonic lattice / covalent dimerCovalent (tetrahedral)Covalent (pyramidal)Ionic lattice / covalentCovalent

Melting and Boiling Points of Chlorides

ChlorideNaClMgCl2AlCl3SiCl4PCl3PCl5SCl2
Melting Point (°C)801714192.6-68.74-93.6160.5-121
Boiling Point (°C)1413141218057.6576.1166.859

Sodium chloride and magnesium chloride are ionic chlorides and have high melting and boiling points. Aluminium chloride has some covalent character, so it has low melting and boiling points. The chlorides of silicon, phosphorus and sulphur are covalent compounds with low melting and boiling points, because their molecules are attracted by weak van der Waals forces. The melting and boiling points of phosphorus pentachloride (PCl5) are higher than those of phosphorus trichloride (PCl3), because in the solid state PCl5 has an ionic lattice structure, while PCl3 is a simple covalent compound whose molecules are attracted by weak van der Waals forces.

Electrical Conductivity of Chlorides

Sodium chloride and magnesium chloride conduct electricity in the molten state or in aqueous solution, because their ions are free to move and carry the electric current. They do not conduct electricity in the solid state, because in the solid state the ions are not free to move. Aluminium chloride exists as a dimer (Al2Cl6) and its bonds are covalent in nature, so it does not conduct electricity. The chlorides of silicon, phosphorus and sulphur are simple covalent compounds with no free electrons or ions, so they do not conduct electricity.

Solubility of Chlorides in Water

Sodium chloride and magnesium chloride are ionic chlorides and are soluble in water. Sodium chloride is neutral, so its aqueous solution has pH almost equal to 7. Magnesium chloride solution is slightly acidic (pH about 6.5), because the Mg2+ ion is small and highly charged, so it hydrolyses water and releases H+ ions. The covalent chlorides react with water (they are hydrolysed) and give acidic solutions:

ChlorideReaction with waterpH
Al2Cl6Al2Cl6 + 6H2O → 2Al(OH)3 + 6HClabout 3
SiCl4SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HClabout 2
PCl3PCl3 + 3H2O → H3PO3 + 3HClabout 2
PCl5PCl5 + 4H2O → H3PO4 + 5HClabout 2

Sulphur chlorides are insoluble in water. Keep in mind: the solubility of the chlorides of Period 3 elements in water decreases, while the acidic character of their aqueous solutions increases, along the period.

Key Points

  • NaCl and MgCl2 are giant ionic lattices with high melting and boiling points.
  • AlCl3 has covalent character and exists as the dimer Al2Cl6 at about 180°C.
  • SiCl4, PCl3 and S2Cl2 are simple covalent molecules with low melting and boiling points.
  • Solid PCl5 is ionic, [PCl4]+[PCl6]-, so it melts higher than PCl3.
  • Ionic chlorides conduct when molten or in solution; covalent chlorides never conduct.
  • Covalent chlorides hydrolyse in water to give strongly acidic solutions (pH about 2-3).

lessons.title: Hydroxides of Period 3 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The hydroxides of sodium (NaOH) and magnesium (Mg(OH)2) are basic in nature. They are white, hygroscopic, crystalline solids. Sodium hydroxide is highly soluble in water, while magnesium hydroxide is slightly soluble in water. Both hydroxides react with dilute hydrochloric acid to form their respective salts:

NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O

Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl → MgCl2 + 2H2O

The hydroxide of aluminium, Al(OH)3, is amphoteric in nature. It reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form aluminium chloride and water, acting as a base:

Al(OH)3 + 3HCl → AlCl3 + 3H2O

It also reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate, acting as an acid:

Al(OH)3 + NaOH → Na[Al(OH)4]

The hydroxides of silicon, phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine do not exist as hydroxides; instead, these elements form oxoacids, in which the -OH groups are covalently bonded to the central atom. Silicon forms orthosilicic acid, Si(OH)4, which is a very weak acid. Phosphorus forms phosphoric acid (H3PO4), sulphur forms sulphuric acid (H2SO4) and chlorine forms perchloric acid (HClO4), which is a very strong acid.

Key Points

  • NaOH and Mg(OH)2 are basic hydroxides; NaOH is highly soluble, Mg(OH)2 only slightly soluble.
  • Basic hydroxides react with acids to form salts and water.
  • Al(OH)3 is amphoteric: it reacts with both HCl and NaOH.
  • Si, P, S and Cl form oxoacids instead of hydroxides: Si(OH)4 (very weak), H3PO4, H2SO4 and HClO4 (very strong).
  • Across the period the hydroxides change from strongly basic to strongly acidic.

lessons.title: Group 1 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group 1 are called alkali metals. The word alkali is an Arabic word which means ashes. The alkali metals are the most active metals and are stored in oil (kerosene). They are not found in the free state in nature. They are soft metals and can be cut with a knife. They are silvery when freshly cut and are good conductors of heat and electricity.

Their valence shell electronic configuration is ns1. They are excellent reducing agents. They form monovalent positive ions (M+) by losing their one valence electron and attain the stable noble gas configuration. They show an oxidation state of +1.

Electronic Configuration of Alkali Metals

ElementAtomic NumberElectronic ConfigurationValence Shell Configuration
Lithium31s2 2s12s1
Sodium111s2 2s2 2p6 3s13s1
Potassium191s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s14s1
Rubidium371s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s15s1
Cesium551s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s16s1
Francium871s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 5d10 6p6 7s17s1

Key Points

  • Group 1 elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) are the alkali metals, the most active metals.
  • They are soft, silvery when freshly cut, good conductors, and are stored under oil.
  • They never occur free in nature because they are so reactive.
  • Valence configuration ns1: they lose one electron to form M+ ions and show oxidation state +1.
  • They are excellent reducing agents.

lessons.title: Atomic and Physical Properties of Group 1 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Atomic Radius

The alkali metals have the largest atomic radii in their respective periods. The atomic radii increase down the group from lithium to francium, due to the addition of a new electronic shell in each element.

ElementLiNaKRbCsFr
Atomic Radius (pm)152186227248265348

Francium is unstable, so the credit for the largest atomic radius goes to cesium.

Ionization Energy

The first ionization energies of alkali metals are the lowest of all the elements in their respective periods, because each has only one electron in the outermost shell, which is loosely bound to the nucleus. For this reason the alkali metals are powerful reducing agents. The ionization energy decreases down the group due to the increase in atomic size.

ElementLiNaKRbCs
First Ionization Energy (kJ/mol)520.3495.8418.9403.0375.7

Electronegativity

The alkali metals are highly electropositive elements with very low electronegativity values, which decrease down the group.

ElementLiNaKRbCs
Electronegativity0.980.930.820.820.79

Melting and Boiling Points

The melting and boiling points of alkali metals are low because of their weak metallic bonds: each atom provides only one delocalized electron, spread over a large atomic volume. They generally decrease down the group because the metallic bond becomes weaker as the atoms get larger.

ElementLiNaKRbCs
Melting Point (°C)180.597.863.738.928.7
Boiling Point (°C)1330892760688670

Density

ElementLiNaKRbCs
Atomic Volume (cm3/mol)12.9723.6845.3655.8069.95
Density (g/cm3)0.540.970.861.531.90

Lithium, sodium and potassium are less dense than water and float on its surface. Density generally increases down the group, but potassium is less dense than sodium because of an abnormal increase in its atomic volume.

Key Points

  • Atomic radius increases down the group (152 pm for Li to 265 pm for Cs) as new shells are added.
  • First ionization energy is the lowest in each period and decreases down the group, so the metals are powerful reducing agents.
  • Electronegativity is very low and decreases down the group.
  • Melting and boiling points are low (weak metallic bonding) and decrease down the group.
  • Li, Na and K float on water; density generally rises down the group, but K is less dense than Na.

lessons.title: Trends in Reactivity of Alkali Metals with Water
lessons.notes_html:
All the alkali metals react with water to produce the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

2M + 2H2O → 2MOH + H2

The reactivity of alkali metals with water increases down the group. Lithium is the least reactive alkali metal, while cesium is the most reactive. This is because the atomic radius increases and the ionization energy decreases down the group, so the valence electron is lost more and more easily.

Key Reactions

MetalReaction with water
Lithium2Li + 2H2O → 2LiOH + H2
Sodium2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2
Potassium2K + 2H2O → 2KOH + H2

Key Points

  • Alkali metals react with water to give the hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
  • Reactivity increases down the group: lithium is the least reactive and cesium the most reactive.
  • Reason: atomic radius increases and ionization energy falls down the group, so the electron is lost more easily.
  • The hydroxide solutions formed are strongly alkaline.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkali Metals with Oxygen
lessons.notes_html:
Alkali metals react with oxygen or air quickly and become tarnished (dull) due to the formation of a film of oxides on their surface. That is why they are stored in kerosene or paraffin oil.

Formation of Oxides

There are three types of oxides: normal oxides, in which the oxidation state of oxygen is -2 (for example Na2O, CO2); peroxides, in which the oxidation state of oxygen is -1 (for example Na2O2, K2O2); and superoxides, in which the oxidation state of oxygen is -1/2 (for example KO2, RbO2).

Lithium mainly forms the normal oxide (lithium oxide) and also some peroxide on burning in air:

4Li + O2 → 2Li2O

2Li + O2 → Li2O2

Sodium mainly forms the peroxide (sodium peroxide) and also some normal oxide on burning in air:

4Na + O2 → 2Na2O

2Na + O2 → Na2O2

Potassium, rubidium and cesium form superoxides on burning in air:

K + O2 → KO2

Rb + O2 → RbO2

Cs + O2 → CsO2

Reaction of Oxides with Water

The oxides of alkali metals react with water to form hydroxides. The peroxides also give hydrogen peroxide, and the superoxides give hydrogen peroxide and oxygen gas:

Li2O + H2O → 2LiOH

Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH

Na2O2 + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2O2

2KO2 + 2H2O → 2KOH + H2O2 + O2

2RbO2 + 2H2O → 2RbOH + H2O2 + O2

Reaction of Oxides with Acids

The normal oxides combine with dilute acids to produce salt and water:

Li2O + 2HCl → 2LiCl + H2O

Na2O + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O

The peroxides are strong oxidizing agents. They combine with dilute acids to produce salt and hydrogen peroxide:

Na2O2 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O2

The superoxides are also strong oxidizing agents. They combine with dilute acids to produce salt, hydrogen peroxide and oxygen gas:

2KO2 + 2HCl → 2KCl + H2O2 + O2

Key Points

  • Alkali metals tarnish quickly in air, so they are stored in kerosene or paraffin oil.
  • Lithium forms mainly the normal oxide Li2O; sodium forms mainly the peroxide Na2O2; K, Rb and Cs form superoxides.
  • In normal oxides oxygen is -2, in peroxides -1, and in superoxides -1/2.
  • Normal oxides give hydroxides with water; peroxides also give H2O2; superoxides give H2O2 and O2.
  • Peroxides and superoxides are strong oxidizing agents.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkali Metals with Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Alkali metals react directly with halogens to produce their respective metal halides:

2M + X2 → 2MX

Here, M represents Li, Na, K, Rb or Cs and X2 represents F2, Cl2, Br2 or I2. For example, when sodium reacts with chlorine, sodium chloride is formed:

2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl

The halides of alkali metals are white crystalline solids and are readily soluble in water. They are good conductors of electricity in the molten state or in solution form.

Key Points

  • Alkali metals react directly with halogens: 2M + X2 → 2MX.
  • The metal halides formed are ionic compounds.
  • Alkali metal halides are white crystalline solids, readily soluble in water.
  • They conduct electricity when molten or in solution, because their ions are free to move.

lessons.title: Effect of Heat on Nitrates, Carbonates and Bicarbonates of Alkali Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Effect of Heat on Nitrates

The nitrates of alkali metals are highly stable towards heat. They decompose into nitrites and oxygen gas on strong heating, except lithium nitrate. Lithium nitrate decomposes more readily into the oxide, nitrogen peroxide (NO2) and oxygen gas.

4LiNO3 → 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2 (on heating)

2NaNO3 → 2NaNO2 + O2 (on heating)

Effect of Heat on Carbonates

The carbonates of alkali metals are highly stable towards heat. Lithium carbonate is significantly less stable towards heat and decomposes more readily. The carbonates of the other alkali metals do not decompose even at higher temperature.

2Li2CO3 → 2Li2O + 2CO2 (on heating)

Effect of Heat on Bicarbonates

The bicarbonates of alkali metals are stable towards heat but are not very stable. They decompose on heating to produce carbonates, carbon dioxide and water vapours.

2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O (on heating)

For all three families of salts, the thermal stability increases down the group. The reason is that the positive ions become larger down the group, so their polarizing power decreases and they distort the nitrate, carbonate or bicarbonate ion less.

Key Reactions

SaltEffect of heat
LiNO34LiNO3 → 2Li2O + 4NO2 + O2
Other nitrates, e.g. NaNO32NaNO3 → 2NaNO2 + O2
Li2CO32Li2CO3 → 2Li2O + 2CO2
Other carbonatesDo not decompose even at high temperature
Bicarbonates, e.g. NaHCO32NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O

Key Points

  • Alkali metal nitrates give nitrites and oxygen on strong heating; LiNO3 is the exception, giving Li2O, NO2 and O2.
  • Alkali metal carbonates are very stable to heat; only Li2CO3 decomposes readily.
  • Bicarbonates decompose on heating to the carbonate, CO2 and water vapour.
  • Thermal stability of all these salts increases down the group as the polarizing power of the cation decreases.
  • Lithium salts behave differently because the small Li+ ion has a high polarizing power.

lessons.title: Flame Tests: Origin of the Flames
lessons.notes_html:
Various metals give very attractive coloured flames when burnt in air. The colours of flames are the result of electrons moving from higher energy levels to lower energy levels in metal atoms. When a sample of an alkali metal or its salt is heated in the Bunsen burner, the heat first excites the electrons to higher energy levels. When the electrons return to the ground state, they release energy as light of a definite colour. The colour of the emitted light (flame) can be used to identify the alkali metals; this process is known as the flame test. Since the amount of energy released during the return of the electron to the ground state is different in different atoms, different colours are imparted by the atoms to the flame.

Flame Colours of Alkali Metals

ElementLithiumSodiumPotassiumRubidiumCesium
Flame ColourCrimsonYellowLilacRed-violetBlue

Key Points

  • Flame colours arise when excited electrons fall back to lower energy levels and emit light.
  • Each metal emits its own characteristic colour, so the flame test identifies the metal.
  • Lithium: crimson; sodium: yellow; potassium: lilac; rubidium: red-violet; cesium: blue.
  • The colour differs from metal to metal because the energy gaps between levels are different in each atom.

lessons.title: Group 2 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group 2 (IIA) are beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium. They are all metals and are known as alkaline earth metals. They are harder, denser and have higher melting and boiling points than the alkali metals. Alkaline earth metals are always found in combined states with other elements. They are the second most active metals in the periodic table. They must be stored in oil (kerosene) to prevent their reaction with oxygen and water vapours in the air, and they are not found as pure elements because of their high chemical reactivity. They are white or silvery, except beryllium, which is grey in colour.

Their valence shell electronic configuration is ns2. They lose both valence electrons to form M2+ ions and attain the stable noble gas configuration, showing an oxidation state of +2. They are less reactive than the alkali metals because two electrons must be removed and their ionization energies are higher.

Electronic Configuration of Alkaline Earth Metals

ElementAtomic NumberElectronic ConfigurationValence Shell Configuration
Beryllium41s2 2s22s2
Magnesium121s2 2s2 2p6 3s23s2
Calcium201s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s24s2
Strontium381s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s25s2
Barium561s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s26s2
Radium881s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 5d10 6p6 7s27s2

Key Points

  • Group 2 elements (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra) are the alkaline earth metals.
  • They are harder, denser and higher-melting than the alkali metals, and are stored under oil.
  • They are the second most active metals and always occur in combined form.
  • Valence configuration ns2: they lose two electrons to form M2+ ions (oxidation state +2).
  • They are white or silvery, except grey beryllium.

lessons.title: Atomic and Physical Properties of the Group 2 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Atomic Radius

The atomic radii of alkaline earth metals are smaller than those of the corresponding alkali metals, because of the greater nuclear charge, but they increase down the group as new shells are added: Be 111 pm, Mg 160 pm, Ca 197 pm, Sr 215 pm, Ba 217 pm.

Ionization Energies

ElementBeMgCaSrBaRa
First Ionization Energy (kJ/mol)899737590549503509
Second Ionization Energy (kJ/mol)1757145011451064965979

The first and second ionization energies decrease down the group due to the increase in atomic radii. The ionization energy of radium is, however, higher than that of barium. Keep in mind: radium has a filled 4f subshell; the 4f electrons shield very poorly, so the nuclear charge for radium is 32 units higher than for barium. The higher nuclear charge available to the radium valence electrons causes a contraction of the 7s orbital and an increase in the ionization energy.

Electronegativity Values

The electronegativity values of alkaline earth metals are small, but they are higher than the values for the alkali metals. They decrease down the group due to the increase in atomic size.

ElementBeMgCaSrBaRa
Electronegativity1.571.311.000.950.890.89

Melting and Boiling Points

The melting and boiling points of these elements are higher than those of the alkali metals, because each atom provides two delocalized electrons for metallic bonding.

ElementBeMgCaSrBaRa
Melting Point (°C)1287649839768727700
Boiling Point (°C)250011051494138118501700

The melting and boiling points of these metals do not show any regular trend, because they adopt different crystal structures.

Key Points

  • Atomic radii are smaller than those of Group 1 metals but increase down the group.
  • First and second ionization energies decrease down the group, except that radium is higher than barium.
  • Radium's exception is due to the poorly shielding filled 4f subshell and the contraction of the 7s orbital.
  • Electronegativity is small (higher than Group 1) and decreases down the group.
  • Melting and boiling points are higher than Group 1 values but show no regular trend.

lessons.title: Trends in Reactivity of Group 2 Elements with Water
lessons.notes_html:
Although alkaline earth metals are less reactive than alkali metals, they are still more reactive than the majority of other metals. Alkaline earth metals (except beryllium) react with water to produce hydroxides with the liberation of hydrogen gas:

Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2

The reactivity of alkaline earth metals increases down the group due to the increase in atomic size (and the fall in ionization energy). Beryllium does not react with water even at high temperature. Magnesium does not react with water at room temperature (25°C), but it will react with steam to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Calcium, strontium and barium react with water at room temperature to produce hydroxides and hydrogen gas, barium being the most vigorous of the three.

Key Points

  • Group 2 metals (except Be) react with water to give the hydroxide and hydrogen.
  • Reactivity increases down the group as atomic size increases and ionization energy falls.
  • Beryllium does not react with water even at high temperature.
  • Magnesium reacts only with steam; Ca, Sr and Ba react with cold water at room temperature.
  • Group 2 metals are less reactive than the corresponding Group 1 metals.

lessons.title: Reactions of Group 2 Elements with Oxygen and Nitrogen
lessons.notes_html:
Formation of Simple Oxides and Peroxides

Alkaline earth metals react with oxygen to form normal oxides, except barium and radium. Barium and radium, however, produce peroxides. The tendency of alkaline earth metals to form peroxides increases from top to bottom in the group. The reactivity of alkaline earth metals with oxygen increases going from the top of the group to the bottom. Beryllium is relatively inert because it has a strong thin layer of oxide on its surface; it reacts with oxygen at 600°C and is much more reactive in the powder form.

Formation of normal oxides:

2Be + O2 → 2BeO

2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

2Ca + O2 → 2CaO

Formation of peroxides:

Ba + O2 → BaO2

Sr + O2 → SrO2

Formation of Nitrides on Heating in Air

All the alkaline earth metals react with nitrogen to produce nitrides of the general formula M3N2:

3Be + N2 → Be3N2

3Mg + N2 → Mg3N2

3Ca + N2 → Ca3N2

Keep in mind: beryllium nitride is a covalent compound due to the small size, high charge density and high ionization energy of beryllium. It has weak intermolecular forces of attraction, which leads to its volatile nature. On the other hand, the nitrides of the other alkaline earth metals are ionic (electrovalent) and are non-volatile.

Key Points

  • Group 2 metals form normal oxides MO; Ba and Ra (and Sr) also form peroxides MO2.
  • The tendency to form peroxides increases down the group.
  • Beryllium is protected by a strong thin oxide layer and reacts with oxygen only at 600°C.
  • On heating in air all Group 2 metals form nitrides, M3N2.
  • Be3N2 is covalent and volatile; the other nitrides are ionic and non-volatile.

lessons.title: Trends in Solubility of the Hydroxides, Sulphates and Carbonates of Group 2 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Solubility of Hydroxides

The solubility of the hydroxides in water increases gradually on going down the group. Be(OH)2 and Mg(OH)2 are almost insoluble in water, whereas the hydroxides of the other alkaline earth metals are slightly soluble in water, Ba(OH)2 being the most soluble. The reason is that down the group the lattice energy of the hydroxides decreases more rapidly than their hydration energy, so dissolution becomes easier.

Solubility of Sulphates

The solubility of the sulphates in water decreases on going down the group, the opposite trend to the hydroxides. BeSO4 is soluble, MgSO4 is soluble, CaSO4 is slightly soluble, SrSO4 is almost insoluble and BaSO4 is insoluble. The reason is that the hydration energy decreases more rapidly than the lattice energy on moving from Be2+ to Ba2+.

Solubility of Carbonates

All the carbonates of alkaline earth metals are sparingly soluble in water, and their solubility decreases down the group. BeCO3 is the most soluble carbonate of the group because of the high hydration energy of the small Be2+ ion.

Compound familyTrend down the group
Hydroxides M(OH)2Solubility increases (Be(OH)2 almost insoluble → Ba(OH)2 most soluble)
Sulphates MSO4Solubility decreases (BeSO4 soluble → BaSO4 insoluble)
Carbonates MCO3All sparingly soluble; solubility decreases (BeCO3 most soluble)

Key Points

  • Hydroxide solubility increases down the group.
  • Sulphate solubility decreases down the group: BaSO4 is insoluble.
  • Carbonates are all sparingly soluble, decreasing down the group; BeCO3 is the most soluble.
  • The trends are decided by the balance between lattice energy and hydration energy.

lessons.title: Trends in Thermal Stability of Nitrates and Carbonates of Group 2 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Thermal Stability of Carbonates

All the carbonates of alkaline earth metals decompose on heating to form the metal oxide and carbon dioxide:

CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 (on heating)

The thermal stability of the carbonates increases down the group, so the decomposition temperature rises: BeCO3 about 100°C, MgCO3 about 540°C, CaCO3 about 900°C, SrCO3 about 1290°C and BaCO3 about 1360°C. The reason is that the ionic radius of the cation increases down the group, which reduces its polarizing power, so the carbonate ion is distorted less and the carbonate becomes more stable.

Thermal Stability of Nitrates

All the nitrates of alkaline earth metals decompose on heating to form the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen:

2Ca(NO3)2 → 2CaO + 4NO2 + O2 (on heating)

The thermal stability of the nitrates also increases down the group, for the same reason: the larger cation has a smaller polarizing power and distorts the nitrate ion less.

Key Points

  • Group 2 carbonates decompose to the oxide and CO2; nitrates decompose to the oxide, NO2 and O2.
  • Thermal stability of both carbonates and nitrates increases down the group.
  • Decomposition temperature of the carbonates rises from about 100°C (BeCO3) to about 1360°C (BaCO3).
  • Reason: larger cations have lower polarizing power, so they distort the anion less.
  • Group 2 carbonates and nitrates are much less stable to heat than those of Group 1.

lessons.title: Peculiar Behaviour of Beryllium
lessons.notes_html:
Beryllium differs from the other members of its group because it is very small and has a high charge density. Its main differences are:

  • Its compounds are largely covalent, not ionic. For example, BeCl2 is a covalent compound; the small Be2+ ion strongly polarizes the electron cloud of the chloride ion.
  • Its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, while those of the other Group 2 metals are basic: Be(OH)2 + 2HCl → BeCl2 + 2H2O, and Be(OH)2 + 2NaOH → Na2[Be(OH)4].
  • It does not react with water, even at high temperature.
  • It does not form a peroxide, and it does not form a stable carbonate in the ordinary way.
  • Its maximum coordination number is 4, while the other Group 2 metals commonly show 6.
  • Its salts are hydrolysed in water.

Beryllium shows a diagonal relationship with aluminium, the element diagonally below it in the periodic table: both have amphoteric oxides and hydroxides, covalent chlorides, and carbides that give methane with water.

Key Points

  • Beryllium is abnormal because of its very small size and high charge density.
  • Its compounds are largely covalent (for example BeCl2).
  • BeO and Be(OH)2 are amphoteric; the other Group 2 oxides and hydroxides are basic.
  • Beryllium does not react with water and has a maximum coordination number of 4.
  • Beryllium resembles aluminium because of the diagonal relationship.

lessons.title: Mining and Extraction of Elements/Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science: Mining is the process of obtaining valuable minerals and metals from the Earth's crust. There are two main types of mining. In surface mining, the minerals are taken from deposits near the surface; it includes open-pit mining and strip mining. In underground mining, the minerals lie deep below the surface and are reached by drift, slope or shaft mines.

The method chosen depends on factors such as the depth of the deposit, its shape and size, the grade (richness) of the ore and the type of rock. Extraction is the separation of the metal from its ore, using physical and chemical processes such as crushing, concentration and reduction. Mining and extraction provide the metals used in buildings, machines, vehicles and everyday articles, but they must be carried out carefully because they can damage the land, water and air.

Key Points

  • Mining obtains valuable minerals and metals from the Earth's crust.
  • Surface mining (open-pit and strip mining) is used for deposits near the surface.
  • Underground mining (drift, slope and shaft) is used for deep deposits.
  • Extraction separates the metal from its ore by physical and chemical processes.
  • The choice of method depends on depth, shape, size, grade of ore and type of rock.

lessons.title: Group 14 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group 14 (IVA) are carbon (C), silicon (Si), germanium (Ge), tin (Sn) and lead (Pb). It is also called the carbon family. All these elements have four electrons in their valence shells, with the general configuration ns2 np2, so they are tetravalent and form mainly covalent compounds.

Electronic Configuration of Group 14 Elements (by shells)

ElementAtomic NumberElectrons in shellsValence Shell Configuration
Carbon62, 42s2 2p2
Silicon142, 8, 43s2 3p2
Germanium322, 8, 18, 44s2 4p2
Tin502, 8, 18, 18, 45s2 5p2
Lead822, 8, 18, 32, 18, 46s2 6p2

Carbon shows the property of catenation (forming long chains with itself) to the maximum extent, and this power decreases down the group. The group shows a gradual change from non-metals at the top to metals at the bottom.

Key Points

  • Group 14 (IVA) is the carbon family: C, Si, Ge, Sn and Pb.
  • All have four valence electrons, ns2 np2, and are tetravalent.
  • Their compounds are mainly covalent.
  • Catenation is strongest in carbon and decreases down the group.
  • Metallic character increases down the group.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Group 14 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in Melting and Boiling Points

The melting and boiling points of Group 14 elements decrease down the group. This is due to the increase in atomic size and the decrease in inter-atomic forces.

ElementCSiGeSnPb
Melting Point (°C)35501420945232327
Boiling Point (°C)48302480285026231751

The melting and boiling points of carbon and silicon are very high because they have tendencies to form macromolecules (giant structures). Tin has the lowest melting point of the group (232°C); the melting point rises slightly again at lead (327°C).

Trends from Non-metal to Metal

Metallic character increases down the group. Carbon and silicon are non-metals, germanium is a semimetal (metalloid), and tin and lead are metals. The electrical properties of silicon are similar to those of a semimetal, which is why silicon is used as a semiconductor.

Key Points

  • Melting and boiling points generally decrease down Group 14 as atomic size increases and inter-atomic forces weaken.
  • Carbon (3550°C) and silicon (1420°C) melt very high because of their giant structures.
  • Tin has the lowest melting point of the group, 232°C.
  • Carbon and silicon are non-metals, germanium is a semimetal, and tin and lead are metals.

lessons.title: Oxidation States of Group 14 Elements and the Inert Pair Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group IVA have four electrons in their valence shells and they have an oxidation state of +4. The first three elements may also have an oxidation state of -4 when they are bonded to more electropositive elements. Tin (Sn) and lead (Pb) also show an oxidation state of +2, which is the only oxidation state in which they produce ionic compounds.

The stability of the +4 oxidation state decreases and that of the +2 oxidation state increases on moving down the group. For example, the compounds of Ge2+ are less stable than Ge4+. The compounds of Ge2+ act as strong reducing agents, while those of Ge4+ act as oxidizing agents. On the other hand, the compounds of Pb2+ (for example PbCl2) are more stable than those of Pb4+ (for example PbCl4). The compounds of Pb2+ are ionic and more common than those of Pb4+, and the compounds of Pb4+ act as oxidizing agents.

Inert Pair Effect and the Nature of Bond

The tendency of the ns2 electrons of the valence shell of metallic elements to remain unshared or unionized is called the inert pair effect. The ability of an electron to get closer to the nucleus is called penetration. The penetration power of the s-orbital is the maximum, and it experiences stronger attraction to the nucleus. As a result, the s-electrons fail to participate in bond formation, so the ns2 electrons need more energy to remove. Hence, the oxidation states of the heavier elements (especially the last two elements of Groups IIIA, IVA, VA and VIA) are two less than what would be expected.

Key Points

  • Group 14 elements show the +4 oxidation state; C, Si and Ge can also show -4 with electropositive elements.
  • Sn and Pb also show +2, the state in which they form ionic compounds.
  • Down the group, +4 becomes less stable and +2 becomes more stable.
  • Ge(II) compounds are reducing agents; Pb(II) compounds (like PbCl2) are the stable, common ones and Pb(IV) compounds are oxidizing agents.
  • The inert pair effect is the reluctance of the ns2 pair to take part in bonding, caused by the strong penetration of s-electrons.

lessons.title: Chlorides of Carbon, Silicon and Lead
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Tetrachlorides

Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is prepared by the chlorination of methane (or of carbon disulphide):

CH4 + 4Cl2 → CCl4 + 4HCl

Silicon tetrachloride (SiCl4) is prepared by heating silicon with chlorine, or by passing chlorine over a heated mixture of silica and carbon:

Si + 2Cl2 → SiCl4

Lead chlorides: lead (II) chloride is prepared by precipitation, for example:

Pb(NO3)2 + 2HCl → PbCl2 + 2HNO3

Thermal Stability

CCl4 is stable to heat. PbCl4 is unstable and decomposes on heating to the more stable PbCl2, because of the inert pair effect, which favours the +2 state of lead:

PbCl4 → PbCl2 + Cl2 (on heating)

Reactions with Water (Hydrolysis)

CCl4 does not hydrolyse in water: it is stable and does not react. SiCl4, in contrast, hydrolyses readily and vigorously in water:

SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl

This difference exists because silicon is a larger atom and can accept a lone pair from water into its vacant d-orbitals, while the small carbon atom in CCl4 is fully shielded by the four chlorine atoms and has no vacant d-orbital available.

Key Points

  • CCl4 is made by chlorinating methane; SiCl4 by heating silicon (or silica with carbon) in chlorine.
  • PbCl2 is made by precipitation; PbCl4 is unstable and decomposes to PbCl2 and Cl2 on heating (inert pair effect).
  • CCl4 does not hydrolyse; SiCl4 hydrolyses readily to SiO2 and HCl.
  • The +2 state becomes more stable down the group, so SnCl2 is more stable than SnCl4.

lessons.title: Oxides of Group 14 Elements: Structure of Carbon Dioxide and Silicon Dioxide
lessons.notes_html:
The important oxides of Group 14 elements are the monoxides, of general formula MO (examples: CO, SnO and PbO), and the dioxides, of general formula MO2 (examples: CO2, SiO2, SnO2 and PbO2). Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous gas and a strong reducing agent; carbon dioxide (CO2) is the acidic gas used by plants in photosynthesis.

Structure of Carbon Dioxide

Carbon dioxide consists of small, discrete molecules, O=C=O. The molecules are held together only by weak van der Waals forces, so CO2 is a gas at room temperature.

Structure of Silicon Dioxide

Silicon dioxide (SiO2) has a giant covalent structure: each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is shared between two silicon atoms, forming a continuous three-dimensional network. A very large amount of energy is needed to break this network, so SiO2 is a hard solid with a very high melting point. SiO2 occurs as quartz and sand and is used in making glass.

PropertyCO2SiO2
StructureSimple molecules, O=C=OGiant covalent network
Forces to breakWeak van der Waals forcesStrong covalent bonds throughout the network
State at room temperatureGasSolid (very high melting point)

Other important oxides: GeO2 is amphoteric; SnO is a basic, blue-black solid; SnO2 is a white amphoteric oxide; PbO (litharge) is a yellow basic oxide; and PbO2 is a brown, strong oxidizing agent used in lead accumulators (car batteries).

Key Points

  • Group 14 oxides are monoxides (MO) and dioxides (MO2).
  • CO2 is a gas of simple molecules held by weak van der Waals forces.
  • SiO2 is a giant covalent network, so it is a hard solid with a very high melting point.
  • This is why SiO2 is a solid while CO2 is a gas.
  • PbO2 is a strong oxidizing agent used in lead accumulators.

lessons.title: Acid-Base Behaviour of Group 14 Oxides
lessons.notes_html:
The acid-base character of the Group 14 oxides changes down the group as the metallic character increases: the oxides pass from acidic at the top to basic and amphoteric at the bottom.

  • CO2 is acidic: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic acid).
  • SiO2 is weakly acidic: it reacts with strong bases: SiO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O.
  • GeO2 is amphoteric.
  • SnO and PbO are basic: they react with acids to form salts.
  • SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric: they react with both acids and bases.

Reactions of Group 14 Elements with Water

Carbon does not react with water at ordinary temperature; with steam at high temperature it gives water gas: C + H2O → CO + H2. Silicon does not react with cold water but reacts with steam and with alkalis. Germanium is unaffected by water. Tin reacts slowly with steam: Sn + 2H2O → SnO2 + 2H2. Lead is unaffected by pure water, but water containing dissolved oxygen slowly attacks it, forming slightly soluble lead hydroxide; this is called plumbosolvency.

Key Points

  • CO2 is acidic and SiO2 is weakly acidic.
  • GeO2 is amphoteric; SnO and PbO are basic; SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric.
  • The oxides become more basic down the group as metallic character increases.
  • Carbon gives water gas with steam at high temperature; tin reacts slowly with steam.
  • Lead is attacked only by water containing dissolved oxygen (plumbosolvency).

lessons.title: Canning Process and the Use of Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science: Food is preserved in cans made of tinplate, which is steel sheet coated with a thin layer of tin. Tin is used for this coating because it is non-toxic and does not react with the food, and it protects the steel underneath from rusting and from attack by the food acids. In this way the canning process keeps food safe and fresh for a long time. Metals are chosen for such uses because of their special properties: they are strong, can be rolled into thin sheets, conduct heat, and some of them resist corrosion.

Key Points

  • Cans are made of steel coated with a thin layer of tin (tinplate).
  • Tin is non-toxic and unreactive towards food, so it protects both the food and the steel.
  • The tin coating stops the steel from rusting and keeps the food fresh for longer.
  • Metals are selected for uses according to their properties, such as strength, malleability and resistance to corrosion.

lessons.title: Group 17 Elements: The Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group 17 (VIIA) — fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I) and astatine (At) — are called halogens, a Greek word meaning salt producers, because they react with metals to form salts. They are the most reactive non-metals and are never found free in nature. They exist as diatomic molecules: F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2.

Halogens have seven electrons in their valence shells, with the general configuration ns2 np5. They need only one electron to complete the octet, so they readily gain an electron to form halide ions, X-, and show an oxidation state of -1. Fluorine shows only the -1 oxidation state, while the other halogens also show positive oxidation states of +1, +3, +5, +6 and +7 in their compounds with more electronegative elements.

Electronic Configuration of Halogens

ElementAtomic NumberElectronic ConfigurationValence Shell Configuration
Fluorine91s2 2s2 2p52s2 2p5
Chlorine171s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p53s2 3p5
Bromine351s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p54s2 4p5
Iodine531s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6 4d10 5s2 5p55s2 5p5

Physical States and Colours of Halogens

HalogenState at room temperatureColour
Fluorine, F2GasPale yellow
Chlorine, Cl2GasGreenish yellow
Bromine, Br2LiquidReddish brown
Iodine, I2SolidViolet-black (gives violet vapours on heating)

Key Points

  • Group 17 elements are the halogens: F, Cl, Br, I and At, the most reactive non-metals.
  • They occur as diatomic molecules X2 and are never found free in nature.
  • Valence configuration ns2 np5: they gain one electron to form X- ions (oxidation state -1).
  • Fluorine shows only -1; the others also show positive oxidation states in compounds.
  • F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid at room temperature.

lessons.title: Atomic and Physical Properties of the Halogens: Atomic Radius, Electronegativity and Electron Affinity
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in Atomic Radius

The atomic radii of Group VIIA elements go on increasing as we move down the group. This is due to the increase in the number of shells.

ElementFClBrI
Atomic Radii (pm)7299114133

Trends in Electronegativity

Halogens have very high values of electronegativity. These values decrease from fluorine to iodine as the atomic number increases. Fluorine is the most electronegative atom among all the elements.

ElementFClBrI
Electronegativity3.983.002.962.56

Trends in Electron Affinity

Electron affinity values decrease from chlorine to iodine. The electron affinity of fluorine is less than that of chlorine. This is due to the smaller size of fluorine: when an extra electron is added to a fluorine atom, high electron density is produced around the fluoride ion. This high electron density increases the repulsion between the electrons already present in the relatively compact 2p orbitals of fluorine and the electron being added. Due to this electron-electron repulsion, the fluorine atom shows a lesser tendency to attract an electron towards itself to form the fluoride ion, and hence the electron affinity of fluorine becomes less than that of chlorine. The correct order of electron affinity values of the halogens is: Cl > F > Br > I.

ElementFClBrI
Electron Affinity (kJ/mol)-328-349-325-295

Key Points

  • Atomic radius increases down the group (72 pm for F to 133 pm for I) as shells are added.
  • Electronegativity decreases down the group; fluorine (3.98) is the most electronegative element of all.
  • Electron affinity decreases from chlorine to iodine, but fluorine's value is lower than chlorine's.
  • Reason: the small fluorine atom has strong electron-electron repulsion in its compact 2p orbitals.
  • Electron affinity order: Cl > F > Br > I.

lessons.title: Melting and Boiling Points and Bond Enthalpies of the Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in Melting and Boiling Points

Halogens have low melting and boiling points. Their melting and boiling points gradually increase down the group, because the London dispersion forces become stronger as the molecules become larger. This is why F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid at room temperature.

HalogenF2Cl2Br2I2
Melting Point (°C)-220-102-7114
Boiling Point (°C)-188-3559184

Bond Enthalpies in Halogens

The bond enthalpy (bond energy) of the X-X bond generally decreases down the group as the atoms become larger and the bond becomes longer and weaker. Fluorine is an exception: the F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond, because the two small fluorine atoms bring their lone pairs very close together, and the strong repulsion between the lone pairs weakens the bond.

BondF-FCl-ClBr-BrI-I
Bond Enthalpy (kJ/mol)158242193151

Bond Enthalpies in Hydrogen Halides

The H-X bond enthalpy decreases steadily down the group, because the halogen atom becomes larger, the bond becomes longer and weaker. This is why the acidic strength and the reducing power of the hydrogen halides increase from HF to HI.

BondH-FH-ClH-BrH-I
Bond Enthalpy (kJ/mol)565432366299

Key Points

  • Melting and boiling points of halogens increase down the group as London dispersion forces strengthen.
  • States at room temperature: F2 gas, Cl2 gas, Br2 liquid, I2 solid.
  • X-X bond enthalpy generally decreases down the group, but F-F (158) is weaker than Cl-Cl (242) due to lone-pair repulsion in the small F2 molecule.
  • H-X bond enthalpy decreases from HF (565) to HI (299 kJ/mol).

lessons.title: Strength of Halogens as Oxidizing Agents
lessons.notes_html:
Halogens are strong oxidizing agents because they readily gain an electron to complete their octet and form halide ions. The oxidizing power of the halogens decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. The oxidizing power of fluorine is maximum among the halogens because of its small size and high electronegativity.

Displacement Reactions

Fluorine can oxidize the chloride, bromide and iodide ions to chlorine, bromine and iodine respectively:

F2 + 2Cl- → 2F- + Cl2

F2 + 2Br- → 2F- + Br2

F2 + 2I- → 2F- + I2

Chlorine can oxidize the bromide and iodide ions, but not the fluoride ion:

Cl2 + 2F- → No action

Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2

Cl2 + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2

Bromine can oxidize only the iodide ions:

Br2 + 2F- → No action

Br2 + 2Cl- → No action

Br2 + 2I- → 2Br- + I2

Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion:

I2 + 2F- → No action; I2 + 2Cl- → No action; I2 + 2Br- → No action.

Key Points

  • Halogens are strong oxidizing agents because they gain an electron to complete the octet.
  • Oxidizing power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • A halogen can displace (oxidize) only the halide ions below it in the group.
  • Fluorine oxidizes all other halide ions; iodine oxidizes none.
  • Fluorine is the strongest oxidizing agent because of its small size and highest electronegativity.

lessons.title: The Acidity of Hydrogen Halides
lessons.notes_html:
All the halogens combine with hydrogen to produce hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), and their aqueous solutions are commonly known as hydrohalic acids or halogen acids. The general formula of hydrogen halides is HX, and all the hydrogen halides are irritant.

H2 + X2 → 2HX

All the hydrogen halide molecules in the gaseous state are essentially covalent and are not able to ionize to give hydrogen ions (protons), but in aqueous solution they ionize to give hydrogen ions. The hydrogen ions combine with water molecules to form hydronium ions, H3O+, and hence hydrogen halide molecules act as acids:

HX + H2O → H3O+ + X-

The acidic strength (proton releasing power) of HX molecules increases from HF to HI, in the order: HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Thus HF is the weakest acid and HI is the strongest acid. HF ionizes only slightly and is therefore a weak acid, whereas HCl, HBr and HI ionize almost completely and are therefore strong acids.

Dissociation Energies of Hydrogen Halides

Hydrogen HalideHFHClHBrHI
Dissociation Energy (kJ/mol)565432366299

The weakest acidic nature of HF is due to the high dissociation energy of the H-F bond: the bond is very strong, so it breaks with great difficulty in water and very few H+ ions are released. Down the group the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, so it breaks more easily and the acid becomes stronger. A related fact: HF cannot be stored in glass containers, because it attacks the silica of glass.

Key Points

  • Hydrogen halides HX dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids: HX + H2O → H3O+ + X-.
  • Acidic strength increases HF < HCl < HBr < HI.
  • HF is a weak acid; HCl, HBr and HI are strong acids.
  • Reason: the H-X bond weakens down the group (565 to 299 kJ/mol), so H+ is released more easily.
  • HF attacks glass and cannot be stored in glass containers.

lessons.title: Halide Ions as Reducing Agents and Trends in Reducing Strength of Halide Ions
lessons.notes_html:
A substance that loses electrons during a chemical reaction is called a reducing agent, while a substance that gains electrons is called an oxidizing agent. The reducing agent reduces other substances (decreases their oxidation states) and is itself oxidized (its oxidation state is increased). The halide ions (or hydrogen halides) reduce oxidizing agents and are themselves oxidized to X2 molecules:

4HX + O2 → 2H2O + 2X2

The trend in the reducing ability of halide ions (or hydrogen halides) is opposite to the trend in the oxidizing power of the halogens. The reducing properties increase from fluoride ion (or HF) to iodide ion (or HI), because the ionic radii of the halide ions increase down the group, so the outer electron is held less firmly and is lost more easily. The order is:

F- < Cl- < Br- < I- or HF < HCl < HBr < HI

The fluoride ion (or HF) is the weakest reducing agent; in fact it has no considerable reducing properties at all. It cannot reduce even very strong oxidizing agents such as SO2 and HI, and it cannot reduce any of the halogens (Cl2, Br2 and I2) to their halide ions: 2F- + Cl2 → No action; 2F- + Br2 → No action; 2F- + I2 → No action.

The chloride ion (or HCl) reduces only strong oxidizing agents like F2, and is itself oxidized to Cl2. It can reduce neither Br2 nor I2:

2Cl- + F2 → 2F- + Cl2

2Cl- + Br2 → No action

2Cl- + I2 → No action

The bromide ion (or HBr) reduces F2 and Cl2, but not I2:

2Br- + F2 → 2F- + Br2

2Br- + Cl2 → 2Cl- + Br2

2Br- + I2 → No action

The iodide ion (or HI), being the strongest reducing agent, can reduce all of the other three halogens to their corresponding halide ions:

2I- + F2 → 2F- + I2

2I- + Cl2 → 2Cl- + I2

2I- + Br2 → 2Br- + I2

We may say that a given halide ion (or halogen acid) can reduce only that halogen molecule which lies above it in Group 17 (VIIA) of the periodic table. The halide ion cannot reduce the halogen molecule which lies below it in the group.

Key Points

  • Halide ions act as reducing agents: they lose electrons and are oxidized to X2.
  • Reducing power increases down the group: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
  • This trend is opposite to the oxidizing power of the halogens.
  • Reason: the ions get larger down the group, so the outer electron is lost more easily.
  • F- is the weakest reducing agent (practically none); I- is the strongest.
  • A halide ion can reduce only the halogens above it in the group.

lessons.title: Properties and Commercial Uses of the Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science:

Properties and Uses of Fluorine

Fluorine is a highly toxic gas. It is the most electronegative and reactive element. It reacts directly with all elements except helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar). It is used in the manufacture of chlorofluorocarbons, commercially known as Freons. Freons are used as refrigerants in refrigerators, as cooling agents in air conditioners, and as aerosol propellants and cleaning agents. Fluorine is also used in the manufacture of Teflon. Teflon is a valuable plastic used for coating electrical wiring; it provides a non-stick surface for frying pans and other cooking-related products.

Properties and Uses of Chlorine

Chlorine (Cl2) is a highly toxic gas with a pale yellow-green colour. Chlorine is chemically less active than fluorine but more active than bromine and iodine. Some of the uses of chlorine depend on its toxic effects: chlorine is used as a disinfectant in swimming pools and water treatment plants. Many organic compounds of chlorine are used in the manufacture of antiseptics, insecticides, weed killers and herbicides. Chlorine is a very strong oxidizing agent and is used commercially as a bleaching agent. Large amounts of chlorine are used to make solvents such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl4), chloroform (CHCl3), dichloroethylene (C2H2Cl2) and trichloroethylene (C2HCl3).
