Properties and Uses of Bromine

Bromine (Br2) is a reddish-orange liquid with an unpleasant, choking odour. The vapours of bromine are irritating to the eyes and throat. The liquid is highly corrosive and can cause serious burns if spilled on the skin. Bromine is chemically less active than fluorine and chlorine but more active than iodine. Bromine is used to prepare flame retardants, fire-extinguishing agents, sedatives, germicides, pesticides, fungicides and insecticides. Bromine can also be used as a disinfectant like chlorine.

Properties and Uses of Iodine

Iodine is an intensely coloured solid with an almost metallic lustre. Iodine vapours are irritating to the eyes and respiratory system. Iodine is chemically less active than the other halogens (not counting astatine). Iodine acts as an antioxidant in our blood. It is also used as a cough expectorant and is helpful in treating allergies, dermatitis, bladder infections and moles. The human body uses iodine to make thyroxine, an important hormone (chemical messenger) produced by the thyroid gland, which plays an important role in metabolism. The deficiency of iodine in the human body can lead to goitre, a swelling around the neck. Iodine can be used as a water purifying agent and as a sterilizing agent, and for the preparation of antiseptics such as iodex and tincture.

Properties and Uses of Bleaching Powder

Bleaching powder is also known as calcium hypochlorite, or sometimes calcium oxychloride, and its chemical formula is CaOCl2. It is a pale yellow powder and has a strong smell of chlorine. It loses chlorine when it reacts with carbon dioxide:

CaOCl2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + Cl2

Key Points

  • Fluorine is used to make Freons (refrigerants, propellants) and Teflon (non-stick plastic).
  • Chlorine is a disinfectant for water and a commercial bleaching agent; it is also used to make solvents like CCl4 and CHCl3.
  • Bromine is used in flame retardants, fire-extinguishing agents, sedatives and pesticides.
  • Iodine is needed to make the hormone thyroxine; its deficiency causes goitre. It is used in antiseptics like tincture and iodex.
  • Bleaching powder, CaOCl2, releases chlorine on reacting with CO2.

lessons.title: Fluoride Toxicity and Deficiency
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science: A small amount of fluoride is useful for health: fluoride in drinking water (about 1 part per million) and fluoride compounds such as sodium fluoride in toothpaste help to prevent tooth decay by making the enamel of the teeth harder and more resistant to acid attack.

Too much fluoride, however, is harmful; this is called fluoride toxicity. Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis, in which the teeth become mottled (marked with patches) and weak. In more severe cases it causes skeletal fluorosis, in which the bones and joints become stiff and painful. On the other hand, deficiency of fluoride increases tooth decay, because the enamel is not protected.

Key Points

  • About 1 ppm fluoride in drinking water helps prevent tooth decay.
  • Fluoride in toothpaste strengthens the enamel against acid attack.
  • Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis (mottled teeth) and skeletal fluorosis (stiff, painful bones and joints).
  • Fluoride deficiency increases tooth decay.

lessons.title: Transition Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Transition elements are the elements in which the d-orbitals are partially filled, either in the atomic state or in any of their common oxidation states. They lie between the s-block and p-block elements. The d-block elements are collectively called transition elements or transition metals, while the f-block elements are called inner transition elements.

Their general electronic configuration is (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2. They are hard, lustrous metals with high melting and boiling points. They show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds, act as catalysts and form alloys.

Series of Transition Elements

SeriesElementsOrbital FilledPeriod
First seriesSc to Zn (10 elements)3d4
Second seriesY to Cd (10 elements)4d5
Third seriesLa and Hf to Hg5d6
Fourth seriesAc and Rf to Cn (incomplete)6d7

The elements of Group 12 (Zn, Cd, Hg) are not counted as transition elements because they have completely filled d-orbitals (d10) in the atomic state and in their common oxidation states. The book also excludes Group 3 elements, whose common ions have an empty d-subshell (d0).

Key Points

  • Transition elements have partially filled d-orbitals in the atom or in a common oxidation state.
  • General configuration: (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2.
  • There are four transition series: 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series.
  • The first series (Sc to Zn) lies in period 4.
  • Zn, Cd and Hg (d10) are excluded from the transition elements.
  • f-block elements are called inner transition elements.

lessons.title: General Characteristics of Transition Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Almost all transition elements show similar properties because their valence shell configurations are similar. Their important general characteristics are:

  • They have high tensile strength, ductility, malleability and thermal and electrical conductivity.
  • They show variable oxidation states.
  • They form coloured compounds.
  • They are used as catalysts.
  • They form complex compounds (coordination compounds).
  • They form interstitial compounds.
  • They form alloys.
  • Many of their compounds are used in paints.
  • Many of them and their compounds are paramagnetic.

Their metallic character comes from the electrons available for metallic bonding. In the 3d series, chromium and copper contribute the most electrons per atom to the metallic bond, while scandium and zinc contribute the fewest.

Key Points

  • Transition metals are hard, strong, ductile and malleable, and conduct heat and electricity well.
  • Variable oxidation states and coloured compounds are their typical features.
  • They form complexes, alloys and interstitial compounds.
  • They and their compounds are widely used as catalysts.
  • Many transition metal compounds are paramagnetic.

lessons.title: Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
In d-block elements the (n-1)d subshell is filled gradually. The general configuration is (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2. When ions are formed, the ns electrons are lost before the (n-1)d electrons. For example, Ti2+ is [Ar]3d2, Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6 and Fe3+ is [Ar]3d5.

First Transition Series (3d)

ElementConfigurationElementConfiguration
Sc (21)[Ar]3d1 4s2Mn (25)[Ar]3d5 4s2
Ti (22)[Ar]3d2 4s2Fe (26)[Ar]3d6 4s2
V (23)[Ar]3d3 4s2Co (27)[Ar]3d7 4s2
Cr (24)[Ar]3d5 4s1Ni (28)[Ar]3d8 4s2
Cu (29)[Ar]3d10 4s1Zn (30)[Ar]3d10 4s2

Cr and Cu are exceptions: one 4s electron moves into 3d to give the extra stable half-filled (d5) and completely filled (d10) configurations. Similar exceptions in the 4d series are Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh and Pd (Pd is 4d10 5s0), and in the 5d series Pt (5d9 6s1) and Au (5d10 6s1).

Key Points

  • General configuration of d-block elements: (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2.
  • On forming ions, ns electrons are removed before (n-1)d electrons.
  • Cr is 3d5 4s1 and Cu is 3d10 4s1 because half-filled and filled d-subshells are extra stable.
  • Fe2+ is 3d6 and Fe3+ is 3d5.
  • Pd has the exceptional configuration 4d10 5s0.

lessons.title: Binding Energies
lessons.notes_html:
The binding energy of an element is the energy needed to separate its atoms. In transition metals it depends on the number of unpaired electrons taking part in metallic bonding.

Binding energy first increases across a series, reaches a maximum in the middle, and then decreases. Elements in the middle of the series, such as Cr, Mo and W, have the maximum number of unpaired electrons, so they have the highest binding energies and the highest melting points. Towards the end of the series the electrons pair up, bonding becomes weaker, and binding energy and melting point fall. Zn, Cd and Hg, with filled d-subshells, have the lowest melting points and are quite volatile.

The same trend is shown by melting points: they rise up to the middle of the series (Cr, Mo, W) and then decrease, with a small dip at Mn and Tc.

Key Points

  • Binding energy measures the strength of bonding between metal atoms.
  • It increases up to the middle of a transition series, then decreases.
  • More unpaired d-electrons mean stronger bonding, higher binding energy and higher melting point.
  • Cr, Mo and W have the highest melting points in their series.
  • Zn, Cd and Hg have low melting points because their d-subshells are filled.

lessons.title: Variable Oxidation State
lessons.notes_html:
Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the ns and (n-1)d orbitals are very close in energy, so electrons from both can be used in bonding. The maximum oxidation state rises across the series up to the middle (it equals the group number for the early groups) and then falls.

Stable Oxidation States (First Series)

ElementStable Oxidation States
Sc+3
Ti+2, +4
V+2, +3, +4, +5
Cr+2, +3, +6
Mn+2, +4, +6, +7
Fe+2, +3
Co+2, +3
Ni+2
Cu+1, +2
Zn+2

Stability depends on electronic configuration. Sc3+ and Ti4+ are stable because they have the noble gas configuration. Fe3+ (d5, half-filled) is more stable than Fe2+ (d6). Ag+ (4d10, filled) is more stable than Ag2+. In water, however, Cu2+ is more stable than Cu+ because the small Cu2+ ion has a much higher (more negative) hydration enthalpy. Lower oxidation states usually form ionic compounds, while higher oxidation states occur in covalent compounds such as oxides and fluorides (for example V2O5).

Key Points

  • Variable oxidation states arise because ns and (n-1)d electrons are close in energy.
  • The most frequent oxidation states of transition elements are +2 and +3.
  • Half-filled (d5) and filled (d10) configurations give extra stability, e.g. Fe3+ and Ag+.
  • Sc3+ and Ti4+ are stable due to the noble gas configuration.
  • In aqueous solution Cu2+ is more stable than Cu+ due to its high hydration enthalpy.

lessons.title: Catalytic Behaviour
lessons.notes_html:
Transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts for two reasons:

  • They have variable oxidation states, so they can form unstable intermediate compounds with the reactants and then return to their original state.
  • Their surfaces adsorb reactant molecules, which weakens their bonds and speeds up the reaction (adsorption theory).

Key Reactions

CatalystProcess / Reaction
FeHaber process: manufacture of NH3
V2O5Contact process: manufacture of H2SO4
PtOstwald process: manufacture of HNO3
NiHydrogenation of oils to make ghee
MnO2Decomposition of KClO3 to give O2
FeCl3Manufacture of CCl4 from CS2 and Cl2
Hot CuOxidation of ethanol to ethanal
Pt, RhCatalytic converters in vehicle exhausts

Key Points

  • Transition metals catalyse reactions through variable oxidation states and surface adsorption.
  • Fe is the catalyst in the Haber process and V2O5 in the Contact process.
  • Ni is used for hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
  • MnO2 speeds up the decomposition of KClO3.

lessons.title: Magnetic Behaviour
lessons.notes_html:
The response of a substance to a magnetic field is its magnetic behaviour.

  • Paramagnetic: substances attracted into a magnetic field. They have unpaired electrons, e.g. most transition metal ions.
  • Diamagnetic: substances repelled by a magnetic field. All their electrons are paired, e.g. Zn2+ and Sc3+ compounds.
  • Ferromagnetic: substances that are strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetised, e.g. Fe, Co and Ni.

The magnetic moment is calculated from the number of unpaired electrons (n): μ = √(n(n+2)) BM (Bohr magneton).

IonUnpaired ElectronsMagnetic Moment (BM)
Sc3+00
Ti3+11.73
V3+22.83
Cr3+33.87
Mn2+, Fe3+55.92
Fe2+44.90
Co2+33.87
Ni2+22.83
Cu2+11.73
Zn2+00

Key Points

  • Unpaired electrons make a substance paramagnetic; paired electrons make it diamagnetic.
  • Magnetic moment μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
  • Mn2+ and Fe3+ (5 unpaired electrons) have the highest magnetic moment, 5.92 BM.
  • Cu2+ is paramagnetic (d9) but Zn2+ is diamagnetic (d10).
  • Fe, Co and Ni are ferromagnetic.

lessons.title: Alloy Formation
lessons.notes_html:
Transition metals form alloys readily because their atomic sizes are very similar (within about 15% of each other), so atoms of one metal can easily replace atoms of another in the crystal lattice. An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal.

Examples: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn) and stainless steel (Fe + Cr).

How Alloy Properties Differ from the Pure Metals

  • Alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals.
  • Their melting points are usually lower than those of the component metals.
  • They resist corrosion better, e.g. stainless steel does not rust like iron.
  • Their appearance and colour can differ, e.g. brass looks golden.
  • Their electrical resistance can be much higher, e.g. nichrome is used in heating elements.

Key Points

  • Alloys form easily because transition metal atoms have similar sizes.
  • Brass is Cu + Zn and bronze is Cu + Sn.
  • Alloys are generally harder, stronger and more corrosion-resistant than pure metals.
  • Alloys usually melt lower than their component metals.

lessons.title: Coordination Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Coordination compounds (complex compounds) contain a central metal atom or ion attached to a group of ligands by coordinate covalent bonds, and the complex can exist independently as a molecule or ion, e.g. [Cu(NH3)4]2+ and [Fe(CN)6]4-.

They differ from double salts: Mohr's salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, gives all its ions (Fe2+, NH4+ and SO4 2-) in solution, but K4[Fe(CN)6] gives only K+ ions and the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4-; it does not give free Fe2+ or CN- ions.

Transition elements form complexes readily because they have small size, high charge, and vacant (n-1)d orbitals that can accept lone pairs from ligands.

Parts of a Complex

  • Central metal atom or ion: the electron-pair acceptor, e.g. Fe in [Fe(CN)6]4-.
  • Ligands: ions or molecules that donate lone pairs to the metal.
  • Coordination sphere: the metal and its ligands, written inside square brackets.
  • Counter-ions: ions outside the brackets that balance the charge.

Types of Ligands

TypeMeaningExamples
MonodentateDonates one lone pairNH3, H2O, Cl-, CN-, OH-
BidentateDonates two lone pairsEthylenediamine (en), oxalate C2O4 2-
PolydentateDonates several lone pairsEDTA (hexadentate)
AmbidentateCan bind through either of two atomsNO2- (through N or O), SCN- (through S or N)
BridgingBinds two metal atoms at onceOH-, Cl- bridges

Key Points

  • A complex has a central metal ion bonded to ligands by coordinate bonds.
  • Unlike double salts, a complex does not give free metal ions in solution.
  • Small size, high charge and vacant d-orbitals favour complex formation.
  • Ligands are classified by the number of lone pairs they donate.
  • EDTA is a hexadentate (chelating) ligand.

lessons.title: Oxidation State and Coordination Number of Central Metal Ion
lessons.notes_html:
The coordination number is the number of lone pairs of electrons provided by the ligands to the central metal atom or ion, that is, the number of coordinate bonds formed. Common coordination numbers are 2, 4 and 6.

Coordination NumberShapeExample
2Linear[Ag(NH3)2]+
4Tetrahedral[Zn(NH3)4]2+
4Square planar[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]
6Octahedral[Fe(CN)6]4-

Finding the Oxidation State

The sum of the oxidation state of the metal and the charges of the ligands equals the charge on the complex ion.

  • In K4[Fe(CN)6]: the complex ion is [Fe(CN)6]4-. x + 6(-1) = -4, so Fe = +2.
  • In [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2: the complex ion is [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+. x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2, so Co = +3.
  • In [Zn(NH3)4]2+: NH3 is neutral, so Zn = +2.

Key Points

  • Coordination number = number of coordinate bonds to the central metal.
  • Common coordination numbers are 2, 4 and 6.
  • Neutral ligands (NH3, H2O) contribute zero charge in oxidation state calculations.
  • In K4[Fe(CN)6] iron is in the +2 oxidation state.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Rules for Naming

  • The cation is named first, then the anion.
  • Inside the complex, ligands are named first (in alphabetical order, ignoring di, tri, etc.), then the central metal.
  • Anionic ligands end in -o: Cl- chloro, CN- cyano, OH- hydroxo, SO4 2- sulphato, C2O4 2- oxalato.
  • Neutral ligands keep their names, with special names: H2O aqua, NH3 ammine, CO carbonyl, NO nitrosyl.
  • The number of ligands is shown by di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa; bis, tris, tetrakis are used for complex ligand names such as ethylenediamine.
  • The oxidation state of the metal is written in Roman numerals in brackets, e.g. iron(III).
  • If the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate, e.g. ferrate, cobaltate, platinate, argentate, stannate.

Worked Examples (from the book)

FormulaName
[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2Pentaamminechlorocobalt(III) chloride
K3[Fe(CN)6]Potassium hexacyanoferrate(III)
K4[Fe(CN)6]Potassium hexacyanoferrate(II)
[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]Diamminedichloroplatinum(II)
[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3Hexaaquachromium(III) chloride
Na2[Sn(OH)6]Sodium hexahydroxostannate(IV)
Na2[Fe(CN)5NO]Sodium pentacyanonitrosylferrate(II)
[Pt(NH3)2Cl4]Diamminetetrachloroplatinum(IV)

Key Points

  • Name the cation before the anion; ligands before the metal.
  • Anionic ligands end in -o; H2O is aqua and NH3 is ammine.
  • Show the metal's oxidation state in Roman numerals.
  • For anionic complexes the metal name ends in -ate.

lessons.title: Shapes of Complex Compound
lessons.notes_html:
The shape (geometry) of a complex depends on its coordination number.

Coordination NumberShapeExamples
2Linear[Ag(NH3)2]+, [Ag(CN)2]-
4Tetrahedral[Zn(NH3)4]2+, [Ni(CO)4]
4Square planar[Cu(NH3)4]2+, [Ni(CN)4]2-, [AuCl4]-
5Trigonal bipyramidal / square pyramidal[Fe(CO)5]
6Octahedral[Fe(CN)6]4-, [Co(NH3)6]3+

The octahedral shape (coordination number 6) is the most common geometry of coordination compounds.

Key Points

  • Coordination number 2 gives a linear shape.
  • Coordination number 4 gives tetrahedral or square planar shapes.
  • Coordination number 6 gives an octahedral shape, the most common one.
  • [Ag(NH3)2]+ is linear and [Fe(CN)6]4- is octahedral.

lessons.title: Colour in Complex Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Most transition metal complexes are coloured. The colour is due to d-d transitions: when ligands surround the metal ion, its five d-orbitals split into two sets of different energy. An electron absorbs visible light and jumps from the lower set to the higher set. The colour absorbed is removed from white light, and we see the complementary colour.

Ions with empty d-orbitals (d0, e.g. Sc3+, Ti4+) or completely filled d-orbitals (d10, e.g. Zn2+) cannot show d-d transitions, so they are colourless. Hydrated copper(II) sulphate, [Cu(H2O)6]2+, is blue, while anhydrous CuSO4 is white. CoCl2 is blue when anhydrous and pink when hydrated.

Iond-ElectronsColour
Sc3+d0Colourless
Ti4+d0Colourless
Ti3+d1Purple (violet)
V4+d1Blue
V3+d2Green
V2+d3Violet

Some very intense colours, such as purple MnO4- and orange Cr2O7 2-, are due to charge-transfer transitions, because Mn(VII) and Cr(VI) have no d-electrons.

Key Points

  • Colour in complexes is caused by d-d transitions between split d-orbitals.
  • The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • d0 and d10 ions (Sc3+, Zn2+) are colourless.
  • [Ti(H2O)6]3+ is violet and [Cu(H2O)6]2+ is blue.
  • The colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligand.

lessons.title: Uses of Transition Metal Compounds in Paints
lessons.notes_html:
Pure transition metals are valued for many reasons. One important reason is their ability to form highly coloured compounds, which are used as pigments in paints.

  • Transition elements such as chromium, iron, copper, cobalt and titanium form numerous coloured compounds with oxygen.
  • Red paint comes from compounds of iron with oxygen.
  • Green and blue paints come from different compounds of copper, chromium and cobalt.
  • Titanium forms a white compound with oxygen, used for white paint.

Key Points

  • Coloured transition metal compounds are used as paint pigments.
  • Iron-oxygen compounds give red paint.
  • Copper, chromium and cobalt compounds give green and blue paints.
  • Titanium gives white paint.

lessons.title: Vanadium
lessons.notes_html:
Vanadium has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d3 4s2. It shows oxidation states from +2 to +5.

Oxidation StateExamplesColour
+5VO3-, V2O5Yellow / orange
+4VO2+, VOCl2Blue
+3V3+, VCl3Green
+2V2+, VCl2Violet

The +5 state is the most stable; stability decreases as the oxidation state falls. Vanadium(II) compounds are strong reducing agents and are quickly oxidised by air to vanadium(III). In acid solution the blue vanadyl ion VO2+ reacts with V2+: VO2+ + 2V2+ + 4H+ → 3V3+ + 2H2O.

Vanadium(V) oxide, V2O5, is amphoteric: it dissolves in acids and in alkalis, forming vanadates. It is used as a catalyst in the Contact process for making sulphuric acid.

Key Reactions

ReactionChange
SO2 + V2O5 → SO3 + 2VO2V(V) oxidises SO2
4VO2 + O2 → 2V2O5Catalyst regenerated
VO2+ + 2V2+ + 4H+ → 3V3+ + 2H2OReaction in acid solution

Key Points

  • Vanadium shows oxidation states +2, +3, +4 and +5, each with a different colour.
  • The +5 state is the most stable; V(II) is a strong reducing agent.
  • V2O5 is amphoteric and forms vanadates with alkalis.
  • V2O5 catalyses the oxidation of SO2 to SO3 in the Contact process.

lessons.title: Chromium
lessons.notes_html:
Chromium has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d5 4s1. Its main oxidation states are +2, +3 and +6.

  • +2 state: chromium(II) compounds are reducing agents and are unstable; they are quickly oxidised to chromium(III).
  • +3 state: the most stable state. Chromium(III) oxide, Cr2O3, is a green solid, and chromium(III) salts such as CrCl3 are violet or green.
  • +6 state: compounds such as K2Cr2O7, K2CrO4 and CrO3 are strong oxidizing agents.

Cr2O3 is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and alkalis. Chromium gives stainless steel its resistance to rusting.

Chromate-Dichromate Equilibrium

ReactionObservation
2CrO4 2- (yellow) + 2H+ ⇌ Cr2O7 2- (orange) + H2OAcid turns yellow chromate into orange dichromate
Cr2O7 2- + 2OH- → 2CrO4 2- + H2OAlkali turns orange dichromate back to yellow chromate

Key Points

  • Chromium shows +2, +3 and +6 oxidation states; +3 is the most stable.
  • Cr2O3 is green and amphoteric.
  • Cr(VI) compounds are strong oxidizing agents.
  • Yellow chromate and orange dichromate interconvert in acid and alkali.
  • Chromium makes stainless steel rust-resistant.

lessons.title: Potassium Dichromate(VI) as an Oxidizing Agent
lessons.notes_html:
Potassium dichromate, K2Cr2O7, is prepared from the mineral chromite, FeCr2O4.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
Roasting chromite4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 → 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2
Acidifying2Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 → Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O
With KClNa2Cr2O7 + 2KCl → K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl

K2Cr2O7 forms orange crystals (melting point 398°C) and is less soluble in water than sodium dichromate. In acid solution it is a powerful oxidizing agent; chromium changes from +6 to +3 and the orange solution turns green:

Cr2O7 2- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

It oxidises iron(II) to iron(III): K2Cr2O7 + 7H2SO4 + 6FeSO4 → 3Fe2(SO4)3 + Cr2(SO4)3 + K2SO4 + 7H2O. Because of this oxidising action it is used in volumetric analysis.

Key Points

  • K2Cr2O7 is made from chromite ore in three steps.
  • It is an orange crystalline solid, melting point 398°C.
  • In acid it oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+ and is itself reduced to green Cr3+.
  • Half-equation: Cr2O7 2- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O.
  • It is used as an oxidising agent in volumetric analysis.

lessons.title: Manganese
lessons.notes_html:
Manganese has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d5 4s2. It shows oxidation states from +2 to +7. The common states are +2 (d5), +4 (d3) and +7 (d0).

The +2 state is the most stable because of the half-filled d5 configuration. Manganese(II) salts such as MnCl2 and MnSO4 are pale pink. Compounds in higher oxidation states, such as potassium manganate(VI), K2MnO4 (+6), and potassium permanganate, KMnO4 (+7), are strong oxidizing agents.

Oxides of Manganese

OxideFormulaOxidation StateNature
Manganese(II) oxideMnO+2Basic
Manganese(IV) oxideMnO2+4Amphoteric
Manganese(VII) oxideMn2O7+7Acidic

The acidic character of manganese oxides increases, and the basic character decreases, as the oxidation state increases.

Key Points

  • Manganese shows oxidation states +2 to +7.
  • Mn2+ (d5) is the most stable state; its salts are pale pink.
  • K2MnO4 and KMnO4 are strong oxidizing agents.
  • MnO is basic, MnO2 is amphoteric and Mn2O7 is acidic.
  • Acidic character of the oxides increases with oxidation state.

lessons.title: Potassium Manganate(VII) as an Oxidizing Agent in Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4 (potassium permanganate), is a powerful oxidizing agent and probably the most useful one in organic chemistry. It can work in acidic, basic or neutral medium. In acid it is reduced to manganese(II) ions, while in alkaline or neutral medium MnO2 is formed.

Oxidizing Properties in Alkaline Medium (Baeyer's Test)

When an alkene is passed through cold 1% alkaline KMnO4 solution (Baeyer's reagent), a vicinal diol (glycol) is formed. The pink colour is discharged and dark brown MnO2 appears. This is Baeyer's test for unsaturation.

3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O → 3CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) + 2KOH + 2MnO2

Oxidizing Properties in Acidic Medium

With acidified KMnO4 an alkene also gives a glycol, but the pink colour disappears because colourless manganese(II) ions are formed:

5CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 2H2O → 5CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) + 2MnSO4 + K2SO4

Use in Titrations

Acidified KMnO4 is used in redox titrations. It acts as its own indicator (self-indicator): the end point is the first permanent pink colour. It oxidises iron(II) ions and oxalic acid:

ReactionUse
MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2OEstimation of iron(II)
2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 5(COOH)2 → K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 8H2O + 10CO2Estimation of oxalates

Key Points

  • KMnO4 oxidises in acid, alkaline and neutral media.
  • In acid it gives Mn2+; in alkaline or neutral medium it gives MnO2.
  • Cold alkaline KMnO4 converts alkenes to glycols (Baeyer's test for unsaturation).
  • KMnO4 is a self-indicator in redox titrations.
  • It is used to estimate iron(II) and oxalates volumetrically.

lessons.title: Iron
lessons.notes_html:
Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. It is highly reactive, corrodes easily and occurs only in the combined state. Its important ores are magnetite (Fe3O4), haematite (Fe2O3) and limonite (2Fe2O3.3H2O). In Pakistan, iron ore deposits are found at Kalabagh (the largest), Nokundi and Chiniot. The largest world producers are China, Australia, Brazil, India and Russia.

Oxidation States

Iron, [Ar]3d6 4s2, shows oxidation states from -2 to +6; the most common are +2 and +3. Iron(II) compounds such as [Fe(H2O)6]2+ and FeSO4.7H2O are reducing agents. Fe2+ (3d6) is easily oxidised to Fe3+ (3d5) because the half-filled d-subshell is extra stable; this is why a cut apple turns brown in air and why Fe2O3 is more stable than FeO.

Iron as Catalyst in Haber's Process

N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (Fe catalyst). Nitrogen comes from air and hydrogen from methane in natural gas. The reaction is reversible and slow, so a catalyst is used to reach equilibrium quickly. The catalyst is magnetite (Fe3O4) mixed with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3. The gases are purified first so the catalyst is not poisoned. Iron is cheap, so it lowers the cost of the process.

Iron as Catalyst in the Reaction between Persulphate and Iodide Ions

Persulphate ions oxidise iodide ions only slowly: S2O8 2- + 2I- → 2SO4 2- + I2. Iron(II) or iron(III) ions catalyse the reaction in two steps:

StepReaction
1S2O8 2- + 2Fe2+ → 2SO4 2- + 2Fe3+
22Fe3+ + 2I- → 2Fe2+ + I2

The iron(II) catalyst is regenerated at the end of the second step.

Key Points

  • Iron's main ores are magnetite, haematite and limonite; Kalabagh has Pakistan's largest deposits.
  • The common oxidation states of iron are +2 and +3.
  • Fe3+ (d5) is extra stable, so Fe2+ compounds are reducing agents.
  • Iron (magnetite) catalyses the Haber process for ammonia.
  • Fe2+/Fe3+ ions catalyse the persulphate-iodide reaction and are regenerated.

lessons.title: Reactions of Hexaaquairon(II) and Hexaaquairon(III) Ions
lessons.notes_html:
Reaction with Water

The pale green hexaaquairon(II) ion, [Fe(H2O)6]2+, and the yellow hexaaquairon(III) ion, [Fe(H2O)6]3+, are both acidic: they donate hydrogen ions to water. The greater the charge density on the metal ion, the more acidic it is, so hexaaquairon(III) is more acidic than hexaaquairon(II).

[Fe(H2O)6]2+ + H2O ⇌ [Fe(H2O)5(OH)]+ + H3O+

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + H2O ⇌ [Fe(H2O)5(OH)]2+ + H3O+

Reaction with Ammonia

Ammonia is a stronger base than water and removes protons from the hexaaqua ions, forming hydroxide precipitates:

[Fe(H2O)6]2+ + 2NH3 ⇌ [Fe(H2O)4(OH)2] + 2NH4+

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3NH3 ⇌ [Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3NH4+

Reaction with Carbonate Ions

The less acidic iron(II) complex gives a green precipitate of iron(II) carbonate: [Fe(H2O)6]2+ + CO3 2- → FeCO3 + 6H2O. The more acidic iron(III) complex instead forms the hydrated hydroxide with effervescence of CO2: 2[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3CO3 2- → 2[Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3H2O + 3CO2.

Reaction with Thiocyanate Ions

This is a ligand exchange reaction. Adding thiocyanate ions to a solution of hexaaquairon(III) ions gives an intense blood-red solution of [Fe(H2O)5(SCN)]2+:

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + SCN- → [Fe(H2O)5(SCN)]2+ + H2O

Hexaaquairon(II) ions do not give this reaction, so it is a test for iron(III).

Key Points

  • Hexaaqua iron ions are acidic; Fe(III) is more acidic than Fe(II) due to higher charge density.
  • Ammonia precipitates the hydrated hydroxides of both ions.
  • Carbonate gives green FeCO3 precipitate with Fe(II), but hydroxide precipitate and CO2 gas with Fe(III).
  • Thiocyanate gives a blood-red colour with Fe(III) only.

lessons.title: Copper
lessons.notes_html:
Copper is a reddish-orange, soft, malleable and ductile metal with high thermal and electrical conductivity. It tarnishes to a dull brownish colour in air. It is used in electrical cables and appliances and in alloys such as brass and bronze. It occurs native and in combined form; in Pakistan it is found at Reko Diq, Balochistan.

Important Ores

OreFormulaCopper Content
CupriteCu2OAbout 88%
ChalcociteCu2SAbout 80%
Azurite (blue)2CuCO3.Cu(OH)2About 65%
Malachite (green)CuCO3.Cu(OH)2About 57%
ChalcopyriteCuFeS2About 34%

Chalcopyrite is the most common source of copper and accounts for about 50% of world copper production.

Oxidation States

Copper, [Ar]3d10 4s1, shows +1 (cuprous, d10) and +2 (cupric, d9) states, e.g. Cu2O and CuO. Copper is the only transition metal for which +1 is important. Copper(II) is the most stable and abundant state in solution and in solids, while copper(I) is more stable in some solids at moderate temperatures. In aqueous solution copper(I) is readily oxidised, Cu+ → Cu2+ + e-, so Cu+ acts as a reducing agent.

Reactions of Hexaaquacopper(II) Ions

  • With hydroxide ions: a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms: [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH- → [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] + 2H2O.
  • With ammonia: a little ammonia gives the same pale blue precipitate; excess ammonia dissolves it to a deep blue solution of tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ions: [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] + 4NH3 → [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ + 2OH- + 2H2O.
  • With carbonate ions: an insoluble precipitate of copper(II) carbonate forms: [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + CO3 2- → CuCO3 + 6H2O.

Key Points

  • Copper is a reddish-orange metal used in cables and alloys; its Pakistani source is Reko Diq.
  • Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is its most common ore.
  • Common oxidation states are +1 (cuprous) and +2 (cupric); Cu(II) is most stable in solution.
  • Cu+ is a reducing agent in aqueous solution.
  • Excess ammonia gives a deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) solution.

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.notes_html:
In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, chemists classified compounds into two classes: organic compounds, obtained from plants or animals (living sources), and inorganic compounds, obtained from non-living sources. For example, acetic acid (from vinegar) and tartaric acid (from grapes) were called organic, while marble and sodium chloride (from rocks) were called inorganic.

Today, organic compounds are the chemical compounds containing carbon, usually with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and the halogens. A few carbon compounds are not counted as organic: carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, cyanides, cyanates, CO, CO2 and CS2.

Carbon is essential to life; all living things are made of carbon compounds. Because carbon can link with itself and with other elements in many ways, there are more than 16 million carbon compounds, and chemists make thousands of new ones every year. More than 90% of all known compounds contain carbon.

The most useful definition is: hydrocarbons and their derivatives are called organic compounds. Compounds of carbon and hydrogen only are hydrocarbons; compounds containing other elements along with carbon and hydrogen are their derivatives. The branch of chemistry in which we study hydrocarbons and their derivatives is called organic chemistry.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds were originally defined as compounds from living sources.
  • Today organic compounds are compounds of carbon; carbonates, CO, CO2 and similar compounds are excluded.
  • More than 16 million carbon compounds are known.
  • Hydrocarbons and their derivatives are called organic compounds.
  • Organic chemistry is the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

lessons.title: Sources of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
There are two main sources of organic compounds: (i) natural sources and (ii) synthetic sources. Natural organic compounds are present in our environment and do not need to be made, while synthetic organic compounds are man-made and do not occur naturally. The natural sources are: (i) fossil remains, i.e. coal, petroleum and natural gas, (ii) plants, and (iii) animals.

Fossil Remains: Coal, Petroleum and Natural Gas

The three major fossil remains are formed by the decay of plants and animals over millions of years.

  • Coal: a black solid fuel formed from plants buried under the Earth's surface for about 300 million years at high temperature and pressure. On destructive distillation it yields coke (mostly carbon) and coal tar (a complex mixture of organic compounds). Its main types, by carbon content, are lignite (about 70% C), bituminous (about 80% C) and anthracite (92-98% C). Higher carbon content means better quality, and older coal has more carbon.
  • Petroleum: formed by bacterial decomposition of plants and animals buried deep under porous rocks by heat and pressure; its deposits are younger than coal. It is a mixture of gaseous and liquid hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation gives gasoline, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil and paraffin wax.
  • Natural gas: a mixture of low molecular mass hydrocarbons (methane, ethane, propane, butane); methane is nearly 85%. It is formed by decay of organic matter and is found in porous rocks near petroleum deposits. It is used as a fuel and as a raw material for fertilizers and petrochemicals.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds come from natural and synthetic sources.
  • Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil remains of plants and animals.
  • Anthracite has the highest carbon content (92-98%) and is the best quality coal.
  • Petroleum gives gasoline, kerosene and diesel on fractional distillation.
  • Natural gas contains nearly 85% methane.

lessons.title: Plants and Natural Products Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Plants and animals are major sources of organic compounds. Many compounds are obtained directly from them by suitable methods of isolation. Compounds obtained from living organisms are called natural products, and the study of such compounds is called natural product chemistry.

Important natural products from animals include proteins, hormones, animal fats, urea and insulin. From plants we get carbohydrates (cellulose, sugars, starches), vitamins, alcohols, acetone, acids, esters, vegetable oils, dyes, drugs, perfumes and fibres (cotton, jute).

Important Medicines Obtained from Plants

MedicineUseMedicinal Plant
CaffeineCNS stimulantTea leaves, coffee beans, kola nuts
AspirinAnalgesic, antipyreticWillow tree and bark
QuinineAntimalarial, antipyreticCinchona bark
CocaineLocal anaestheticCoca plant
MorphineAnalgesicOpium poppy

Plant medicines have long been used in the Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha systems of medicine, and by the ancient Chinese, Egyptians and Native Americans.

Key Points

  • Compounds obtained from living organisms are called natural products.
  • Animals give proteins, fats, urea, hormones and insulin.
  • Plants give carbohydrates, vitamins, oils, dyes, drugs and fibres.
  • Aspirin comes from willow bark and quinine from cinchona bark.
  • Morphine is obtained from the opium poppy.

lessons.title: Partial and Total Synthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Many useful organic compounds, including ether, glycol, drugs, rubber, fibres, dyes and plastics, are synthesized in the laboratory. Today synthesis is the most important source of organic compounds. Compounds synthesized in the laboratory are called synthetic compounds, and the study of such compounds is called synthetic chemistry.

Synthesis is of two types, and the difference between them is the starting material:

  • Partial synthesis (semi-synthesis): the desired product is obtained from an intermediate product of a reaction. For example, ethanoic acid is obtained by the oxidation of ethanal (an intermediate), instead of starting from the alkane: CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH (K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4).
  • Total synthesis: the starting material is converted into the desired product through various steps. For example, ethanoic acid can be obtained from ethane through several steps: ethane → ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
1CH3-CH3 + [O] → CH3CH2OH (ethane to ethanol, Cu catalyst)
2CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO (ethanol to ethanal, K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4)
3CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH (ethanal to ethanoic acid, K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4)

Key Points

  • Laboratory-made compounds are called synthetic compounds.
  • Synthesis is now the most important source of organic compounds.
  • Partial synthesis starts from an intermediate product.
  • Total synthesis builds the product from a simple starting material through many steps.

lessons.title: Products of Biotechnology
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology involves the use of living organisms, especially microorganisms, or other biological systems in the manufacture of products and in industrial, agricultural, medical and technological applications. The compounds obtained by means of biotechnology are called products of biotechnology.

Important products of biotechnology include ethylene glycol, ethyl alcohol, hormones, acids, vitamins, vaccines and antibiotics. Genetically engineered bacteria are used to make medicines such as insulin, and fermentation by yeast gives alcohol and bread.

Key Points

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms or biological systems to manufacture products.
  • Its products include ethyl alcohol, ethylene glycol, hormones and vitamins.
  • Vaccines and antibiotics are also products of biotechnology.
  • Biotechnology is applied in industry, agriculture and medicine.

lessons.title: Destructive Distillation of Coal
lessons.notes_html:
Coal is a most important source of organic compounds. When coal is heated strongly at 500-1000°C in the absence of air, it is converted into various useful organic and inorganic products. This process is called destructive distillation of coal. The major products are coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor and coke.

Products

  • Coal gas: a mixture of hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), carbon monoxide (CO) and other gases. It is an excellent fuel; in the past it was used for domestic cooking and lighting, and nowadays as an industrial fuel.
  • Coal tar: a liquid product containing more than 215 organic compounds. On fractional distillation it yields benzene, toluene, xylene, phenol, cresol, naphthalene and anthracene, which are used in explosives, pesticides, perfumes, synthetic fibres, naphthalene balls, dyes and paints. The residue left is called pitch, used for metalling roads and as a binder in roof making.
  • Ammoniacal liquor: ammonium compounds obtained during the distillation dissolve in water to form ammoniacal liquor. It is used to make nitrogenous fertilizers such as ammonium sulphate and ammonium superphosphate.
  • Coke: the solid product, an almost pure form of carbon. It is an excellent fuel that burns without smoke. It is used in the manufacture of steel, calcium carbide, graphite, silicon carbide and carbon disulphide, as a reducing agent, and for making fuel gases such as water gas (CO + H2) and producer gas (CO + N2).

Key Points

  • Destructive distillation is heating coal strongly (500-1000°C) without air.
  • Its four products are coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor and coke.
  • Coal tar is a source of benzene, toluene, phenol and naphthalene.
  • Ammoniacal liquor is used to make nitrogenous fertilizers.
  • Coke is almost pure carbon and burns without smoke.

lessons.title: Conversion of Coal to Petroleum
lessons.notes_html:
Coal can be converted into liquid fuels such as gasoline, kerosene and diesel by the Fischer-Tropsch process. In this process, the coal gas obtained during the destructive distillation of coal is converted into high quality, ultraclean liquid fuel products.

The Fischer-Tropsch process is a collection of chemical reactions that converts water gas into liquid hydrocarbons. The water gas is mixed with half its volume of hydrogen. The reactions occur at 150-300°C and at pressures of 1 to 10 atmospheres, in the presence of metal catalysts such as cobalt, iron, nickel and ruthenium.

Key Reactions

ReactionConditions
CO + H2 → Mixture of hydrocarbons + H2OCobalt catalyst, 150-300°C, 1-10 atm

Liquid coal can become a petroleum substitute (gasoline, kerosene or diesel) for the transportation industry. It is also used in synthetic lubricants and synthetic waxes.

Key Points

  • Coal is converted to liquid fuels by the Fischer-Tropsch process.
  • Water gas (CO + H2) is converted into liquid hydrocarbons.
  • Extra hydrogen, equal to half the volume of water gas, is mixed in.
  • Conditions: 150-300°C, 1-10 atm pressure, Co, Fe, Ni or Ru catalyst.
  • The products can replace petroleum in transport.

lessons.title: Characteristic of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Organic compounds obey all the fundamental laws of chemistry, just like inorganic compounds, and there is no clear-cut division between their properties. Even so, organic compounds are studied as a separate branch because of the following characteristic features:

  • Catenation: the self-linking property by which an atom combines with other atoms of the same element to form long chains and cyclic structures. Carbon forms long chains, loops, sheets and rings.
  • Isomerism: compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas are isomers; organic compounds show this phenomenon widely.
  • Non-polar character: most organic compounds are non-polar and are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
  • Solubility: most organic compounds do not dissolve in water but dissolve in organic solvents such as ether, benzene, alcohol and acetone.
  • Rate of reactions: organic compounds are generally covalent, so their reactions are usually slow and may need heating, thorough mixing and a catalyst.
  • Melting and boiling points: generally low, because of weak intermolecular forces; such compounds also have high vapour pressure.
  • Flammability: they are generally volatile and flammable; fuels such as natural gas, coal and oil burn to give energy as heat and light.
  • Stability: most organic compounds are thermally unstable and decompose on heating (above 500°C).

Key Points

  • Catenation and isomerism are special features of carbon compounds.
  • Organic compounds are mostly non-polar covalent compounds.
  • They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
  • Weak intermolecular forces give them low melting and boiling points.
  • Their reactions are slow and they decompose on strong heating.
  • Most organic compounds are flammable.

lessons.title: Uses of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Organic compounds play an important role in our daily life. The food we eat, the clothes we wear, the medicines we take, the paper we write on, cosmetics and soaps are all organic compounds.

UseExamples
FoodProteins, carbohydrates, fats
ClothesCotton, silk, wool, nylon, rayon
FuelsWood, coal, natural gas
Medicines and drugsPenicillin, aspirin, cocaine, morphine
Insecticides and herbicidesDDT, malathion, treflan
DyesIndigo, alizarin, malachite green
ExplosivesTrinitrotoluene (TNT), nitroglycerine
Daily life materialsSoaps, detergents, perfumes, flavours, cosmetics, plastics, rubber, resins, paints, varnishes, inks, leather, preservatives, fertilizers

Key Points

  • Food, clothes, fuels and medicines are all organic compounds.
  • Penicillin and aspirin are organic medicines.
  • DDT and malathion are organic insecticides.
  • TNT and nitroglycerine are organic explosives.
  • Soaps, plastics, paints and fertilizers are everyday organic products.

lessons.title: New Allotrope of Carbon: Bucky Balls (Fullerenes)
lessons.notes_html:
Until the mid-1980s, scientists thought that pure carbon existed in only two allotropic forms: diamond and graphite. In 1985 a new allotropic form, buckminsterfullerene, commonly called a bucky ball, was discovered by Richard Smalley, Robert Curl and Harry Kroto. The 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to them for this discovery.

Fullerenes (bucky balls) consist of molecules composed entirely of carbon atoms arranged in the form of hollow spheres, ellipsoids or tubes. Each molecule generally has both pentagonal and hexagonal faces.

  • The most common bucky ball is C60: 60 carbon atoms joined in a shape like a soccer ball, with 32 faces — 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
  • The smallest fullerene has 20 carbon atoms (C20); fullerenes up to 100 carbon atoms are commonly obtained, and the largest has more than 600 carbon atoms.
  • Fullerenes are rare in nature. Small amounts of C60, C70, C76, C82 and C84 have been found in soot and in the residue of carbon arc lamps; they are also formed by lightning discharges in the atmosphere.
  • Bucky balls are a new family of aromatic organic molecules and are soft like graphite. Doped fullerenes can conduct electricity and even act as superconductors at low temperature.

Key Points

  • Bucky ball (buckminsterfullerene) is the third allotrope of carbon, after diamond and graphite.
  • It was discovered in 1985 by Smalley, Curl and Kroto (Nobel Prize 1996).
  • C60 has 32 faces: 12 pentagonal and 20 hexagonal, like a soccer ball.
  • Fullerenes are hollow spheres, ellipsoids or tubes of carbon atoms.
  • They occur in small amounts in soot and arc-lamp residue.

lessons.title: Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Carbon forms millions of compounds, so they are divided into families on the basis of their functional groups to make their study easy. A functional group is an atom or group of atoms in a molecule that is mainly responsible for the chemical behaviour of the molecule. Double and triple bonds are also functional groups.

Compounds with the same functional group have similar chemical properties, whatever the rest of the molecule is. For example, methanol (CH3OH), ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and propanol have similar properties because all contain the -OH group. Replacing one functional group by another changes the properties: methanol (CH3OH) and methanoic acid (HCOOH) behave differently. The functional group is the reactive part of the molecule, while the hydrocarbon portion is inert. A compound with two or more functional groups is called a polyfunctional compound.

Key Points

  • A functional group decides the chemical behaviour of a molecule.
  • Compounds with the same functional group have similar chemical properties.
  • The functional group is the reactive part; the hydrocarbon part is inert.
  • Compounds with two or more functional groups are polyfunctional.
  • Examples: -OH alcohols (-ol), -COOH acids (-oic acid), -NH2 amines (-amine).

lessons.title: Homologous Series
lessons.notes_html:
A group of organic compounds in which each member differs from the next member by a methylene group (-CH2-) is called a homologous series. Its members are called homologs. For example, butane (CH3CH2CH2CH3) and pentane (CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3) are homologs. Removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane gives an alkyl group, CnH2n+1.

General Characteristics of a Homologous Series

  • All members have the same functional group and the same general formula.
  • They have similar chemical properties because of the same functional group.
  • Their physical properties differ because their molecular masses differ.
  • Successive members differ by a CH2 group, so their molecular masses differ by 14 units (CH2 = 12 + 2 = 14).
  • All members contain the same type of elements and are prepared by the same methods.

  • Members of a homologous series differ from each other by one -CH2- group.
  • Successive homologs differ in molecular mass by 14 units.
  • All members share one functional group and one general formula.
  • Chemical properties are similar; physical properties change gradually.
  • Alkanes follow the general formula CnH2n+2.

lessons.title: Preparation of Lassaigne's Solution and Detection of Nitrogen
lessons.notes_html:
All organic compounds contain carbon, and most of them (except CCl4, CS2, etc.) contain hydrogen, so these two elements are usually not tested. Oxygen is generally present, but there is no direct method for its detection. Other elements that may be present — nitrogen, sulphur, halogens and phosphorus — are detected by Lassaigne's test.

Preparation of Lassaigne's Solution (Sodium Extract)

  • Take a small, freshly cut piece of sodium metal (pea size) in a fusion tube and heat it until the sodium melts. Sodium is stored under kerosene oil and must never be touched with fingers; use forceps.
  • Add a small amount of the unknown organic compound and heat, first gently and then strongly, until the bottom of the tube becomes red hot.
  • Plunge the red-hot tube into a china dish containing about 10-15 mL of cold distilled water.
  • Crush the contents, boil and filter. The filtrate is Lassaigne's solution (sodium extract).

Fusion with sodium converts the covalently bound elements into ionic sodium salts that can be tested. The extract is divided into portions for the detection of nitrogen, sulphur and halogens.

Key Reactions

ReactionProduct
Na + C + N → NaCNSodium cyanide
Na + C + N + S → NaCNSSodium sulphocyanide
2Na + S → Na2SSodium sulphide
Na + X → NaXSodium halide

Detection of Nitrogen

Boil the sodium extract with freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution and a little sodium hydroxide. Cool the mixture, then add a few drops of ferric chloride solution and excess concentrated hydrochloric acid. A green or Prussian blue colour confirms nitrogen. Fresh FeSO4 is used because Fe2+ is easily oxidised by air to Fe3+.

ReactionNote
FeSO4 + 2NaOH → Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4Green precipitate
Fe(OH)2 + 6NaCN → Na4[Fe(CN)6] + 2NaOHSodium ferrocyanide
3Na4[Fe(CN)6] + 4FeCl3 → Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 + 12NaClFerric ferrocyanide, Prussian blue

Key Points

  • Lassaigne's test detects nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in organic compounds.
  • The compound is fused with sodium to form ionic sodium salts.
  • The filtrate of the fused mixture is called the sodium extract.
  • Prussian blue colour with FeSO4 and FeCl3 confirms nitrogen.
  • Sodium is handled with forceps and stored under kerosene oil.

lessons.title: Detection of Sulphur and Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Detection of Sulphur

Sodium nitroprusside test: add sodium nitroprusside solution to the sodium extract. A deep violet colour confirms sulphur:

Na2S + Na2[Fe(CN)5NO] → Na4[Fe(CN)5NOS] (deep violet)

Lead acetate test: add freshly prepared lead acetate solution to the extract in the presence of dilute acetic acid. A black precipitate of lead sulphide confirms sulphur:

Na2S + (CH3COO)2Pb → PbS (black) + 2CH3COONa

If sulphur is present along with nitrogen, the extract contains NaCNS, which gives a blood-red colouration of ferric sulphocyanide with FeCl3: 3NaCNS + FeCl3 → Fe(CNS)3 + 3NaCl.

Detection of Halogens

Boil the sodium extract with concentrated nitric acid for some time to expel HCN or H2S, which would otherwise give a white precipitate of silver cyanide or a black precipitate of silver sulphide with silver nitrate. Cool the mixture and add silver nitrate solution:

Precipitate with AgNO3Solubility in NH4OHHalogen Present
White (AgCl)Soluble in cold NH4OHChlorine
Light yellow (AgBr)Sparingly soluble in cold, soluble in hot concentrated NH4OHBromine
Yellow (AgI)Insoluble in NH4OHIodine

Key Reactions

ReactionNote
2Na + X2 → 2NaXFusion forms sodium halide
NaX + AgNO3 → AgX↓ + NaNO3Silver halide precipitate
AgCl + 2NH4OH → [Ag(NH3)2]Cl + 2H2OSoluble complex
AgBr + 2NH4OH → [Ag(NH3)2]Br + 2H2OSparingly soluble

Key Points

  • Deep violet colour with sodium nitroprusside confirms sulphur.
  • Black PbS precipitate with lead acetate also confirms sulphur.
  • Before the halogen test, the extract is boiled with conc. HNO3 to remove HCN and H2S.
  • White AgCl soluble in NH4OH shows chlorine; yellow AgI insoluble in NH4OH shows iodine.
  • Nitrogen and sulphur together give a blood-red colour with FeCl3.

lessons.title: Types of Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds. They are made of carbon and hydrogen only, joined by covalent bonds. Examples are methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), acetylene (C2H2) and benzene (C6H6). They are classified as aliphatic or aromatic, depending on whether a benzene ring is present or not.

Two Main Types

  • Aliphatic hydrocarbons: straight chained, branched or non-aromatic compounds. They may be linear or cyclic. Most of them are volatile and flammable.
  • Aromatic hydrocarbons: compounds that contain at least one benzene ring in their structure.

Saturated and Unsaturated Hydrocarbons

  • Saturated hydrocarbons contain carbon-carbon single bonds only. They include the alkanes and the cycloalkanes.
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond or triple bond. They include the alkenes and the alkynes.

In a straight chain, a carbon atom is never bonded to more than two other carbon atoms. In a branched chain, a carbon atom may be bonded to three or four carbon atoms at a time.

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only, joined by covalent bonds.
  • They are classified as aliphatic (no benzene ring) or aromatic (at least one benzene ring).
  • Saturated hydrocarbons have single bonds only: alkanes and cycloalkanes.
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons have at least one double or triple bond: alkenes and alkynes.
  • Most aliphatic hydrocarbons are volatile and flammable.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes are hydrocarbons that contain only single bonds. They are also called paraffins, from the Latin words parum (little) and affin (affinity): paraffins have little affinity, so they are the least reactive hydrocarbons. Petroleum and natural gas are composed of alkanes.

General Formula of Alkanes

The general formula of alkanes is CnH2n+2, where n is the number of carbon atoms.

AlkanenHydrogen atoms (2n + 2)Molecular formula
Methane12 × 1 + 2 = 4CH4
Ethane22 × 2 + 2 = 6C2H6
Propane32 × 3 + 2 = 8C3H8
Butane42 × 4 + 2 = 10C4H10

Cycloalkanes

Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which the carbon atoms are linked by single covalent bonds to form a ring. They are also called cycloparaffins. Their general formula is CnH2n: a cycloalkane has two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane, because of the ring formation.

Key Points

  • Alkanes contain single bonds only and are called paraffins (little affinity, least reactive).
  • General formula of alkanes: CnH2n+2.
  • Petroleum and natural gas are composed of alkanes.
  • Cycloalkanes are ring compounds with single bonds only; general formula CnH2n.
  • A cycloalkane has two hydrogens less than the alkane with the same number of carbons.

lessons.title: Nomenclature: Common and IUPAC Systems
lessons.notes_html:
Nomenclature is the system used for naming chemical compounds. There are two systems: the common system and the IUPAC system.

The Common System

  • In early days, compounds were named after the plants or animals from which they were obtained, or sometimes after their discoverer.
  • Methane was called marsh gas because it was found in marshy places.
  • Acetic acid got its name from the Latin word acetum, meaning vinegar.
  • Methyl alcohol was called wood spirit because it was obtained by the destructive distillation of wood.
  • Barbituric acid was supposedly named by Adolf von Baeyer after a girl called Barbara.
  • The common system follows no formal rules. It is impossible to give common names to the millions of compounds now known, and impossible to remember them all. Common names are still in wide use today.
  • Common names are useful when the IUPAC name is lengthy and complicated: for example, tartaric acid instead of 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid.

The IUPAC System

  • A commission of 34 chemists from nine countries met at Geneva (Switzerland) in 1892 and developed a system of nomenclature, called the Geneva system.
  • The group later became the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), pronounced “eye-you-pack”.
  • The IUPAC rules have been continually revised and improved since 1892.
  • The fundamental principle is that each different compound should have a different and unambiguous (clear, single-meaning) name.

Key Points

  • Nomenclature is the system of naming chemical compounds.
  • Common names come from sources or discoverers and follow no formal rules.
  • Examples: methane = marsh gas; methyl alcohol = wood spirit; acetic acid from acetum (vinegar).
  • The IUPAC system began at Geneva in 1892; its rules are still revised today.
  • IUPAC principle: every different compound gets one different, unambiguous name.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Straight Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
The first four alkanes are known by their common names: methane, ethane, propane and butane. The names of alkanes with more than four carbons are formed from a Latin or Greek prefix that shows the number of carbon atoms, plus the suffix -ane.

Parts of an IUPAC Name

  • Root: shows the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain.
  • Suffix: shows the family of the compound; for alkanes the suffix is -ane.
  • Prefix: shows the identity, position and number of substituents (side groups).

Parent Names of Alkanes

CarbonsRootAlkaneCarbonsRootAlkane
1MethMethane11UndecUndecane
2EthEthane12DodecDodecane
3PropPropane13TridecTridecane
4ButButane14TetradecTetradecane
5PentPentane15PentadecPentadecane
6HexHexane16HexadecHexadecane
7HeptHeptane17HeptadecHeptadecane
8OctOctane18OctadecOctadecane
9NonNonane19NonadecNonadecane
10DecDecane20IcosIcosane

Common Prefixes n-, iso- and neo-

  • In the common system, all isomeric alkanes have the same parent name: the three isomeric C5H12 alkanes are all pentanes. The prefixes n, iso and neo show which isomer is meant.
  • n- (normal): all carbon atoms are joined in one continuous, unbranched chain, e.g. n-pentane, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3.
  • iso-: one methyl group is bonded to the second carbon of the continuous chain, e.g. isopentane, isohexane.
  • neo-: two methyl groups are bonded to the second carbon of the continuous chain, e.g. neohexane, neoheptane.

Alkyl Groups

A group formed by the removal of one hydrogen atom from an alkane is called an alkyl group. It is represented by the symbol R (R-H → R- on removal of H). An alkyl group is named by replacing “ane” with “yl”: methane gives methyl (CH3-), ethane gives ethyl (CH3CH2-). From propane, removal of H from a primary (1°) carbon gives n-propyl (CH3CH2CH2-), and from a secondary (2°) carbon gives isopropyl.

A primary carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, a secondary carbon to two, a tertiary carbon to three and a quaternary carbon to four other carbons.

Key Points

  • Alkane name = root (number of carbons in longest chain) + suffix -ane.
  • An IUPAC name has three parts: prefix, root and suffix.
  • Common prefixes: n- = unbranched chain; iso- = one methyl on carbon 2; neo- = two methyls on carbon 2.
  • Alkyl group = alkane minus one H; named by changing -ane to -yl (methyl, ethyl).
  • Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary carbons are bonded to 1, 2, 3 and 4 other carbons.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Branched Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Branched chain alkanes are named by the following IUPAC rules.

Rules

  • Rule 1: Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms and name it as the parent (stem) name. The longest chain is not always in a straight line; sometimes it “turns a corner”.
  • Rule 2: Show the position of each substituent by the number of the carbon atom to which it is bonded, e.g. a methyl branch on carbon 4 of octane gives 4-methyloctane.
  • Rule 3: Number the longest chain from the end nearer to the substituents, so that the substituents get the lowest numbers: 3-methylhexane is correct, not 4-methylhexane.
  • Rule 4: For two or more identical substituents, use the prefixes di, tri, tetra or penta, e.g. 2,4-dimethylpentane.
  • Rule 5: If the first substituent is at the same distance from both ends, number the chain so that the second substituent gets the lower number. Always look for the first point of difference: 2,4,7-trimethyloctane is correct, not 2,5,7-trimethyloctane.
  • Rule 6: Name different substituents in alphabetical order, e.g. 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane. The prefixes di, tri, tetra, penta, sec and tert are ignored in alphabetizing, but iso and cyclo are not ignored.
  • If the same set of numbers is obtained in both directions, number from the end that gives the lower number to the substituent that comes first alphabetically.
  • Rule 7: If two or more chains of equal length can be selected, choose the chain with the greater number of substituents: 3-ethyl-2-methylheptane is correct, not 3-isopropylheptane.

The branch name and the parent name are written as a single word, with a hyphen after the number. Numbers for identical substituents are separated by commas, and a hyphen is placed between a number and a word.

Key Points

  • The parent is the longest continuous carbon chain, even if it turns a corner.
  • Number from the end nearer the substituents; use the first point of difference for ties.
  • Identical substituents take di, tri, tetra; different substituents are listed alphabetically.
  • di, tri, sec, tert are ignored in alphabetizing; iso and cyclo are counted.
  • Between equal-length chains, choose the one with more substituents.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Rules

  • Rule 1: Add the prefix cyclo- to the name of the corresponding alkane with the same number of carbons as the ring: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane. A cycloalkane is drawn as a geometric figure (triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon); each corner stands for one carbon atom and two hydrogen atoms.
  • Rule 2: For a ring with only one substituent, no position number is needed, because all positions of the ring are equivalent: methylcyclopropane, ethylcyclobutane.
  • Rule 3: For two or more substituents, number the ring so that the substituent carbons get the lowest possible numbers, and name the substituents in alphabetical order: 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane; 1,3-dimethylcyclopentane; 1-ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane; 1-ethyl-2,5-dimethylcyclohexane.
  • Rule 4: If the substituent has more carbon atoms than the ring, the substituent is taken as the parent and the ring is named as a substituent: 1-cyclopropylbutane; 2-cyclobutylpentane.

Key Points

  • Cycloalkane name = cyclo- + alkane name for the ring size.
  • One substituent on a ring needs no locant (number).
  • With two or more substituents, number for the lowest locants and list alphabetically.
  • If the side chain is longer than the ring, the chain is the parent and the ring is a substituent (cyclopropyl, cyclobutyl).

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties of Alkanes

  • The first four members (methane to butane) are colourless, odourless gases at room temperature. They are used as fuels.
  • Members with 5 to 17 carbons are colourless, odourless liquids at room temperature. They are found in gasoline, kerosene, diesel and jet fuels.
  • Members with 18 or more carbons are colourless waxy solids, used as lubricants. Vaseline is a semisolid mixture of alkanes having more than 25 carbon atoms.
  • Alkanes are mostly non-polar. They are insoluble in polar solvents like water, but soluble in solvents like benzene, ether, carbon tetrachloride and acetone.
  • Boiling points and melting points increase with the number of carbon atoms; the rise in melting point is not very regular. The boiling point increases by 20-30°C for each added methylene group (-CH2-).
  • A straight chain alkane has a higher boiling point than its branched isomer, because its larger surface area of contact gives stronger van der Waals forces: n-butane boils at -0.5°C, isobutane at -10.2°C.
  • Densities increase gradually with the number of carbons, from about 0.62 g/mL to about 0.79 g/mL. Alkanes are less dense than water (1.0 g/mL), so they float on water.
  • Viscosity increases with molecular mass.

Solid alkanes are used in the waxy coatings of fruits such as apples, plums, oranges and pears, and of vegetables such as cucumber, turnips and green tomatoes. The coating prevents loss of water (keeping firmness and juiciness), improves appearance and freshness, and slows down microbial degradation.

Physical Properties of Cycloalkanes

  • Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are gases at room temperature; cycloalkanes with five or more carbons are liquids.
  • They are soluble in non-polar solvents like benzene and ether, and insoluble in polar solvents.
  • Their melting and boiling points increase gradually with molecular mass.
  • They have low densities, like alkanes; alkanes and cycloalkanes are the least dense of all groups of organic compounds.
  • Liquid cycloalkanes are soluble in one another.
