Key Points

  • Alkanes: C1-C4 gases, C5-C17 liquids, C18 and above waxy solids; all colourless and odourless.
  • Alkanes are insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents, and less dense than water.
  • Boiling point rises 20-30°C per -CH2- group; straight chains boil higher than branched isomers.
  • Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are gases; higher cycloalkanes are liquids.
  • Melting point, boiling point and density of cycloalkanes rise gradually with molecular mass.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of Alkanes

The simplest alkane is methane, CH4. Its four hydrogen atoms are arranged around the central carbon atom as far apart from each other as possible. Methane therefore has a tetrahedral geometry, with bond angles of 109.5°. In the higher alkanes too, the four bonds about each carbon atom are still tetrahedral, and all bond angles are nearly 109.5°.

Structure of Cycloalkanes

The simplest cycloalkane is cyclopropane. The line-angle formula of a cycloalkane is drawn as a regular polygon with the same number of sides as the number of carbon atoms in the ring: a triangle for cyclopropane, a square for cyclobutane, a pentagon for cyclopentane and a hexagon for cyclohexane.

Key Points

  • Methane is tetrahedral; the H-C-H bond angle is 109.5°.
  • Every carbon in every alkane is tetrahedral, with bond angles near 109.5°.
  • Cycloalkanes are drawn as regular polygons (line-angle formulas).
  • The number of sides of the polygon equals the number of carbons in the ring.

lessons.title: Relative Stability and Reactivity of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Relative Stability

  • Alkanes are relatively stable compounds. Branched chain alkanes are more stable than straight chain alkanes: 2-methylpropane is more stable than n-butane.
  • Cycloalkanes are also stable, except cyclopropane and cyclobutane.

Why Alkanes Are Inert

  • The C-H bond is the least polar bond.
  • The C-C bond is completely non-polar.
  • There is no unshared pair of electrons.
  • There is no point of unsaturation.
  • There is no electrophilic or nucleophilic centre.

Reactivity

Alkanes contain only strong sigma bonds. The electrons in the C-H and C-C sigma bonds are shared equally between the atoms, so no atom carries a significant charge. An alkane is therefore neither an electrophile nor a nucleophile, and alkanes are the least reactive organic compounds. They do not react with acids, bases, strong oxidizing agents or other reagents at room temperature. Their most useful reactions take place under drastic conditions and are of two types: (i) substitution reactions and (ii) thermal and catalytic reactions.

Cycloalkanes behave like alkanes, except cyclopropane and cyclobutane. The reactivity of cyclopropane and cyclobutane is due to their largest ring strain.

Key Points

  • Branched alkanes are more stable than straight chain alkanes.
  • Alkanes are inert: non-polar bonds, no lone pairs, no unsaturation, no electrophilic or nucleophilic centre.
  • Alkanes do not react with acids, bases or strong oxidizers at room temperature.
  • Useful alkane reactions need drastic conditions: substitution, and thermal and catalytic reactions.
  • Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are reactive because of ring strain.

lessons.title: Radical Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
A radical (free radical) is a highly reactive species that contains an atom with an unpaired electron. It is formed by the homolysis (homolytic cleavage) of a covalent bond: A-B → A• + B•. Each atom keeps one electron of the shared pair. Free radicals are electrically neutral, but very reactive and unstable because of their incomplete octet. A radical process involves a single electron, and the movement of one electron is shown by a half-headed arrow.

In heterolytic cleavage (heterolysis), both electrons of the bond stay with one atom: A-B → A+ + :B-, or A:- + B+.

Overview of Radical Substitution

  • In a substitution reaction, an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group.
  • Alkanes react with Cl2 or Br2 to form alkyl chlorides and alkyl bromides.
  • Reactivity order of alkanes: tertiary → secondary → primary → methyl (tertiary most reactive).
  • Reactivity order of halogens: F2 → Cl2 → Br2 → I2 (F2 most reactive).
  • Chlorination gives the less stable radical; bromination gives the most stable radical.
  • The reaction proceeds by a radical chain mechanism involving radical intermediates.
  • Termination steps have a low probability, because the concentration of radical species is low, so the chances of collision between radicals are very low.

Key Points

  • A free radical has an unpaired electron and an incomplete octet; it is neutral, reactive and unstable.
  • Homolysis: each atom keeps one electron. Heterolysis: one atom takes both electrons, giving ions.
  • Alkane reactivity: tertiary, then secondary, then primary, then methyl.
  • Halogen reactivity: F2, then Cl2, then Br2, then I2.
  • Halogenation of alkanes follows a radical chain mechanism.

lessons.title: Reaction Mechanism of Free Radical Halogenation
lessons.notes_html:
The halogenation of alkanes proceeds by a free radical mechanism in three steps, shown here for the chlorination of methane.

Step 1: Initiation

The Cl-Cl bond of a chlorine molecule breaks by homolytic fission in the presence of heat or light, giving two chlorine free radicals: Cl2 →(Heat or Light) 2Cl•.

Step 2: Propagation

  • The chlorine radical abstracts (removes) a hydrogen atom from methane, forming HCl and a methyl radical: Cl• + CH3-H → HCl + •CH3.
  • The methyl radical abstracts a chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule, forming chloromethane and a new chlorine radical: •CH3 + Cl-Cl → CH3-Cl + Cl•.
  • These two steps repeat again and again, so the reaction is a chain reaction. They are called propagation steps because they propagate (carry forward) the reaction.

Step 3: Termination

Two radicals combine to form a neutral molecule, and the chain ends: •CH3 + •CH3 → CH3-CH3; Cl• + Cl• → Cl2; •CH3 + Cl• → CH3-Cl. Termination ends the reaction by decreasing the number of radicals available to propagate the chain.

Chlorination of methane also produces more highly halogenated products: CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4, together with more HCl.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
InitiationCl2 →(Heat or Light) 2Cl•
Propagation 1Cl• + CH4 → HCl + •CH3
Propagation 2•CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•
Termination•CH3 + •CH3 → C2H6; Cl• + Cl• → Cl2; •CH3 + Cl• → CH3Cl

Key Points

  • Initiation: heat or light splits Cl2 into two chlorine radicals.
  • Propagation: each step consumes one radical and produces a new one, so the chain continues.
  • Termination: two radicals combine; the supply of radicals falls and the reaction stops.
  • Further chlorination of methane gives CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Oxidation means an increase in the oxygen content, or a decrease in the hydrogen content, of a compound. The reverse process is reduction. Oxidation and reduction always take place simultaneously; such a reaction is a redox reaction.

Complete Oxidation (Combustion)

Alkanes such as natural gas, gasoline and diesel burn readily in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water vapours and energy. Burning in oxygen is called combustion. Methane, the main part of natural gas used for cooking and heating, burns as: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH = -891 kJ/mol. The heat of combustion is the heat evolved when one mole of a hydrocarbon is completely burnt to carbon dioxide and water.

Incomplete Oxidation

When the supply of oxygen or air is insufficient, alkanes burn incompletely and produce carbon monoxide, water vapours and carbon black (soot): 3CH4(g) + 4O2(g) → 2CO(g) + 6H2O(g) + C(s) + Energy.

Catalytic Oxidation

When lower alkanes are burnt in the presence of a metallic catalyst at high temperature and pressure, many useful products are formed. With a copper catalyst at 400°C and 200 atm, methane is oxidized in stages to methyl alcohol, then formaldehyde, then formic acid.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
Complete combustion of methaneCH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O (ΔH = -891 kJ/mol)
Incomplete combustion of methane3CH4 + 4O2 → 2CO + 6H2O + C
Catalytic oxidation, step 1CH4 + [O] →(Cu catalyst, 400°C, 200 atm) CH3OH
Catalytic oxidation, step 2CH3OH + [O] → HCHO + H2O
Catalytic oxidation, step 3HCHO + [O] → HCOOH

Key Points

  • Oxidation = gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is the reverse; together they form a redox reaction.
  • Complete combustion gives CO2 + H2O + energy; methane gives ΔH = -891 kJ/mol.
  • Incomplete combustion (less oxygen) gives CO + H2O + carbon black.
  • Catalytic oxidation of methane (Cu, 400°C, 200 atm) gives methanol, then formaldehyde, then formic acid.
  • Heat of combustion is measured for one mole of hydrocarbon burnt completely.

lessons.title: Alkenes and Their Nomenclature
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds. They are also called olefins, from the French word olefiant (oil forming), because the lower members react with chlorine or bromine to give oily products. Alkenes occur in small amounts in natural gas, coal gas and gasoline, and are produced in large amounts by the cracking of petroleum. Alkenes with one double bond (monoenes) have the general formula CnH2n. Ethylene is the first member of the series.

Nomenclature of Alkenes

  • Alkenes are normally named by the IUPAC system, but older common names are still used: ethene is called ethylene, and propene is called propylene.
  • The IUPAC name is formed by replacing the ending “ane” of the corresponding alkane with “ene”: CH2=CH2 is ethene; CH3CH=CH2 is propene.
  • Step 1: Select the longest chain that contains the double bond, and name it (for example, a five-carbon chain gives pentene).
  • Step 2: Number the longest chain from the end closer to the double bond. Alkenes of two or three carbons do not need numbers.
  • Step 3: Show the position of the double bond by the number of the lower-numbered carbon of the double bond: a double bond between carbons 2 and 3 gives 2-pentene (pent-2-ene).
  • Step 4: Name substituents as for alkanes, before the parent name and with their numbers. The double bond suffix must get the lowest possible number: 4-methyl-2-pentene (4-methylpent-2-ene).
  • Step 5: For two or more double bonds, replace “ene” with diene, triene or tetraene: CH2=CH-CH=CH2 is 1,3-butadiene (buta-1,3-diene).

Key Points

  • Alkenes contain at least one C=C double bond; general formula CnH2n; also called olefins.
  • Large amounts of alkenes come from the cracking of petroleum.
  • The parent chain must contain the double bond, and it is numbered from the end nearer the double bond.
  • The double bond position is shown by its lower-numbered carbon.
  • Two or three double bonds are shown by diene and triene.

lessons.title: Relative Stability of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The stability of an alkene depends on three factors.

Degree of Substitution

The stability of alkenes increases with an increase in the number of R (alkyl) groups attached to the doubly bonded carbons: CH2=CH2 → RCH=CH2 → RCH=CHR → R2C=CHR → R2C=CR2, in order of increasing stability. Ethene is the least stable and the tetra-substituted alkene is the most stable.

Stereochemistry

Trans alkenes are more stable than cis alkenes. A cis alkene has more steric hindrance, because its bulky groups lie on the same side of the double bond and crowd each other. A trans alkene has less steric hindrance, because its bulky groups lie on opposite sides. For example, trans-2-butene is more stable than cis-2-butene.

Conjugation

Conjugated alkenes are more stable than isolated alkenes: 1,3-pentadiene (conjugated) is more stable than 1,4-pentadiene (isolated).

Key Points

  • More alkyl groups on the C=C carbons means a more stable alkene.
  • Trans isomers are more stable than cis isomers (less steric hindrance).
  • Conjugated alkenes are more stable than isolated alkenes.
  • Order: CH2=CH2 is least stable; R2C=CR2 is most stable among substituted ethenes.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
In ethene, the carbon-carbon double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The doubly bonded carbons are sp2 hybridized. Each such carbon has three sp2 hybrid orbitals and one pure p-orbital.

  • The sp2 orbitals overlap with the orbitals of other atoms to form sigma bonds. A sigma bond is formed by the head-to-head overlap of hybrid orbitals.
  • The remaining pure p-orbitals overlap sideways (side-to-side) to form the pi bond.
  • All six atoms of ethene lie in the same plane; the molecule is trigonal planar.
  • The HCH and HCC bond angles are approximately 120°.
  • The C=C bond length is 134 pm and the C-H bond length is 109 pm.

Key Points

  • A C=C double bond = one sigma bond + one pi bond.
  • Double-bonded carbons are sp2 hybridized: three sp2 orbitals plus one pure p-orbital.
  • Sigma bonds form by head-to-head overlap; the pi bond by side-to-side overlap of p-orbitals.
  • Ethene is planar (trigonal planar), with angles near 120°.
  • C=C = 134 pm; C-H = 109 pm.

lessons.title: Preparation of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are generally prepared by β-elimination reactions: two atoms or groups present on adjacent (neighbouring) carbon atoms are removed, and a double bond is formed between those carbons.

Dehydration of Alcohols

  • Water is removed from adjacent carbons by heating the alcohol with a dehydrating agent. The best dehydrating reagents are conc. H2SO4, Al2O3 and P2O3, and all of them work at high temperature.
  • The -OH group is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon.
  • Ease of dehydration: tertiary (3°) alcohols dehydrate most easily, then secondary (2°), then primary (1°).
  • Primary: ethyl alcohol with conc. H2SO4 at 170-180°C gives ethene: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O.
  • Secondary: 75% H2SO4 at 100-140°C (the book's example works at 108°C).
  • Tertiary: tert-butyl alcohol with only 5% H2SO4 at 50°C gives 2-methylpropene + H2O.

Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halides

  • Hydrogen halide (HX) is removed from adjacent carbons by heating the alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH.
  • The halogen (X) is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon.
  • Example: chloroethane + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) CH2=CH2 + KCl + H2O.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
Dehydration (1° alcohol)CH3CH2OH →(Conc. H2SO4, 170-180°C) CH2=CH2 + H2O
Dehydration (3° alcohol)tert-Butyl alcohol →(5% H2SO4, 50°C) 2-methylpropene + H2O
DehydrohalogenationCH3CH2Cl + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) CH2=CH2 + KCl + H2O

Key Points

  • Alkene preparations are β-eliminations: groups leave from adjacent carbons.
  • Dehydration removes -OH from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon.
  • Ease of dehydration: 3° alcohols, then 2°, then 1°; stronger acid and higher temperature are needed for 1° alcohols.
  • Dehydrohalogenation removes HX with hot alcoholic KOH.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkenes: Hydrogenation, Hydrohalogenation, Hydration and Halogenation
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the pi bond. The pi bond is formed by the parallel overlap of p-orbitals, so its electrons lie much farther from the carbon nuclei and are less firmly bound. The pi bond is weaker than the sigma bond and breaks easily when an electrophilic reagent attacks. The most important reactions of alkenes are addition reactions, in which two molecules combine to form a single product molecule, and the double bond changes into a single bond.

Catalytic Hydrogenation

Hydrogen adds to the double bond in the presence of a catalyst (Pt, Ni or Pd) at moderate pressure (1-5 atm), giving the saturated hydrocarbon (alkane): CH2=CH2 + H2 →(Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C) CH3-CH3. The heat of hydrogenation is the heat evolved when one mole of an alkene is hydrogenated; it is about 120 kJ/mol for each double bond. The reaction is used in industry to convert vegetable oil into vegetable ghee with a nickel catalyst.

Hydrohalogenation

Hydrogen halides (HX) add to alkenes to form alkyl halides. The reaction is carried out in a solvent such as acetic acid, or by passing dry gaseous HX over the alkene: CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3-CH2Br (ethyl bromide). The reactivity order of HX is HI → HBr → HCl (in decreasing order). The mechanism has two steps: first the alkene and HBr form a carbocation and Br-; then the carbocation combines with Br- (the nucleophile) to give the alkyl bromide.

Markovnikov's rule: when an unsymmetrical molecule (polar reagent) such as HX is added to an unsymmetrical alkene like propene, the negative part of the adding molecule goes to the carbon atom that has the least number of hydrogen atoms. So propene + HBr gives 2-bromopropane.

Hydration

Water adds to alkenes in the presence of H2SO4 at 100°C to form alcohols. In step 1, ethene reacts with sulphuric acid (H-OSO3H) to form ethyl hydrogensulphate. In step 2, ethyl hydrogensulphate reacts with water (H-OH) to give ethyl alcohol, and the sulphuric acid is regenerated.

Halogenation

Chlorine and bromine add to alkenes in an inert solvent (CCl4) in the dark, giving vicinal dihalides (halogens on adjacent carbons): propene + Cl2 → 1,2-dichloropropane. The mechanism has two steps: first the alkene and X2 form a halonium ion and X-; then the halonium ion combines with X- to give the vicinal dihalide.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HydrogenationCH2=CH2 + H2 →(Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C) CH3-CH3
HydrohalogenationCH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br; propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov)
HydrationCH2=CH2 + H2O →(H2SO4, 100°C) CH3CH2OH
HalogenationPropene + Cl2 →(CCl4, dark) 1,2-dichloropropane

Key Points

  • The weak, exposed pi bond makes alkenes reactive; their main reactions are additions.
  • Hydrogenation (Ni/Pt/Pd, 1-5 atm) gives alkanes; heat of hydrogenation ≈ 120 kJ/mol per double bond.
  • HX addition follows Markovnikov's rule; HX order: HI, then HBr, then HCl.
  • Hydration with H2SO4 at 100°C gives alcohols, through ethyl hydrogensulphate.
  • Halogenation in CCl4 in the dark gives vicinal dihalides through a halonium ion.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkenes: Halohydration, Epoxidation, Ozonolysis and Polymerization
lessons.notes_html:
Halohydration

This is the addition of a hypohalous acid to an alkene. Aqueous solutions of halogens (Cl2 or Br2) react with alkenes to form halohydrins, which carry a halo group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons: propene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloro-2-propanol + HCl.

Epoxidation

This is the addition of oxygen (O2) to an alkene. Alkenes react with oxygen in the presence of a silver catalyst under high pressure and temperature to form epoxides: 2CH2=CH2 + O2 →(Ag, 300°C) 2 ethylene oxide. Propene similarly gives propylene oxide.

Ozonolysis

Ozonolysis is the reaction of ozone (O3) with an alkene, in which the C=C double bond is broken. In an inert solvent such as ether, ozone first forms an unstable molozonide, which rearranges into an ozonide. Ozonides are explosive and are not isolated. Decomposition of the ozonide with zinc and water gives an aldehyde and/or a ketone: ethylene ozonide + Zn →(H2O, 100°C) 2HCHO (formaldehyde) + ZnO. Ozonolysis is used to find the position of the double bond, because the molecule is cleaved at the double bond.

Polymerization

Polymerization is the process in which small molecules (monomers) combine to form large molecules (polymers). Ethylene polymerizes in the presence of a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to form polythene (polyethylene): n CH2=CH2 →(400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2) -[CH2-CH2]n-. Polythene is a plastic used for toys, bags, boxes, purses, carpet backing, buckets, rain coats, dustbins, shoe soles and pipes.

The reaction of ethene with bromine is very important: it is used for the detection of unsaturation in a compound.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HalohydrationPropene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloro-2-propanol + HCl
Epoxidation2CH2=CH2 + O2 →(Ag, 300°C) 2 ethylene oxide
OzonolysisEthylene ozonide + Zn →(H2O, 100°C) 2HCHO + ZnO
Polymerizationn CH2=CH2 →(400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2) polythene

Key Points

  • Halohydration gives halohydrins: -X and -OH on adjacent carbons.
  • Epoxidation with O2 and a silver catalyst gives epoxides such as ethylene oxide.
  • Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond and gives aldehydes and/or ketones; it locates the double bond.
  • Polymerization joins monomers into polymers: ethene gives polythene.
  • Bromine water reaction with ethene is the test for unsaturation.

lessons.title: Conjugation in Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The word conjugation comes from Latin and means “to link together”. It describes conjugated (pi) systems, such as double bonds, that are linked together. The focus here is on dienes, alkenes with two double bonds. Dienes are divided into three classes by the closeness of their pi bonds.

Three Classes of Dienes

  • Cumulated dienes (cumulenes or allenes): the two double bonds are adjacent (next to each other), e.g. 1,2-pentadiene, CH2=C=CH-CH2-CH3. They are relatively rare.
  • Isolated dienes (non-conjugated): the double bonds are separated by more than one single bond, e.g. 1,4-pentadiene, CH2=CH-CH2-CH=CH2.
  • Conjugated dienes: the double bonds are separated by exactly one single bond, e.g. 1,3-pentadiene, CH2=CH-CH=CH-CH3. The simplest conjugated diene is 1,3-butadiene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2.

Why Conjugation Gives Stability

Conjugation takes place whenever p-orbitals overlap on three or more adjacent atoms. In 1,3-butadiene, all four carbons are sp2 hybridized and each carries a pure p-orbital with an unpaired electron. The four p-orbitals on adjacent carbons overlap, so the pi electrons are delocalized over the whole molecule. The electron density of the pi bonds is spread over all four atoms, which lowers the energy and makes the molecule more stable. In 1,4-pentadiene, the pi bonds are separated by more than one sigma bond; they are too far apart to conjugate, so it behaves differently from 1,3-butadiene.

Key Points

  • Dienes have two double bonds: cumulated (adjacent), isolated (far apart) or conjugated (one single bond between them).
  • Conjugation needs p-orbitals overlapping on three or more adjacent atoms.
  • In 1,3-butadiene the pi electrons delocalize over all four carbons, lowering the energy.
  • Conjugated dienes are more stable than isolated dienes.

lessons.title: Isomerism and Chiral Centres
lessons.notes_html:
Compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas are called isomers, and the phenomenon is called isomerism. For example, n-butane and isobutane are isomers: both have the formula C4H10 but different structures. Isomers have different physical, chemical and biological properties. The number of isomers of a compound depends on the number of carbon atoms, and it increases as the number of carbon atoms increases: butane has 2 isomers, pentane 3, heptane 9 and decane 75.

There are two main types of isomerism: constitutional isomerism and stereoisomerism.

Chiral Centres

  • Tetrahedral atoms, usually carbon, that carry four different substituents are called chiral centres (or stereogenic centres).
  • A molecule that contains a chiral centre will be chiral; a molecule without a chiral centre will be achiral.
  • A molecule with a single chiral centre is always chiral. A molecule with two or more chiral centres may or may not be chiral.
  • Example: in the amino acid alanine, the central carbon is bonded to four different groups (CH3, H, COOH and NH2), so it is a chiral centre and the molecule is chiral.
  • The word chiral comes from the Greek word cheir, meaning “hand”. Left and right hands are chiral: each is the mirror image of the other, and the two do not superimpose (do not fit exactly on each other).

Key Points

  • Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formulas, different properties.
  • The number of isomers grows quickly with carbon number (decane has 75).
  • Two main types: constitutional isomerism and stereoisomerism.
  • A chiral centre is a tetrahedral atom (usually C) with four different substituents.
  • One chiral centre always makes a molecule chiral; two or more may or may not.

lessons.title: Optical Activity and Optical Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Optical Activity

  • Ordinary light consists of waves vibrating in many planes. When it passes through a polarizer (a Nicol prism or a Polaroid lens), it vibrates in one plane only; this is plane polarized light.
  • Compounds that can rotate the plane of polarized light clockwise or anticlockwise are called optically active compounds, and this property is called optical activity. It is measured with an instrument called a polarimeter.
  • When plane polarized light passes through a solution of a chiral (optically active) compound, the beam is rotated by a certain number of degrees.
  • Dextrorotatory: rotates the plane clockwise; shown by the prefix d or (+). Dextro is Latin for “to the right”.
  • Levorotatory: rotates the plane anticlockwise; shown by the prefix l or (-). Levo is Latin for “to the left”. Sometimes d and l are used rather than (+) and (-).

Optical Isomers

  • Optically active compounds that have the same molecular formulas and the same structural formulas, but differ in their interaction with plane polarized light, are called optical isomers; the phenomenon is optical isomerism.
  • Optical isomers have the same physical and chemical properties; they differ only in their behaviour towards plane polarized light.
  • Lactic acid has two optical isomers: (+) lactic acid is dextrorotatory and (-) lactic acid is levorotatory. The (+) form is the mirror image of the (-) form.
  • An equal mixture of the (+) and (-) forms is called a racemic mixture or racemate, written (±). In it, the two rotations cancel each other, so no rotation is observed.

Key Points

  • Plane polarized light vibrates in one plane only; optical activity is measured by a polarimeter.
  • Dextrorotatory = clockwise rotation, d or (+); levorotatory = anticlockwise, l or (-).
  • Optical isomers share formula and structure and all physical and chemical properties, except the direction of rotation.
  • (+) and (-) lactic acid are mirror images of each other.
  • An equal mixture of both forms is a racemate (±), which shows no rotation.

lessons.title: Stereoisomers and Geometrical Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Stereoisomers (configurational isomers) have the same molecular formulas and the same structural formulas, but differ in the arrangement of their atoms or groups in space. They are of two types: geometrical isomers and optical isomers.

Geometrical (Cis-Trans) Isomers

  • Geometrical isomers have the same formulas but restricted rotation in the molecule. Restricted rotation is produced by carbon-carbon double bonds, or by carbon-carbon single bonds in cyclic compounds.
  • Cis (from Latin cisoid, same side): the similar groups lie on the same side of the double bond.
  • Trans (from Latin transoid, opposite side): the similar groups lie on opposite sides of the double bond.
  • In cis-2-butene the two hydrogen atoms are on the same side; in trans-2-butene they are on opposite sides.
  • Cis and trans isomers are different compounds with different physical and chemical properties. The trans isomer is more stable, because in the cis isomer the bulky groups on the same side repel each other.
  • Cyclic compounds with two substituents on different carbons also show cis-trans isomerism: in cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane both methyl groups are on the same side of the ring; in the trans form they are on opposite sides.

Conditions for Geometrical Isomerism

  • The compound must have a double bond.
  • Two different atoms or groups must be bonded to each carbon of the double bond.

Key Points

  • Stereoisomers differ only in the arrangement of atoms in space; they are geometrical or optical.
  • Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation (double bond or ring).
  • Cis = similar groups on the same side; trans = on opposite sides.
  • Trans isomers are more stable than cis isomers.
  • Each double-bond carbon must carry two different atoms or groups.

lessons.title: Constitutional Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Constitutional isomers (structural isomers) have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas; they differ in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule. There are five types.

Chain Isomers (Skeleton Isomers)

These have different carbon chains or skeletons. The three chain isomers of pentane (C5H12) are n-pentane (a five-carbon chain), isopentane (longest chain of four carbons) and neopentane (longest chain of three carbons).

Position Isomers

These differ in the position of the same functional group. Examples: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane (C4H9Cl); 1-butene and 2-butene (C4H8), which differ in the position of the double bond.

Functional Group Isomers

These have different functional groups. Examples: ethyl alcohol, CH3CH2OH, and dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3 (both C2H6O); methyl acetate and propionic acid (both C3H6O2).

Metamers

These have the same molecular formula and the same functional group, but differ in the distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group. Diethyl ether, CH3CH2OCH2CH3, and methyl-n-propyl ether, CH3OCH2CH2CH3, are metamers; trimethylamine and ethylmethylamine are also metamers. Metamers belong to the same homologous series.

Tautomers

Tautomers are two forms of the same compound that differ in the position of protons and electrons; the phenomenon is called tautomerism. The keto and enol forms are readily interconvertible and exist in dynamic equilibrium. In ethyl acetoacetate at 25°C, the keto form is 93% and the enol form is 7%. Usually the keto form is more stable, but in some cases the enol form is more stable.

Key Points

  • Constitutional isomers differ in the arrangement of atoms: chain, position, functional group, metamers, tautomers.
  • Chain isomers: different carbon skeletons (n-pentane, isopentane, neopentane).
  • Position isomers: same group at different positions (1-butene and 2-butene).
  • Functional group isomers: different functional groups (ethanol and dimethyl ether).
  • Metamers: different carbon distribution around the same functional group.
  • Tautomers: keto and enol forms in dynamic equilibrium (ethyl acetoacetate: 93% keto, 7% enol at 25°C).

lessons.title: Alkynes and Their Nomenclature
lessons.notes_html:
Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain one or more carbon-carbon triple bonds. The simplest alkyne is ethyne, commonly called acetylene, and the common name of the alkyne family is acetylenes, after this simplest member. The general formula of alkynes is CnH2n-2, where n = 2, 3, 4, 5, ... Acetylene has the structure H-C#C-H (# shows a triple bond). Alkynes are less common in nature than alkenes, although more than 1000 different alkynes have been isolated from natural sources. They are also produced during the cracking of petroleum.

Nomenclature of Alkynes

  • Alkynes are named like alkenes: replace the ending “ane” with “yne”. CH#CH is ethyne; CH3C#CH is propyne.
  • Step 1: Select the longest chain that contains the triple bond.
  • Step 2: Number the chain from the end closer to the triple bond. Alkynes of two or three carbons do not need numbers.
  • Step 3: Show the position of the triple bond by the number of its lower-numbered carbon, e.g. 2-hexyne.
  • Step 4: Name substituents as for alkanes; the triple bond suffix must get the lowest possible number, e.g. 4-methyl-2-hexyne.
  • Step 5: For two or more triple bonds, use diyne, triyne or tetrayne: HC#C-C#CH is 1,3-butadiyne (buta-1,3-diyne).

Alkenynes

Hydrocarbons that contain both double and triple bonds are called alkenynes. If the double and triple bonds are at different positions from the two ends, number from the end closer to a double or triple bond (3-penten-1-yne; 1-penten-3-yne). If they are at the same positions from the ends, the double bond is given preference in numbering (1-penten-4-yne).

Key Points

  • Alkynes contain at least one C#C triple bond; general formula CnH2n-2.
  • Ethyne (acetylene) is the first member; the family is also called acetylenes.
  • The parent chain must contain the triple bond and is numbered from the end nearer it.
  • Two triple bonds are shown by diyne; compounds with both bond types are alkenynes.
  • In alkenynes, a tie in numbering is given to the double bond.

lessons.title: Relative Stability and Structure of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Relative Stability of Alkynes

The book relates the stability of alkynes to the smaller bond length of the triple bond. Two factors decide the stability of an alkyne.

  • Position of the triple bond: internal alkynes, in which the triple bond is at a position other than the end of the chain, are more stable than terminal alkynes, in which the triple bond is at the end. 2-Pentyne is more stable than 1-pentyne.
  • Number of substituents: branched alkynes are more stable than unbranched alkynes. 2,5-Dimethyl-3-hexyne is more stable than 3-hexyne.

Structure of Alkynes

  • In acetylene, the triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The carbon atoms are sp hybridized; each carbon has two sp hybrid orbitals and two pure p-orbitals.
  • One sp orbital of each carbon overlaps with the half-filled s orbital of a hydrogen atom, forming a C-H sigma bond. The other sp orbital overlaps with the sp orbital of the second carbon, forming the C-C sigma bond.
  • The two remaining pure p-orbitals form two pi bonds by sidewise overlapping.
  • Acetylene is a linear molecule; all bond angles are 180°.
  • The C#C bond length is 120 pm and the C-H bond length is 106 pm.

Key Points

  • Internal alkynes are more stable than terminal alkynes; branched alkynes are more stable than unbranched ones.
  • A triple bond = one sigma bond + two pi bonds; the carbons are sp hybridized.
  • Acetylene is linear, with bond angles of 180°.
  • C#C = 120 pm; C-H = 106 pm.

lessons.title: Physical Properties and Preparation of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties of Alkynes

  • The first three members are gases, the next eight members are liquids, and the higher members are solids.
  • They are colourless and odourless, except acetylene, which has a garlic-like smell.
  • They are generally non-polar compounds, soluble in non-polar solvents like ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride.
  • Their melting points, boiling points and densities increase gradually with molecular mass.

Preparation of Alkynes

Alkynes are prepared by the elimination of atoms or groups from adjacent carbon atoms.

Dehydrohalogenation of Dihalides

  • A vicinal dihalide is heated with alcoholic KOH. The reaction takes place in two steps: in the first step one HX is removed and a vinyl halide is formed; in the second step a second HX is removed and the alkyne is formed.
  • Step 1: 1,2-dibromoethane + alcoholic KOH →(Heat) vinyl bromide + KBr + H2O.
  • Step 2: vinyl bromide + alcoholic KOH →(Heat) acetylene + KBr + H2O. Removal of the second HX is difficult and needs a strong base.
  • This method is useful because vicinal dihalides are readily prepared from alkenes by the addition of halogens.

Dehalogenation of Tetrahalides

  • A vicinal tetrahalide is heated with zinc dust in ethanol. The reaction again takes place in two steps: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + Zn →(Heat) 1,2-dibromoethene + ZnBr2; then 1,2-dibromoethene + Zn →(Heat) acetylene + ZnBr2.
  • This method is not used in practice, because tetrahalides themselves are prepared by the halogenation of alkynes.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
From vicinal dihalide, step 11,2-Dibromoethane + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) vinyl bromide + KBr + H2O
From vicinal dihalide, step 2Vinyl bromide + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) acetylene + KBr + H2O
From tetrahalide1,1,2,2-Tetrabromoethane + 2Zn →(Heat) acetylene + 2ZnBr2 (in two steps)

Key Points

  • Alkynes: first three gases, next eight liquids, higher members solids; colourless and non-polar.
  • Melting point, boiling point and density rise gradually with molecular mass.
  • Dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide removes two HX in two steps; the second step needs a strong base.
  • Dehalogenation of a tetrahalide uses zinc dust in ethanol, but the method is not used in practice.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alkynes and Acidity of Terminal Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Reactivity of Alkynes

  • The triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The electron density between the carbon atoms is very high, and this draws the atoms very close to each other.
  • The electrons of the triple bond are less exposed than the electrons of a double bond.
  • Therefore alkynes are less reactive towards electrophilic reagents than alkenes.

Acidity of Terminal Alkynes

  • The triply bonded carbon atom is sp hybridized. An sp hybridized carbon is highly electronegative and strongly electron withdrawing.
  • Because of this, the hydrogen attached to a terminal triple-bonded carbon is slightly acidic (the carbon carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogen a partial positive charge).
  • This hydrogen is replaced readily by metals such as Na, Ag and Cu, forming ionic compounds (metal acetylides).

Key Points

  • High electron density in the triple bond holds its electrons close, so they are less exposed than double-bond electrons.
  • Alkynes react with electrophiles more slowly than alkenes.
  • The sp carbon of a terminal alkyne is highly electronegative, so its hydrogen is weakly acidic.
  • Terminal alkyne hydrogen is replaced by Na, Ag or Cu to form ionic acetylides.

lessons.title: Addition Reactions of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkynes undergo addition reactions like alkenes, but they add two molecules of the reagent instead of one. The reaction takes place in two steps: in the first step the triple bond changes into a double bond, and in the second step the double bond changes into a single bond.

Hydrogenation (Addition of H2)

Hydrogen adds in the presence of a finely divided metal catalyst (Ni, Pt or Pd) at or above room temperature, in two steps: HC#CH + H2 →(Ni, 250-300°C) CH2=CH2 (ethene); then CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3-CH3 (ethane).

Dissolving Metal Reduction

This is one of the most useful and oldest reduction methods. The reduction uses a solution of a strongly electropositive metal (Na, K or Zn) in an inert solvent such as liquid ammonia or THF, containing a proton source. With sodium in liquid ammonia, acetylene forms sodium acetylide: HC#CH + Na →(Liquid NH3) HC#CNa + 1/2 H2. Sodium acetylides are used to convert lower alkynes into higher alkynes: HC#CNa + CH3I → HC#C-CH3 + NaI. In these reactions the “H2” is added as 2e- and 2H+.

Hydrohalogenation (Addition of HX)

Alkynes add HX to form dihaloalkanes. The reaction follows Markovnikov's rule: the halogen adds to the carbon with the lesser number of hydrogen atoms. It takes place in two steps: propyne + HBr → 2-bromopropene; then 2-bromopropene + HBr → 2,2-dibromopropane. The reactivity order of HX is HI → HBr → HCl → HF (in decreasing order).

Hydration (Addition of H2O)

Alkynes react with water in the presence of mercuric sulphate and sulphuric acid to form unstable enols, which rearrange to carbonyl compounds. Acetylene gives an aldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones. The addition follows Markovnikov's rule: propyne + H2O →(HgSO4, H2SO4) propen-2-ol (enol), which rearranges to propanone (acetone).

Bromination (Addition of Br2)

With less bromine, alkynes form dibromides; with excess bromine they form tetrabromides: propyne + Br2 → 1,2-dibromopropene; then + Br2 → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane.

Ozonolysis (Addition of O3)

Ozone breaks the carbon-carbon triple bond. First, ozone adds across the pi bond (in CCl4) to form a molozonide, which rearranges into an ozonide. The ozonide is then hydrolysed by water to a 1,2-dicarbonyl compound and H2O2, and the dicarbonyl compound is cleaved by the H2O2 into a mixture of carboxylic acids. Ozonolysis is used to find the position of the triple bond, because the molecule is cleaved at the triple bond.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HydrogenationHC#CH + 2H2 →(Ni, 250-300°C) CH3-CH3 (through CH2=CH2)
Sodium acetylide formationHC#CH + Na →(Liquid NH3) HC#CNa + 1/2 H2
HydrohalogenationPropyne + 2HBr → 2,2-dibromopropane (Markovnikov, two steps)
HydrationPropyne + H2O →(HgSO4, H2SO4) propanone (through propen-2-ol)
BrominationPropyne + 2Br2 → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane (through 1,2-dibromopropene)

Key Points

  • Alkynes add two molecules of reagent in two steps: triple bond, then double bond, is saturated.
  • Full hydrogenation gives the alkane; the first step gives the alkene.
  • HX addition follows Markovnikov's rule twice and gives a geminal dihalide.
  • Hydration (HgSO4/H2SO4) gives an enol that rearranges: acetylene to an aldehyde, other alkynes to ketones.
  • Bromination gives dibromides or tetrabromides; ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond to carboxylic acids.

lessons.title: Benzene and Substituted Benzenes
lessons.notes_html:
Michael Faraday, an English scientist, isolated benzene from whale oil in 1825. Twenty years later, in 1845, benzene was found in coal tar by Hoffman.

Benzene is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (arene). Its formula is C6H6: it consists of a ring of six carbon atoms, with one hydrogen atom bonded to each carbon. It is represented by the Kekulé structure (a hexagon with alternating double bonds) or by a hexagon with a circle inside it. Compounds that contain a benzene ring are called aromatic compounds, because many benzene compounds had fragrant odours.

Types of Substituted Benzene Derivatives

  • Monosubstituted: one hydrogen of benzene is replaced by another atom or group.
  • Disubstituted: two hydrogens are replaced.
  • Polysubstituted: more than two hydrogens are replaced.

Key Points

  • Faraday isolated benzene from whale oil in 1825; it was found in coal tar in 1845.
  • Benzene, C6H6, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon: a six-carbon ring, one H on each carbon.
  • It is drawn as a hexagon with alternating double bonds, or with a circle inside.
  • Derivatives are mono-, di- or polysubstituted, according to how many hydrogens are replaced.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Monosubstituted and Disubstituted Benzene Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
The nomenclature of aromatic hydrocarbons is more complex than that of aliphatic hydrocarbons.

Monosubstituted Benzene Derivatives

  • They are named by placing the name of the substituent in front of the word benzene: chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, ethylbenzene.
  • Some monosubstituted derivatives have common names that are accepted by IUPAC. These names have to be memorized.
SubstituentCommon nameSubstituentCommon name
-CH3Toluene-CHOBenzaldehyde
-OHPhenol-COCH3Acetophenone
-OCH3Anisole-COC6H5Benzophenone
-NH2Aniline-CH=CH2Styrene
-COOHBenzoic acid-CNBenzonitrile
IsopropylCumene-SO3HBenzenesulphonic acid

Disubstituted Benzene Derivatives

  • A disubstituted benzene has three isomers, with substitution at the 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4- positions. They are designated by the prefixes ortho, meta and para: 1,2- is ortho (Greek: correct or straight), 1,3- is meta (Greek: between, in the middle) and 1,4- is para (Greek: beyond). They are abbreviated o-, m- and p-.
  • Relative to one substituent, a benzene ring has two ortho positions, two meta positions and one para position.
  • Positions are shown either by the ortho, meta and para descriptors or by locants (1,2- for ortho). For two identical substituents the prefix di is used. The dimethyl derivatives of benzene are called xylenes: 1,2-dimethylbenzene (o-xylene), 1,3-dimethylbenzene (m-xylene) and 1,4-dimethylbenzene (p-xylene).
  • For two different substituents, position 1 is given to the group of higher priority. The priority order is: -COOH, -CN, -CHO, -COCH3, -OH, -NH2, -OR, -R. Examples: 2-aminobenzaldehyde, 3-hydroxybenzoic acid, 4-methylanisole.
  • If there is no priority order, the substituents are named in alphabetical order, and the last-named substituent is assumed to be at position 1: 2-bromochlorobenzene, 3-fluoronitrobenzene, 4-chloroiodobenzene.
  • If one substituent is part of a common root, the compound is named as a derivative of that monosubstituted benzene: 2-bromophenol, 3-nitroaniline, 4-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid.
  • Some disubstituted derivatives are better known by common names: catechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene), resorcinol (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) and hydroquinone (1,4-dihydroxybenzene).

Key Points

  • Monosubstituted: substituent name + benzene (chlorobenzene), or an accepted common name (toluene, phenol, aniline).
  • Disubstituted positions: 1,2- = ortho (o-), 1,3- = meta (m-), 1,4- = para (p-).
  • Dimethylbenzenes are the three xylenes.
  • With two different groups, position 1 goes to the higher-priority group: -COOH has the highest priority in the book's list.
  • Without a priority order, name alphabetically with the last-named group at position 1.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Polysubstituted Benzene Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Rules

  • Identical substituents: when the ring has more than two identical substituents, use the prefix tri for three, tetra for four, penta for five and hexa for six, and assign the lowest possible numbers: 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene; 1,3,5-tribromobenzene; 1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene.
  • Different substituents: when the ring has more than two different substituents, name them in alphabetical order; the last-named substituent is assumed to be at position 1: 4-bromo-3-chloroiodobenzene; 3-bromo-5-fluoronitrobenzene; 2,4-dichloro-5-iodonitrobenzene.
  • Common roots: if the substituents are part of common roots, name the compound as a derivative of that monosubstituted benzene, and the substituent that includes the common root is placed at position 1: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol; 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene; 2,4,6-triiodophenol.
  • Some polysubstituted derivatives are better known by common names: phloroglucinol (1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene), mesitylene (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene), durene (1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene), picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) and TNT (2,4,6-trinitrotoluene).

Key Points

  • More than two identical groups: tri, tetra, penta, hexa, with the lowest locants.
  • More than two different groups: alphabetical order, last-named group at position 1.
  • With a common root (phenol, toluene), the compound is named as its derivative.
  • Picric acid = 2,4,6-trinitrophenol; TNT = 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
• Benzene is a colourless liquid with a peculiar smell.
  • It has a burning taste.
  • Its melting point is 5.5°C and its boiling point is 80.1°C.
  • It is insoluble in water.
  • It is highly inflammable and burns with a luminous and smoky flame.
  • It is miscible with alcohol and ether in all proportions.
  • Its specific gravity is 0.884 g/cm3 at 15°C.
  • It is a good solvent for many organic and inorganic substances, such as fats, resins, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.
  • Its vapours are highly toxic: on inhalation they produce loss of consciousness, and in the long run they destroy the red and white blood cells.

Key Points

  • Benzene is a colourless liquid, melting point 5.5°C, boiling point 80.1°C.
  • It is insoluble in water but miscible with alcohol and ether.
  • It burns with a luminous, smoky flame and is highly inflammable.
  • Specific gravity 0.884 g/cm3 at 15°C; a good solvent for fats, resins, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.
  • Benzene vapours are highly toxic and damage blood cells.

lessons.title: Structure of Benzene (Molecular Orbital Aspects)
lessons.notes_html:
The hexagonal planar structure of benzene is best explained by molecular orbital theory.

The Sigma Framework

  • Each carbon in benzene has three sp2 hybrid orbitals, which are half filled and are used in bond formation.
  • Two sp2 orbitals of each carbon form sigma bonds with the adjacent carbon atoms (sp2-sp2 overlapping), and the third sp2 orbital forms a sigma bond with a hydrogen atom (sp2-s overlapping).
  • All the sigma bonds lie in the same plane and all bond angles are 120°, which confirms the regular hexagonal structure of benzene.

The Pi System

  • Each carbon also has one pure p-orbital with an unpaired electron, so there are six p-orbitals in all. They stand perpendicular to the plane of the sigma bonds.
  • The six pure p-orbitals form pi-molecular orbitals. One half of this pi molecular orbital lies above the plane of the sigma bonds and the other half lies below it.
  • The six electrons of the p-orbitals cover all six carbon atoms; they are said to be delocalized.
  • Delocalization forms stronger pi bonds and a more stable molecule. It makes benzene less reactive, so benzene undergoes substitution reactions rather than addition.
  • Because of delocalization, all the bond lengths in benzene are equal. The delocalization of the six pi electrons is shown by a circle in the ring.

Key Points

  • Each benzene carbon is sp2 hybridized; the sigma framework is planar with 120° angles.
  • Six p-orbitals, one on each carbon, stand perpendicular to the ring plane.
  • They form pi-molecular orbitals above and below the plane, holding six delocalized electrons.
  • Delocalization gives equal bond lengths, extra stability and low reactivity.
  • Benzene therefore prefers substitution over addition.

lessons.title: Resonance, Resonance Energy and Stabilization
lessons.notes_html:
Resonance

  • Resonance is another term used for delocalization. The process in which two or more structures are written for a compound, differing only in the arrangement of electrons, is called resonance.
  • The different structures are called resonance structures, also known as canonical structures or contributing structures.
  • No single structure alone can explain the characteristics of such a molecule. The actual structure is a hybrid of all the resonance structures.
  • Resonance structures are hypothetical; they cannot be isolated. In writing them, we are allowed to move electrons, not atoms. Resonance is shown by a double-headed arrow (↔) between the structures.
  • For benzene, the two major contributing structures are the two Kekulé forms. Each carbon-carbon bond is single in one structure and double in the other, so the actual bond length, 139 pm, is intermediate between a carbon-carbon single bond (153 pm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (134 pm). The three alternate single and double bonds are called conjugate bonds or resonating bonds.
  • The resonance hybrid (drawn with a circle in the hexagon) is more stable than either structure, because in a single canonical form the pi-electrons are localized, while in the hybrid they are delocalized over the six atoms of the ring.

Resonance Energy and Stability of Benzene

  • The difference between the energy of the actual molecule (the resonance hybrid) and the energy of the most stable resonance structure is called resonance energy. It is also known as delocalization energy.
  • Resonance energy explains the unusual stability of benzene and its lack of reactivity towards addition. It is found from the difference between the calculated and experimental heats of hydrogenation.
  • The heat of hydrogenation of cyclohexene (one double bond) is -120 kJ/mol.
  • For 1,3-cyclohexadiene (two double bonds) the expected value is 2 × -120 = -240 kJ/mol; the observed value is -232 kJ/mol, slightly smaller because a conjugated diene is more stable than two isolated double bonds.
  • For benzene, treated as 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene (three double bonds), the expected value is 3 × -120 = -360 kJ/mol, but the observed value is only -208 kJ/mol.
  • The observed value is 152 kJ/mol less than expected. This difference is the resonance energy of benzene: benzene is resonance stabilized by 152 kJ/mol, which makes it more stable than the other unsaturated hydrocarbons.

Key Formulae

QuantityValue
Heat of hydrogenation, cyclohexene-120 kJ/mol
Expected for benzene (3 × -120)-360 kJ/mol
Observed for benzene-208 kJ/mol
Resonance energy of benzene360 - 208 = 152 kJ/mol
C-C bond length in benzene139 pm (single 153 pm, double 134 pm)

Key Points

  • Resonance structures differ only in electron arrangement; the real molecule is their hybrid.
  • Resonance is shown by a double-headed arrow; structures cannot be isolated.
  • All C-C bonds in benzene are equal at 139 pm, between single and double bond lengths.
  • Resonance energy = energy of most stable structure minus energy of the hybrid.
  • Benzene's resonance energy is 152 kJ/mol, from heats of hydrogenation.

lessons.title: Reactivity and Reactions of Benzene: Addition Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Reactivity of Benzene

Benzene is highly unsaturated and has six pi-electrons delocalized in six p-orbitals, yet it does not undergo addition reactions as readily as other unsaturated hydrocarbons such as alkenes and alkynes. In alkenes and alkynes the pi-electrons are localized and easily available for addition reactions; in benzene they are delocalized and not easily available. Benzene is therefore less reactive than alkenes and alkynes towards electrophilic addition. The most common reactions of benzene are electrophilic substitution reactions. Benzene does undergo two addition reactions.

Addition of Hydrogen (Catalytic Hydrogenation)

Benzene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst such as Pt, Pd or Ni at high temperature and pressure to produce cyclohexane: C6H6 + 3H2 →(Ni, 200°C, 25 atm) cyclohexane.

Addition of Halogens

Benzene reacts with Cl2 (or Br2) in the presence of sunlight to form benzene hexachloride, which is used as an insecticide: C6H6 + 3Cl2 →(Sunlight) C6H6Cl6. The reaction of F2 with benzene is vigorous, and the reaction of I2 with benzene is very slow. These addition reactions indicate that benzene is unsaturated and contains three double bonds.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HydrogenationC6H6 + 3H2 →(Ni, 200°C, 25 atm) cyclohexane
Chlorine additionC6H6 + 3Cl2 →(Sunlight) benzene hexachloride, C6H6Cl6

Key Points

  • Delocalized pi-electrons make benzene less reactive towards addition than alkenes and alkynes.
  • Benzene's common reactions are electrophilic substitutions, not additions.
  • Hydrogenation (Ni, 200°C, 25 atm) gives cyclohexane.
  • Chlorine adds in sunlight to give benzene hexachloride, an insecticide.
  • Addition reactions show that benzene is unsaturated, with three double bonds.

lessons.title: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
The most important reactions of benzene are electrophilic substitution reactions. In these reactions, one hydrogen atom (proton) of the benzene ring is replaced by an electrophile. They are carried out in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeX3 or AlX3, which helps in the generation of the electrophile. The electrophile is either a positive ion or the slightly positive end of a polar molecule.

General Mechanism

  • Step 1: Formation of the arenium ion. The electrophile attacks the pi-electrons of the benzene ring and forms a sigma bond with one carbon atom. This generates a positively charged intermediate (a cyclohexadienyl carbocation) called the arenium ion or sigma complex. The sigma complex is not aromatic, because the carbon that bonds to the electrophile becomes sp3 hybridized and has no p-orbital; only five carbons remain sp2 with p-orbitals, so there is no continuous system of overlapping p-orbitals. The positive charge is distributed over three carbon atoms by resonance, which makes the ion partially stable.
  • Step 2: Regeneration of catalyst and formation of product. The sigma complex is highly reactive and loses its proton from the sp3 carbon to a Lewis base. The electrons that held the proton move into the ring and restore its aromaticity. The proton is always removed from the carbon that formed the new bond with the electrophile.
  • Step 1 is the rate determining step and is relatively slow, because an aromatic compound is being converted into a much less stable non-aromatic intermediate. Step 2 is fast, because the aromaticity of the ring is restored.

The five most useful electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions are nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and Friedel-Crafts acylation.

Key Points

  • In electrophilic substitution, a ring hydrogen is replaced by an electrophile; the aromatic ring survives.
  • Lewis acid catalysts (FeX3, AlX3) generate the electrophile.
  • Step 1 forms the arenium ion (sigma complex): slow and rate determining; aromaticity is lost.
  • Step 2 removes the proton and restores aromaticity: fast.
  • The five key reactions: nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.

lessons.title: Nitration and Sulphonation of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
Nitration

  • The replacement of a hydrogen of an organic compound by a nitro group is called nitration.
  • Benzene reacts with a mixture of conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 at 50-55°C to produce nitrobenzene: C6H6 + HONO2 →(Conc. H2SO4, 50-55°C) C6H5NO2 + H2O.
  • Conc. H2SO4 acts as a catalyst and increases the rate by increasing the concentration of the electrophile, NO2+ (the nitronium ion).
  • Mechanism: the NO2+ electrophile is produced by an acid-base reaction between HNO3 and H2SO4. Step 1: nitric acid acts as a base and accepts a proton from the stronger sulphuric acid, forming protonated nitric acid. Step 2: protonated nitric acid dissociates to form the nitronium ion and water. Step 3: the electrophile attacks the benzene ring to form the arenium ion (slow). Step 4: the arenium ion loses a proton to a Lewis base, producing nitrobenzene (fast).

Sulphonation

  • The replacement of a hydrogen of an organic compound by a sulphonic acid (-SO3H) group is called sulphonation.
  • Benzene reacts with fuming sulphuric acid (H2SO4 + SO3) at room temperature to give benzenesulphonic acid: C6H6 + SO3 →(Conc. H2SO4, 25°C) C6H5SO3H.
  • Mechanism: Step 1: sulphuric acid ionizes in water to produce hydrogen sulphate and hydronium ions: H2SO4 + H2O → HSO4- + H3O+. Step 2: the electrophile (SO3) attacks the benzene ring to form the arenium ion (slow). Step 3: a Lewis base removes the proton from the arenium ion to produce the benzenesulphonate ion (fast). Step 4: the benzenesulphonate ion accepts a proton from a hydronium ion to produce benzenesulphonic acid (fast).

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation and electrophile
NitrationC6H6 + HNO3 →(Conc. H2SO4, 50-55°C) C6H5NO2 + H2O; electrophile NO2+
SulphonationC6H6 + SO3 →(Fuming H2SO4, 25°C) C6H5SO3H; electrophile SO3

Key Points

  • Nitration: conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 at 50-55°C gives nitrobenzene; electrophile is NO2+.
  • H2SO4 in nitration raises the concentration of the nitronium ion.
  • Sulphonation: fuming sulphuric acid at room temperature gives benzenesulphonic acid; electrophile is SO3.
  • Both mechanisms pass through the arenium ion: attack (slow), then loss of proton (fast).

lessons.title: Halogenation and Friedel-Crafts Alkylation of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
Halogenation

  • The replacement of a hydrogen of an organic compound by a halogen is called halogenation.
  • Benzene reacts with halogens (Cl2 or Br2) in the presence of Lewis acids such as ferric chloride or ferric bromide to produce a halobenzene: C6H6 + Cl2 →(FeCl3, 25°C) chlorobenzene + HCl; C6H6 + Br2 →(FeBr3, Heat) bromobenzene + HBr.
  • The reactions of iodine and fluorine are not synthetically useful, because iodine reacts too slowly and fluorine too fast.
  • Mechanism (chlorination): Step 1: chlorine reacts with FeCl3 to produce a Lewis acid-base complex (the electrophile); the complex has a weak, polar Cl-Cl bond and acts as a source of the chloronium ion (Cl+). Step 2: the benzene ring donates an electron pair to the terminal chlorine, forming a new carbon-chlorine sigma bond and the arenium ion, along with the base FeCl4- (slow). Step 3: the base FeCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion to form chlorobenzene and regenerate the catalyst (fast).

Friedel-Crafts Alkylation

  • Charles Friedel, a French chemist, and James Crafts, an American chemist, discovered new methods for the preparation of alkylbenzenes and acylbenzenes in 1877; these are the Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation reactions.
  • The replacement of a hydrogen of benzene by an alkyl group (-R) is called alkylation. Benzene reacts with an alkyl halide in the presence of a Lewis acid such as aluminium chloride to produce an alkylbenzene: C6H6 + R-Cl →(AlCl3) C6H5-R + HCl.
  • Mechanism: Step 1: the Lewis acid AlCl3 reacts with the alkyl chloride to produce a Lewis acid-base complex, which serves as a source of the electrophile. Step 2: the benzene ring donates an electron pair to the alkyl group, forming the arenium ion and the base AlCl4- (slow). Step 3: the base AlCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion to form the alkylbenzene and regenerate the catalyst (fast).

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
ChlorinationC6H6 + Cl2 →(FeCl3, 25°C) C6H5Cl + HCl
BrominationC6H6 + Br2 →(FeBr3, Heat) C6H5Br + HBr
Friedel-Crafts alkylationC6H6 + R-Cl →(AlCl3) C6H5-R + HCl

Key Points

  • Halogenation needs a Lewis acid (FeCl3 or FeBr3); iodine is too slow and fluorine too fast to be useful.
  • In chlorination, the FeCl3 complex supplies the Cl+ electrophile.
  • Friedel-Crafts alkylation (1877) puts an alkyl group on the ring using R-Cl and AlCl3.
  • Both mechanisms follow the same pattern: complex formation, arenium ion (slow), proton removal (fast).

lessons.title: Friedel-Crafts Acylation of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
• The replacement of a hydrogen of benzene by an acyl group (-COR) is called acylation.
  • Benzene reacts with acyl halides (also called acid halides) or with an acid anhydride, in the presence of a Lewis acid, to produce an acylbenzene: C6H6 + R-COCl →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + HCl; and C6H6 + (RCO)2O →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + R-COOH.
  • Mechanism: Step 1: the Lewis acid AlCl3 reacts with the acyl chloride to produce a Lewis acid-base complex, which serves as a source of the electrophile. Step 2: the benzene ring donates an electron pair to the carbon of the carbonyl group of the complex, forming the arenium ion and the base AlCl4- (slow). Step 3: the base AlCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion to form the acylbenzene and regenerate the catalyst (fast).

Key Reactions

ReagentEquation
Acyl chlorideC6H6 + R-COCl →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + HCl
Acid anhydrideC6H6 + (RCO)2O →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + R-COOH

Key Points

  • Acylation replaces a ring hydrogen with an acyl group (-COR).
  • Reagents: an acyl halide or an acid anhydride, with AlCl3 as Lewis acid.
  • The product is an acylbenzene (an aromatic ketone).
  • Mechanism: complex formation, arenium ion (slow), proton removal by AlCl4- (fast).

lessons.title: Substituent Effects on Benzene Ring
lessons.notes_html:
Electrophilic substitution on benzene itself gives only one product, because all the available sites of the ring are equivalent. On a ring that already has a substituent, the substituent affects the reaction in two ways: (a) it affects the reactivity of the ring, and (b) it affects the orientation of the reaction.

A) The Effect of Substituents on Reactivity

  • An activating group donates electrons to the ring. It makes the ring more electron rich, so the ring becomes more reactive towards electrophilic aromatic substitution and the reaction occurs faster. For example, in aromatic nitration the hydroxyl group (-OH) makes the ring 1000 times more reactive than benzene.
  • A deactivating group withdraws electrons from the ring. It makes the ring electron poor, so the ring becomes less reactive and the reaction occurs slower. For example, in aromatic nitration the nitro group (-NO2) makes the ring more than 10 million times less reactive than benzene.
  • The hydrogen atom is taken as the standard and is regarded as having no effect.
  • Activating groups are alkyl groups or phenyl groups, or they have an atom, especially N or O, with a lone pair of electrons attached directly to the ring. Deactivating groups are either halogens, or they have an atom with a full or partial positive charge attached to the ring.
Activating: StrongActivating: ModerateActivating: WeakDeactivating: StrongDeactivating: ModerateDeactivating: Weak
-O-, -NR2, -NH2, -OH, -OR-NHCOR, -OCOR-R, -C6H5, -CH=CR2-NO2, -NR3+, -SO3H, -CN, -CF3-COCl, -COOH, -COOR, -COR, -CHO-X (halogens)

B) The Effect of Substituents on Orientation

  • Orientation is the process of determining the position of the second incoming substituent on a monosubstituted benzene. It depends on the nature of the first substituent already present.
  • Ortho-para directing groups direct the incoming electrophile towards the ortho and para positions. They are electron releasing groups and activate primarily the ortho and para positions. All activating substituents, and the weakly deactivating halogens, are ortho-para directors. Example: nitration of toluene gives o-nitrotoluene (59%), m-nitrotoluene (4%) and p-nitrotoluene (37%), so the methyl group is ortho-para directing.
  • Meta directing groups direct the incoming electrophile towards the meta positions. They are electron withdrawing groups; they deactivate primarily the ortho and para positions, so attack occurs at the meta positions. All moderately and strongly deactivating substituents are meta directors. Example: nitration of benzoic acid at 100°C gives about 80% m-nitrobenzoic acid, 18% o-nitrobenzoic acid and 2% p-nitrobenzoic acid, so the carboxyl group is meta directing.
  • Monosubstituted benzenes that give mainly ortho and para products usually react faster than benzene; those that give mainly the meta product always react more slowly than benzene.

Key Points

  • A substituent changes both the reactivity of the ring and the position of the next substitution.
  • Activating groups donate electrons (faster reaction); deactivating groups withdraw electrons (slower reaction).
  • -OH activates strongly (1000 times benzene in nitration); -NO2 deactivates strongly (over 10 million times slower).
  • Ortho-para directors: all activators plus halogens. Meta directors: moderate and strong deactivators.
  • Toluene nitration: 59% ortho, 4% meta, 37% para. Benzoic acid nitration: 80% meta.

lessons.title: Formation of Polysubstituted Benzenes
lessons.notes_html:
The substitution pattern of electrophilic substitution reactions can be controlled by the substituent group already present on the benzene ring. An activating group such as methyl, hydroxyl or methoxy directs the electrophile to the ortho and para positions, whereas deactivating groups such as nitro, carboxyl and aldehyde (except halogens) direct the electrophile to the meta positions. If there is competition between ortho-para and meta directing groups, the ortho-para directing groups predominate.

Formation of Disubstituted Benzenes

  • The position of the second substituent depends on the nature of the first substituent bonded to the ring.
  • Example: in the nitration of anisole, the methoxy group is an electron releasing, ortho-para directing group. It sends the second substituent (the electrophile) mostly to the ortho and para positions, giving o-nitroanisole and p-nitroanisole as the major products.
  • The ortho and para products can be separated by several methods, because they have different physical properties.

Formation of Trisubstituted Benzenes

  • The position of the third substituent depends on the nature of both substituents already bonded to the ring.
  • Example 1 (both groups direct to the same positions): neither group dominates. In p-nitrotoluene, the methyl group is an ortho-para director and the nitro group is a meta director. The methyl group directs the incoming substituent to its ortho positions only (its para position is already blocked), and the nitro group directs it to the position meta to itself. Both groups direct to the same positions, and the two positions are identical, so only one product is formed: nitration gives 2,4-dinitrotoluene.
  • Example 2 (groups direct to different positions): the more powerful group predominates. In m-nitroanisole, the methoxy group is a stronger activating group than the nitro group, so substitution takes place ortho and para to the methoxy group. The isomer with the sulphonic acid group (-SO3H) between the -OCH3 and -NO2 groups is a very minor product, because of steric hindrance.

Key Points

  • Existing groups control where the next electrophile goes: activators to ortho/para, deactivators (except halogens) to meta.
  • In a competition, ortho-para directors predominate over meta directors.
  • Anisole nitration gives o- and p-nitroanisole as major products.
  • If both groups direct to the same position, one product forms (p-nitrotoluene → 2,4-dinitrotoluene).
  • If groups direct differently, the stronger group wins; crowded positions are avoided (steric hindrance).

lessons.title: Importance of Various Hydrocarbons as Fuels for the Future Energy Needs
lessons.notes_html:
Fuels are naturally occurring combustible substances that act as a source of heat energy, or as raw materials for the chemical industry. Hydrocarbons (compounds of hydrogen and carbon) are mainly used as fuels. Fuels include hydrocarbons from methane up to higher hydrocarbons containing seventeen carbon atoms. Important hydrocarbon fuels are LPG, natural gas, gasoline, kerosene oil and diesel. Higher hydrocarbons with more than seventeen carbon atoms are present in heavy oil fractions; they can be cracked to get gasoline and other hydrocarbons that can be used as fuel in various sectors. Energy is obtained from fuels through the combustion (burning) process.

Uses of Hydrocarbons as Fuels

  • LPG (liquefied petroleum gas): a refined petroleum gas, used as a camping and domestic fuel.
  • Natural gas: a fossil fuel that exists in a gaseous state and is composed mainly of methane (CH4). It is used as a fuel in industries, electric power stations and homes.
  • CNG (compressed natural gas): natural gas under pressure. It can be used as a cheaper, greener and more efficient alternative to the traditional petrol and diesel fuels for vehicles.
  • Gasoline: used as a fuel for cars, motorbikes, trucks, boats and other transport vehicles.
  • Kerosene oil: widely used to power the jet engines of aeroplanes and some rocket engines. It is used to fuel lamps and lanterns because it has a low explosion hazard and burns relatively cleanly, and it is also used in stoves for cooking.
  • Diesel: used as a fuel for trucks, buses, tractors, tanks and central heating systems, and in diesel engine generators to generate electricity.
  • Coal: not a hydrocarbon; it is made up almost entirely of carbon. It is mainly used in power generation, and also as a household fuel for cooking and heating.
  • Fuel oil: derived from crude petroleum, either as a distillate or as a residue at the oil refinery. It is the most widely used liquid fuel for power generation and ships. Fuel oil has more than sixteen carbon atoms.
  • Paraffin wax: an alkane with approximately 25 carbon atoms, used as a fuel for candles.

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons from methane to C17 compounds are the main fuels; heavier fractions are cracked into fuel-range hydrocarbons.
  • Natural gas is mainly methane; CNG is its compressed form for vehicles.
  • Gasoline runs road vehicles; kerosene runs jet engines; diesel runs trucks, buses and generators.
  • Coal is not a hydrocarbon: it is almost entirely carbon.
  • Paraffin wax (about C25) is the candle fuel.

lessons.title: Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are organic compounds containing a halogen atom covalently bonded to one of the saturated carbon atoms of an alkyl group. They are also called haloalkanes.

Classification

Alkyl halides are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to the nature of the carbon atom to which the halogen is attached.

  • Primary (1°) alkyl halide: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon atom, e.g. R-CH2-X.
  • Secondary (2°) alkyl halide: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to two other carbon atoms.
  • Tertiary (3°) alkyl halide: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to three other carbon atoms.

The general formula of alkyl halides is CnH2n+1X, where X may be fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br) or iodine (I).

Key Points

  • Alkyl halides have a halogen atom covalently bonded to a saturated carbon of an alkyl group.
  • They are also known as haloalkanes.
  • They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon bearing the halogen.
  • Their general formula is CnH2n+1X, where X = F, Cl, Br or I.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are named by two systems: the common system and the IUPAC system.

Common System

The names consist of two words. The first word is the name of the alkyl group and the second word is fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide. Examples: CH3Cl = methyl chloride, CHCl3 = chloroform, CH2Cl2 = methylene chloride, CCl4 = carbon tetrachloride, (CH3)3CBr = tert-butyl bromide, (CH3)2CHCl = isopropyl chloride.

IUPAC System

In this system alkyl halides are named as haloalkanes and the names consist of one word only.

  • Select the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the halogen atom.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer to the halogen atom.
  • Name the halogen as a prefix: fluoro, chloro, bromo or iodo.
  • Show the position of the halogen by a number before its name.
  • If different substituents are present, name them in alphabetical order.

Examples: chloromethane, fluoroethane, 1-iodopropane, 2-chloropropane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, tetrachloromethane, 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, 2,4-dibromopentane, 3-bromo-5-chloro-2-methylhexane.

Key Points

  • Common names have two words: alkyl group name + fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide.
  • IUPAC names are one-word haloalkane names.
  • The longest chain containing the halogen is selected and numbered from the end nearer the halogen.
  • Halogens are named fluoro, chloro, bromo and iodo as prefixes, with position numbers.
  • Different substituents are listed in alphabetical order.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
• The lower members of the series (CH3Cl, CH3Br, CH3F and CH3CH2Cl) are gases at room temperature. Alkyl halides up to C18 are colourless liquids, and beyond C18 they are colourless solids.
  • Alkyl halides are practically insoluble in water, because they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. They are, however, soluble in organic solvents.
  • For a given halogen, the boiling point increases with the increase in the size and mass of the alkyl group.
  • For a given alkyl group, the boiling points follow the order RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
  • For a given halogen, the density decreases with the increase in the size and mass of the alkyl group.

Key Points

  • Lower alkyl halides are gases; members up to C18 are liquids; higher members are solids.
  • They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
  • Boiling point rises with the size and mass of the alkyl group.
  • For the same alkyl group, boiling points follow RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
  • Density falls as the alkyl group becomes larger and heavier.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
The structure of alkyl halides can be explained by taking methyl chloride as an example. The carbon atom of an alkyl halide is sp3 hybridized.

  • The carbon-halogen sigma bond is formed by the overlap of an sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon with the half-filled p-orbital of the halogen atom.
  • The carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds are formed by the overlap of sp3 hybrid orbitals of carbon with the s-orbitals of hydrogen atoms.
  • The H-C-H and H-C-X bond angles are approximately 109.5°.
  • The molecule therefore has a tetrahedral shape around carbon.

Key Points

  • The carbon atom in an alkyl halide is sp3 hybridized.
  • The C-X sigma bond forms from an sp3 orbital of carbon and a p-orbital of the halogen.
  • Bond angles are about 109.5°, so the shape around carbon is tetrahedral.

lessons.title: Preparation of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
From Alcohols and Hydrogen Halides

Alcohols react with hydrogen halides in the presence of anhydrous ZnCl2, which acts as a dehydrating agent: CH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O (with ZnCl2). The reactivity of the hydrogen halides is in the order HI > HBr > HCl, and the reactivity of alcohols is 3° > 2° > 1°.

From Alcohols and Other Halogenating Agents (SOCl2, PX3)

Alkyl halides are prepared by heating alcohols with thionyl chloride (SOCl2) in the presence of pyridine: CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl. This is the best method for preparing alkyl halides, because both by-products (SO2 and HCl) are gases and can be removed easily. Alcohols also react with phosphorus halides (PX3): 3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3.

Radical Halogenation of Alkanes

Alkanes react with halogens in diffused sunlight or UV light: CH3CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + HCl (UV light). This is not a good method, because halogen derivatives containing two or more halogen atoms are also formed along with the alkyl halide.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
Alcohol + HXCH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O (ZnCl2)
Alcohol + SOCl2CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl (pyridine)
Alcohol + PCl33CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3
Alkane + halogenCH3CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + HCl (UV light)

Key Points

  • Alcohols react with HX in the presence of anhydrous ZnCl2 to give alkyl halides.
  • Reactivity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl; reactivity of alcohols: 3° > 2° > 1°.
  • The SOCl2 method is the best, because SO2 and HCl are gases and escape easily.
  • Phosphorus halides (PX3) also convert alcohols into alkyl halides.
  • Radical halogenation of alkanes is a poor method because polyhalogen products are also formed.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are very reactive compounds. The extent of their reactivity depends on two factors: (i) the bond polarity of the carbon-halogen bond, and (ii) the bond energy of the carbon-halogen bond.

Bond Polarity of the Carbon-Halogen Bond

The halogen atom is more electronegative than carbon, so the alkyl halide molecule is polarized: carbon carries a partial positive charge and the halogen a partial negative charge. The greater the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) between carbon and the halogen, the greater is the polarity of the C-X bond. Greater polarity means greater bond strength and lesser reactivity of RX.

HalomethaneElectronegativity of halogenEN difference (C and X)Dipole moment (Debye)

Bond Energy of the Carbon-Halogen Bond

Bond energy is the measure of bond strength. The greater the bond energy, the greater is the bond strength and the lesser is the reactivity of the C-X bond.

BondBond energy (kJ/mol)
C-F467
C-Cl346
C-Br290
C-I228

From the bond energies, the order of reactivity of alkyl halides is: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

Key Points

  • Reactivity of alkyl halides depends on C-X bond polarity and C-X bond energy.
  • The C-X bond is polarized because the halogen is more electronegative than carbon.
  • Bond energies fall in the order C-F (467) > C-Cl (346) > C-Br (290) > C-I (228) kJ/mol.
  • The weakest bond (C-I) breaks most easily, so reactivity is RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

lessons.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
