The reactions in which an electron-rich nucleophile replaces another nucleophile (the leaving group) to form a new molecule are called nucleophilic substitution reactions, or SN reactions: Nu- + R-C-X → R-C-Nu + X-.

  • In these reactions the nucleophile is always a Lewis base. It may be neutral or negatively charged.
  • The substrate is frequently an alkyl halide, and the leaving group is a halide ion.
  • The partial positive carbon atom of the alkyl halide acts as an electrophile and accepts a pair of electrons from the attacking nucleophile. In this way a new bond is formed between the nucleophile and the carbon of the alkyl halide.
  • SN reactions take place by two mechanisms: SN1 and SN2.

Key Points

  • In an SN reaction a nucleophile replaces a leaving group on carbon.
  • The nucleophile is a Lewis base and may be neutral or negatively charged.
  • The substrate is usually an alkyl halide and the leaving group is a halide ion.
  • The partially positive carbon is the electrophile that accepts the electron pair.
  • SN reactions occur by the SN1 or the SN2 mechanism.

lessons.title: Important Concepts: Carbocations, Nucleophiles and Leaving Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Carbocations and Their Stability

Carbocations are very reactive, unstable, electron-deficient species. Anything that donates electron density to the electron-deficient centre helps to stabilize them. Alkyl groups are weak electron-donating groups, so they stabilize a nearby carbocation. More substituted carbocations are therefore more stable: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl (the methyl carbocation is the least stable).

Nucleophile and Base

Both nucleophiles and Lewis bases are electron-pair donor species. A base is a species that donates an electron pair to hydrogen (a proton), while a nucleophile donates an electron pair to an atom other than hydrogen, particularly a carbon atom. For example, the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile in a substitution reaction (it donates electrons to carbon) but as a base in an elimination reaction (it donates electrons to hydrogen).

Reactivity classNucleophileRelative reactivity
Very good nucleophileI-, HS-> 10^5
Good nucleophileBr-, HO-, RO-, CN-10^4
Fair nucleophileNH3, Cl-, F-10^3
Weak nucleophileH2O, ROH10^0
Very weak nucleophileRCOOH10^-2

Substrate and Leaving Group

The substrate is the carbon-containing compound on which substitution takes place: it is the reactant to which the nucleophile becomes bonded and from which the leaving group departs. The leaving group is the species that departs from the substrate and takes a pair of electrons with it. The best leaving groups are those that become the most stable ions after they depart; they are weakly basic. Halide ions are weak bases, so they are good leaving groups. Poor leaving groups are strongly basic, e.g. hydroxide and amide ions.

ClassLeaving group
Good leaving groupsI-, Br-, Cl-, H2O
Moderate leaving groupsHS-, CN-, NH3
Poor leaving groupsF-, HO-, RO-
Very poor leaving groupsNH2-, H-, R-

Key Points

  • Carbocations are reactive, unstable and electron deficient.
  • Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl.
  • A base donates its electron pair to a proton; a nucleophile donates its pair to carbon.
  • I- and HS- are very good nucleophiles; RCOOH is a very weak nucleophile.
  • The substrate is the molecule attacked; the leaving group departs with the bonding electron pair.
  • Good leaving groups are weak bases; strongly basic groups leave poorly.

lessons.title: SN1 Mechanism
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation SN1, S stands for substitution, N for nucleophilic and 1 for unimolecular: only one molecule is involved in the rate-determining step. In this mechanism, the breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group is fully completed before bond making with the nucleophile starts. The reaction of a tertiary alkyl halide occurs in two steps.

Step 1 (Slow, Rate-Determining)

The tert-alkyl halide ionizes in a polar solvent to produce a planar carbocation and the leaving group: R3C-X → R3C+ + X-. The tertiary carbocation is stable because of its three electron-donating alkyl groups. This step involves the breakage of a covalent bond, so it is slow and rate-determining.

Step 2 (Fast)

The nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation to produce the tert-alkyl product. This step is fast because it is a combination of a cation and an anion.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [R3CX], so Rate = k[R3CX]. The rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate (tert-alkyl halide), not on the concentration of the nucleophile. Doubling the concentration of the tert-alkyl halide doubles the rate; changing the nucleophile concentration has no effect. The reaction is first order overall.

Stereochemical Evidence

The positively charged carbon of the carbocation is sp2 hybridized, with an empty p-orbital having one lobe on each side of the plane. The nucleophile can attack from either side of the plane, so some product has retained configuration and some has inverted configuration.

Key Points

  • SN1 is a two-step, unimolecular mechanism typical of tertiary alkyl halides.
  • Step 1 is the slow ionization to a planar carbocation; it is the rate-determining step.
  • Step 2 is the fast attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation.
  • Rate = k[R3CX]: first order, independent of nucleophile concentration.
  • Attack from either side gives products with retained and inverted configurations.

lessons.title: SN2 Mechanism
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation SN2, S stands for substitution, N for nucleophilic and 2 for bimolecular: two molecules (the alkyl halide and the nucleophile) are involved in the rate-determining step. The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group and the formation of the bond between the nucleophile and the electrophile occur simultaneously. The reaction of a primary alkyl halide occurs in one step.

The Transition State

In the transition state, the bond to the nucleophile is partially formed and the bond to the leaving group (halide) is partially broken. The transition state has a very short-lived existence. This single step is the slow, rate-determining step.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [RH2CX][Nu-], so Rate = k[RH2CX][Nu-]. The rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the nucleophile. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate; doubling both quadruples it. The reaction is first order in each reactant and second order overall.

Stereochemical Evidence

In a primary alkyl halide the electrophilic carbon carries one alkyl group and two small hydrogen atoms, so there is no steric hindrance. The nucleophile attacks from the back side of the leaving group, because the leaving group blocks the front side. The product therefore has an inverted configuration compared with the reactant alkyl halide. (Keep in mind: methyl and primary alkyl halides undergo SN2 only; tertiary alkyl halides undergo SN1 only; secondary alkyl halides can undergo both, depending on the solvent and the alkyl groups.)

Comparison of SN1 and SN2 Mechanisms

SN1SN2
Two-step mechanismOne-step mechanism
Unimolecular, first-order kineticsBimolecular, second-order kinetics
Proceeds through a carbocationProceeds through a transition state
Rate depends on [RX] only: Rate ∝ [RX]Rate depends on [RX] and [Nu-]: Rate ∝ [RX][Nu-]
Reactivity order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl; methyl and primary halides fail to reactReactivity order: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3°; tertiary halides fail to react
Products have both retained and inverted configurationsProduct has the inverted configuration
Favoured by polar solventsFavoured by non-polar solvents
Favoured by weaker nucleophilesFavoured by stronger nucleophiles

Key Points

  • SN2 is a one-step, bimolecular mechanism typical of primary alkyl halides.
  • Bond breaking and bond making happen at the same time, through a transition state.
  • Rate = k[RX][Nu-]: second order overall.
  • The nucleophile attacks from the back side, so the product is inverted.
  • Complete inversion in a substitution shows the mechanism is SN2, not SN1.

lessons.title: 1,2-Elimination Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
In addition to SN reactions, alkyl halides also undergo elimination reactions. An elimination reaction is a type of organic reaction in which two substituents are removed from two adjacent saturated carbon atoms of a substrate molecule.

When an alkyl halide undergoes elimination, the halogen atom is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen is removed from the β-carbon. As a result, a double bond is formed between the α-carbon and the β-carbon, and the product is an alkene. The removal of a proton (hydrogen ion) and a halide ion is called dehydrohalogenation.

The most common bases used in elimination reactions are HO-, RO- and H2N-. There are two important mechanisms for elimination reactions: E1 and E2, just like the SN reactions.

Key Points

  • Elimination removes two substituents from two adjacent saturated carbons.
  • The halogen leaves from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon.
  • A double bond forms between the α- and β-carbons, giving an alkene.
  • Removal of H+ and halide ion together is called dehydrohalogenation.
  • Common bases are HO-, RO- and H2N-; the mechanisms are E1 and E2.

lessons.title: E1 Mechanism (Unimolecular Elimination)
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation E1, E stands for elimination and 1 for unimolecular: only one molecule is involved in the rate-determining step. The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group is fully completed before any reaction occurs with the base to lose a hydrogen. The reaction of a tert-alkyl halide with a base occurs in two steps.

Step 1 (Slow, Rate-Determining)

The tert-butyl halide ionizes in a polar solvent to produce a planar carbocation and the leaving group. The bond breaks between the halogen atom and the α-carbon atom. This step involves the breakage of a covalent bond, so it is slow and rate-determining.

Step 2 (Fast)

The base (HO-) removes a proton from one of the β-carbons, and a new π-bond is formed between the α- and β-carbons, giving the alkene.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [(CH3)3CX], so Rate = k[(CH3)3CX]. The rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate (tert-butyl halide) and not on the concentration of the base. The reaction is first order overall.

Key Points

  • E1 is a two-step, unimolecular elimination through a carbocation.
  • Step 1 is the slow ionization of the tert-alkyl halide; it is rate-determining.
  • Step 2 is the fast removal of a β-proton by the base, forming the π-bond.
  • Rate = k[(CH3)3CX]: first order, independent of base concentration.

lessons.title: E2 Mechanism (Bimolecular Elimination)
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation E2, E stands for elimination and 2 for bimolecular: both the alkyl halide and the base are involved in the rate-determining step. The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group and the reaction with the base to lose a proton (hydrogen) occur simultaneously. The reaction of a primary alkyl halide with a base occurs in one step.

The Transition State

In the transition state, the bond of the base to one of the β-hydrogens and the bond between the α- and β-carbon atoms are partially formed, while the bond of the β-hydrogen to carbon and the bond between the α-carbon and the leaving group are partially broken. This is the slow, rate-determining step. The product is an alkene, e.g. ethene from a primary halide.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [RH2CX][OH-], so Rate = k[RH2CX][OH-]. The rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the base. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate; doubling both quadruples it. The reaction is second order. (Keep in mind: primary alkyl halides undergo E2 reactions only; secondary and tertiary alkyl halides undergo both E1 and E2 reactions.)

Key Points

  • E2 is a one-step, bimolecular elimination.
  • Proton removal and leaving-group departure happen at the same time.
  • The reaction passes through a single transition state.
  • Rate = k[RX][OH-]: second order overall.
  • Primary halides follow E2 only; secondary and tertiary halides can follow E1 and E2.

lessons.title: Substitution versus Elimination
lessons.notes_html:
All nucleophiles are possible bases and all bases are possible nucleophiles, because the reactive part of both is an unshared electron pair. Elimination reactions therefore occur simultaneously with substitution reactions: there is always a competition between them, and the reaction of a nucleophile (base) with an alkyl halide produces a mixture of elimination (alkene) and substitution products.

If the nucleophile attacks the α-carbon, substitution occurs. If it attacks a β-hydrogen, elimination occurs. The ratio of products depends on the relative rates of the two reactions, which are affected by these factors:

  • Nature of solvent: polar solvents favour substitution, while non-polar solvents favour elimination. In an aqueous medium (more polar), substitution is the main reaction and elimination is a side reaction; in an alcoholic medium (less polar), elimination is the main reaction and substitution is a side reaction.
  • Nature of base: strong bases favour elimination reactions.
  • Effect of temperature: an increase in temperature favours elimination over substitution.
  • Nature of substrate: crowding within the substrate favours elimination over substitution.
  • Nature of alkyl halide: primary alkyl halides favour mainly substitution; tertiary alkyl halides favour mainly elimination; secondary alkyl halides favour both.

Alkyl Halides as Precursors

A compound that participates in a chemical reaction and produces another compound is called a precursor. Alkyl halides act as precursors and produce many other organic chemicals in the laboratory, such as thiols, Grignard reagents and dialkyl disulphides.

  • R-X + KOH + H2S → R-SH + H2O + KX (thiols).
  • R-X + Mg → R-Mg-X in pure diethyl ether, in the absence of moisture, CO2 or O2 (Grignard reagents).
  • R-X + thiourea, with triethylamine (Et3N) in CCl4 at 50°C for about 12 hours → R-S-S-R (dialkyl disulphides), which are used to make other chemicals.

Key Points

  • Substitution and elimination always compete; a mixture of products is formed.
  • Attack at the α-carbon gives substitution; attack at a β-hydrogen gives elimination.
  • Polar (aqueous) solvents favour substitution; less polar (alcoholic) media favour elimination.
  • Strong bases, high temperature and a crowded substrate favour elimination.
  • Primary halides favour substitution; tertiary halides favour elimination.
  • Alkyl halides are precursors for thiols, Grignard reagents and dialkyl disulphides.

lessons.title: Organometallic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Compounds that have a metal-carbon bond are called organometallic compounds. For example, alkyl magnesium halides (RMgX) are organometallic compounds because they have metal-carbon bonds.

Alkyl magnesium halides are also known as Grignard reagents. They are named after the French chemist Victor Grignard, who discovered them in 1900 and received the Nobel Prize in 1912. Grignard reagents are used in the preparation of alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids. Their general formula is RMgX, where R is an alkyl or aryl group and X is chlorine, bromine or iodine.

Key Points

  • Organometallic compounds contain a direct metal-carbon bond.
  • Alkyl magnesium halides, RMgX, are called Grignard reagents.
  • They are named after Victor Grignard (discovered 1900; Nobel Prize 1912).
  • They are used to prepare alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.
  • In RMgX, R is an alkyl or aryl group and X is Cl, Br or I.

lessons.title: Preparation of Grignard Reagents
lessons.notes_html:
Grignard reagents are prepared in the laboratory by the reaction of an alkyl or aryl halide with magnesium metal in the presence of pure diethyl ether, in the absence of moisture, CO2 or O2.

Key Reactions

ReactantsProduct
R-X + Mg (ether)RMgX (Grignard reagent)
CH3-Cl + Mg (ether)CH3-MgCl (methylmagnesium chloride)

Key Points

  • An alkyl or aryl halide reacts with magnesium metal to form a Grignard reagent.
  • The reaction is carried out in pure diethyl ether.
  • Moisture, CO2 and O2 must be absent, because the reagent reacts with them.
  • General equation: R-X + Mg → RMgX.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Grignard Reagents
lessons.notes_html:
Grignard reagents are highly reactive compounds because of the highly polar carbon-magnesium bond. Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so carbon has a partial negative charge (δ-) and magnesium a partial positive charge (δ+): R(δ-)-Mg(δ+)-X.

The partial negative charge on carbon makes the alkyl group highly reactive towards electrophiles, and the reagent acts as a source of a nucleophile (the carbon is nucleophilic, not electrophilic).

  • For the same alkyl group, the order of reactivity of halides towards magnesium is: RI > RBr > RCl. Alkyl iodide is more reactive than alkyl bromide, which is more reactive than alkyl chloride.
  • For a given halogen, the order of reactivity of alkyl groups is: CH3X > C2H5X > C3H7X. Methyl halide is more reactive than ethyl halide, which is more reactive than propyl halide.

Key Points

  • The C-Mg bond is highly polar: carbon is δ- and magnesium is δ+.
  • The negatively charged carbon attacks electrophiles; the reagent is a source of nucleophile.
  • Halide reactivity towards Mg: RI > RBr > RCl.
  • Alkyl group reactivity: CH3X > C2H5X > C3H7X.

lessons.title: Reactions of Grignard Reagents with Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Grignard reagents react with organic and inorganic compounds to form a variety of valuable compounds. Their reactions with carbonyl compounds first give an addition product, which on acid hydrolysis gives an alcohol. These reactions can be used to increase the length of the carbon chain.

  • With formaldehyde: the addition product on acid hydrolysis forms a primary alcohol. Example: HCHO + CH3MgCl → addition product → (H2O/H+) CH3CH2OH, ethyl alcohol, a 1° alcohol.
  • With other aldehydes: the addition products on acid hydrolysis form secondary alcohols. Example: CH3CHO + CH3MgCl → addition product → (H2O/H+) isopropyl alcohol, a 2° alcohol.
  • With ketones: the addition products on acid hydrolysis form tertiary alcohols. Example: CH3COCH3 (acetone) + CH3MgCl → addition product → (H2O/H+) tert-butyl alcohol, a 3° alcohol.

Key Reactions

Carbonyl compoundProduct after hydrolysis
Formaldehyde (HCHO)Primary (1°) alcohol
Other aldehydes (RCHO)Secondary (2°) alcohol
Ketones (RCOR)Tertiary (3°) alcohol

Key Points

  • Grignard reagents add to the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones.
  • Acid hydrolysis of the addition product gives an alcohol.
  • Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol; other aldehydes give secondary alcohols; ketones give tertiary alcohols.
  • These reactions increase the length of the carbon chain.

lessons.title: Reactions of Grignard Reagents with Esters
lessons.notes_html:
The reaction of a Grignard reagent with an ester takes place in two steps.

Step 1

Ethyl formate reacts with the Grignard reagent to produce an unstable intermediate, which expels an alkoxide ion to produce an aldehyde. Example: ethyl formate + CH3MgCl → unstable intermediate → CH3CHO (acetaldehyde).

Step 2

The acetaldehyde reacts with a second molecule of the Grignard reagent to produce an unstable intermediate, which on acid hydrolysis forms a secondary alcohol: CH3CHO + CH3MgCl → intermediate → (H2O/H+) isopropyl alcohol, a 2° alcohol.

Keep in mind: esters other than ethyl formate react in the same way with an excess of Grignard reagent to form tertiary alcohols.

Key Points

  • Ethyl formate reacts with a Grignard reagent in two steps.
  • Step 1 gives an aldehyde through an unstable intermediate.
  • Step 2 adds a second Grignard molecule; hydrolysis gives a secondary alcohol.
  • Other esters with excess Grignard reagent give tertiary alcohols.

lessons.title: Reactions of Grignard Reagents with Carbon Dioxide
lessons.notes_html:
A Grignard reagent reacts with CO2 to produce an unstable intermediate, which on acid hydrolysis forms a carboxylic acid. Example: CH3MgCl + CO2 → unstable intermediate → (H2O/H+) CH3COOH, acetic acid. The product acid has one carbon more than the alkyl group of the reagent.

Organometallic Compounds in Medicines

Organometallic compounds play an important role in medicines, mainly in cancer therapy. Salvarsan, the first important organometallic medicine, was discovered in 1908 and used as an anti-syphilis drug. Cisplatin is a chemotherapy drug, highly effective in treating several cancers such as ovarian and testicular cancers. Carboplatin is used to treat ovarian cancer. Thimerosal (trade name merthiolate) is used as a preservative in vaccines, some cosmetics and eye drops, and as a disinfectant in pharmaceuticals. Merbromin (mercurochrome) is a weak antiseptic for minor cuts, bedsores and abrasions. Ferroquine is a next-generation drug with good antimalarial activity, and vanadoceneacetylacetonate (VDacac) shows anti-HIV properties.

Haemoglobin and Chlorophyll

Haemoglobin and chlorophyll are both pigments found in organisms, and both have a metallic element at the centre of the molecule. They differ in important ways: chlorophyll has magnesium at its centre, while haemoglobin has iron. Chlorophyll is found in the chloroplast of plant cells and gives the green colour to leaves, seaweed, algae and vegetables; it absorbs light energy from the sun and changes it into chemical energy by photosynthesis, so it is called the blood of plants. Haemoglobin is found in the blood of all vertebrates and some invertebrates; it gives the red colour to the blood (in RBCs) and transports oxygen from the lungs to various parts of the body.

Key Points

  • Grignard reagent + CO2, followed by acid hydrolysis, gives a carboxylic acid.
  • Example: CH3MgCl + CO2 → CH3COOH (acetic acid) after hydrolysis.
  • Organometallic compounds are used in medicines, e.g. salvarsan, cisplatin and carboplatin.
  • Chlorophyll has magnesium at its centre; haemoglobin has iron.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis; haemoglobin transports oxygen.

lessons.title: Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

Classification

  • Primary amine: one alkyl group is bonded to the nitrogen atom, R-NH2.
  • Secondary amine: two alkyl groups are bonded to the nitrogen atom, R2NH.
  • Tertiary amine: three alkyl groups are bonded to the nitrogen atom, R3N.

Amines are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the number of alkyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom.

Key Points

  • Amines are derivatives of ammonia with one or more H atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
  • Primary amines have one alkyl group on nitrogen.
  • Secondary amines have two alkyl groups on nitrogen.
  • Tertiary amines have three alkyl groups on nitrogen.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Common Names

Common names are obtained by adding the suffix amine to the name of the alkyl or aryl group; the whole name is written as one word. If there are two or more identical alkyl or aryl groups, the prefix di- or tri- is used. If there are two or more different groups, their names are arranged in alphabetical order. Examples: methylamine, ethylamine, ethylmethylamine, ethyldimethylamine, trimethylamine. In the common system, most primary amines are named as alkylamines.

IUPAC Names: Primary Amines

Primary amines with more complex groups are named as alkanamines.

  • Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms containing the amino group.
  • Replace the ending -e of the parent alkane by the suffix amine.
  • Number the parent chain from the end nearer to the amino group.
  • When another functional group is present, the amino group is generally listed as a substituent (amino-).

Examples: methanamine, ethanamine, 2-propanamine, 3-amino-2-butanol, 2-methyl-2-butanamine, 2,3-dimethyl-2-pentanamine.

IUPAC Names: Secondary and Tertiary Amines

  • They are named as derivatives of primary amines.
  • The longest chain bonded to the nitrogen atom is taken as the parent chain; the remaining alkyl groups are named as substituents.
  • The locant N is used to show substituents bonded to the nitrogen atom.
  • If the same alkyl group appears more than once, the prefix di or tri is used; different groups are named individually in alphabetical order.
  • Secondary amines are named as N-alkylalkanamines; tertiary amines as N,N-dialkylalkanamines (same groups) or N-alkyl-N-alkylalkanamines (different groups).

Examples: N-methylethanamine, N-ethylethanamine, N,N-dimethylmethanamine, N-ethyl-N-methyl-2-propanamine.

Key Points

  • Common names: alkyl group name + amine, written as one word.
  • IUPAC primary amines are alkanamines: longest chain with -NH2, -e replaced by -amine.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer the amino group.
  • Substituents on nitrogen are shown by the locant N.
  • Secondary amines are N-alkylalkanamines; tertiary amines are N,N-dialkylalkanamines.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Physical State

Lower amines are gases. Higher amines with three or more carbon atoms are liquids, and still higher ones are solids.

Odour

Methylamine and ethylamine have an ammoniacal smell, but higher amines have a fishy smell.

Boiling Points

Amines are polar compounds; their polarity is due to the nitrogen atom. Primary and secondary amines form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. The hydrogen bonds in alcohols are much stronger than in amines, because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen. Amines therefore have higher boiling points than the corresponding hydrocarbons, but lower boiling points than the corresponding alcohols or carboxylic acids. Tertiary amines do not form hydrogen bonds with each other, so their boiling points are similar to those of the corresponding alkanes.

Solubility

Lower amines are soluble in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl group (the hydrophobic part) increases, and higher members are predominantly insoluble in water. Amines are more soluble in water than the corresponding alcohols and ethers, which may be due to the increased basicity of the amines.

NameMolar mass (g/mol)Boiling point (°C)Solubility at 25°C in water
Methylamine31.16Miscible
Ethylamine45.0817Miscible
Propylamine59.1148Miscible
Butylamine73.4178Miscible
Dimethylamine45.087Miscible
Diethylamine73.1456Miscible
Trimethylamine59.113Miscible
Triethylamine101.1989Slightly soluble

Key Points

  • Lower amines are gases, C3 and higher members are liquids, and the highest are solids.
  • Lower amines smell ammoniacal; higher amines smell fishy.
  • Primary and secondary amines hydrogen-bond with each other; tertiary amines do not.
  • Amines boil higher than hydrocarbons but lower than alcohols and carboxylic acids.
  • Lower amines are miscible with water; solubility falls as the alkyl group grows.

lessons.title: Structure of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
The nitrogen atom in amines is sp3 hybridized. Nitrogen has five electrons in its valence shell: three unpaired electrons and one lone pair of electrons. The three unpaired electrons form sigma bonds with hydrogen atoms or with carbon atoms of alkyl groups.

According to VSEPR theory, a molecule with three bond pairs and one lone pair has a trigonal pyramidal shape. Hence the structure of amines is trigonal pyramidal. The C-N-C angle in amines is less than 109.5°; the angles in amines are approximately 108°.

Key Points

  • The nitrogen atom of an amine is sp3 hybridized.
  • Nitrogen forms three sigma bonds and carries one lone pair.
  • With three bond pairs and one lone pair, the shape is trigonal pyramidal.
  • The C-N-C bond angle is about 108°, less than the tetrahedral 109.5°.

lessons.title: Basicity of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are basic in nature because of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. Alkanamines are more basic than ammonia because of the electron-releasing alkyl groups: the alkyl groups concentrate the electron density on nitrogen and make the lone pair more easily available for sharing with acids. The expected order of basicity is therefore 3° alkylamines > 2° alkylamines > 1° alkylamines.

The methylamines follow this expected order in the gas phase. In aqueous solution, however, they do not follow the expected trend, and the order changes to: (CH3)2NH (pKb = 3.29) > CH3NH2 (pKb = 3.36) > (CH3)3N (pKb = 4.28). The larger the value of pKb, the smaller is the tendency to accept a proton from water. Basic strength in aqueous solution depends not only on the electron-releasing effect of the alkyl groups, but also on the steric effect and the hydration effect: due to the high steric effect, a 3° alkylamine cannot easily donate its electron pair to a proton.

Key Points

  • Amines are basic because nitrogen carries a lone pair of electrons.
  • Alkyl groups release electrons, so alkanamines are more basic than ammonia.
  • Expected (gas phase) order: 3° > 2° > 1° alkylamines.
  • In water the order is (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N, by their pKb values 3.29, 3.36 and 4.28.
  • A larger pKb means a weaker base (less tendency to accept a proton).
  • Steric and hydration effects also control basic strength in aqueous solution.

lessons.title: Alkylation of Ammonia by Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
An alkyl halide reacts with an aqueous or alcoholic solution of ammonia in a sealed tube on heating to produce primary, secondary and tertiary amines. This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction. The process of cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond by an ammonia molecule is known as ammonolysis.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
1NH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI
2CH3NH2 + CH3I → (CH3)2NH + HI
3(CH3)2NH + CH3I → (CH3)3N + HI
4(CH3)3N + CH3I → [(CH3)4N]+ I- (quaternary ammonium salt)

The primary amine is the major product when ammonia is present in excess. Conversely, the tertiary amine is the major product when the alkyl halide is present in excess. The resulting ammonium salt, on treatment with a base, regenerates the amine: [(CH3)4N]+I- + NaOH → (CH3)3N + NaI + CH3OH.

Key Points

  • Alkyl halides react with ammonia (aqueous or alcoholic, sealed tube, heating) to give amines.
  • This cleavage of the C-X bond by ammonia is called ammonolysis; it is an SN2 reaction.
  • The reaction continues stepwise: 1° amine → 2° amine → 3° amine → quaternary ammonium salt.
  • Excess ammonia makes the primary amine the major product.
  • Excess alkyl halide makes the tertiary amine the major product.

lessons.title: Reduction of Nitrogen Containing Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are obtained by the reduction of nitrogen-containing functional groups such as nitriles, nitro compounds and amides.

Reduction of Nitriles

Nitriles are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4 or by catalytic hydrogenation: CH3CN + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 (LiAlH4); CH3CN + 2H2 → CH3CH2NH2 (Ni). This method is used for increasing the length of the carbon chain.

Reduction of Nitro Compounds

Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4, or Zn/HCl, or H2/Ni, or H2/Pt: CH3NO2 + 6[H] → CH3NH2 + 2H2O (LiAlH4); CH3NO2 + 3H2 → CH3NH2 + 2H2O (Pt).

Reduction of Amides

Amides are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4: CH3CONH2 (acetamide) + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 + H2O (LiAlH4).

Key Reactions

Starting materialReagentProduct
CH3CN (nitrile)LiAlH4 or H2/NiCH3CH2NH2
CH3NO2 (nitro compound)LiAlH4 or H2/PtCH3NH2
CH3CONH2 (amide)LiAlH4CH3CH2NH2

Key Points

  • Reduction of nitriles, nitro compounds and amides gives primary amines.
  • Nitriles are reduced by LiAlH4 or catalytic hydrogenation; the chain grows by one carbon.
  • Nitro compounds are reduced by LiAlH4, Zn/HCl, H2/Ni or H2/Pt.
  • Amides are reduced by LiAlH4.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines can act both as bases and as nucleophiles. Their main reactions are due to the presence of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. These electrons attack the electron-deficient centres (positive or slightly positive parts) of other molecules.

Important Reactions of Amines as Nucleophiles

  • Amines are alkylated by alkyl halides through nucleophilic substitution, forming a mixture of products (higher amines and quaternary salts).
  • Amines react with acid halides (or acid anhydrides) through nucleophilic acyl substitution to form substituted amides.
  • Amines react with aldehydes and ketones to form carbinolamines, which dehydrate to imines.
  • Acting as bases, amines react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts.

Key Points

  • The lone pair on nitrogen makes amines both bases and nucleophiles.
  • Amines attack electron-deficient centres of other molecules.
  • With alkyl halides they are alkylated by nucleophilic substitution.
  • With acid halides they form substituted amides by nucleophilic acyl substitution.
  • With nitrous acid they form diazonium salts.

lessons.title: Alkylation of Amines by Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Amines react with primary alkyl halides to form alkylated ammonium halides. The alkylation proceeds step by step: each product amine reacts further with more alkyl halide.

Key Reactions

StepReactionProduct type
1CH3NH2 + CH3CH2Br → CH3-NH-CH2CH3 + HBr2° amine
2CH3-NH-CH2CH3 + CH3CH2Br → CH3-N(CH2CH3)2 + HBr3° amine
3CH3-N(CH2CH3)2 + CH3CH2Br → [CH3-N(CH2CH3)3]+ Br-Quaternary salt

Key Points

  • Amines are alkylated by primary alkyl halides in a stepwise manner.
  • A primary amine gives a secondary amine, then a tertiary amine.
  • Further alkylation of a tertiary amine gives a quaternary ammonium salt.
  • Because the reaction does not stop at one stage, a mixture of products is obtained.

lessons.title: Reaction of Amines with Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes react with primary amines to form a carbinolamine, which dehydrates to produce an aldimine (a Schiff's base). Example: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3CHO → carbinolamine → (heat) CH3CH2-N=CH-CH3 + H2O.

Ketones react with primary amines in the same way: they form a carbinolamine, which dehydrates to produce a ketimine (a Schiff's base). Example: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3COCH3 → carbinolamine → (heat) CH3CH2-N=C(CH3)2 + H2O.

Key Points

  • Primary amines add to aldehydes and ketones to form carbinolamines.
  • The carbinolamine loses water (dehydrates) on heating.
  • Aldehydes give aldimines; ketones give ketimines.
  • Aldimines and ketimines are called Schiff's bases.

lessons.title: Preparation of Amides
lessons.notes_html:
Amines attack the carbonyl group of an acid chloride and form amides (nucleophilic acyl substitution). A base such as NaOH or pyridine is used to neutralize the HCl produced.

Key Reactions

ReactionProduct
CH3CH2NH2 + CH3COCl (NaOH)CH3CO-NH-CH2CH3 (N-ethylethanamide) + HCl
NaOH + HClNaCl + H2O (the base neutralizes the acid)

Key Points

  • Amines react with acid chlorides to form substituted amides.
  • The reaction is a nucleophilic acyl substitution at the carbonyl carbon.
  • HCl is formed as a by-product.
  • NaOH or pyridine is added to neutralize the HCl.

lessons.title: Preparation of Diazonium Salts
lessons.notes_html:
Amines react with nitrous acid to produce diazonium salts: R-NH2 + HNO2 + HCl → [R-N≡N]+Cl- + 2H2O.

The diazonium salts are highly unstable. They decompose spontaneously by losing nitrogen to give carbocations: [R-N≡N]+Cl- → R+ + Cl- + N2. The carbocations then change into mixtures of products:

  • Alkenes (by loss of H+).
  • Alcohols (by reaction with H2O, with H+ formed).
  • Alkyl halides (by reaction with Cl-).

Key Points

  • Primary amines react with nitrous acid (HNO2 + HCl) to form diazonium salts.
  • Diazonium salts are highly unstable.
  • They decompose spontaneously, losing N2 to give carbocations.
  • The carbocations give mixtures of alkenes, alcohols and alkyl halides.

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols, phenols and ethers are hydrocarbon derivatives whose functional groups contain one oxygen atom in two single bonds. They all contain the hydroxyl group (—OH) or an oxygen atom like the oxygen of water, so they are also called the oxygen family of organic compounds.

Their structures are derived from the structure of water (H—O—H). If one hydrogen of water is replaced by an alkyl group, an alcohol (R—O—H) is formed. If it is replaced by a phenyl group, a phenol (C6H5—O—H) is formed. If both hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, an ether (R—O—R) is formed.

Alcohols and phenols both have a hydroxyl (—OH) group, but alcohols are the hydroxyl derivatives of alkanes, while phenols are the hydroxyl derivatives of benzene. These compounds occur widely in nature and have many pharmaceutical, biological and industrial applications.

Key Points

  • Alcohols, phenols and ethers form the oxygen family of organic compounds.
  • All three are derived from water: alcohol = R—O—H, phenol = C6H5—O—H, ether = R—O—R.
  • Alcohols are hydroxyl derivatives of alkanes.
  • Phenols are hydroxyl derivatives of benzene.
  • They are widely used in medicines, biology and industry.

lessons.title: Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are the compounds in which a hydroxyl (—OH) group is bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Their general formula is R—OH.

Classification of Alcohols

Alcohols are classified in two ways.

1. By the number of hydroxyl groups:

  • Monohydric alcohols have only one —OH group, e.g. ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol.
  • Polyhydric alcohols have two or more —OH groups, e.g. glycol (two —OH groups) and glycerol (three —OH groups).

2. By the type of carbon bearing the —OH group (for monohydric alcohols):

  • Primary (1°) alcohol: the —OH group is on a carbon attached to only one other carbon.
  • Secondary (2°) alcohol: the —OH group is on a carbon attached to two other carbons.
  • Tertiary (3°) alcohol: the —OH group is on a carbon attached to three other carbons.

Key Points

  • In alcohols, the —OH group is bonded to a saturated carbon atom.
  • Monohydric alcohols have one —OH group; polyhydric alcohols have two or more.
  • Glycol and glycerol are polyhydric alcohols.
  • Monohydric alcohols are primary, secondary or tertiary according to the carbon bearing the —OH group.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are named by two systems: the common system and the IUPAC system.

Common System

The name of the alkyl group is written first, followed by the word alcohol, e.g. methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol, n-propyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol and tert-butyl alcohol. Common names are generally used for simple alcohols with one to four carbon atoms.

IUPAC System

In the IUPAC system, alcohols are called alkanols. The rules are:

  • Select the longest carbon chain containing the —OH group.
  • Drop the ending -e of the alkane name and add the suffix -ol.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer to the —OH group. The —OH group gets precedence over alkyl groups, halogens and double or triple bonds.
  • Show the position of the —OH group and of all other substituents by numbers.
  • For two, three or four —OH groups, use the suffixes -diol, -triol and -tetraol.
  • In compounds containing a carbonyl group (aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and their derivatives), the —OH group is only a side group and is named as hydroxy with its position number.

Examples: methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol, 3-methyl-1-butanol, 2,4-pentanediol, 4-penten-2-ol, 3-hydroxybutanal.

Isomerism in Alcohols

  • Functional isomerism: alcohols with two or more carbon atoms are functional isomers of ethers, e.g. ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether (both C2H6O).
  • Position isomerism: alcohols with three or more carbon atoms show position isomerism, e.g. 1-propanol and 2-propanol.

Key Points

  • Common name = alkyl group + alcohol.
  • IUPAC name = alkanol: longest chain with —OH, -e replaced by -ol.
  • Number the chain so that the —OH group gets the lowest number.
  • Diols, triols and tetraols have two, three and four —OH groups.
  • Alcohols are functional isomers of ethers and also show position isomerism.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
• Lower alcohols are colourless liquids; higher alcohols are colourless waxy solids.
  • They have a characteristic alcoholic smell and a burning taste.
  • They are volatile in nature and inflammable.
  • Their boiling points are higher than those of the corresponding alkanes, ethers and haloalkanes.
  • Alcohols with up to four carbon atoms are readily soluble in water. From five carbon atoms onwards, they are insoluble in water.
  • Water solubility is due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding with water. Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl group increases, and increases with branching of the chain.
  • Alcohols are lighter than water. The density of methanol is 0.792 g/mL and that of ethanol is 0.789 g/mL at 20°C, while the density of water is 0.998 g/mL at 20°C.

Key Points

  • Lower alcohols are colourless liquids with an alcoholic smell and burning taste.
  • Hydrogen bonding gives alcohols high boiling points and water solubility.
  • Alcohols up to C4 dissolve readily in water; C5 and above do not.
  • Solubility falls as the alkyl group grows and rises with branching.
  • Alcohols are less dense than water.

lessons.title: Structure of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
In alcohols, the oxygen atom is sp3 hybridized. It has four sp3 hybrid orbitals. Two of them form sigma (σ) bonds, one with carbon and one with hydrogen. The other two orbitals contain the lone pairs of electrons of oxygen.

Because of the lone pairs, the molecule has a bent shape around oxygen. In methanol, the C—O—H bond angle is 108.9°. The C—O bond length is 142 pm and the O—H bond length is 96 pm.

Key Points

  • The oxygen of an alcohol is sp3 hybridized.
  • Oxygen forms two sigma bonds (to C and to H) and carries two lone pairs.
  • The C—O—H angle in methanol is 108.9°.
  • C—O bond length is 142 pm and O—H bond length is 96 pm.

lessons.title: Acidity of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are acidic in nature because of the polar O—H bond. The greater the polarity of the —OH group, the greater is the acidity of the alcohol.

Alkyl groups are electron-releasing. They push electrons towards oxygen, decrease the polarity of the O—H bond and make the alcohol a weaker acid. More alkyl groups on the alpha carbon means lower acidity, so the order of acidity is:

Primary alcohol > secondary alcohol > tertiary alcohol

For example, tert-butyl alcohol is a weaker acid than methyl alcohol or ethyl alcohol.

Compared with water, methanol is more acidic than water, ethanol is almost as acidic as water, and alcohols with more than two carbon atoms are slightly weaker acids than water. Overall, alcohols are only weak acids.

Key Points

  • Alcohols are acidic because the O—H bond is polar.
  • Greater polarity of the O—H bond means greater acidity.
  • Electron-releasing alkyl groups decrease acidity.
  • Acidity order: primary > secondary > tertiary.
  • Methanol is more acidic than water; higher alcohols are weaker acids than water.

lessons.title: Preparations of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Hydration of Alkenes

Alkenes react with cold concentrated H2SO4 and then give alcohols on hydrolysis. The addition follows Markovnikov's rule.

Hydrolysis of Alkyl Halides

Alkyl halides are hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH or KOH to give alcohols.

CH3CH2Br + KOH → CH3CH2OH + KBr

Reaction of Grignard Reagents with Aldehydes and Ketones

Grignard reagents (RMgX) add to aldehydes and ketones. The addition product gives an alcohol on protonation with aqueous acid.

  • Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, e.g. HCHO + CH3MgCl → (addition product) → CH3CH2OH (ethyl alcohol).
  • Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols, e.g. acetaldehyde + CH3MgCl gives isopropyl alcohol.
  • Ketones give tertiary alcohols, e.g. acetone + CH3MgCl gives tert-butyl alcohol.

Reduction of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols by NaBH4 or LiAlH4. Aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols. NaBH4 is commonly used in polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol.

Reaction of Grignard Reagents with Esters

  • Formate esters first give aldehydes, which react with another molecule of Grignard reagent to give secondary alcohols.
  • Other esters first give ketones, which react further with Grignard reagent to give tertiary alcohols.

Reduction of Carboxylic Acids and Esters

Carboxylic acids and esters are reduced to alcohols by LiAlH4, a strong reducing agent, e.g. acetic acid gives ethyl alcohol, and methyl acetate gives ethyl alcohol and methyl alcohol.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
Hydrolysis of alkyl halidesCH3CH2Br + KOH → CH3CH2OH + KBr
Grignard + formaldehydeHCHO + CH3MgCl → CH3CH2OH (1° alcohol)
Reduction of acidsCH3COOH + 4[H] (LiAlH4) → CH3CH2OH + H2O

Key Points

  • Alkenes give alcohols by acid-catalysed hydration (Markovnikov addition).
  • Aqueous KOH or NaOH hydrolyzes alkyl halides to alcohols.
  • Grignard reagents give 1° alcohols from formaldehyde, 2° from other aldehydes and 3° from ketones.
  • NaBH4 or LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes to 1° alcohols and ketones to 2° alcohols.
  • Formate esters give 2° alcohols and other esters give 3° alcohols with Grignard reagents.
  • LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are reactive compounds. They can act both as electrophiles and as nucleophiles, because:

  • Both the C—O and O—H bonds are polar, as oxygen is an electronegative element.
  • Oxygen is an electron-rich centre because it has two lone pairs of electrons.

Alcohols react with polar or ionic reagents in two ways:

  • When a nucleophile attacks the alcohol, the C—O bond breaks.
  • When an electrophile attacks the alcohol, the O—H bond breaks.

The reactivity order for breaking of the C—O bond is: tertiary > secondary > primary > CH3OH.

The reactivity order for breaking of the O—H bond is the reverse: CH3OH > primary > secondary > tertiary.

Key Points

  • Alcohols act as both electrophiles and nucleophiles.
  • Nucleophilic attack breaks the C—O bond; electrophilic attack breaks the O—H bond.
  • C—O bond breaking is easiest for tertiary alcohols.
  • O—H bond breaking is easiest for methanol.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Reaction with Halogen Acids

Alcohols react with halogen acids to form alkyl halides:

R—OH + HX → R—X + H2O

Ethyl alcohol reacts with HCl in the presence of ZnCl2 catalyst to give ethyl chloride. HBr and HI react without a catalyst. The mixture of HCl and ZnCl2 is used in the Lucas test, which differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols. The reactivity order of the halogen acids is HI > HBr > HCl.

Reaction with Thionyl Chloride and Phosphorus Trihalides

Alcohols react with SOCl2 in the presence of pyridine to give alkyl chlorides:

R—OH + SOCl2 → R—Cl + SO2 + HCl

With phosphorus trihalides, three molecules of alcohol react:

3R—OH + PX3 → 3R—X + H3PO3

Key Reactions

ReagentProduct
HXAlkyl halide + H2O
SOCl2 / pyridineAlkyl chloride + SO2 + HCl
PX3Alkyl halide + H3PO3

Key Points

  • Halogen acids convert alcohols into alkyl halides.
  • HCl needs a ZnCl2 catalyst; HBr and HI do not.
  • The HCl + ZnCl2 mixture is the Lucas reagent, used to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
  • Reactivity of halogen acids: HI > HBr > HCl.
  • SOCl2 and PX3 also replace the —OH group by halogen.

lessons.title: Dehydration of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Dehydration is the removal of a water molecule from two adjacent carbon atoms of an alcohol. It is carried out with an acid catalyst such as concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4. The —OH group leaves from the alpha carbon and a hydrogen leaves from the beta carbon.

The product depends on the type of alcohol, the temperature and the concentration of the acid. The ease of dehydration follows the order of carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary.

  • Primary alcohols are the most difficult to dehydrate and need high temperature and strong acid. Ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at 170–180°C gives ethylene (ethene). With excess ethanol at 140°C, diethyl ether is formed instead.
  • Secondary alcohols dehydrate at lower temperatures (100–140°C). 2-Butanol with 75% H2SO4 at 100°C gives 2-butene.
  • Tertiary alcohols dehydrate very easily, slightly above room temperature (25–80°C). 2-Methyl-2-propanol with 5% H2SO4 at 50°C gives 2-methylpropene.

Key Reactions

AlcoholConditionsProduct
Ethanol (1°)Conc. H2SO4, 170–180°CEthene
Ethanol (excess)Conc. H2SO4, 140°CDiethyl ether
2-Butanol (2°)75% H2SO4, 100°C2-Butene
2-Methyl-2-propanol (3°)5% H2SO4, 50°C2-Methylpropene

Key Points

  • Dehydration removes —OH from the alpha carbon and H from the beta carbon.
  • Acid catalysts used are concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4.
  • Ease of dehydration: tertiary > secondary > primary.
  • Ethanol gives ethene at 170–180°C but diethyl ether at 140°C.
  • Tertiary alcohols dehydrate under very mild conditions.

lessons.title: Preparation of Esters
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 to form esters. This reaction is called esterification:

R—COOH + R—OH ⇌ R—COOR + H2O

For example, acetic acid reacts with ethyl alcohol to give ethyl acetate and water:

CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O

The reaction is reversible. Concentrated H2SO4 removes the water formed, so almost all the reactants are converted into the ester.

Key Points

  • Esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form an ester.
  • Concentrated H2SO4 is used as catalyst and dehydrating agent.
  • The reaction is reversible.
  • Removing water shifts the reaction towards the ester.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
The addition of oxygen to a compound is called oxidation. Alcohols are oxidized by K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4. The product depends on the type of alcohol and the reaction conditions, so oxidation is used to differentiate primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

  • Methyl alcohol is oxidized first to formaldehyde and then to formic acid.
  • Primary alcohols are oxidized first to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids, e.g. ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetic acid. The oxidation can be stopped at the aldehyde stage by removing the aldehyde from the oxidizing medium as it forms.
  • Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones. Ketones are not oxidized further easily, because that needs breaking of a C—C bond. Under drastic conditions they give carboxylic acids, e.g. acetone gives acetic acid, carbon dioxide and water.
  • Tertiary alcohols are not oxidized under acidic conditions, because the carbon bearing the —OH group is attached to three other carbons and cannot form a C=O double bond.

Cleavage of 1,2-Diols (Glycols)

Vicinal diols (glycols) are cleaved into two carbonyl compounds by periodic acid (HIO4) or lead tetraacetate. The products are aldehydes or ketones, depending on the glycol.

Ethylene glycol + HIO4 → 2HCHO (formaldehyde) + HIO3 + H2O

1,2-Propanediol + HIO4 → CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) + HCHO (formaldehyde) + HIO3 + H2O

Key Points

  • K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4 is the common oxidizing agent for alcohols.
  • Primary alcohols give aldehydes, then carboxylic acids.
  • Secondary alcohols give ketones.
  • Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under acidic conditions.
  • Oxidation behaviour distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
  • HIO4 or lead tetraacetate cleaves 1,2-diols into two carbonyl compounds.

lessons.title: The Sulphur Analogous (Thiols, RSH)
lessons.notes_html:
Thiols are the sulphur analogues of alcohols. They are also called thioalcohols. They contain the mercapto group (—SH) instead of the hydroxyl group (—OH).

Thiols form strong complexes with mercuric oxide, i.e. they capture mercury:

2CH3CH2SH + HgO → (CH3CH2S)2Hg + H2O

Because of this mercury-capturing property, thiols are also called mercaptans.

Nomenclature of Thiols

  • Common system: name the alkyl group and add the word mercaptan, e.g. methyl mercaptan, ethyl mercaptan, phenyl mercaptan.
  • IUPAC system: name the alkane and add the suffix -thiol (alkanethiol), e.g. methanethiol, ethanethiol, 2-propanethiol, benzenethiol.
  • Select the longest chain containing the —SH group and number it from the end nearer to —SH. The —SH group has priority over alkyl groups and halogens.
  • If a higher-priority group is present, —SH is named as the prefix sulfanyl (or mercapto-). The —OH group has priority over the —SH group, e.g. 3-sulfanyl-2-pentanol.

Physical Properties of Thiols

  • Methanethiol is a gas; the higher members are colourless volatile liquids.
  • They have much lower boiling points than the corresponding alcohols because their intermolecular forces are weaker, e.g. methanethiol boils at 6°C while methanol boils at 65°C.
  • They are less soluble in water than alcohols of similar molecular mass.
  • Lower thiols have strong repulsive odours, like garlic and rotten eggs. Methanethiol and ethanethiol are used as odorants to detect leakage of natural gas.

Structure and Acidity of Thiols

The —SH group is bonded to an sp3 hybridized carbon, so the structure of thiols is similar to that of alcohols. The C—S—H bond angle in methanethiol is 100.3°. The S—H bond is less polar than the O—H bond because sulphur is less electronegative than oxygen.

Thiols are stronger acids than alcohols. The pKa of ethanethiol is 10.5, while the pKa of ethanol is 15.9 in dilute aqueous solution.

Key Points

  • Thiols (RSH) are the sulphur analogues of alcohols, with a —SH (mercapto) group.
  • They are called mercaptans because they capture mercury as complexes.
  • IUPAC names end in -thiol; common names end in mercaptan.
  • Thiols boil lower and dissolve less in water than alcohols.
  • Lower thiols have very unpleasant odours and are used as gas-leak odorants.
  • Thiols are stronger acids than alcohols (ethanethiol pKa 10.5, ethanol pKa 15.9).

lessons.title: Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
The name phenol comes from phen, the old name of benzene, and ol, the suffix for a hydroxyl group.

Phenols are compounds in which one or more hydroxyl (—OH) groups are directly bonded to a carbon atom of the benzene ring. The simplest phenol is phenol itself (C6H5OH). Phenols are classified as monohydric or polyhydric according to the number of —OH groups.

Aromatic compounds in which the —OH group is not directly attached to the benzene ring are not phenols. They are aromatic alcohols, because they behave as derivatives of aliphatic alcohols, e.g. phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol) and 2-phenylethanol.

Key Points

  • In phenols, the —OH group is directly bonded to the benzene ring.
  • The simplest phenol is phenol, C6H5OH.
  • Phenols may be monohydric or polyhydric.
  • If —OH is on a side chain, the compound is an aromatic alcohol, not a phenol.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
Phenol is the specific name for hydroxybenzene and is also used as the parent name. Substituted phenols are named as derivatives of phenol or as benzenols; common names are also used.

  • Give position 1 to the carbon bearing the —OH group, then number the substituents, e.g. 2-chlorophenol (o-chlorophenol), 3-ethylphenol (m-ethylphenol), 4-nitrophenol (p-nitrophenol).
  • Two —OH groups: 1,2-benzenediol (catechol), 1,3-benzenediol (resorcinol), 1,4-benzenediol (hydroquinone).
  • 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is commonly called picric acid.
  • Methylphenols are called cresols: 2-methylphenol (o-cresol), 3-methylphenol (m-cresol), 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).
  • Dimethylphenols are called xylenols, e.g. 2,6-xylenol, 3,5-xylenol.
  • If a functional group of higher priority is present, the compound is named as a hydroxy derivative, e.g. 3-hydroxybenzoic acid, 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde.

Isomerism in Phenols

Phenols show position isomerism when two or more substituents are present on the ring. Cresol has three position isomers: ortho, meta and para. Xylenol has six isomers.

Key Points

  • Phenol is the parent name; the —OH carbon is position 1.
  • Catechol, resorcinol and hydroquinone are the 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-benzenediols.
  • Methylphenols are cresols; dimethylphenols are xylenols.
  • 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is picric acid.
  • Phenols show position isomerism (cresol: 3 isomers; xylenol: 6 isomers).

lessons.title: Structure of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
In phenol, the —OH group is bonded to the aromatic ring. The oxygen atom has two bond pairs and two lone pairs of electrons, so phenol has a bent shape like water.

  • The C—O—H bond angle is 109°, slightly less than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.
  • The C—O bond length is 136 pm.
  • Phenol is a polar compound. Its dipole moment is 1.54 D.

Key Points

  • Phenol has a bent shape around oxygen, like water.
  • Its C—O—H angle is 109° and its C—O bond length is 136 pm.
  • Phenol is polar, with a dipole moment of 1.54 D.
  • The oxygen of phenol has two bond pairs and two lone pairs.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
• Pure phenols are generally colourless solids at room temperature. They turn reddish on exposure to air due to oxidation.
  • They have a characteristic phenolic odour.
  • They are generally insoluble in water, but phenol itself and dihydric and trihydric phenols are fairly soluble in water.
  • They have higher boiling points than aliphatic alcohols, because of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding and high molecular masses.
  • Phenol itself is a colourless, crystalline, hygroscopic solid with a low melting point (43°C) and a medicinal odour.
  • Phenol is less soluble in water but more soluble in alcohol and chloroform. It becomes completely soluble in water above 68.5°C.
  • Phenol vapours are toxic, and phenol produces painful blisters on the skin. A 5% aqueous solution of phenol is called carbolic acid.

Key Points

  • Phenols are colourless solids with a phenolic odour; they turn reddish in air.
  • Hydrogen bonding gives phenols high boiling points.
  • Phenol melts at 43°C and is fully miscible with water above 68.5°C.
  • Phenol is toxic and blisters the skin; its 5% solution is carbolic acid.

lessons.title: Acidity of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
Phenol is more acidic than alcohols but less acidic than carboxylic acids:

Carboxylic acid > Phenol > Alcohol

The acidic behaviour of phenol is shown by the following facts:

  • It turns blue litmus red.
  • It reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen gas: 2C6H5OH + 2Na → 2C6H5ONa + H2.
  • It produces H+ ions in water.
  • It reacts with a strong base to form a salt and water: C6H5OH + NaOH → C6H5ONa + H2O.
  • After losing H+, it forms a stable phenoxide (phenolate) ion.

The phenoxide ion is more stable than an alkoxide ion because its negative charge is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance. This resonance stabilization makes phenol lose its proton more easily than an alcohol.

Key Points

  • Acidity order: carboxylic acid > phenol > alcohol.
  • Phenol turns blue litmus red and reacts with Na and NaOH.
  • Phenol forms sodium phenoxide with sodium hydroxide.
  • The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance delocalization into the ring.
  • Resonance stabilization of phenoxide makes phenol more acidic than alcohols.

lessons.title: Preparation of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
From Benzene Sulphonic Acid

Benzene sulphonic acid reacts with NaOH at room temperature to give sodium benzene sulphonate. This is fused with NaOH at about 300°C to give sodium phenoxide, which gives phenol on hydrolysis with HCl. This is the oldest method of preparing phenol and is not used nowadays.

From Chlorobenzene (Dow's Method)

Chlorobenzene is heated with 10% NaOH at 350°C and 300 atm pressure to give sodium phenoxide, which gives phenol on acid hydrolysis. This method has limited laboratory application.

From Acidic Oxidation of Cumene

Cumene is oxidized by air to cumene hydroperoxide. Hydrolysis of cumene hydroperoxide with HCl gives phenol and acetone. Most of the phenol produced in the world today is made by this method.

From Hydrolysis of Diazonium Salts

Benzenediazonium chloride is warmed with water and then acidified. It gives phenol, with nitrogen gas released.

Key Points

  • Fusion of sodium benzene sulphonate with NaOH is the oldest method; it is no longer used.
  • Dow's method: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 350°C and 300 atm gives phenol.
  • The cumene method gives phenol and acetone, and is the main industrial method today.
  • Warming benzenediazonium chloride with water also gives phenol.
  • In every method, sodium phenoxide is acidified to get free phenol.

lessons.title: Reactions of Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
The —OH group of phenol is electron donating. It increases the electron density at the ortho and para positions of the ring by donating its electron pair to the ring. So the benzene ring of phenol is more reactive towards electrophilic substitution than benzene itself, and phenols behave as nucleophiles in most reactions.

Phenols give two types of reactions: reactions due to the —OH group and reactions due to the benzene ring.

Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution

The —OH group is an ortho-para director.

  • Nitration: with dilute HNO3 at room temperature, phenol gives o-nitrophenol (30–40%) and p-nitrophenol (20%). With concentrated HNO3, it gives picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol): C6H5OH + 3HNO3 → C6H2(NO2)3OH + 3H2O.
  • Halogenation: with bromine water, phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr.

Reaction with Sodium Metal

On warming with sodium metal, phenol gives sodium phenoxide, a water-soluble salt, and hydrogen gas.

Oxidation

Phenol is oxidized to p-benzoquinone by stronger oxidizing agents such as silver oxide, lead tetraacetate, dichromate and atmospheric oxygen. Phenols are more easily oxidized than simple alcohols.

Key Points

  • The —OH group activates the ring and directs electrophiles to ortho and para positions.
  • Dilute HNO3 gives o- and p-nitrophenol; concentrated HNO3 gives picric acid.
  • Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol at once.
  • Phenol reacts with sodium to form sodium phenoxide and hydrogen.
  • Strong oxidizing agents convert phenol into p-benzoquinone.

lessons.title: Difference between Alcohols and Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
AlcoholsPhenols
The —OH group is bonded to an alkyl groupThe —OH group is bonded to an aryl group
Hydroxyl derivatives of alkanesHydroxyl derivatives of benzene
General formula R—OHGeneral formula Ar—OH
Less acidicMore acidic
pKa values about 16–20pKa values about 10
Lower alcohols are colourless liquidsColourless crystalline solids
Characteristic sweet smellPhenolic smell
No action with bromine waterWhite precipitate with bromine water
Do not react with NaOH solutionReact with NaOH solution to form phenoxides

Antiseptics and Disinfectants

Antiseptics are mild antimicrobial chemicals applied to living tissue such as skin and wounds; they are safe for the body. Examples: surgical spirit (ethyl alcohol 60–70% or isopropyl alcohol at least 70%), iodine, dettol, boric acid and hydrogen peroxide.

Disinfectants are strong antimicrobial chemicals applied to non-living surfaces such as floors, doors and instruments; they can be harmful and corrosive. Examples: phenol, dettol, formalin and sodium hypochlorite.

Alcohols (ethyl and isopropyl) are widely used as antiseptics and disinfectants because they kill bacteria and viruses. Phenols are widely used as disinfectants in household products.

Key Points

  • In alcohols —OH is on an alkyl group; in phenols it is directly on the benzene ring.
  • Phenols (pKa about 10) are much more acidic than alcohols (pKa about 16–20).
  • Phenols react with NaOH and give a white precipitate with bromine water; alcohols do neither.
  • Antiseptics are mild and used on living tissue; disinfectants are strong and used on surfaces.
  • Alcohols and phenols are both used to kill bacteria and viruses.

lessons.title: Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers are compounds in which an oxygen atom is bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups. They may be considered as derivatives of water in which both hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

The two groups R and R' may be alkyl, aryl or vinyl groups. The general formula of ethers is R—O—R'. The bond angle at oxygen is somewhat greater than in water; in dimethyl ether it is 110°.

Types of Ethers

  • Symmetrical (simple) ethers: both groups on oxygen are the same, e.g. dimethyl ether and diphenyl ether.
  • Unsymmetrical (mixed) ethers: the two groups on oxygen are different, e.g. ethyl methyl ether and methyl phenyl ether.

Key Points

  • Ethers have the general formula R—O—R' and are derivatives of water.
  • Symmetrical ethers have two identical groups on oxygen.
  • Unsymmetrical (mixed) ethers have two different groups on oxygen.
  • The C—O—C bond angle in dimethyl ether is 110°.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Common System

The two groups attached to oxygen are named in alphabetical order, followed by the word ether. If both groups are the same, the prefix di- is used, e.g. dimethyl ether, ethyl methyl ether, diphenyl ether.

IUPAC System

In the IUPAC system, ethers are named as alkoxy derivatives of hydrocarbons:

  • The larger group is taken as the parent alkane.
  • The smaller group, together with oxygen, is named as an alkoxy group (methoxy, ethoxy, etc.).

Examples: CH3—O—CH3 is methoxymethane; CH3—O—CH2CH3 is methoxyethane; CH3—O—CH(CH3)2 is 2-methoxypropane; CH3CH2—O—CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2-ethoxybutane.

The common system is generally used, but the IUPAC system is used for compounds containing more than one ether linkage.

Key Points

  • Common name: groups in alphabetical order + ether; di- for identical groups.
  • IUPAC name: alkoxy group + parent alkane (larger group).
  • Dimethyl ether is methoxymethane in the IUPAC system.
  • The IUPAC system is used for compounds with more than one ether linkage.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
• Lower ethers such as dimethyl ether and ethyl methyl ether are gases. Higher ethers are colourless, volatile liquids.
  • They have a pleasant odour.
  • They are highly inflammable.
  • They have low boiling points, because there is no hydrogen bonding between ether molecules.
  • They are slightly soluble in water, because they can form hydrogen bonds with water. Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl groups increases.
  • They are readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene and chloroform.
  • They are lighter (less dense) than water.
  • Because of these properties, ethers are used as solvents.

Key Points

  • Lower ethers are gases; higher ethers are volatile, pleasant-smelling liquids.
  • Ethers are highly inflammable and have low boiling points.
  • They cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, but can hydrogen-bond with water.
  • They are less dense than water and slightly soluble in it.
  • Ethers are widely used as solvents.

lessons.title: Preparation of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Williamson's Synthesis

An alcohol is first treated with sodium metal to form a sodium alkoxide. The alkoxide then reacts with an alkyl halide to form an ether:

R—ONa + R'—X → R—O—R' + NaX

This is the most important and widely used method for the preparation of ethers.

Reaction of Alkyl Halides with Dry Silver Oxide

Alkyl halides react with dry silver oxide on heating to form ethers:

2R—X + Ag2O → R—O—R + 2AgX

Key Points

  • Williamson's synthesis: sodium alkoxide + alkyl halide gives an ether.
  • Williamson's synthesis is the most important method for preparing ethers.
  • Dry silver oxide converts alkyl halides into ethers on heating.
  • In Williamson's synthesis, the alkoxide is made by reacting the alcohol with sodium metal.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers are stable compounds. They are less reactive than alcohols but more reactive than alkanes.

Ethers are less reactive because they have no active hydrogen bonded to oxygen, as alcohols have. They become reactive only when the oxygen is protonated in an acidic medium.

Ethers do not react with bases, dilute acids, metallic sodium, reducing agents or oxidizing agents in the cold state. However, they show some characteristic reactions with concentrated acids.

Key Points

  • Ethers are stable and much less reactive than alcohols.
  • They have no active (O—H) hydrogen.
  • They react only after protonation of oxygen in acidic medium.
  • They do not react with bases, dilute acids, sodium, or cold oxidizing and reducing agents.

lessons.title: Reactions of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Reaction with Cold Concentrated Acids

Ethers react with cold concentrated HCl or H2SO4 to produce oxonium salts:

(C2H5)2O + HCl → [(C2H5)2OH]+ Cl− (diethyl oxonium chloride)

(C2H5)2O + H2SO4 → [(C2H5)2OH]+ HSO4− (diethyl oxonium hydrogen sulphate)

Reaction with Hot Concentrated Acids

With hot concentrated HCl or HI, the ether is cleaved into an alcohol and an alkyl halide:

C2H5—O—C2H5 + HCl → C2H5OH + C2H5Cl

If excess acid is used, the alcohol formed reacts further with HX to give more alkyl halide.

Use of Ether as Anesthesia

Diethyl ether is a colourless, volatile and highly flammable liquid with a characteristic smell. It was one of the first chemicals used as an anesthetic in hospitals. An anesthetic causes loss of sensation or consciousness so that surgery can be done without pain. The three important early anesthetics were diethyl ether, chloroform and nitrous oxide. Diethyl ether is safer than chloroform and more effective than nitrous oxide, and it remained the standard general anesthetic until the 1960s. It is no longer used in advanced countries because it is extremely flammable and recovery from its anesthesia is prolonged; safer fluorinated hydrocarbons are used instead. It is still used in some developing countries because it is cheap.

Key Points

  • Cold concentrated acids convert ethers into oxonium salts.
  • Hot concentrated HCl or HI cleaves ethers into an alcohol and an alkyl halide.
  • With excess acid, the alcohol is also converted into alkyl halide.
  • Diethyl ether was the standard general anesthetic until the 1960s.
  • Ether is little used as an anesthetic now because it is highly flammable.

lessons.title: Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones are carbonyl compounds: they contain the carbonyl group, C=O. They play an important role in chemistry, biology and biochemistry, and they are responsible for many flavours and odours.

  • Vanillin, an aldehyde, gives the vanilla flavour.
  • Benzaldehyde, an aldehyde, gives the almond flavour.
  • R-carvone, a ketone, gives the spearmint flavour.
  • The male and female sex hormones, testosterone and progesterone, also contain carbonyl groups.

In an aldehyde, one alkyl (or aryl) group and one hydrogen atom are bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group: general formula RCHO. Formaldehyde is the exception, because it has two hydrogen atoms bonded to the carbonyl carbon. In a ketone, two alkyl (or aryl) groups are bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group: general formula RCOR.

Key Points

  • Aldehydes and ketones are carbonyl compounds, containing the C=O group.
  • They give many natural flavours and odours, e.g. vanillin, benzaldehyde and R-carvone.
  • An aldehyde has one alkyl (or aryl) group and one H on the carbonyl carbon (RCHO).
  • Formaldehyde is the exception: it has two H atoms on the carbonyl carbon.
  • A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups on the carbonyl carbon (RCOR).

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Aldehydes
lessons.notes_html:
Both common and IUPAC names are used for aldehydes.

Common System

The common names of aldehydes are derived from the names of the corresponding carboxylic acids by replacing the ending -ic acid with the word -aldehyde. The position of substituents on the chain is shown by Greek letters α, β, γ, δ, etc. The α-carbon is the carbon directly bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group. Examples: formaldehyde (HCHO), acetaldehyde (CH3CHO), propionaldehyde (CH3CH2CHO), β-methylbutyraldehyde, γ-chloro-α,β-dimethylvaleraldehyde.

IUPAC System

The IUPAC names of aldehydes are derived from the names of the corresponding alkanes by replacing the ending -e with -al. Aldehydes are therefore named as alkanals: a three-carbon aldehyde is propanal and a four-carbon aldehyde is butanal. For higher aldehydes with substituents, find the longest chain containing the aldehyde group and number it so that the aldehyde group gets position one. There is no need to indicate the position of the aldehyde group, because it always lies at the end of the chain and is given position number one.

IUPAC examples: methanal, ethanal, propanal, 3-methylbutanal, 4-bromo-3-chloro-2-methylbutanal, 4-chloro-2,3-dimethylpentanal, 3,3-dimethylhexanal.

Key Points

  • Common names come from the corresponding acid: -ic acid is replaced by -aldehyde.
  • Substituent positions in common names use Greek letters α, β, γ, δ from the carbonyl carbon.
  • IUPAC names are alkanals: the alkane ending -e is replaced by -al.
  • The aldehyde carbon is always C-1, so its position is not written.
  • Examples: HCHO = methanal (formaldehyde); CH3CHO = ethanal (acetaldehyde).

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Common System

The common names of ketones are obtained by naming the two alkyl (or aryl) groups bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group, in alphabetical order, and adding the word ketone as a separate word. If the two groups are the same, the prefix di is used. The position of substituents on the chain is indicated by Greek letters (α, β, γ, δ, etc.), starting with the carbon next to the carbonyl group, and substituents are named in alphabetical order. Examples: dimethyl ketone, ethyl methyl ketone, ethyl isopropyl ketone, diphenyl ketone, methyl phenyl ketone.

Some ketones are known by their historical names: dimethyl ketone is always named acetone, diphenyl ketone is called benzophenone, and methyl phenyl ketone is known as acetophenone.

IUPAC System

The IUPAC names of ketones are derived from the names of the corresponding alkanes by replacing the ending -e with -one. Ketones are therefore named as alkanones: a four-carbon ketone is butanone and a five-carbon ketone is pentanone. For open-chain ketones, find the longest chain containing the carbonyl group and number it so that the carbonyl group is assigned the lowest possible number; the position of the carbonyl carbon is indicated before the stem name. If two or more ketonic groups are present, the suffixes dione, trione, tetraone are used. The positions of substituents are shown by the numbers of the carbons to which they are attached.

IUPAC examples: propanone, butan-2-one, 2-methylpentan-3-one, 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one, 4-hydroxy-2-methylhexan-3-one, 6-chloro-4,5-dimethylheptan-3-one.

Key Points

  • Common ketone names: the two groups on the carbonyl carbon (alphabetical) + ketone.
  • Identical groups take the prefix di, e.g. dimethyl ketone.
  • Historical names: acetone, benzophenone and acetophenone.
  • IUPAC names are alkanones: the alkane ending -e is replaced by -one.
  • Number the longest chain so the carbonyl group gets the lowest possible number.
  • Two or more keto groups are shown by dione, trione, tetraone.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
• The carbonyl group is polar, because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon. Due to this polarity, aldehydes and ketones show dipole-dipole interactions, which make their boiling points higher than those of the corresponding alkanes of comparable molecular masses.
  • They cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, because they have no O-H bond. They are therefore less polar than alcohols and carboxylic acids, and have lower boiling points than alcohols and carboxylic acids.
  • Aldehydes and ketones having five or fewer carbon atoms are soluble in water, because they can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
  • Those having more than five carbon atoms are insoluble in water, because the non-polar hydrocarbon portion is too large to dissolve in polar water.
  • Methanal and ethanal are gases; the other lower aldehydes and ketones are colourless liquids at room temperature. Higher aldehydes with more than twenty carbon atoms and ketones with more than thirty carbon atoms are solids at room temperature.
  • Lower aldehydes have pungent smells and higher aldehydes have pleasant smells; camphor, a ketone, has a sweet smell.
  • The density of aldehydes and ketones is less than that of water.

Formaldehyde: Sources, Health Risks and Recommendations

Formaldehyde is a colourless, flammable gas with a pungent, irritating odour. Its aqueous solution is called formalin. All organisms (such as bacteria, fish and humans) naturally produce formaldehyde as part of cell metabolism. It is commonly used as a preservative in medical laboratories and mortuaries, and as an industrial fungicide, germicide, fumigant and disinfectant. It is used in making chemical resins, rubber products, paper products and cosmetics, and is found in adhesives, glues, varnishes, paints, household products, plywood and fibreboard. It is also present in combustion products such as vehicle exhaust and tobacco smoke.

Health risks: short-term exposure irritates the eyes, nose and throat and can cause coughing and a sore throat; at high concentration it irritates the lungs, causing chest pain and shortness of breath. Long-term exposure makes all these symptoms worse and can cause allergic reactions of the skin (dermatitis), the eyes and the lungs (asthma). Repeated contact can cause numbness and hardening of the skin, and at high concentration formaldehyde can cause cancer in the nose, throat or lungs. Formalin is a skin irritant (smarting, drying, cracking and scaling), and formaldehyde can decrease fertility and increase the risk of spontaneous miscarriage in humans. Recommendation: students, teachers and workers who may be exposed should wear safety goggles, gloves, a face shield and an apron of appropriate materials before entering the workplace.

Key Points

  • The polar carbonyl group gives dipole-dipole interactions and higher boiling points than alkanes.
  • With no O-H bond, they cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, so they boil lower than alcohols and acids.
  • Members with five or fewer carbons dissolve in water; larger members do not.
  • Methanal and ethanal are gases; most others are liquids; the highest members are solids.
  • Formaldehyde is a pungent, irritating gas; its aqueous solution is formalin.
  • Formaldehyde is harmful on long exposure; protective equipment must be worn when handling it.

lessons.title: Structure of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
The carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones is composed of one sigma bond and one pi bond. Both the carbon and the oxygen of the carbonyl group are sp2 hybridized. The fourth p-orbital of carbon remains unhybridized.

  • The three sp2 hybrid orbitals of carbon form three sigma bonds: one with oxygen and two with the other groups bonded to it.
  • The fourth, unhybridized p-orbital of carbon forms the pi bond with oxygen.
