  • The three atoms or groups attached to the carbon of the carbonyl group lie in the same plane.
  • The bond angles between the bonded atoms or groups are around 120°, so the carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar.

Key Points

  • The C=O group has one sigma bond and one pi bond.
  • Both carbonyl carbon and oxygen are sp2 hybridized.
  • The unhybridized p-orbital of carbon forms the pi bond with oxygen.
  • The three groups on the carbonyl carbon lie in one plane, with angles of about 120°.

lessons.title: Ozonolysis of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes react with ozone to form an explosive compound called an ozonide. On subsequent reductive cleavage with zinc dust and water, the ozonide produces aldehydes or ketones, or both, depending on the structure of the alkene.

Key Reactions

AlkeneProducts after O3, then Zn/H2O
R-CH=CH-R2 R-CHO (aldehydes)
R2C=CR22 R2C=O (ketones)

Each carbon of the double bond becomes a carbonyl carbon: a double-bond carbon carrying a hydrogen gives an aldehyde, and a double-bond carbon carrying two alkyl groups gives a ketone.

Key Points

  • Ozone adds to an alkene to form an ozonide, which is explosive.
  • Reductive cleavage with Zn/H2O breaks the double bond completely.
  • The products are aldehydes, ketones, or both, depending on the alkene's structure.

lessons.title: Hydration of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkynes undergo hydration according to Markovnikov's rule in the presence of mercuric sulphate and sulphuric acid. The reaction forms an unstable enol, which on rearrangement gives aldehydes or ketones, or both, depending on the structure of the alkyne. Acetylene (ethyne) produces an aldehyde, while all other alkynes under the same conditions produce the corresponding ketones.

Key Reactions

AlkyneConditionsProduct
HC≡CH (acetylene)H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4CH3CHO (acetaldehyde), through an enol intermediate
HC≡C-CH3 (propyne)H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4CH3COCH3 (dimethyl ketone, acetone), through an enol intermediate

Key Points

  • Water adds to alkynes by Markovnikov's rule with HgSO4/H2SO4.
  • An unstable enol forms first and rearranges to the carbonyl compound.
  • Acetylene gives acetaldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
The controlled oxidation of primary alcohols in the presence of an acidified solution of potassium dichromate or potassium permanganate produces aldehydes, whereas secondary alcohols result in the formation of ketones.

Key Reactions

AlcoholConditionsProduct
CH3CH2OH (ethyl alcohol, 1°)[O], K2Cr2O7/H2SO4CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) + H2O
CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 (sec-propyl alcohol, 2°)[O], K2Cr2O7/H2SO4CH3COCH3 (acetone) + H2O

Key Points

  • Controlled oxidation of a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde.
  • Oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
  • The oxidizing agents are acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4.

lessons.title: Friedel-Crafts Acylation of Aromatic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
An aromatic compound (benzene) reacts with an acyl halide in the presence of a Lewis acid (AlCl3) to produce an aryl ketone.

Key Reactions

ReactantsConditionsProduct
Benzene + CH3COCl (acetyl chloride)AlCl3Methyl phenyl ketone (acetophenone) + HCl

Key Points

  • Benzene reacts with an acyl halide to give an aryl ketone.
  • AlCl3 is the Lewis acid catalyst.
  • Example: benzene + acetyl chloride → methyl phenyl ketone + HCl.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Carbonyl Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones both contain a carbon-oxygen double bond. A ketone has an alkyl or aryl group on each side of the carbonyl, while an aldehyde has a hydrogen on one side and an alkyl or aryl group on the other side.

Oxygen of the carbonyl group is more electronegative than carbon. Therefore, the less tightly held pi electrons are strongly attracted by the oxygen atom. This makes the carbonyl group highly polar: a partial negative charge (δ-) develops on oxygen and a partial positive charge (δ+) develops on the carbon of the carbonyl group.

The positively charged carbon atom therefore acts as an electrophile, and the most characteristic reaction of aldehydes and ketones is nucleophilic addition to the carbon-oxygen double bond. During addition of a reagent to the carbonyl group, the negative part of the reagent adds to the carbon of the carbonyl group and the positive part adds to the oxygen of the carbonyl group.

Key Points

  • The C=O bond is highly polar: carbon is δ+ and oxygen is δ-.
  • The π electrons are pulled strongly towards the more electronegative oxygen.
  • The carbonyl carbon is an electrophile and is attacked by nucleophiles.
  • The characteristic reaction is nucleophilic addition to the C=O bond.
  • In addition, the negative part of the reagent joins the carbon and the positive part joins the oxygen.

lessons.title: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones react with nucleophiles to produce a wide variety of useful derivatives. They undergo addition of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nucleophiles. The carbon of the carbonyl group is highly electrophilic because of its partial positive charge, so the nucleophile adds to the electrophilic carbon. As the nucleophile adds, the hybridization of carbon changes from sp2 to sp3. These reactions can be catalyzed by an acid or by a base.

Base Catalyzed Nucleophilic Addition

These reactions occur in the presence of a strong nucleophile. The strong nucleophile is produced by the reaction of the base with the reagent: H-Nu + OH- → Nu- + H2O. The nucleophile uses its pair of electrons to make a bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the electrons of the π-bond are forced out onto the oxygen atom, producing an alkoxide anion. The alkoxide intermediate is then protonated on treatment with water, and the base is regenerated: alkoxide + H2O → addition product (an alcohol) + OH-.

Acid Catalyzed Nucleophilic Addition

These reactions occur in the presence of a weak nucleophile. A small amount of acid is used to initiate the reaction. The proton of the acid attacks the carbonyl oxygen atom to produce a protonated carbonyl group. Protonation increases the electrophilic character of the carbonyl carbon and makes it more reactive towards the nucleophile. The nucleophile then uses its pair of electrons to bond to the carbonyl carbon, the π-bond electrons are forced onto the oxygen, and the addition product (an alcohol) is formed.

Key Points

  • Nucleophilic addition is the most common reaction of aldehydes and ketones.
  • H, C, N and O nucleophiles all add to the carbonyl carbon.
  • On addition, the carbonyl carbon changes from sp2 to sp3.
  • Base catalysis works by producing a strong nucleophile; an alkoxide intermediate is protonated by water.
  • Acid catalysis works by protonating the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic for a weak nucleophile.

lessons.title: Relative Reactivity of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition reactions. An alkyl group is an electron-donating group, so it makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic. The carbonyl carbon of a ketone has two alkyl groups, so it is less reactive towards nucleophiles than an aldehyde, which has only one alkyl group. The order of reactivity is: formaldehyde > aldehydes > ketones.

Steric effects are also important in the transition state. An aldehyde has only one alkyl (or aryl) group, so its transition state is less crowded. A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups, so its transition state is more crowded. Because of this greater steric crowding in the transition state, ketones are less reactive towards nucleophilic attack than aldehydes.

Key Points

  • Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
  • Reactivity order: formaldehyde > aldehydes > ketones.
  • Electronic reason: two electron-donating alkyl groups make the ketone carbonyl carbon less positive.
  • Steric reason: the ketone transition state is more crowded than the aldehyde transition state.

lessons.title: Reduction to Hydrocarbon (Clemmensen Reduction)
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones undergo reduction in the presence of different reducing agents to produce hydrocarbons, alcohols or glycols. On reduction with zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl, aldehydes and ketones produce hydrocarbons: the carbonyl group is reduced completely to a CH2 group. This reduction is known as Clemmensen reduction.

Key Reactions

CompoundConditionsProduct
CH3CHO (acetaldehyde)Zn-Hg, conc. HClCH3CH3 (ethane) + H2O
CH3COCH3 (acetone)Zn-Hg, conc. HClCH3CH2CH3 (propane) + H2O

Key Points

  • Zn-Hg and conc. HCl reduce the carbonyl group completely to CH2.
  • Aldehydes and ketones are converted into hydrocarbons.
  • This is called Clemmensen reduction.
  • Example: acetaldehyde → ethane; acetone → propane.

lessons.title: Reduction to Alcohols (Reduction with NaBH4)
lessons.notes_html:
Metal hydrides such as NaBH4 (sodium borohydride) or LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride) are reducing agents. They reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Reduction with NaBH4 needs polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol.

Key Reactions

CompoundConditionsProduct
CH3CHO (acetaldehyde)NaBH4, H2OCH3CH2OH (ethyl alcohol, 1°)
CH3COCH3 (acetone)NaBH4, H2OCH3-CH(OH)-CH3 (isopropyl alcohol, 2°)

Key Points

  • NaBH4 and LiAlH4 are metal hydride reducing agents.
  • Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols.
  • Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.
  • NaBH4 reduction is carried out in polar solvents such as water or ethanol.

lessons.title: Reduction with Carbon Nucleophiles
lessons.notes_html:
The carbon in HCN, in organometallic compounds such as RLi, in terminal alkynes and in Grignard's reagent acts as a nucleophile and adds to aldehydes and ketones to give various compounds (the book groups these addition reactions under reduction with carbon nucleophiles).

Addition of HCN: Cyanohydrin Formation

Hydrogen cyanide is a weak acid that adds to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins: RCHO + HCN → R-CH(OH)-CN. Examples: formaldehyde + HCN → formaldehyde cyanohydrin, HO-CH2-CN; acetaldehyde + HCN → acetaldehyde cyanohydrin, CH3-CH(OH)-CN; acetone + HCN → acetone cyanohydrin, (CH3)2C(OH)-CN.

Mechanism: the conjugate base of HCN, the cyanide ion, acts as a strong nucleophile. In step 1, the cyanide ion adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion. In step 2, the alkoxide ion takes a proton from HCN to produce the cyanohydrin, and the cyanide ion is regenerated.

Addition of Grignard's Reagent (RMgX)

The reaction of an aldehyde or ketone with Grignard's reagent, followed by protonation in aqueous acid, forms a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol containing a new carbon-carbon bond: formaldehyde + CH3MgCl → ethyl alcohol (1°) after hydrolysis; acetaldehyde + CH3MgCl → isopropyl alcohol (2°); acetone + CH3MgCl → tert-butyl alcohol (3°).

Key Reactions

ReagentProduct type
HCNCyanohydrin, R-CH(OH)-CN
RMgX, then H2O/H+Alcohol with a new C-C bond (1°, 2° or 3°)

Key Points

  • Carbon nucleophiles include HCN, RLi, terminal alkynes and RMgX.
  • HCN adds to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins.
  • The cyanide ion is the real nucleophile; it adds first, then the alkoxide is protonated.
  • Grignard addition followed by hydrolysis gives alcohols and forms a new C-C bond.

lessons.title: Reduction with Nitrogen Nucleophiles
lessons.notes_html:
The nitrogen in ammonia and its derivatives acts as a nucleophile and reacts with aldehydes and ketones to give various compounds. In each case an addition product forms first, and then water is eliminated.

Addition of Ammonia

Ammonia adds to aldehydes to form imines: CH3CHO + NH3 → CH3-CH=NH + H2O. Mechanism: in step 1, ammonia adds to the aldehyde to form an unstable addition product; in step 2, a proton is transferred to give the carbinolamine-type intermediate; in step 3, water is eliminated to produce the imine.

Addition of Ammonia Derivatives

  • Alkyl amines: primary amines add to aldehydes and ketones to form an addition product, which undergoes elimination of water to produce imines: CH3CHO + R-NH2 → CH3-CH=N-R + H2O.
  • Hydroxylamine: hydroxylamine adds to aldehydes and ketones; elimination of water produces an oxime: (CH3)2C=O + NH2OH → (CH3)2C=N-OH (propanone oxime) + H2O.
  • Hydrazine: hydrazine adds to aldehydes and ketones; elimination of water produces a hydrazone: (CH3)2C=O + H2N-NH2 → (CH3)2C=N-NH2 (propanone hydrazone) + H2O.
  • Phenylhydrazine reacts in the same way to give phenylhydrazones.

Key Points

  • Ammonia and its derivatives attack through nitrogen.
  • Ammonia + aldehyde → imine + water.
  • Primary amines give imines; hydroxylamine gives oximes; hydrazine gives hydrazones.
  • All these reactions are addition followed by elimination of water.

lessons.title: Reduction with Oxygen Nucleophiles
lessons.notes_html:
The oxygen in water, alcohols, etc. acts as a nucleophile and reacts with aldehydes and ketones to give various products.

Addition of Water (Hydration)

Water adds to aldehydes or ketones to produce a germinal diol (gem-diol). The reaction is catalyzed by an acid or a base: R2C=O + H2O → R2C(OH)2. Examples: formaldehyde + water → formaldehyde hydrate, H2C(OH)2; acetaldehyde + water → acetaldehyde hydrate (1,1-ethanediol); acetone + water → acetone hydrate (2,2-propanediol). A 37% solution of formaldehyde in water is known as formalin and is used to preserve biological specimens.

Addition of Alcohols

Alcohols add to aldehydes (or ketones) in the presence of dry HCl to produce acetals. The reaction occurs in two steps. First, one molecule of alcohol adds to produce a hemiacetal, which is unstable. The hemiacetal then reacts with a second molecule of alcohol to produce the acetal: CH3CHO + CH3CH2OH → hemiacetal CH3-CH(OH)(OCH2CH3); hemiacetal + CH3CH2OH → acetal CH3-CH(OCH2CH3)2 (1,1-diethoxyethane) + H2O. On hydrolysis, the acetal converts back to the original aldehyde.

An acetal obtained from a ketone is often called a ketal. A ketone does not react with alcohols readily to form hemiketals or ketals because of steric hindrance. Acetals are common compounds: sucrose (table sugar) and cotton fabric are composed of acetals.

Key Points

  • Water adds to the carbonyl group to give a gem-diol (a hydrate).
  • Hydration is catalyzed by an acid or a base.
  • Formalin is a 37% aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used to preserve specimens.
  • Alcohols add in dry HCl: first a hemiacetal, then an acetal.
  • Acetals hydrolyse back to the original aldehyde; ketone acetals are called ketals.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Aldehydes
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones show generally similar behaviour towards nucleophilic addition, but their behaviour towards oxidizing agents is quite different. Aldehydes are much more easily oxidized to carboxylic acids than ketones; ketones are oxidized to carboxylic acids only under drastic conditions.

Aldehydes can be oxidized by mild oxidizing agents such as silver oxide, Ag2O (Tollens' reagent), and cupric oxide, CuO (Fehling's solution or Benedict's solution). They can also be oxidized by strong oxidizing agents such as potassium permanganate or potassium dichromate in acidic medium: CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4).

Composition of the Test Reagents

ReagentComposition
Tollens' reagentMixture of AgNO3 and NH4OH
Fehling's solutionMixture of CuSO4, NaOH and tartaric acid
Benedict's solutionMixture of CuSO4, NaOH and citric acid

Key Points

  • Aldehydes are easily oxidized to carboxylic acids with the same number of carbons.
  • Even mild oxidizers (Tollens', Fehling's, Benedict's) oxidize aldehydes.
  • Strong oxidizers KMnO4 and acidified K2Cr2O7 also oxidize aldehydes.
  • Example: acetaldehyde + [O] → acetic acid.
  • These mild-oxidizer tests distinguish aldehydes from ketones.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Ketones cannot be oxidized by mild oxidizing agents. They can be oxidized only by strong oxidizing agents such as potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate, at higher temperatures and at higher concentrations of acid or base. The oxidation of ketones produces a mixture of two carboxylic acids, because a carbon-carbon bond next to the carbonyl group breaks.

Key Reactions

KetoneConditionsProducts
CH3COCH3 (acetone) + 3[O]K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, strong conditionsCH3COOH (acetic acid) + HCOOH (formic acid)

Glucose and Fructose: Aldehydes and Ketones in Nature

Carbonyl compounds are found extensively in nature and play important roles in living things. Monosaccharides, the simplest carbohydrates, are either aldehydes or ketones with one or more hydroxyl groups. Glucose is a six-carbon aldehyde with five hydroxyl groups, while fructose is a six-carbon ketone with five hydroxyl groups. A monosaccharide with an aldehyde group is called an aldose, and one with a ketone group is called a ketose.

Key Points

  • Mild oxidizing agents do not oxidize ketones.
  • Strong oxidizers (KMnO4, K2Cr2O7) at high temperature oxidize ketones with bond cleavage.
  • Ketone oxidation gives a mixture of two carboxylic acids.
  • Example: acetone + 3[O] → acetic acid + formic acid.
  • Glucose is an aldose (an aldehyde sugar); fructose is a ketose (a ketone sugar).

chapters.title: Chapter 20: Carboxylic Acids and their Functional Derivatives

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids are organic compounds containing the carboxyl group (—COOH) in their structures. Their general formula is R—COOH, where R is an aliphatic or aromatic group.

The name carboxyl is obtained from carbonyl and hydroxyl, because both these groups are present in carboxylic acids. The most important chemical property of carboxylic acids, as shown by their name, is their acidity.

Carboxylic Acid Derivatives

Compounds obtained by replacing the hydroxyl group (—OH) of the carboxyl group by halogen (—X), alkoxy (—OR), amino (—NH2) or carboxylate (—OCOR) are called carboxylic acid derivatives. There are four types of acid derivatives:

  • Acyl halides (acid halides): —OH replaced by —X, giving R—CO—X.
  • Esters: —OH replaced by —OR', giving R—CO—OR'.
  • Amides (acid amides): —OH replaced by —NH2, giving R—CO—NH2.
  • Acid anhydrides: —OH replaced by —OCOR', giving R—CO—O—CO—R'.

Carboxylic acids and their functional derivatives are important classes of organic compounds. They are the most abundant of all organic compounds.

Key Points

  • Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, —COOH; general formula R—COOH.
  • Carboxyl = carbonyl + hydroxyl.
  • Acidity is the most important property of carboxylic acids.
  • The four acid derivatives are acyl halides, esters, amides and acid anhydrides.
  • Derivatives are formed by replacing the —OH of the carboxyl group.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Common System

Carboxylic acids with six or less carbon atoms are often known by their common names. These names are derived from the Latin or Greek word that shows the original source of the acid, and all common names end in -ic acid.

StructureCommon NameDerivation
HCOOHFormic acidLatin: formica, ant
CH3COOHAcetic acidLatin: acetum, vinegar
CH3CH2COOHPropionic acidGreek: propion, first fat
CH3(CH2)2COOHButyric acidLatin: butyrum, butter
CH3(CH2)3COOHValeric acidLatin: valeriana, a flowering plant
CH3(CH2)4COOHCaproic acidLatin: caper, goat

In substituted acids, the position of a substituent is shown by Greek letters α, β, γ, δ. The α-carbon is the carbon directly bonded to the carboxyl carbon. Examples: α-aminopropionic acid, β-methylbutyric acid.

Formic acid is found in ants, bees and other stinging insects. Acetic acid is found in vinegar. Butyric acid is found in rancid butter, and caproic acid in goat's milk.

IUPAC System

The IUPAC names of monocarboxylic acids are derived from the corresponding alkanes by replacing the ending -e with -oic acid. They are called alkanoic acids: methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid, and so on. The carboxyl group lies at the end of the chain, so its position is not shown.

For substituted acids, take the longest chain containing the carboxyl group and give the carboxyl carbon position number 1. The carboxyl group has priority over all other functional groups. Examples: 2-methylpropanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid, 2-aminobutanoic acid.

Dicarboxylic Acids

Dicarboxylic acids, also called diacids, have two carboxyl groups. They are named by adding the suffix -dioic acid to the parent alkane name. Examples: ethanedioic acid (oxalic acid), propanedioic acid (malonic acid), butanedioic acid (succinic acid).

Key Points

  • Common names come from the natural source of the acid and end in -ic acid.
  • In common names, substituent positions are shown by α, β, γ, δ from the carboxyl carbon.
  • IUPAC names end in -oic acid; the carboxyl carbon is always C-1.
  • The carboxyl group has priority over other functional groups.
  • Diacids have two —COOH groups and names ending in -dioic acid.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acid Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Acyl Halides

Acyl halides are named by replacing the suffix "ic acid" of the parent carboxylic acid name (common or IUPAC) with "yl halide". Examples: methanoyl chloride (formyl chloride), ethanoyl chloride (acetyl chloride), propanoyl bromide (propionyl bromide), 3-methylpentanoyl chloride.

Amides

Amides are named by replacing the suffix "ic acid" (common names) or "oic acid" (IUPAC names) of the parent acid with "amide". Examples: methanamide (formamide), ethanamide (acetamide), propanamide (propionamide), 4-chloropentanamide.

Esters

Ester names have two words. The first word is the name of the alkyl group bonded to the oxygen atom. The second word is obtained by replacing the suffix "ic acid" of the parent acid with "ate". Examples: methyl methanoate (methyl formate), ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate), methyl propanoate (methyl propionate).

Acid Anhydrides

Symmetrical anhydrides are named by replacing the word "acid" in the parent acid name with "anhydride", e.g. ethanoic anhydride (acetic anhydride). Unsymmetrical (mixed) anhydrides, made from two different acids, are named by writing the names of both acids in alphabetical order and replacing "acid" by "anhydride", e.g. ethanoic methanoic anhydride (acetic formic anhydride).

Key Points

  • Acyl halides: acid name with "ic acid" replaced by "yl halide".
  • Amides: acid name with "ic acid" or "oic acid" replaced by "amide".
  • Esters: alkyl group name + acid name ending in "ate".
  • Anhydrides: acid name with "acid" replaced by "anhydride".
  • Common names of derivatives are often written in brackets after the IUPAC name.

lessons.title: Physical Characteristics of Carboxylic Acid
lessons.notes_html:
• The first six members of carboxylic acids are colourless liquids; the higher members are wax-like solids.
  • The first three members have a pungent smell. The next six members, up to C9, have a smell of rancid butter. The higher members have almost no smell.
  • The first four members are completely soluble in water due to hydrogen bonding. Solubility decreases as the length of the carbon chain increases.
  • Melting points increase irregularly with molecular mass. Acids with an even number of carbon atoms have markedly higher melting points than odd members, e.g. propanoic acid (3 carbons) melts at −21°C, butanoic acid (4 carbons) at −7°C and pentanoic acid (5 carbons) at −35°C.
  • Boiling points are relatively high due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The acids exist in the form of cyclic dimers.
FormulaBoiling Point
HCOOH101°C
CH3COOH118°C
CH3CH2COOH141°C

Key Points

  • Lower acids are colourless, pungent liquids; higher acids are wax-like solids.
  • The first four members are completely soluble in water.
  • Solubility falls as the carbon chain grows.
  • Even-carbon acids melt higher than odd-carbon acids.
  • Hydrogen-bonded cyclic dimers give carboxylic acids high boiling points.

lessons.title: Structure of Carboxylic Acids and Their Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
The carbon atom of the carboxyl group in carboxylic acids and their derivatives is sp2 hybridized.

The three sp2 hybrid orbitals of the carboxyl carbon form three sigma bonds: one with the carbonyl oxygen, one with the oxygen of the hydroxyl group, and one with a hydrogen atom or another group bonded to it.

The remaining unhybridized p orbital of the carboxyl carbon overlaps with the p orbital of the carbonyl oxygen to form a pi bond.

The three atoms or groups bonded to the carboxyl carbon lie in the same plane, and the bond angles between them are approximately 120°. Hence the carboxyl group shows trigonal planar geometry.

Key Points

  • The carboxyl carbon is sp2 hybridized.
  • It forms three sigma bonds and one pi bond (with the carbonyl oxygen).
  • All three groups on the carboxyl carbon lie in one plane.
  • Bond angles are about 120°, so the geometry is trigonal planar.

lessons.title: Acidity of Carboxylic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids are the most acidic organic compounds. Their acidic behaviour is explained as follows:

  • A carboxylic acid gives a hydrogen ion (H+) in water, and a conjugate base, the carboxylate ion, is produced: R—COOH ⇌ R—COO− + H+.
  • The carboxylate ion is more stable in water than the carboxylic acid, because its negative charge is delocalized. The carboxylate ion is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent structures.
  • The carboxylate ion is more effectively resonance-stabilized than the conjugate bases of alcohols and phenols. The greater the stability of the resonance hybrid, the greater is the strength of the acid.

Acid strength is also shown by pKa values: the greater the pKa, the weaker the acid. The pKa values of HCl, H2SO4, CH3COOH, C6H5OH, H2O and C2H5OH are −7, −3, 4.75, 10, 14 and 16 respectively.

So carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than water, alcohols and phenols, but they are not as strong as mineral acids such as HCl and H2SO4.

Order of acidity: Mineral acids > carboxylic acids > phenol > water > alcohol

Key Points

  • Carboxylic acids ionize in water to give carboxylate ions and H+ ions.
  • The carboxylate ion is stabilized by resonance delocalization of the negative charge.
  • Greater resonance stabilization means a stronger acid.
  • Acetic acid has pKa 4.75, phenol 10 and ethanol 16.
  • Acidity order: mineral acids > carboxylic acids > phenol > water > alcohol.

lessons.title: Preparations of Carboxylic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Carbonation of Grignard's Reagent

Grignard reagents react with CO2 to give an addition product, which gives a carboxylic acid on acid hydrolysis:

CH3MgCl + CO2 → CH3COOMgCl → (H2O/HCl) CH3COOH + Mg(OH)Cl

This is a convenient way to convert an alkyl or aryl halide into a carboxylic acid.

Hydrolysis of Nitriles

Alkyl nitriles (alkyl cyanides) react with a hot aqueous solution of an acid (mineral acid) or alkali to produce carboxylic acids:

R—C≡N + 2H2O → (HCl) R—COOH + NH3

Oxidation of Primary Alcohols

Primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes, which on further oxidation give carboxylic acids. The oxidizing agent is K2Cr2O7 in H2SO4; KMnO4 can also be used:

CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O; CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH

Oxidation of Aldehydes

Aldehydes are oxidized to carboxylic acids by mild oxidizing agents such as silver oxide (Ag2O), and also by strong oxidizing agents such as potassium permanganate or potassium dichromate in acidic medium:

R—CHO + [O] → R—COOH

Oxidation of Alkyl Benzenes

Alkyl groups attached directly to the benzene ring are oxidized to a carboxylic acid group. Toluene is oxidized to benzoic acid. Alkyl benzenes give the same product, benzoic acid, whether the side chain is methyl, ethyl or any other alkyl group; the rest of the side chain is converted into carbon dioxide and water.

Key Reactions

MethodStarting Material
Carbonation of Grignard reagentRMgX + CO2, then acid hydrolysis
Hydrolysis of nitrilesR—C≡N + hot aqueous acid or alkali
Oxidation of primary alcoholsR—CH2OH with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 or KMnO4
Oxidation of aldehydesR—CHO with Ag2O or strong oxidants
Oxidation of alkyl benzenesAlkyl benzene → benzoic acid

Key Points

  • Grignard reagents + CO2 give acids with one extra carbon atom.
  • Nitrile hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid and ammonia.
  • Primary alcohols oxidize through aldehydes to acids.
  • Aldehydes are easily oxidized, even by mild Ag2O.
  • Every alkyl benzene oxidizes to benzoic acid, whatever the side chain.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Carboxyl Group
lessons.notes_html:
The carboxyl group is made up of a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group attached to an alkyl group. Because of these groups, carboxylic acids show the following types of reactions:

  • (i) Reactions in which the hydrogen atom of the carboxyl group is involved. Salts are formed in these reactions.
  • (ii) Reactions in which an alkyl group is involved.
  • (iii) Reactions in which the carbonyl group is involved.
  • (iv) Reactions in which the hydroxyl group (—OH) is involved.
  • (v) Reactions in which the carboxyl group (—COOH) as a whole is involved.

Key Points

  • The carboxyl group contains a carbonyl part and a hydroxyl part.
  • Reactions may involve the H atom, the alkyl group, the carbonyl group, the —OH group, or the whole —COOH group.
  • Reactions of the H atom form salts.
  • Reactions involving the —OH group give the carboxylic acid derivatives.

lessons.title: Reactions involving Replacement of —OH Group
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acid derivatives are obtained by the replacement of the hydroxyl group (—OH) of the carboxyl group by halogen (—X), alkoxy (—OR), amino (—NH2) or carboxylate (—OCOR).

Conversion to Acyl Halides (Acid Halides)

Carboxylic acids react with phosphorus halides (PCl5, PCl3) or thionyl chloride (SOCl2) to give acyl halides:

  • R—COOH + PCl5 → R—COCl + POCl3 + HCl
  • 3R—COOH + PCl3 → 3R—COCl + H3PO3
  • R—COOH + SOCl2 → R—COCl + SO2 + HCl

All these reagents give acid chlorides in good yield. The best reagent is thionyl chloride, because it forms gaseous by-products (SO2 and HCl) that are easily removed.

Conversion to Acid Anhydrides

Carboxylic acids react with acyl chlorides in the presence of pyridine to give acid anhydrides:

R—COOH + R—COCl → (pyridine) (RCO)2O + HCl

Acid anhydrides can also be prepared by strongly heating the carboxylic acid in the presence of a dehydrating agent such as phosphorus pentoxide:

2CH3COOH → (P2O5, heat) (CH3CO)2O + H2O

Key Points

  • Replacing the —OH of —COOH gives the four acid derivatives.
  • PCl5, PCl3 and SOCl2 convert acids into acyl chlorides.
  • SOCl2 is the best reagent because its by-products are gases.
  • Acid + acyl chloride (pyridine) gives an acid anhydride.
  • Heating an acid with P2O5 also gives its anhydride.

lessons.title: Conversion to Esters
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of a strong acid such as H2SO4 or HCl to form esters. This reaction is reversible and is known as esterification:

CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH ⇌ CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O

Esters can also be prepared by the reaction of acyl chlorides with alcohols:

CH3COCl + CH3CH2OH → CH3COOCH2CH3 + HCl

This is one of the best methods to prepare an ester, and it does not need an acid catalyst.

Esters have a fruity smell and are used as artificial flavours.

EsterFlavourEsterFlavour
Amyl acetateBananaEthyl butyratePineapple
Benzyl acetateJasmineOctyl acetateOrange
Amyl butyrateApricotIsoamyl valerateApple
Isobutyl formateRaspberry

Key Points

  • Esterification: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, with strong acid catalyst.
  • Esterification is a reversible reaction.
  • Acyl chloride + alcohol is a better ester preparation and needs no catalyst.
  • Esters have fruity smells and are used as artificial flavours.

lessons.title: Conversion to Amides
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids react with aqueous ammonia to form ammonium salts of the carboxylic acid, which on heating give amides:

CH3COOH + NH3 → CH3COONH4 (ammonium acetate)

CH3COONH4 → (heat) CH3CONH2 (acetamide) + H2O

This is not a good method for the preparation of amides.

Amides can also be obtained by the reaction of acid anhydrides with ammonia (or amines):

(CH3CO)2O + 2NH3 → CH3CONH2 + CH3COONH4

Key Points

  • Acid + ammonia first gives an ammonium salt.
  • Heating the ammonium salt gives the amide and water.
  • This route is not a good preparation of amides.
  • Acid anhydrides + ammonia also give amides.

lessons.title: Interconversion of Carboxylic Acid Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acid derivatives are compounds that can be converted to carboxylic acids through simple acidic or basic hydrolysis. The most important acid derivatives are esters, amides, acid halides and acid anhydrides.

The carboxylic acid derivatives are a family of closely related functional groups. Carboxylic acids and all their derivatives contain carbonyl groups, and many of them can be easily interconverted.

  • All acid derivatives can be converted to carboxylic acids.
  • A derivative can be converted into a less reactive derivative, but it cannot be converted into a more reactive derivative. For example, esters can be converted to amides, but not into acid halides or anhydrides.

Order of reactivity: Acyl chloride > Acid anhydride > Ester = Carboxylic acid > Amide

Interconversion of Acid Chloride

  • Acid → acid chloride: with SOCl2 or PCl5.
  • Acid chloride → acid anhydride: with a carboxylic acid (the book's scheme uses CH3COOH with P2O5 and heat).
  • Acid chloride → ester: with an alcohol, e.g. CH3COCl + CH3OH → CH3COOCH3 + HCl.
  • Acid chloride → acid: hydrolysis with water.
  • Acid chloride → amide: with ammonia: R—COCl + 2NH3 → R—CONH2 + NH4Cl.

Key Points

  • All derivatives hydrolyze to carboxylic acids.
  • Conversions go from more reactive to less reactive derivatives only.
  • Reactivity order: acyl chloride > anhydride > ester = acid > amide.
  • Acid chlorides can be changed into anhydrides, esters, acids and amides.

lessons.title: Interconversion of Acid Anhydride
lessons.notes_html:
• Acid → acid anhydride: a carboxylic acid reacts with an acyl chloride in the presence of pyridine: R—COOH + R'—COCl → (RCO)2O type anhydride + HCl. Example: acetic acid + acetyl chloride gives acetic anhydride.
  • Acid anhydride → ester: with an alcohol, the anhydride gives an ester and a carboxylic acid: (CH3CO)2O + CH3OH → CH3COOCH3 + CH3COOH.
  • Acid anhydride → acid: hydrolysis with water gives two molecules of carboxylic acid: (CH3CO)2O + H2O → 2CH3COOH.
  • Acid anhydride → amide: with ammonia, the anhydride gives an amide and a carboxylic acid: (CH3CO)2O + NH3 → CH3CONH2 + CH3COOH.

Key Points

  • Acids form anhydrides with acyl chlorides in pyridine.
  • Anhydrides react with alcohols to give an ester plus an acid.
  • Hydrolysis of an anhydride gives two acid molecules.
  • Ammonia converts an anhydride into an amide plus an acid.

lessons.title: Interconversion of Ester
lessons.notes_html:
• Acid → ester: a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of HCl: R—COOH + R'OH → R—COOR' + H2O. Example: acetic acid + methanol gives methyl acetate.
  • Ester → acid: hydrolysis of the ester with water in the presence of HCl gives the carboxylic acid and an alcohol: CH3COOCH3 + H2O → CH3COOH + CH3OH.
  • Ester → amide: with ammonia, the ester gives an amide and an alcohol: CH3COOCH3 + NH3 → CH3CONH2 + CH3OH.

Key Points

  • Esters are made from acids and alcohols with an acid catalyst.
  • Hydrolysis converts an ester back into an acid and an alcohol.
  • Ammonia converts an ester into an amide.
  • Esters are less reactive than acid chlorides and anhydrides, so they cannot be converted back into them.

lessons.title: Interconversion of Amide
lessons.notes_html:
• Acid → amide: the acid is treated with ammonia to form the ammonium salt, which on heating (Δ) gives the amide: R—COOH → (NH3) R—COONH4 → (Δ) R—CONH2 + H2O.
  • Amide → acid: hydrolysis with water in the presence of HCl gives the carboxylic acid and ammonium chloride: R—CONH2 + H2O → (HCl) R—COOH + NH4Cl.

Amides are the least reactive of all the acid derivatives, so they cannot be converted into more reactive derivatives such as esters, acid anhydrides and acyl halides.

Key Points

  • Amides form from acids through their ammonium salts on heating.
  • Acid hydrolysis converts amides back into carboxylic acids.
  • Amides are the least reactive derivatives and cannot be converted upwards.
  • Amide hydrolysis is also the second step in the hydrolysis of nitriles to acids.

lessons.title: Reactions involving Carboxyl Group
lessons.notes_html:
Reduction to Alcohols

Two reagents are commonly used to reduce carbonyl compounds: LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride), a stronger reducing agent, and NaBH4 (sodium borohydride), a weaker reducing agent. NaBH4 is used to reduce aldehydes and ketones, but it is not used for carboxylic acids because the carboxyl group is resistant to reduction.

The most common reagent for the reduction of carboxylic acids is the most powerful reducing agent, LiAlH4. It reduces carboxylic acids, through aldehydes, to primary alcohols. The aldehyde formed as an intermediate cannot be isolated, because it is reduced more easily than the original carboxylic acid.

CH3COOH → (1. LiAlH4, ether; 2. H2O, H+) CH3CH2OH + LiOH + Al(OH)3

On complete reduction with HI in the presence of red phosphorus, carboxylic acids give alkanes:

CH3COOH + 6HI → (red P) CH3CH3 + 2H2O + 3I2

Decarboxylation Reactions

The loss of carbon dioxide from the carboxyl group of a molecule is called decarboxylation. Carboxylic acids are decarboxylated at high temperature in the presence of soda lime (a mixture of lime, CaO, and caustic soda, NaOH) to produce alkanes:

CH3COONa → (NaOH, heat) CH4 (methane) + Na2CO3

An acid containing a carbonyl group β to the carboxyl group (a β-keto acid) is decarboxylated on moderate heating, without soda lime. For example, 3-oxobutanoic acid (acetoacetic acid) gives acetone and carbon dioxide on warming:

CH3COCH2COOH → (warm) CH3COCH3 + CO2

Key Points

  • LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols; NaBH4 does not reduce them.
  • The aldehyde intermediate in this reduction cannot be isolated.
  • HI with red phosphorus reduces acids completely to alkanes.
  • Decarboxylation removes CO2 from the carboxyl group.
  • Soda lime decarboxylation converts acid salts into alkanes.
  • β-Keto acids decarboxylate on gentle warming alone.

lessons.title: Reactions of Acyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis (Reaction with Water)

Acyl halides react spontaneously with water to produce carboxylic acids and HCl:

CH3COCl + H2O → CH3COOH + HCl

The reaction of low molecular mass acid halides with water is fast, and that of high molecular mass acid halides is slow, because the higher acid halides are less soluble in water.

Reduction

Acyl chlorides are reduced to primary alcohols by LiAlH4:

CH3COCl + 4[H] → (LiAlH4) CH3CH2OH + HCl

Acid chlorides are more reactive than the other acid derivatives. Either LiAlH4 (stronger) or NaBH4 (weaker) converts acid chlorides into primary alcohols.

Friedel-Crafts Acylation

Acid halides react with aromatic hydrocarbons in the presence of aluminium chloride to form aromatic ketones. In this reaction, a hydrogen of benzene is replaced by an acyl group:

CH3COCl + C6H6 → (AlCl3) C6H5COCH3 (methyl phenyl ketone) + HCl

Key Points

  • Acyl halides hydrolyze spontaneously to acids and HCl.
  • Low molecular mass acyl halides hydrolyze faster than heavy ones.
  • LiAlH4 or NaBH4 reduces acyl chlorides to primary alcohols.
  • Acyl chlorides are the most reactive acid derivatives.
  • With benzene and AlCl3, acyl halides give aromatic ketones (Friedel-Crafts acylation).

lessons.title: Reactions of Acid Anhydrides
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis

Acid anhydrides react with water to produce carboxylic acids:

(CH3CO)2O + H2O → 2CH3COOH

Reduction

LiAlH4 reduces anhydrides to primary alcohols:

(RCO)2O + 8[H] → (LiAlH4) 2R—CH2OH + H2O

For example, acetic anhydride gives two molecules of ethyl alcohol.

In general form: (RCO)2O + H2O → 2R—COOH.

Key Points

  • Hydrolysis of an anhydride gives two molecules of carboxylic acid.
  • LiAlH4 reduces anhydrides to primary alcohols.
  • One anhydride molecule gives two alcohol molecules on reduction.
  • In reactivity, anhydrides stand below acyl chlorides but above esters and amides.

lessons.title: Reactions of Esters
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis

Esters react with water to produce a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. The reaction is catalyzed by strong mineral acids such as HCl or H2SO4 and by heat:

CH3COOCH3 + H2O → (HCl, heat) CH3COOH + CH3OH

Reduction

LiAlH4 reduces esters to primary alcohols. The ester gives the primary alcohol of its acid part and the alcohol of its alkoxy part:

CH3COOCH3 + 4[H] → (LiAlH4, ether) CH3CH2OH + CH3OH

Reaction with Grignard's Reagent

Esters other than formates react with Grignard's reagent to form ketones, which react further with another molecule of Grignard's reagent to form a tertiary alcohol as the final product. In step 1, the Grignard reagent attacks the ester carbonyl and an unstable intermediate breaks down to a ketone. In step 2, the ketone reacts with a second Grignard molecule and, after hydrolysis, gives the tertiary alcohol.

Formate esters react in the same way with excess Grignard's reagent, but they form secondary alcohols.

Key Points

  • Acid hydrolysis of esters gives a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
  • LiAlH4 reduces esters to primary alcohols.
  • Esters react with two molecules of Grignard reagent.
  • Ordinary esters finally give tertiary alcohols; formates give secondary alcohols.

lessons.title: Reactions of Amides
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis

Amides are the most stable of the acid derivatives, and considerably more vigorous conditions are needed for their hydrolysis. Amides do not react with water under normal conditions. They react with water when the mixture is heated in the presence of an acid or a base:

CH3CONH2 + H2O → (acid or base, heat) CH3COOH + NH3

Reduction

Lithium aluminium hydride reduces amides to amines. The product is a primary, secondary or tertiary amine, depending on the degree of substitution on the amide:

  • Acetamide → ethylamine (1° amine).
  • N-Methylacetamide → ethylmethylamine (2° amine).
  • N,N-Dimethylacetamide → ethyldimethylamine (3° amine).

Key Points

  • Amides are the most stable acid derivatives.
  • Amide hydrolysis needs heating with an acid or a base.
  • Hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid and ammonia.
  • LiAlH4 reduces amides to amines (1°, 2° or 3° according to substitution).

lessons.title: Reactions of Nitriles
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrolysis

Nitriles are more stable compounds than amides and esters, so they are hard to hydrolyze and require severe conditions. When heated with water in the presence of an acid or alkali, nitriles are hydrolyzed to carboxylic acids. They first produce an amide, which is then hydrolyzed to the carboxylic acid:

CH3—C≡N → (acid or base) CH3CONH2 → (H2O, heat) CH3COOH + NH3

Reduction

Lithium aluminium hydride reduces nitriles to primary amines:

CH3—C≡N + 4[H] → (LiAlH4, ether) CH3CH2NH2 (ethylamine)

Reaction with Grignard's Reagent

Nitriles react with Grignard's reagent to form ketimines, which on acid hydrolysis give ketones:

CH3—C≡N + CH3MgCl → ketimine → (2H2O/H+) CH3COCH3 (acetone) + NH3

Sources and Uses of Carboxylic Acids

Most of the simpler saturated carboxylic acids are found in fruits, vegetables and other natural products, which they give a distinct flavour or tang. Carboxylic acids are mainly used as antibacterial and antifungal preservatives and as flavouring agents in foods and pharmaceutical products.

  • Formic acid: in insect stings and nettles.
  • Acetic acid: in vinegar; used in food preservation and in pickles; stops the growth of bacteria.
  • Butyric acid: in butter; responsible for the smell of rancid butter and the odour of sweat.
  • Palmitic acid: in palm oil. Stearic acid: in chocolate, waxes, soaps, animal fats and oils.
  • Oxalic acid: in spinach and rhubarb; used as a cleaning agent for rust stains on fabric and porcelain.
  • Citric acid: in citrus fruits, pineapple and tomatoes; preservative and flavouring agent in foods and soft drinks.
  • Malic acid: in unripe fruits such as green apples and pears. Tartaric acid: in grapes, bananas, potatoes and tamarinds; gives wine its tartness.
  • Lactic acid: in sour milk such as yoghurt; used as a preservative. Benzoic acid: in berries, plums and prunes.
  • Adipic acid: in beets and sugar cane. Tannic acid: in the bark of trees; used for tanning, staining wood and dyeing cotton.
  • Amino acids are a special form of carboxylic acids; their groupings make up the proteins, and skin, hair and muscle are composed of protein.

Key Points

  • Nitrile hydrolysis goes through an amide and needs severe conditions.
  • LiAlH4 reduces nitriles to primary amines.
  • Nitriles + Grignard reagent give ketones after hydrolysis of the ketimine.
  • Carboxylic acids occur widely in natural foods and are used as preservatives and flavours.
  • Amino acids are special carboxylic acids that build proteins.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the substances present in living organisms, their structures, functions and interactions. This chapter studies the main biomolecules: carbohydrates, proteins, enzymes, lipids, nucleic acids and minerals.

Carbohydrates are the most abundant naturally occurring compounds. They are widely distributed in plants and animals. Plants are their major source: carbohydrates form about three-fourths of the dry weight of plants, but less than 1% of animal matter. Glucose, glycogen and starch supply energy, while cellulose gives structural support.

The name carbohydrate means hydrate of carbon, because the general formula is Cx(H2O)y. In modern terms, carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or compounds that give such compounds on hydrolysis. Examples are glucose, lactose, sucrose and starch. They exist mainly in hemiacetal or acetal forms. They are also called saccharides (from words meaning sugar) because the low molecular mass carbohydrates taste sweet. Green plants and algae make carbohydrates by photosynthesis.

Classification of Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are classified into monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides.

Monosaccharides are simple sugars that cannot be hydrolysed into simpler carbohydrates. Their general formula is Cx(H2O)y and they contain 3 to 6 carbon atoms. They are sweet in taste and soluble in water. They are of two types: aldoses, which have an aldehyde group (for example glyceraldehyde and glucose), and ketoses, which have a ketone group (for example dihydroxyacetone and fructose). Glucose is also called dextrose, grape sugar or blood sugar. It occurs free in sweet fruits and honey and in small amounts in human blood and urine, and in combined form in disaccharides and polysaccharides. Fructose occurs free and in combined form and is used as a sweetening agent in confectionery as a substitute for cane sugar.

Oligosaccharides (from a Greek word meaning few) give 2 to 10 monosaccharide molecules on hydrolysis. Disaccharides give two units (sucrose, lactose, maltose), trisaccharides give three (raffinose, rabinose) and tetrasaccharides give four (scorodose, stachyose).

Polysaccharides give more than 10 monosaccharide molecules on hydrolysis. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polysaccharides with the formula (C6H10O5)n. They are polymers of hundreds or thousands of monosaccharide units, have high molecular mass, and are tasteless, amorphous, water-insoluble solids, so they are called non-sugars. Plants store glucose as starch, while animals store it as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

Key Reactions

HydrolysisProducts
C12H22O11 (sucrose) + H2O →C6H12O6 (glucose) + C6H12O6 (fructose)
C18H32O16 (raffinose) + 2H2O →glucose + fructose + galactose
C24H42O21 (stachyose) + 3H2O →glucose + fructose + 2 galactose
C6H12O6 (monosaccharide) + H2O →No reaction (cannot be hydrolysed)

Key Points

  • Biochemistry studies the substances of living organisms and their structures, functions and interactions.
  • Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, with the old general formula Cx(H2O)y.
  • Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) cannot be hydrolysed; aldoses have an aldehyde group and ketoses a ketone group.
  • Oligosaccharides give 2 to 10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; sucrose gives glucose and fructose.
  • Polysaccharides such as starch, glycogen and cellulose give more than 10 units and are non-sugars.
  • Plants store glucose as starch; animals store it as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

lessons.title: Function of Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates perform many important functions in living organisms.

  • They provide energy for all cell activities, including the working of the heart, brain, kidneys and muscles.
  • They regulate the functioning of nerve tissue.
  • They act as a substrate (starting material) for respiration.
  • Ribose and deoxyribose are parts of RNA and DNA.
  • Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver. Glucose is also changed into fats and non-essential amino acids. The stored glycogen is used in starvation.
  • Carbohydrates are constituents of many hormones, vitamins and enzymes.
  • As components of other biomolecules, they take part in blood clotting, immunity and fertilization.
  • They clear the gut and prevent constipation.
  • Starch and its fibres play an important role in digestion.
  • They are constituents of cellular organelles such as the cell membrane, mitochondria, nucleus and endoplasmic reticulum, and maintain their structural integrity.
  • Cellulose gives structural support to plant cells.
  • The exoskeleton of arthropods such as insects, lobsters, crabs and other crustaceans is made of chitin, a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide, which gives support and protection.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates are the main energy source for cells, the brain, heart, kidneys and muscles.
  • Ribose and deoxyribose are the sugars of RNA and DNA.
  • Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and can be changed into fats and non-essential amino acids.
  • Carbohydrates help in blood clotting, immunity, fertilization and digestion, and prevent constipation.
  • Cellulose supports plant cells, and chitin forms the exoskeleton of arthropods.

lessons.title: Nutritional Importance of Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
Foods such as fruits, grains, vegetables, breads and dairy products are rich in carbohydrates. They give us glucose, the main source of energy for the brain, kidneys, heart, muscles and the central nervous system. Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver and is used during exercise. Carbohydrates provide nutrients for the good bacteria in the gut and protect the muscles, because the body uses carbohydrates for energy first; otherwise proteins and fats would be used and less protein would remain for building muscles.

Hypoglycaemia is low blood sugar, below the normal value. It is associated with diabetes, but can also occur in healthy people who lack carbohydrates. Its symptoms are tiredness, weakness, light-headedness, confusion and hunger.

Hyperglycaemia is high blood sugar, above the normal value. It can cause heart disease, eye damage and kidney failure. Lifestyle changes help to control it, and complex carbohydrates are encouraged instead of simple carbohydrates because they lower the rise in blood sugar.

Fibre is essential for the prevention of cancer and for healthy digestion, and whole grains lower the risk of constipation. Ketosis is a normal metabolic process that occurs in the absence of carbohydrates: when glycogen stores are used up, the body burns fat and makes ketones. A balanced diet keeps ketosis under control.

Glycogen Storage and Muscular Activity

Most body glycogen is stored in the skeletal muscles (about 500 g) and the liver (about 100 g), with small amounts in the heart, kidneys and brain. Eating more carbohydrates increases muscle glycogen, so the stores last longer. The liver releases glucose into the bloodstream for other tissues, but muscles do not release glucose directly. During intense activity such as a marathon, muscle glycogen is broken down and released as lactate into the blood; the liver changes the lactate back into glucose, which returns to the muscles. Muscle glycogen is important for running, cycling, weight lifting, climbing, dancing, yoga, football, hockey and push-ups. If muscle glycogen runs out, the athlete must slow down, so simple carbohydrates are eaten before and during intense activity.

Carbohydrates and Joint Lubrication

Complex carbohydrates attached to amino acids, proteins and lipids by glycosidic linkages form glycoconjugates, which provide lubrication to the elbow and knee. Glucosamine, an aminosaccharide, helps in repairing and lubricating joints such as the elbow, knee and shoulder, and improves flexibility and mobility. Glucosaminoglycans (GAGs) such as chondroitin sulphate are jelly-like substances in cartilage, tendons and connective tissues that lubricate joint surfaces. Hyaluronic acid is present in synovial fluid, the viscous slippery fluid in synovial joint cavities. Chondroitin sulphate and hyaluronic acid reduce friction between cartilage and the tissues of the elbows and knees. Proteoglycans (mucoproteins), in which proteins are bonded at many sites to GAGs, are present in connective tissues and also act as joint lubricants.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrate foods give glucose, the main fuel of the brain, heart, kidneys, muscles and nervous system.
  • Hypoglycaemia is low blood sugar; hyperglycaemia is high blood sugar and can damage the heart, eyes and kidneys.
  • Fibre keeps digestion healthy and prevents constipation; ketosis is fat burning when glycogen runs out.
  • About 500 g of glycogen is stored in skeletal muscles and about 100 g in the liver.
  • Glucosamine, chondroitin sulphate, hyaluronic acid and proteoglycans lubricate the joints.

lessons.title: Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are high molecular mass organic compounds that give amino acids on complete hydrolysis. The word protein comes from the Greek word Proteios, meaning first, because proteins are of first importance: life is impossible without them. They are present in all living organisms, for example in skin, hair, wool, feathers, nails, horns, hoofs and nerves. Proteins contain carbon (51%), hydrogen (7%), oxygen (23%), nitrogen (16%), sulphur (1-3%) and phosphorus (less than 1%), and may also contain copper, iodine, manganese and zinc.

Classification of Proteins

On the basis of their physical and chemical properties, proteins are classified into simple, compound and derived proteins.

Simple proteins give only amino acids or their derivatives on hydrolysis. Examples are albumins, globulins, legumin, glutelins, histones and collagen. They are the most abundant proteins in animals, forming 25-35% of body protein. Albumins occur in blood, egg white and wheat; globulins in blood, muscle and potatoes; legumin and collagen in connective tissues; glutelins in wheat and rice; and histones in the thymus gland, pancreas and nucleoproteins.

Compound (conjugated) proteins give amino acids along with a non-protein group, called the prosthetic group, on hydrolysis. Examples are phosphoproteins, which contain phosphoric acid, and lipoproteins, which contain lipids such as cholesterol and fatty acids.

Derived proteins are obtained from simple and conjugated proteins. Examples are polypeptides and proteoses.

Key Points

  • Proteins give amino acids on complete hydrolysis and are essential for all living organisms.
  • Proteins contain C, H, O and N, with small amounts of S and P.
  • Simple proteins give only amino acids on hydrolysis, for example albumins, globulins and histones.
  • Conjugated proteins give amino acids plus a non-protein prosthetic group, for example phosphoproteins and lipoproteins.
  • Derived proteins, such as polypeptides and proteoses, are obtained from simple and conjugated proteins.

lessons.title: Structure of Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are built from amino acids. In an amino acid, a central carbon atom carries an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom and an alkyl group (R). Amino acids are written with a three-letter code and also with a one-letter symbol.

SymbolAmino AcidCodeSymbolAmino AcidCode
GGlycineGlySSerineSer
AAlanineAlaPProlinePro
LLeucineLeuVValineVal
MMethionineMetIIsoleucineIle
FPhenylalaninePheCCysteineCys
WTryptophanTrpYTyrosineTyr
KLysineLysHHistidineHis
QGlutamineGlnRArginineArg
EGlutamic acidGluNAsparagineAsn
DAspartic acidAspTThreonineThr

Four Levels of Protein Structure

Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain, held together by peptide bonds formed during protein biosynthesis. It is described from the N-terminal (amino terminal) end to the C-terminal (carbonyl terminal) end, for example Met-Arg-Leu-Ala-Val-Phe. It is very important, because many genetic diseases result from abnormal amino acid sequences, which cause improper folding and loss or impairment of normal function. Haemoglobin is the best example of primary structure.

Secondary structure consists of regular coiled or zigzag structures held by hydrogen bonding between -NH and -CO groups of the chain.

Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional twisting and folding of the polypeptide chain. Myoglobin is its best example. Insulin has primary, secondary and tertiary structures.

Quaternary structure is formed when two or more polypeptide chains (tertiary structures) join together; the chains may be similar or different. Most proteins have only one chain, so they have no quaternary structure. Haemoglobin (four chains) and collagen (three chains) have quaternary structure. Every protein has primary, secondary and tertiary structure, but only some have quaternary structure.

Key Points

  • An amino acid has a central carbon carrying -NH2, -COOH, H and an R group; 20 amino acids build proteins.
  • Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held by peptide bonds, read from the N-terminal to the C-terminal end.
  • Secondary structure is regular coiling or zigzag folding held by hydrogen bonds.
  • Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of one chain, as in myoglobin.
  • Quaternary structure joins two or more chains, as in haemoglobin (4 chains) and collagen (3 chains).

lessons.title: Properties of Protein
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Proteins

  • Proteins contain C, H and O, with a small amount of sulphur.
  • They are complex compounds in which amino acids are linked by peptide bonds.
  • They act as biological catalysts, give structural support and secrete hormones.
  • They are amphoteric, so they react with both acids and bases.
  • Denaturing is the disruption of the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures of a protein. It is caused by heat, change of pH and strong oxidising or reducing agents. Coagulation is the most common observation of denaturing: the albumin of egg white coagulates when an egg is heated.

Importance of Proteins

  • Proteins form the protoplasm of cells.
  • They take part in muscle contraction, digestion of food and clotting of blood.
  • Almost all enzymes are proteins, so proteins act as organic catalysts.
  • Haemoglobin transports oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.
  • Insulin regulates glucose metabolism, and myosin is present in muscles.
  • Protamine, a strongly basic protein, is found in the nucleic acids of sperm cells, and nucleoproteins such as histones and protamine are carriers of heredity.
  • In industry, proteins are used in the tanning of leather (precipitation of proteins with tannic acid), in making buttons, buckles and paper sizing from casein of milk, and in making gelatine from bones, skins and tendons, used in jelly, glue and photography.

Fibrous Proteins

Fibrous proteins have elongated polypeptide chains. They are found only in animals, are insoluble in water and give structural support to cells and tissues. They construct connective tissues, tendons, bone matrix and muscle fibre. Examples are keratins, collagens and elastins. Keratin, found in skin, hair and nails, keeps hair and nails healthy and protects the skin from damage and stress. Collagen, found in bone, cartilage, tendons and ligaments, gives tensile strength. Elastin, found in connective tissues, has elastic properties, so tissues resume their shape after stretching or contracting, for example the skin returns to its shape after being poked or pinched.

Key Points

  • Proteins are amphoteric and are denatured by heat, pH change and strong oxidising or reducing agents.
  • Coagulation of egg albumin on heating is an example of denaturing.
  • Proteins form protoplasm, enzymes and hormones; haemoglobin carries oxygen and insulin controls glucose.
  • Casein is used for buttons and paper sizing, and gelatine for jelly, glue and photography.
  • Fibrous proteins (keratin, collagen, elastin) are insoluble, elongated and give support, strength and elasticity.

lessons.title: Enzymes
lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes are proteins that act as catalysts and increase the rate of chemical reactions in living organisms, such as respiration, photosynthesis and the formation of new proteins. Examples are lipase, zymase, glycosidase and isomerase. Enzymes are produced only by living cells and catalyse reactions inside and outside the cells. Without enzymes, life processes would be too slow and life would be practically impossible. Enzymes increase the rate of reaction by 10^4 to 10^20 times. They are highly specific: one enzyme catalyses only one type of reaction. For example, sucrase hydrolyses only sucrose, and glucokinase catalyses only glucose. An enzyme has two parts: the protein part, called the apo-enzyme, and the non-protein part, called the co-enzyme or co-factor.

Role of Enzymes as Biocatalysts

A natural substance that initiates or increases the rate of a reaction in a living body is called a biocatalyst. Enzymes play this role in metabolism, respiration and digestion. The body produces digestive enzymes, which digest food, and metabolic enzymes, which run all the biochemical reactions in the cells.

Amylase is made in two places. Salivary amylase, present in saliva, converts about 30% of the carbohydrates (starch and sugar) in food into simple sugars in the mouth; this is why bread tastes sweet when it is chewed for a long time. Pancreatic amylase, present in pancreatic juice from the pancreas, does the same work.

Lipase, present in pancreatic juice, breaks down dietary fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Fat digestion in the small intestine is helped by bile, which is made in the liver and breaks fat into small droplets on which lipase can act. Bile itself is not an enzyme.

Protease is the general term for pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin. Pepsin, present in the gastric juice of the stomach, breaks proteins into peptides. Trypsin and chymotrypsin are produced in the pancreas and released into the small intestine through the pancreatic duct; they complete the digestion of proteins into simple amino acids. Vitamins, minerals and water are not digested, because they are already small enough to be absorbed, and digestive enzymes cannot break down dietary fibre.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up reactions by 10^4 to 10^20 times and are highly specific.
  • An enzyme consists of a protein apo-enzyme and a non-protein co-enzyme or co-factor.
  • Amylase digests carbohydrates, lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol, and proteases digest proteins.
  • Pepsin works in the stomach; trypsin and chymotrypsin from the pancreas work in the small intestine.
  • Bile helps fat digestion by making small fat droplets, but bile is not an enzyme.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
lessons.notes_html:
Concentration

The rate of reaction increases with the enzyme concentration: for example, the rate of digestion increases as the concentration of pepsin increases. The rate is also directly proportional to the substrate concentration.

Temperature

Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to about 45°C. Above 45°C enzymes, being proteins, are denatured and become inactive, and at 100°C they are completely destroyed. At low temperature (0°C) activity is reduced but the enzyme is not destroyed. The optimum temperature for enzymes of the mammalian body is about 37°C to 40°C, and it differs for different enzymes.

Effect of pH

The pH at which an enzyme shows maximum activity is its optimum pH. The optimum pH of salivary amylase is 6.4 to 6.9, while that of pepsin of the stomach is 1.4. Pepsin is inactive in neutral and alkaline solutions. The optimum pH of enzymes is never found above 10.

Effect of Other Substances

Co-enzymes are the non-protein part of an enzyme; the protein part is the apo-enzyme, so Enzyme = Co-enzyme + Apo-enzyme. Vitamins are examples of co-enzymes, and certain enzymes cannot function without them. Activators are inorganic substances that increase enzyme activity, for example Mg2+ for phosphatase and Zn2+ for carbonic anhydrase. Inhibitors reduce or destroy enzyme activity; sulpha drugs, penicillin and streptomycin act as inhibitors and cure many infections.

Radiation

Enzymes are generally inactivated by ultraviolet light and by beta, gamma and X-rays.

Key Points

  • Reaction rate increases with both enzyme concentration and substrate concentration.
  • Activity rises with temperature up to about 45°C; above this enzymes denature, and at 100°C they are destroyed.
  • The optimum temperature for mammalian enzymes is about 37°C to 40°C.
  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH: salivary amylase 6.4-6.9 and pepsin 1.4.
  • Vitamins act as co-enzymes; Mg2+ and Zn2+ act as activators; sulpha drugs and penicillin act as inhibitors.
  • UV light and beta, gamma and X-rays inactivate enzymes.

lessons.title: Industrial Application of Enzymes
lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes are among the most efficient catalysts known. They are used in the food, beverage, cosmetic, detergent, leather, agriculture and medicine industries, and in making biofuels and biopolymers.

Food Industry

Enzymes process carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Amylase, lactases and cellulases break complex sugars into simple sugars, and lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

Beverage Industry

Enzymes increase the yield of juice and decrease energy consumption. Pectinase breaks down pectins in fruit juice and makes the juice less viscous. Cellulases and hemicellulases break the plant cell wall for efficient liquefaction of fruit pulp. Neutral proteases, alpha amylase, beta-glucanase and cellulases are used in alcoholic beverages such as beer, wine, brandy, whiskey and rum.

Detergent Industry

Proteases, lipases, amylases and cellulases are added to detergents. They break down and remove dirt and stains from cloth fibres.

Leather Industry

Enzymes are used in the soaking, dehairing and dyeing of leather. Proteases remove hair from hides, and pancreatic enzymes increase the softness of leather.

Paper Industry

Amylases, xylanases, cellulases, laccase, lipase and ligninases are used in the pulp and paper industry. They lower viscosity, help in coating paper, remove colour, smooth the fibres, enhance water drainage and increase softness.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are used in food, beverages, detergents, leather, paper, medicines, biofuels and biopolymers.
  • Pectinase clarifies fruit juice; cellulases and hemicellulases liquefy fruit pulp.
  • Proteases, lipases, amylases and cellulases in detergents remove dirt and stains.
  • Proteases dehair hides in the leather industry, and pancreatic enzymes soften leather.
  • Xylanases, laccase and ligninases are used in pulp and paper making.

lessons.title: Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are a naturally occurring heterogeneous group of organic compounds of animals and plants. They are soluble in organic solvents such as acetone, benzene and CCl4, but insoluble in water. Fats, oils and waxes are lipids. The word lipid comes from the Greek word Lipas, meaning fats. Fats and oils are the most important lipids in nature: lipids that are solid at ambient temperature are called fats, and those that are liquid are called oils.

Classification of Lipids

Simple lipids are esters of fatty acids with glycerol. The common fats and oils belong to this class.

Compound lipids have additional radicals along with fatty acids and alcohols. Examples are phospholipids and lipoproteins.

Derived lipids are obtained by the hydrolysis of simple or compound lipids and are also called associated lipids. Examples are sterols, vitamin D and terpenes. Steroids are lipids with high molecular mass tetracyclic compounds; cholesterol is an example.

The book also names edible lipids: the lipids which have fats, oils and waxes are called edible lipids.

Structure of Lipids (Fats and Oils)

Lipids do not have a single common structure. Fats and oils are triesters of glycerol with fatty acids, called triglycerides or glycerides. One glycerol molecule reacts with three fatty acid molecules to form a triglyceride and three water molecules. Common oils and fats are mixtures of saturated and unsaturated triglycerides. Solid or semi-solid triesters of long-chain saturated fatty acids are fats, while liquid triesters of long-chain unsaturated fatty acids are oils.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
Formation of a triglycerideGlycerol + 3 fatty acids → Triglyceride + 3H2O

Key Points

  • Lipids are soluble in organic solvents and insoluble in water; solid lipids are fats and liquid lipids are oils.
  • Simple lipids are esters of fatty acids with glycerol, such as fats and oils.
  • Compound lipids contain extra groups, for example phospholipids and lipoproteins.
  • Derived lipids come from hydrolysis of simple or compound lipids, for example sterols, vitamin D and terpenes.
  • Fats and oils are triglycerides: triesters of glycerol with three fatty acids.
  • Steroids are tetracyclic lipids; cholesterol is the common example.

lessons.title: Properties of Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

  • Pure fats and oils are colourless, odourless and tasteless.
  • They are liquids or non-crystalline solids at room temperature.
  • They are insoluble in water but readily soluble in organic solvents.
  • They form emulsions when shaken with water in the presence of a base such as NaOH.
  • They are poor conductors of heat and electricity, so they are excellent insulators for the animal body.

Chemical Properties

Hydrolysis: oils and fats give glycerol and fatty acids on hydrolysis with the enzyme lipase.

Saponification: the reaction of fats and oils with NaOH to give soap and glycerol is called saponification.

Hardening of oils: when hydrogen is passed through an unsaturated glyceride (an oil) in the presence of a nickel catalyst, a saturated glyceride (a fat) is obtained. This process is called hardening or hydrogenation. Glycerol trioleate (an oil) takes up 3H2 and forms glycerol tristearate (a fat). Hardened oils are used to make vegetable ghee and margarine, and also in soaps and candles.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
Hydrolysis (lipase)Triglyceride + 3H2O → Glycerol + 3 fatty acids
SaponificationTriglyceride + 3NaOH → Glycerol + 3 soap (R-COONa)
Hydrogenation (Ni)Glycerol trioleate (oil) + 3H2 → Glycerol tristearate (fat)

Key Points

  • Pure fats and oils are colourless, odourless and tasteless, and are insoluble in water.
  • Lipids form emulsions with water in the presence of a base and act as insulators in the body.
  • Hydrolysis with lipase gives glycerol and fatty acids.
  • Saponification with NaOH gives soap and glycerol.
  • Hydrogenation over nickel hardens oils into fats, used for vegetable ghee, margarine, soaps and candles.

lessons.title: Nutritional and Biological Importance of Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
• The main role of lipids is to provide energy for muscles and body processes. Fat gives 9 kcal per gram, while protein and carbohydrate give only 4 kcal per gram.
  • Lipids provide energy to digest and absorb food.
  • The essential lipids linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid cannot be synthesised in the body, so they must be taken in the diet. They are necessary for the regulation of blood pressure, blood clotting, liver function and immune and inflammatory responses, for the proper development and functioning of the brain and nervous system, and for healthy skin and hair.
  • Phospholipids, the second most common lipids, are structural components of cell membranes. The membranes act as barriers and prevent charged particles and large molecules from moving across them.
  • Cholesterol is the starting material for vitamin D and for bile acids, which aid the digestion and absorption of fats.
  • Cholesterol is also used in the synthesis of sex hormones.
  • Lipids are components of the nervous system.
  • Lipids act as carriers of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K from the intestine to the bloodstream.

Hibernating Animals Accumulate Fat

Hibernation is a state of inactivity during winter in which body temperature, heart rate, breathing and metabolic rate all fall. The animal goes into a deep sleep and conserves energy, because food is stored in the body as fat. Fat is a rich and efficient energy source, giving 9 kcal per gram compared with 4 kcal per gram from carbohydrates and proteins. The hibernation period depends on the species, the time of year and the body condition of the animal, and may last for days, weeks or months.

Key Points

  • Fats give 9 kcal per gram, more than double the energy from carbohydrates or proteins (4 kcal per gram).
  • Essential fatty acids (linoleic and alpha-linolenic) must come from the diet.
  • Phospholipids form cell membranes, which act as selective barriers.
  • Cholesterol is the starting material for vitamin D, bile acids and sex hormones.
  • Lipids carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
  • Hibernating animals store food as fat because it is the most efficient energy store.

lessons.title: Nucleic Acids
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are high molecular mass biopolymers of nucleotides. They are present in the nucleus of all eukaryotic living cells and in viruses, and they are the carriers of hereditary information. They were first isolated from the nuclei of pus cells (white blood corpuscles) in 1869 by Friedrich Miescher. They are called nucleic acids because they are present in the nucleus and are acidic in nature.

There are two main classes: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid). DNA is the master blueprint for life and is the genetic material in all free-living organisms and most viruses. RNA is the genetic material of certain viruses and is also present in all living cells, where it plays a role in making proteins. Both DNA and RNA are formed from a large number of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and phosphoric acid joined by ester linkage.

Nitrogenous Bases

The bases are purine and pyrimidine derivatives. Pyrimidines have a single six-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3; their derivatives are cytosine, thymine and uracil. Purines have two rings, a pyrimidine ring and an imidazole ring (C3H4N2); their derivatives are adenine and guanine. DNA contains cytosine, thymine, adenine and guanine; in RNA thymine is absent and uracil takes its place.

Pentose Sugar and Phosphoric Acid

The sugar in DNA is D-2-deoxyribose and the sugar in RNA is D-ribose. The carbon atoms of the sugar are numbered with a prime symbol, for example 1', 3' and 5'. Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) forms the phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides.

ComponentDNARNA
PurinesAdenine, GuanineAdenine, Guanine
PyrimidinesCytosine, ThymineCytosine, Uracil
Pentose sugarD-2-deoxyriboseD-ribose
AcidPhosphoric acidPhosphoric acid

Key Points

  • Nucleic acids are biopolymers of nucleotides and carry hereditary information.
  • DNA is the genetic material of almost all organisms; RNA is the genetic material of some viruses and helps in protein making.
  • Each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and phosphoric acid.
  • Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine and uracil.
  • DNA has deoxyribose and thymine; RNA has ribose and uracil instead of thymine.

lessons.title: Nucleic Acid Polymers
lessons.notes_html:
DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides, so they are called polynucleotides. A nucleotide is made of three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. The pentose sugar is the central component: the base is attached to carbon 1 of the sugar and the phosphate group is attached to carbon 5.

Nucleotides are linked to each other by phosphate ester bonds. The hydroxyl group of the phosphate on one nucleotide condenses with a hydroxyl group on the carbohydrate ring of another nucleotide, and in this way polynucleotides are built up. The phosphodiester bond joins the phosphate group at position 5 of one pentose sugar to the hydroxyl group at position 3 of the next sugar. DNA is a polydeoxyribonucleotide and RNA is a polyribonucleotide.

Storage of Genetic Information

Nucleic acids have two main functions: the storage of genetic information and the synthesis of proteins. DNA stores biological information in the sequences of its four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. A sequence of bases forms a gene. Genes are located on the chromosomal thread that runs along the entire length of a chromosome, and each gene occupies a specific position on the chromosome. Genes provide the instructions for making proteins, and proteins determine the structure and function of each cell. In this way, genes are responsible for inheritance.

Key Points

  • A nucleotide = base + pentose sugar + phosphate; the base is on carbon 1 and the phosphate on carbon 5 of the sugar.
  • Nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds between the 5' phosphate of one sugar and the 3' hydroxyl of the next.
  • DNA is a polydeoxyribonucleotide; RNA is a polyribonucleotide.
  • DNA stores information in the sequence of its four bases.
  • Genes are base sequences on chromosomes that give instructions for making proteins and control inheritance.

lessons.title: Minerals of Biological Importance
lessons.notes_html:
Minerals are inorganic compounds that are essential in small amounts for good health and for the prevention of diseases. Major minerals are required in amounts of 100 mg or more per day; they include sodium, potassium, calcium and manganese, and the non-metals chlorine, sulphur and phosphorus. Trace minerals are required in only a few milligrams per day; they include iron, copper, zinc, selenium and iodine. The most important minerals are iron, calcium, phosphorus and zinc. Minerals are not synthesised in the body, so they must be obtained from the diet. Daily requirements differ slightly for children, youngsters, and during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Sources of Important Minerals

MineralSources
CalciumDairy products, green leafy vegetables, salmon, turnips, spinach, almonds, broccoli, cabbage, kale, tofu, apricots, garlic, dates, sardines, papaya
