IronRed meat, poultry, fish, liver, legumes, egg yolk, dark green vegetables, dried fruits, whole iron-enriched grains
PhosphorusProtein-rich foods: dairy products, nuts, seeds, legumes, meat, fish
ZincMeats, mushrooms, liver, poultry, seafood, nuts, whole grains, soybeans, milk and dairy products
MagnesiumNuts, seeds, whole grains, apricots, beans, green leafy vegetables, potatoes, banana, milk, spinach; found especially in plant foods
PotassiumSpinach, apples, tomatoes, bananas, strawberries, fresh orange juice, papaya, apricots, pineapple, dried fruits, rice, cucumbers, garlic, ginger, legumes

Key Points

  • Minerals are inorganic and essential in small amounts; the body cannot make them, so they come from food.
  • Major minerals are needed at 100 mg or more per day; trace minerals at only a few milligrams per day.
  • Iron, calcium, phosphorus and zinc are the most important minerals.
  • Calcium comes mainly from dairy products and green leafy vegetables.
  • Iron comes from red meat, liver, egg yolk, legumes and dark green vegetables.
  • Magnesium is found especially in plant foods such as nuts, seeds and green leafy vegetables.

lessons.title: Biological Significance of Iron, Calcium, Phosphorus and Zinc
lessons.notes_html:
Iron

Iron is an essential mineral. It plays an important role in the production of red blood cells and helps the red blood cells to carry oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. It also plays an important role in the immune system and prevents us from feeling tired. Lack of iron in the red blood cells causes anaemia, whose symptoms are weakness, tiredness and shortness of breath.

Calcium

Calcium is essential for building strong bones and teeth in children and teens. It helps the muscles to contract and relax, and it is important in blood clotting, blood pressure regulation and the immune system. It also supports nerve transmission. Calcium deficiency may cause osteoporosis (brittle bones in adults), rickets (softening of bones in children), poor growth and mental depression.

Phosphorus

Phosphorus is important for healthy bones and teeth; more than 80% of the phosphorus in the human body is located in the bones as calcium phosphate. It has a role in energy production as a component of ATP, and it is a component of the nucleic acids DNA and RNA, which regulate protein synthesis. It is a constituent of plant cells and is essential for cell division and the development of new tissues, for the repair of body cells and tissues, for acid-base balance (regulating pH) in the body, and for the working of the muscular system, including the beating of the heart. Phosphorus deficiency is relatively uncommon, but it may cause rickets in children and osteomalacia (softening of bones) in adults, especially in pregnant women. An improper balance of phosphorus and calcium may cause osteoporosis. Symptoms of deficiency include poor formation of teeth, irregular breathing pattern, and joint stiffness and pain.

Zinc

Zinc is an essential element. It is important for normal growth, wound healing, the nervous system and especially the defensive (immune) system. It is needed for cell division, tissue growth and repair, and for the breakdown of carbohydrates. It enhances the action of insulin and is important for a proper sense of taste and smell. Lack of zinc may be associated with skin problems, slow healing of wounds, loss of appetite, weight loss and a decreased ability to taste food.

Hormones and Insulin

Hormones are chemical substances that act as chemical messengers in the body. They are secreted by specific organs and glands and travel in the bloodstream or other body fluids to their target organs. They control and regulate growth, development, reproduction, energy use and storage, and water and electrolyte balance. By chemical structure, hormones are of three groups: cholesterol-derived (steroid) hormones, secreted by the adrenal cortex, the gonads and the placenta; amino acid-derived hormones, made from tyrosine and tryptophan, such as epinephrine and norepinephrine from the medulla of the adrenal glands and thyroxine from the thyroid gland; and peptide (protein) hormones, such as insulin, glucagon, leptin, ADH and oxytocin.

Insulin is a protein hormone secreted by the pancreas. It lowers the glucose level in the bloodstream and promotes the storage of glucose in the liver, muscles and other tissues. It facilitates glucose transport, stimulates protein synthesis and enhances free fatty acid uptake and storage. Insulin is often described as a key that unlocks the cell to allow sugar to enter and be used for energy. In diabetes mellitus, insulin is either not produced by the pancreas (type 1 diabetes) or is produced in insufficient amounts (type 2 diabetes), so too much sugar is left in the blood. Symptoms include frequent urination, fatigue, weight loss, and excessive thirst and hunger. It can cause kidney failure, heart disease, stroke and loss of sight. Treatment includes changes in diet, oral medications and, in some cases, daily injections of insulin.

Key Points

  • Iron makes red blood cells and carries oxygen; its deficiency causes anaemia.
  • Calcium builds bones and teeth and is needed for clotting, muscles and nerves; its deficiency causes osteoporosis and rickets.
  • More than 80% of body phosphorus is in the bones as calcium phosphate; phosphorus is also part of ATP and nucleic acids.
  • Zinc is needed for growth, wound healing, immunity and the senses of taste and smell.
  • Hormones are chemical messengers of three types: steroid, amino acid-derived and peptide hormones.
  • Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus, with high blood sugar and symptoms such as excessive thirst, hunger and frequent urination.

lessons.title: Introduction to Chemical Industry
lessons.notes_html:
Industrial chemistry is the branch of chemistry which is concerned with using physical and chemical processes for the transformation of raw materials into useful and profitable products. These products are used both as consumer goods and as intermediates for the manufacture of other, more complex products, such as household appliances and automobiles. Industrial chemistry has raised the standard of living of people, and it brings prosperity to a nation by increasing exports and earning valuable foreign exchange.

An industry is the branch of economic activity that is concerned with the processing of raw materials and the manufacture of goods in factories. Industries that produce chemicals are called chemical industries. They convert raw materials such as oil, natural gas, air, water, metals and minerals into thousands (more than 70,000) of different products that we use in our day-to-day life. The chemical industry has touched all aspects of life, such as agriculture, environment, food, hygiene, decor and transportation. It provides:

  • Food chemicals such as preservatives, taste enhancers and flavours, which keep food edible and increase its shelf life (the period for which a product can be stored and remain fresh and suitable for use).
  • Fertilizers and pesticides to the farmers, which are essential for crop production.
  • Polymers and plastics, used in clothing, home decor, PVC piping, water tanks and many other things.
  • Medicines and drugs for saving the life of people and animals.
  • Toiletries such as soaps, detergents, shampoos, body wash, face wash, toothpaste, toothbrush and deodorant.

The chemical industry is a very important contributor to the wealth of a country. In Pakistan, the average growth in the chemical industry sector was recorded at about 10.01% during 2014-15 and 2015-16. The major chemical industries of the country include sulphuric acid (the king of chemicals), soda ash, caustic soda, paints, varnish, petrochemicals, polymer and plastic products, fertilizers, cement, limestone, gypsum and soaps. Most of these products are used inside the country, which saves valuable foreign exchange, and some amount is also exported, which earns foreign exchange.

Key Points

  • Industrial chemistry changes raw materials into useful and profitable products by physical and chemical processes.
  • Chemical industries convert oil, natural gas, air, water, metals and minerals into more than 70,000 products.
  • They provide food chemicals, fertilizers, pesticides, polymers, medicines and toiletries.
  • Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals.
  • Pakistan's chemical industry grew by about 10.01% during 2014-15 and 2015-16.
  • Chemical products save foreign exchange when used at home and earn it when exported.

lessons.title: Raw Materials Used in Chemical Industries
lessons.notes_html:
All chemicals are derived from raw materials available in nature. The price of chemicals depends on the availability of their raw materials, so major chemical industries have developed around the most plentiful raw materials. The natural environment is the source of raw materials for the chemical industry.

Raw Materials from the Atmosphere

The atmosphere is a useful source of raw materials. The six important industrial gases, nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, krypton and xenon, are separated from liquid air by fractional distillation. Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere and oxygen is the second most abundant; the other gases are present in much smaller proportions.

Raw Materials from the Hydrosphere

Seawater is a useful source of raw materials. Sodium chloride, magnesium, bromine and sodium hydroxide are obtained from seawater. Sodium chloride is obtained by evaporating seawater. The electrolysis of an aqueous solution of sodium chloride (brine) produces three useful products: hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide. The electrolysis of molten sodium chloride produces two useful products: sodium and chlorine.

Raw Materials from the Lithosphere

The lithosphere provides minerals, which are natural compounds formed through geological processes. Many elements such as gold, silver, copper, aluminium and iron are obtained from the earth's crust in the form of mineral ores, and are used to make automobiles, airplanes, computer chips, windows and many other valuable things. In addition to minerals and ores, the lithosphere gives coal, natural gas and crude petroleum, which meet our energy needs. The lithosphere is also a source of valuable gemstones such as diamond and amethyst, which are used in jewellery and other adornments.

Raw Materials from the Biosphere

Before industrialization, the majority of our materials came from the biosphere. Now it is estimated that we get 70% of all materials from the lithosphere. Oils, fats, waxes, resins, sugar, leather, cotton, wool, silk and other natural fibres are products obtained from the biosphere.

Key Points

  • Raw materials come from the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere.
  • Nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, krypton and xenon are separated from liquid air by fractional distillation.
  • Electrolysis of brine gives hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide; electrolysis of molten NaCl gives sodium and chlorine.
  • The lithosphere gives mineral ores, coal, natural gas, crude petroleum and gemstones.
  • About 70% of all materials now come from the lithosphere; the biosphere gives oils, fats, waxes, resins, sugar, leather and natural fibres.

lessons.title: Safety Considerations in Process Industries
lessons.notes_html:
Chemical industries involve the processing of reactive chemicals, flammable liquids, vapours, gases and powders. The safety record of the chemical industry is good, but uncontrolled fires, explosions and chemical reactions can result in hazardous situations. A safety strategy is therefore required, so that chemical manufacturing activities are carried out safely. Its objective is to establish and maintain safe manufacturing practices in a manner compatible with the plant design, the operating conditions, production demands, commercial requirements and economic factors.

The following safety considerations ensure the health and safety of workers and reduce the chances of damage to machinery and equipment:

  • Proper safety training should be given to all workers before permitting them to work.
  • The government has to make legislations in order to ensure industrial safety.
  • A safety committee should be made to create safety consciousness.
  • Communication in the workplace should be increased, so that employees communicate about potential problems effectively and reduce potential hazards.
  • Workers should take regular breaks, which help them stay fresh and more alert.
  • Tools and machines should be used properly and shortcuts avoided; tools and equipment should be regularly cleaned and inspected to ensure they are safe.
  • Clear access to equipment shutoffs should be kept, equipment should be placed in proper storage areas after use, and the work area and emergency exits should be kept clear.
  • The correct safety equipment should be worn, such as safety goggles, hard hats, gloves or a full-face mask, and it should be checked that the safety equipment is itself safe.
  • Extra care should be taken in the receipt, storage, handling and disposal of chemicals and other hazardous materials.
  • Fire extinguishers and fire buckets should be provided at all fire-hazardous locations, and the extinguishers should be inspected, serviced and maintained.
  • Inspection and maintenance of equipment should be scheduled regularly, so that the equipment is safe to use and its lifetime is extended.
  • Passageways should be kept clear and spills cleaned to prevent tripping or slipping; workplaces should be checked for holes, loose boards or nails projecting from the floor.
  • Combustible materials should be stored away from sources of ignition, and combustible waste should be stored in metal containers and discarded daily.

Industries that have an increased risk of workplace accidents must be extra attentive about potential hazards and implement key safety measures to keep their workers happy, healthy and productive.

Key Points

  • Process industries handle reactive chemicals and flammable liquids, vapours, gases and powders, so a safety strategy is essential.
  • All workers must receive proper safety training before starting work.
  • Workers must wear correct protective equipment such as goggles, hard hats, gloves and face masks.
  • Fire extinguishers must be provided at fire-hazardous places and regularly inspected and serviced.
  • Combustible materials must be stored away from ignition sources, and waste must be discarded daily in metal containers.
  • Regular inspection, clear passageways and good communication reduce accidents.

lessons.title: Dyes
lessons.notes_html:
Dyes are organic compounds that are widely used for imparting colour to various substrates such as paper, leather, fur, hair, drugs, food, cosmetics, waxes, greases, plastics and textile materials. Dyes are normally water-soluble or water-dispersible organic compounds that are capable of being absorbed into the substrate. The dye molecules are usually chemically bonded to the surface and become a part of the material on which they are applied. A dye must have high colour intensity, which depends on how strongly it absorbs radiation in the visible region, from 400 to 800 nm. A dye should be resistant to the action of water, dilute acids and alkalies, because detergents and soaps are alkaline in nature.

Chemical Composition of Dyes

A dye is made up of two kinds of parts: chromophores and auxochromes. Chromophores are unsaturated groups; an organic compound looks coloured because of these groups. Important chromophores are the nitroso group (-NO), the nitro group (-NO2), the azo group (-N=N-), the ethylene group (C=C) and the carbonyl group (C=O). The intensity of colour increases with the number of chromophores or the degree of conjugation. Compounds that have chromophore groups are called chromogens. Auxochromes are groups that deepen or intensify the colour in the presence of a chromophore, so they are called colour-intensifying groups. Examples are the hydroxyl group (-OH), carboxyl group (-COOH), sulphonic acid group (-SO3H), amino group (-NH2), secondary amine group (-NHR) and tertiary amine group (-NR2). These groups impart no colour in the absence of a chromophore, and a chromogen without an auxochrome can never act as a dye: azobenzene is red coloured yet it is not a dye, while p-amino azobenzene is a yellow dye.

Classification of Dyes

Dyes are classified on the basis of their source, application, structure and the nature of their chromophores. On the basis of source there are two types. Natural dyes are derived from biological sources such as plants (roots, berries, bark, leaves, seeds, stem and flowers), insects (cochineal, lac and tyrian purple) or minerals (iron oxide and buff); fungi and lichens are other organic sources. Prominent examples are alizarin (red dye) and indigo (blue dye). Logwood is obtained from plants, tyrian purple from animals, and Prussian blue is an inorganic dye obtained from naturally occurring minerals. Natural dyes have limited shades and are not durable. Synthetic dyes are man-made dyes manufactured in the laboratory or industry, mostly from petroleum, sometimes in combination with mineral-derived components. The first man-made organic aniline dye, mauveine, was discovered by William Henry Perkin in 1856. Synthetic dyes are used everywhere, from clothes to paper and from food to wood, because they are cheaper to produce, brighter, more colour-fast and easy to apply to fabric. Examples are acid dyes, azo dyes, basic dyes and mordant dyes.

A mordant dye is a colourant that combines with the dye and the fibre. Mordants are commonly available in the form of salts of metals such as chromium, tin, copper, aluminium and iron; the metal ion acts as a bridge between the dye and the fibre. These dyes are economical and are generally used to produce dark shades such as dark blues, dark greens and blacks. They are most readily used for natural protein fibres, particularly wool, and sometimes for synthetic fibres, particularly nylon.

Key Points

  • Dyes are water-soluble organic compounds that bond chemically to the material and give it colour.
  • A dye has a chromophore (colour-producing group) and an auxochrome (colour-intensifying group).
  • Chromophores include -NO, -NO2, -N=N-, C=C and C=O; a compound with a chromophore is a chromogen.
  • Azobenzene is coloured but not a dye; p-amino azobenzene is a yellow dye.
  • Natural dyes (alizarin, indigo) have limited shades; synthetic dyes are cheaper, brighter and more colour-fast.
  • Mauveine, the first synthetic dye, was discovered by William Henry Perkin in 1856.

lessons.title: Pesticides
lessons.notes_html:
Pesticides are chemicals used to control pests, insects, weeds, fungus and so on. They are generally used on fruit, vegetable and horticulture crops. Traditional pest control methods were in use for a long time, but with the increase in human population the demand for food increased many times, and a need was felt to control the diseases and insects that destroy a large part of vegetative crops. Newer chemical methods were therefore developed.

Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) was synthesized in 1943 and was found to be effective against many insects such as mosquitoes. Due to its hazardous nature, DDT is no longer used nowadays. Other chemicals of a similar nature but safer were synthesized, such as aldrin, dieldrin, heptachlor, mirex and chlordane. These have a targeted action: they control only the desired species and do not affect the good, helpful insects.

Classification of Pesticides

Pesticides are classified on the basis of their action on the specific species that spread disease or affect the crops:

  • Insecticides: substances used to control insects.
  • Fungicides: substances used to control fungus.
  • Herbicides: chemicals used to control unwanted herbs (weeds) in the crops.
  • Miticides: used to kill mites and ticks of the crops.
  • Rodenticides: a large quantity of crop is damaged by rodents such as rats, mice and raccoons; birds and big mammals also affect the crops adversely. These are controlled by rodenticides.
  • Nematicides: chemicals that control harmful nematodes, the tiny hair-like worms that live in the earth and feed on plant roots and the juices from plant roots.
  • Repellents: chemicals that repel harmful pests, insects and other mammals.

Key Points

  • Pesticides are chemicals that control pests, insects, weeds and fungi, mainly on fruit, vegetable and horticulture crops.
  • DDT was effective against mosquitoes but is no longer used because of its hazardous nature.
  • Newer pesticides such as aldrin, dieldrin and chlordane have targeted action on specific species.
  • Insecticides kill insects, fungicides kill fungi and herbicides kill unwanted weeds.
  • Miticides kill mites and ticks, rodenticides control rodents, and nematicides control nematodes.
  • Repellents drive harmful pests and insects away instead of killing them.

lessons.title: Petrochemicals
lessons.notes_html:
The chemicals derived from petroleum products and used for a variety of commercial purposes are called petrochemicals. Petrochemicals can be converted into thousands of industrial and consumer products, including plastics, paints, rubber, pesticides, cosmetics, fertilizers, detergents, dyes, textiles and solvents.

Raw Materials for Petrochemicals

A raw material, also known as a feedstock or unprocessed material, is a basic material used to produce goods, finished products or energy, or intermediate materials which are themselves feedstock for future finished products. Petrochemicals are derived mainly from two feedstocks: natural gas liquids and oil refinery streams.

Natural gas liquids (NGL) are obtained from natural gas processing plants. They are mainly ethane, propane and butanes. They are cracked at high temperatures to yield the primary petrochemicals ethylene, propylene, butylenes and butadiene.

Oil refinery streams are obtained from the fractional distillation of crude oil. They include naphtha, kerosene oil and gas oil. They are cracked to produce higher ratios of propylene, butylenes and butadiene, plus the aromatic products benzene, toluene and xylenes, along with other co-products. Primary petrochemicals are reacted to form secondary petrochemicals and other chemical products, or polymerized to form synthetic resins, which are incorporated into a great variety of industrial and consumer products.

Primary raw materials are naturally occurring substances that have not been subjected to chemical changes after being recovered, for example olefins (ethylene, propylene, butadiene), aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes) and methanol. Secondary raw materials (intermediates) are produced by the chemical conversion of primary raw materials into more complicated derivative products, for example ethylene glycol, polyvinyl acetate, polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene resins and phenol-formaldehyde resins. Final products are obtained from secondary raw materials, for example detergents, dyes, cosmetics, solvents, polymers and fertilizers. The chain is: Feedstock → Primary petrochemicals → Secondary petrochemicals → Final products.

Classification of Petrochemical Feedstocks

GroupMain MembersUses
OlefinsEthylene, propylene, butadieneEthylene: antifreeze, detergents, plastics, synthetic rubber. Propylene: resins, fibres and many chemical products. Butadiene: synthetic rubbers and polymer resins.
AromaticsBenzene, toluene, xyleneSecondary products such as synthetic detergents, polyurethanes, plastics and synthetic fibres.
Synthesis gasCarbon monoxide + hydrogenAmmonia and methyl alcohol; ammonia is further used to make urea fertilizer.

Key Points

  • Petrochemicals are chemicals derived from petroleum, used for plastics, paints, rubber, fertilizers, detergents, dyes and solvents.
  • The two main feedstocks are natural gas liquids and oil refinery streams.
  • NGL (ethane, propane, butanes) are cracked to ethylene, propylene, butylenes and butadiene.
  • Refinery streams (naphtha, kerosene, gas oil) are cracked to olefins and the aromatics benzene, toluene and xylenes.
  • Feedstocks are classified as olefins, aromatics and synthesis gas (CO + H2).
  • Synthesis gas is used to make ammonia and methanol; ammonia is used for urea fertilizer.

lessons.title: Synthetic Polymers
lessons.notes_html:
Polymers, also called macromolecules, are high molecular mass compounds formed either by the addition of many smaller molecules (monomers), as in polyvinyl chloride (PVC), or by the condensation of many smaller molecules with the removal of water or alcohol, as in nylon. The process by which monomers are converted into polymers is called polymerization. Polymers are of two types: natural polymers and synthetic polymers.

Natural polymers, also known as biopolymers, are derived from natural sources. Examples are silk, rubber, cellulose, wool, starch, proteins and DNA. Synthetic polymers are man-made polymers prepared by a chemical reaction, often in a laboratory. Examples are polyethylene, PVC, synthetic rubber and nylon.

Formation and Uses of PVC

Polyvinyl chloride, commonly abbreviated as PVC, is formed by the addition of vinyl chloride monomer units at 52°C and 9 atmosphere pressure in the presence of benzoyl peroxide catalyst. PVC is the most widely used plastic after polyethylene. It is used in the manufacture of pipes, floor coverings (tiles), bottles, electrical wiring and cables, window frames, blood storage bags, stationery, seat coverings, packaging, credit cards, synthetic leather, rain coats, shower curtains and many other useful materials.

Key Reactions

PolymerFormation
PVC (addition polymerization)n CH2=CHCl (vinyl chloride) → -(CH2-CHCl)n- , with benzoyl peroxide at 52°C and 9 atm

Key Points

  • Polymers are high molecular mass compounds made from many monomer units; the process is polymerization.
  • Addition polymerization joins monomers directly (PVC); condensation polymerization removes water or alcohol (nylon).
  • Natural polymers include silk, rubber, cellulose, wool, starch, proteins and DNA.
  • Synthetic polymers include polyethylene, PVC, synthetic rubber and nylon.
  • PVC is made from vinyl chloride at 52°C and 9 atm with benzoyl peroxide catalyst.
  • PVC is used for pipes, tiles, bottles, cables, window frames, credit cards and rain coats.

lessons.title: Formation and Uses of Nylon
lessons.notes_html:
Nylons are high molecular mass polyamides. They are of various types, such as nylon 4,6, nylon 6, nylon 6,6, nylon 6,12 and nylon 12. Nylon 6,6 (read as nylon six, six) is the best-known example. It is prepared by the condensation reaction of adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine at about 252°C. Nylon 6,6 got its name from its monomers, adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine, each of which provides six carbon atoms.

Key Reactions

PolymerFormation
Nylon 6,6 (condensation polymerization)n HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH (adipic acid) + n H2N-(CH2)6-NH2 (hexamethylene diamine) → Nylon 6,6 + (2n-1)H2O, at about 252°C

Nylon has high strength, medium stiffness and resistance to high temperature (+85°C), fuel, lubricants and most chemicals. It is also used in combination with other materials, for example with cotton, for more strength and durability of the product, and it is believed to be as strong as steel metal.

Uses of Nylon

  • In the manufacture of carpets, textile fibres and bristles of brushes.
  • In dress socks, swimwear, activewear, shorts, track pants, windbreakers and bedspreads.
  • For making elastic hosiery.
  • As a substitute for metals in bearings and gears.
  • For food packaging.
  • For making rope.
  • In tyre cord.

Key Points

  • Nylons are polyamides; nylon 6,6 is the best-known type.
  • Nylon 6,6 is made by condensation of adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine at about 252°C, with loss of water.
  • Each monomer of nylon 6,6 provides six carbon atoms, which gives the name 6,6.
  • Nylon is strong and resists heat, fuel, lubricants and most chemicals.
  • Nylon is used for carpets, fibres, brush bristles, clothing, bearings, gears, ropes and tyre cord.

lessons.title: Cosmetics
lessons.notes_html:
Cosmetics are the substances used to enhance natural beauty and to promote good health. They may also be defined as any substance to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, or introduced into or applied to any part of the human body, for cleaning, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance. Cosmetics make the skin feel soft, healthy and flawless. Colour cosmetics are designed to add colour to the skin and enhance the appearance of good health and youth; their pigments make the cheeks rosy, the lips ruby and the eyes smoky. Colour cosmetics applied to the face to enhance its appearance are often called make-up, for example lipsticks, eye liners, nail varnish and powder. Make-up also helps in protection from the harmful rays of the sun. The first known people who used cosmetics to enhance their beauty were the Egyptians. Cosmetics are available in the form of creams, lipsticks, shampoos, hair dyes, body wash, eye liners, eye shadows, perfumes, sunscreens, talcum powder, toothpastes, and nail varnish and remover.

Lipsticks

Lipstick is one of the inexpensive cosmetic products and is most widely used by women to give an attractive colour and appearance to the lips. Lipsticks are manufactured as moulded sticks. They are made from waxes, oils, pigments and emollients, with antioxidants, preservatives and fragrances as other important additives. The waxes used include beeswax, carnauba, candelilla wax and ozokerite. The oils used include castor oil, coconut oil, mineral oil, vegetable oil and petrolatum (petroleum jelly). Important emollients are cocoa butter, shea butter, vitamin E and aloe vera.

Each ingredient has a role. The wax gives the lipstick its shape and ease of application. Oils are added to reflect light and provide shine; they give the lipstick the ability to be easily applied, keeping the wax soft enough to spread easily. Pigments are the colours: they give colour to the lipstick and improve the appearance of the lips. Emollients soften and smooth the surface of the lips. Antioxidants prevent the lipstick from becoming rancid, preservatives extend its shelf life, and a little fragrance (perfume) is added by many manufacturers to give it a nice smell when it is being applied.

Key Points

  • Cosmetics are substances applied to the body for cleaning, beautifying or altering appearance.
  • Colour cosmetics applied to the face are called make-up; the Egyptians were the first known users of cosmetics.
  • Lipsticks are moulded sticks made of waxes, oils, pigments and emollients.
  • Wax gives shape, oils give shine and easy spreading, and pigments give colour.
  • Emollients soften the lips; antioxidants prevent rancidity and preservatives extend shelf life.

lessons.title: Nail Varnish and Nail Varnish Remover
lessons.notes_html:
Nail varnish is applied to the fingernails or toenails to colour them or make them shiny. It is used mainly by women, and it protects and beautifies the nail plates. The correct name of nail varnish is nail lacquer; the terms nail varnish, nail polish, nail enamel, nail paint and nail lacquer are used interchangeably. Nail varnish is sold in liquid form in small bottles and is applied by painting the nail with a tiny brush. It is a flexible lacquer that does not easily crack and flake with nail movement. People want brands that are easy to apply, dry quickly, look glossy and last a long time without chipping.

Ingredients of Nail Varnish

There is no single formula for nail varnish. The four major ingredients in most brands are resins, plasticizers, organic solvents and colouring agents.

  • Resins are types of polymers that act as thickening and hardening agents and serve as a colourless nail protector. Two types are used: hard glossy resins (for example nitrocellulose) and soft pliable resins (tosylamide/formaldehyde resin).
  • Plasticizers (for example camphor, dibutyl phthalate and adipates) make the polish more flexible after drying and increase its durability.
  • Solvents dissolve the ingredients and make the polish spreadable. The most common organic solvents are ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, and the varnish must dry quickly to increase the ease of application.
  • Colouring agents (pigments) create the colour of each polish; naturally occurring and synthetic pigments are mixed together to create varying shades.

Sometimes nail polish also contains particles such as mica, bismuth, pearl essence (guanine) and aluminium powder as sparkling and reflective particles, which give a shimmery look to the polish.

Nail Varnish Remover

Nail varnish (or nail polish) remover is a powerful solvent that can quickly remove polish from the nails, cuticles and surrounding skin. It works by softening the dried nail polish and returning it to its liquid state. Remover mainly consists of volatile organic solvents such as ethyl acetate or acetone, and may contain oils, scents and colouring. Acetone is one of the main components of nail polish remover; it is found naturally in the environment and is also produced in factories. It is a colourless, flammable liquid that evaporates easily. Removers that contain acetone work very quickly and effectively, but acetone can be harmful to nails and skin: it can irritate the nose, eyes, throat, lungs and skin, it can make nails dry and brittle, and it can also remove artificial nails made of acrylic or cured gel. Mild non-acetone removers are therefore preferred for strong, healthy nails. The most commonly used alternatives are ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, which are colourless, volatile liquids and are less harsh and toxic than acetone.

Key Points

  • Nail varnish (nail lacquer) colours and protects the nails; it is a flexible lacquer that does not crack easily.
  • Its four major ingredients are resins, plasticizers, organic solvents and colouring agents.
  • Nitrocellulose is a hard glossy resin; camphor and dibutyl phthalate are plasticizers.
  • Ethyl acetate and butyl acetate are the common solvents in nail varnish.
  • Acetone-based removers work fastest but dry and damage nails; ethyl acetate and butyl acetate removers are less harsh.

lessons.title: Hair Dyes
lessons.notes_html:
Hair dyes (also called hair colours) are chemicals that are used to change the hair colour; the preferred professional term is hair colour. The first safe commercial hair colour was created in 1909 by the French chemist Eugene Schueller, using the chemical paraphenylenediamine. This compound is present in colouring products along with ammonia and peroxide in varying proportions. Most hair dyes contain dyes, modifiers, antioxidants, alkalizers, soaps, ammonia, wetting agents, fragrance and a variety of other chemicals in small amounts, which impart special qualities to the hair, such as softening the texture, or give a desired action to the dye, such as making it more or less permanent. The dye chemicals are usually amino compounds, and metal oxides such as titanium dioxide and iron oxide are often used as pigments.

Types of Hair Dyes

Hair dyes are classified by the types of colour molecules used and the length of time they last. There are three main types.

Temporary hair dyes only coat the surface of the hair. They cannot penetrate into the hair shaft and are easily removed with one or two washings. They do not contain ammonia, so the hair shaft is not opened up during processing, and the natural colour of the hair is retained once the product washes out.

Semi-permanent hair dyes have smaller molecules than temporary dyes, so they can penetrate the surface of the hair into the cuticle layer. They are generally not formulated with ammonia, so they do not require any development. They last for five to ten washings, longer than temporary dyes.

Permanent hair dyes are the most common type of hair colouring. The change in hair colour is permanent, or lasts at least until new hair grows. They contain ammonia and hydrogen peroxide: the ammonia opens the cuticle and the hydrogen peroxide is used as the developer. The dyes used are actually dye precursors; their small monomer molecules penetrate into the hair all the way to the cortex. The shades of permanent hair dyes are often more natural-looking, but they can be more damaging to the hair, because the chemicals used are stronger and the mixture usually has to be left on for a longer period of time. Permanent hair dyes are usually packaged with the developer in a separate bottle; the developer is most often based on hydrogen peroxide.

Side Effects of Hair Dyes

The chemicals used in hair dyes remain at safe levels. However, some ingredients found in hair dye, such as resorcinol and parabens, are suspected to be endocrine-disrupting chemicals.

Key Points

  • Hair dyes change hair colour; the first safe commercial hair colour (1909) used paraphenylenediamine.
  • Hair dyes contain dyes, ammonia, peroxide, modifiers, antioxidants, alkalizers, soaps, wetting agents and fragrance.
  • Temporary dyes only coat the hair and wash out in one or two washings.
  • Semi-permanent dyes enter the cuticle and last five to ten washings.
  • Permanent dyes use ammonia to open the cuticle and hydrogen peroxide as developer, and colour the cortex until new hair grows.
  • Resorcinol and parabens in hair dyes are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals.

lessons.title: Adhesives
lessons.notes_html:
An adhesive, also known as glue, is a substance that is applied to one surface, or both surfaces, of two separate objects and binds them together and resists their separation. Adhesives are used to pack gifts, re-join broken materials, connect parts of toys, mend shoes and paste a photograph into an album. They have been used successfully for centuries, and their usefulness is increasing rapidly.

Natural Adhesives

On the basis of origin there are two types of adhesives: natural and synthetic. Natural adhesives (also called bioadhesives) are produced or extracted from natural resources such as plants or animals. Examples are starch, dextrin, casein glues, blood albumin glue, natural gums, bees wax and resin (tree sap). They are inexpensive, easy to apply and have a long shelf life. They develop tack quickly but have low strength. Natural adhesives have been used since the earliest times: the ancient Egyptians used flour paste in the making of papyrus (paper reed) and glue made from animal skin and bones for woodworking. They are still used in corrugated board, envelopes, bottle labels, book bindings, cartons, furniture, and laminated film and foils, although synthetic adhesives have replaced them for most applications.

Synthetic Adhesives

Synthetic adhesives are not found in nature; they are designed and manufactured by chemists in the laboratory or factory. On the basis of chemical composition they are classified as thermosetting, thermoplastic, elastomeric, or alloys (hybrids) of these.

Thermosetting adhesives are essentially infusible and insoluble. They show good heat and solvent resistance and good creep (flow-under-load) resistance, and little elastic deformation under load at elevated temperature. They are recommended for use at temperatures from 93-260°C and are used for high load assemblies and severe service conditions such as heat, cold and radiation. Examples are epoxies, polyesters, polyamides and phenolics. The emphasis is on structural applications. They are available as solvent-free liquids, pastes and solids, in one-part and two-part systems; the two-part systems have longer shelf lives.

Thermoplastic adhesives are fusible and soluble: they can soften or melt when heated, without undergoing any chemical change, and they harden upon cooling from a melt state or by evaporation of a solvent. Wood glues are thermoplastic emulsions, common household items, which harden by evaporation of water from the emulsion. They have poor creep resistance and fair peel strength (the measure of the bond strength of a material). They are not usually recommended for use above 66°C, although they can be used up to 90°C in some applications, and are normally used for low load assemblies under mild service conditions. They bond non-metallic materials, especially wood, leather, plastics and paper, and are not usually used for structural applications. Examples are polyvinyl alcohol, polyvinyl acetates (PVA), cellulose acetate, polyamides, cyanoacrylates and polyacrylates. They are available as one-part systems.

Elastomeric adhesives are based on synthetic or naturally occurring polymers. They have great toughness and elongation: their polymeric resins are capable of high degrees of extension and compression and return rapidly to their initial dimensions and shape after the load is removed. They are used for their high degree of flexibility and good peel strength; their bond strengths are relatively low but their flexibility is excellent. They are used in unstressed joints on lightweight materials, so they cannot be considered structural adhesives. Most of them are modified with synthetic resins for bonding rubber, fabric, foil, paper, leather and plastic films, and they are also used as tapes. They may be supplied as solutions in organic solvents, as pressure-sensitive tapes, and as single or multiple part solvent-free liquids or pastes. Examples are natural rubber, nitrile rubber, neoprene, polysulphide and silicones.

Hybrid adhesives are made by combining thermosetting, thermoplastic or elastomeric resins into a single adhesive formulation. The thermoset resin, chosen for its high strength, is plasticised by the second resin, which is usually a thermoplastic or elastomer, making the alloy tougher, more flexible and more resistant to impact. These adhesives are generally stronger over wider ranges of temperature than other adhesives and are suitable as structural adhesives where the highest and strictest end-use conditions must be met, irrespective of cost, such as in military applications. They bond metals, ceramics, glass and thermosetting plastics, and they also bond well to oily substrates, because the oil on the substrate is adsorbed into the formulation and acts as another flexibilizer. Examples are epoxy-phenolics, epoxy-nylon, epoxy-polysulphide and nitrile-phenolic.

Peel strength is the measure of the bond strength (adhesive strength) of two bonded materials such as tape, rubber, plastic, textile, wood, paper, foil, plastic films and leather. It is calculated through a peel test, which measures the average force required per unit width to separate bonded materials at a constant speed. Peel tests at 90° and 180° are commonly used.

Key Points

  • An adhesive (glue) binds two surfaces together and resists their separation.
  • Natural adhesives (bioadhesives) come from plants and animals, for example starch, casein glue and natural gums; they are cheap but weak.
  • Thermosetting adhesives (epoxies, phenolics) are infusible, heat-resistant and used for structural, high-load work at 93-260°C.
  • Thermoplastic adhesives soften on heating, for example PVA wood glue, and are used for low-load, non-structural work.
  • Elastomeric adhesives are flexible with good peel strength but low bond strength, and are used as tapes and for lightweight materials.
  • Hybrid adhesives combine resins for the highest strength and flexibility, for example epoxy-phenolics and epoxy-nylon.

Environmental chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the study of the sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of chemical substances in the environment — in air, water and soil — and their effect on human health and the natural environment. It is a multi-disciplinary science that includes physics, life sciences, medical sciences, public health and sanitary engineering.

The environment is everything that is around us. It belongs to all living beings and is important for all.

Segments of the Environment

  • Lithosphere (Greek lithos, stone): the upper rigid and rocky layer of the earth's crust. It includes soil, earth, rocks and mountains, and extends to a depth of about 100 km. Soil, its most important part, is a complex mixture of minerals, organic matter and water, and is used as a medium for growing crops.
  • Hydrosphere (Greek hydor, water): the water-containing part of the earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, streams, polar ice caps, glaciers and groundwater reservoirs. About 75% of the earth's surface is covered by water, so the earth is called the blue planet. Oceans hold about 97% of all water (salt water, unusable by most land animals), about 2% is stored in glaciers and polar ice caps, and only about 1% is available as fresh water.
  • Biosphere (Greek bios, life): the region of the earth where all living species exist, above as well as below sea level.
  • Atmosphere (Greek atmos, vapour, and sphaira, globe): the layers of gases surrounding the earth. It consists of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide, with trace amounts of hydrogen, ozone, methane, carbon monoxide, helium, neon, krypton and xenon, and water vapours. It protects us from harmful ultraviolet radiation and cosmic rays of the sun.

Layers of the Atmosphere

LayerHeight above Earth
Troposphere0-11 km
Stratosphere (contains the ozone layer)11-50 km
Mesosphere50-85 km
Thermosphere85-500 km
ExosphereBeyond the thermosphere, to outer space

Key Points

  • Environmental chemistry studies the sources, reactions, effects, transport and fate of chemicals in air, water and soil.
  • The environment has four segments: lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere.
  • Lithosphere = rocky crust and soil; hydrosphere = all water; biosphere = all living things; atmosphere = the gas layers.
  • Earth is called the blue planet because about 75% of its surface is covered by water.
  • Only about 1% of the earth's water is available as fresh water.
  • The atmosphere is divided into troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.
lessons.title: Environmental Chemistry and Segments of the Environment

lessons.notes_html:
The troposphere is the layer of the atmosphere nearest to the earth's surface. It extends up to about 11 km and accounts for about 70% of the atmospheric mass, because gravity concentrates the molecules of the atmosphere near the surface. Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude: the average pressure at sea level is 760 torr, while at 100 km altitude it is only 0.0023 torr.

The temperature in the troposphere decreases uniformly with increasing altitude, reaching a minimum of about -56°C at about 11 km. The important chemical species in this region are nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapours. The troposphere is the region most easily disturbed by human activities and has the greatest effect on the earth's surface conditions; air pollution, acid rain and global warming are particularly important effects.

Chemical Reactions in the Atmosphere

Many chemical and photochemical reactions occur in the atmosphere. Chemical reactions initiated by sunlight are called photochemical reactions. These reactions depend upon composition, temperature, pressure, humidity and the intensity of sunlight, so different processes are observed under different atmospheric conditions. Diatomic oxygen (O2) plays an important role in the troposphere, and ozone (O3) plays an important role in the stratosphere.

Primary and Secondary Pollutants

  • Primary pollutants are directly emitted from a source, for example from the chimneys of industrial units and the exhaust of automobiles. Examples: total suspended particulates (tiny particles of smoke, dust, fumes, etc.) and oxides of carbon, nitrogen and sulphur.
  • Secondary pollutants are created in the atmosphere as a result of chemical reactions such as oxidation and photochemical reactions involving primary pollutants. Examples: hydrogen peroxide, ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), sulphuric and nitric acids and their salts.

Key Points

  • The troposphere extends to about 11 km and holds about 70% of the atmospheric mass.
  • Its temperature falls with height, to about -56°C at 11 km.
  • Pressure falls from 760 torr at sea level to 0.0023 torr at 100 km.
  • Reactions started by sunlight are called photochemical reactions.
  • Primary pollutants are emitted directly; secondary pollutants are formed by reactions in the air.
  • O2 is the key reactive gas of the troposphere; O3 is the key gas of the stratosphere.
lessons.title: Chemistry of the Troposphere

lessons.notes_html:
About 21% by volume of the gas in the atmosphere is oxygen. Oxygen plays a key role in the troposphere because it is very reactive and acts as a strong oxidizing agent; the presence of a large amount of oxygen makes the atmosphere thermodynamically oxidizing. In the atmosphere, oxygen is produced by photosynthesis and is consumed by animals through respiration.

Rusting of Iron

Iron and steel rust when they come into contact with oxygen and water vapours: Iron + Oxygen + Water → Hydrated iron (III) oxide (rust).

Formation of Ozone

Diatomic oxygen absorbs an ultraviolet photon and produces two free radicals, oxygen atoms. These free radicals react with another molecule of diatomic oxygen to produce triatomic oxygen (ozone). M is a third body (N2 or O2) that absorbs the excess energy liberated by ozone formation and thereby stabilizes the ozone in the stratosphere.

Reaction of Nitrogen Oxides

The important oxides of nitrogen present in the atmosphere are nitrous oxide (N2O), nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2). They undergo many reactions in the atmosphere, both in the presence and in the absence of sunlight. Nitrous oxide is produced through microbial activities, while nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide are produced from the combustion of coal, oil, natural gas and other human activities. NO and NO2 are collectively designated as NOx. Due to photochemical reactions, NO and NO2 are converted to HNO3; this nitric acid is removed from air as acid rain. HNO3 also reacts with bases such as ammonia and particulate lime to produce particulate nitrates, which come down either by rainfall or as dust.

Key Reactions

ReactionProcess
O2(g) →(hv) O•(g) + O•(g)Oxygen split by ultraviolet light into oxygen-atom free radicals
O•(g) + O2(g) + M (N2 or O2) → O3(g) + MFormation of ozone; M absorbs excess energy
Iron + Oxygen + Water → Hydrated iron (III) oxideRusting of iron
NO and NO2 →(photochemical reactions) HNO3Nitric acid formation; removed as acid rain or as particulate nitrates

Key Points

  • Oxygen is about 21% of the atmosphere and is a strong oxidizing agent.
  • Oxygen is produced by photosynthesis and consumed in respiration.
  • Rust is hydrated iron (III) oxide, formed by iron + oxygen + water.
  • Ultraviolet light splits O2 into oxygen atoms, which form ozone (O3).
  • NO and NO2 together are called NOx; N2O comes from microbial activity.
  • NOx is converted to HNO3, which falls as acid rain or as particulate nitrates.
lessons.title: Reactions of Oxygen and Nitrogen Oxides in the Atmosphere

lessons.notes_html:
The oxides of sulphur present in the atmosphere are sulphur dioxide (SO2) and sulphur trioxide (SO3). These are colourless gases and have a pungent odour. Some of the oxides of sulphur originate from biological processes and from volcanoes (67%). They are also produced by the burning of fuels like coal and petroleum.

Sulphur burns in oxygen to give SO2. The SO2 is then oxidized to SO3 in the atmosphere, and the sulphur trioxide, in the presence of water vapours, is converted to sulphuric acid (H2SO4). The rate of photochemical oxidation of sulphur dioxide leading to the formation of H2SO4 aerosol is greatly accelerated in the presence of olefins and oxides of nitrogen, which are present in photochemical smog.

Reaction of Organic Compounds

Generally, organic compounds such as hydrocarbons, aldehydes and ketones undergo redox and photochemical reactions. The reactions of organic compounds, through a series of steps, produce secondary pollutants in the atmosphere. The organic compounds in the lower atmosphere produce photochemical smog.

Key Reactions

ReactionProcess
S + O2 → SO2Burning of sulphur and sulphur-containing fuels
2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3Oxidation of sulphur dioxide in the atmosphere
SO3 + H2O → H2SO4Formation of sulphuric acid (acid rain)

Key Points

  • The atmospheric sulphur oxides are SO2 and SO3: colourless gases with a pungent odour.
  • About 67% of sulphur oxides come from biological processes and volcanoes; the rest mainly from burning coal and petroleum.
  • SO2 is oxidized to SO3, and SO3 + water vapour gives H2SO4.
  • Olefins and nitrogen oxides in photochemical smog speed up the oxidation of SO2.
  • Hydrocarbons, aldehydes and ketones undergo redox and photochemical reactions.
  • Reactions of organic compounds produce secondary pollutants and photochemical smog.
lessons.title: Reactions of Sulphur Oxides and Organic Compounds in the Atmosphere

lessons.notes_html:
Pollutants can be defined as any substance in air that has a harmful effect on living organisms or their environment. Some important air pollutants are: (i) oxides of carbon, (ii) oxides of nitrogen, (iii) volatile organic compounds (VOCs), (iv) oxides of sulphur and (v) ozone.

Carbon Monoxide

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas. It is lighter than air and is insoluble in water. It is produced by: (i) incomplete combustion of fuel, namely coal, gas, charcoal, oil, etc.; (ii) forest fires and incineration of biomass (burning of forest debris, bushes, crop residue, weeds and vegetation); and (iii) industrial operations such as petroleum refining, the paper industry, coal mining, and electric and blast furnaces.

Harmful effects of CO: it is extremely toxic and causes suffocation if inhaled. Exposure to a high concentration of CO causes headache, fatigue and unconsciousness, and eventually death may occur if such exposure is experienced for a longer time.

Carbon Dioxide

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a colourless gas. It is odourless at low concentrations and has a sharp and acidic odour at high concentrations. It is soluble in water. It is added to the atmosphere through human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels and biomass and the production of cement. It is added naturally through the respiration system of plant and animal cells, forest fires and the eruption of volcanoes. The high rate of CO2 emissions is because of deforestation, the increase of automobiles and high population growth, etc.

Harmful effects of CO2: it is usually considered non-toxic and harmless, but more than 65% of the anthropogenic greenhouse effect is attributed to CO2 gas.

Key Reactions

ReactionProcess
2C + O2 → 2COIncomplete combustion of carbon fuels gives carbon monoxide

Key Points

  • A pollutant is any substance in air that harms living organisms or their environment.
  • CO is colourless, odourless, tasteless, lighter than air and insoluble in water.
  • CO comes from incomplete combustion, forest fires, biomass burning and industry.
  • CO is extremely toxic: headache, fatigue, unconsciousness and death on long exposure.
  • CO2 comes from fossil fuels, biomass, cement making, respiration, forest fires and volcanoes.
  • CO2 is normally harmless, but it causes more than 65% of the man-made greenhouse effect.
lessons.title: Air Pollutants: Oxides of Carbon

lessons.notes_html:
Oxides of Nitrogen (NOx)

There are eight possible oxides of nitrogen. Out of these, only three oxides, namely N2O, NO and NO2, are the important components of the atmosphere. N2O is high in concentration in the atmosphere, but it is not generally considered a pollutant. NO and NO2 are more significant pollutants and are usually represented together as NOx.

NO is a colourless, odourless gas, but NO2 has a reddish-brown colour and a pungent suffocating odour. The major man-made sources of oxides of nitrogen are the combustion of coal, oil, natural gas, gasoline and other organic matter. Oxides of nitrogen can also be discharged by natural bacterial activity. The average residence time of NO in the atmosphere is about 4 days and that of NO2 is 3 days.

Harmful effects of NOx: NO and NO2 are both toxic, but NO is less toxic than NO2. NOx gases cause irritation in the airways and lungs, and long-term exposure may cause asthma. These gases also contribute to the formation of fine particles and ground-level ozone, both of which are associated with adverse health effects. Nitrogen dioxide, ozone and hydrocarbons in sunlight form peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), responsible for photochemical smog.

Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs)

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) include a variety of chemical gases emitted from certain liquids and solids. They are released from burning fuel such as diesel, gasoline, wood, coal or natural gas. They are also released from solvents, paints, glues and other products used and stored at home and at work. They are also found in paint thinners, varnishes, air fresheners, cosmetics, tobacco smoke, flooring, carpet, wood preservatives, aerosol sprays and dry cleaning fluids. Some common examples of VOCs in daily life are benzene, formaldehyde, toluene, xylene, styrene, tetrachloroethylene and ethylene glycol.

Harmful effects of VOCs: short-term exposure to high levels of some VOCs can cause headaches, dizziness, light-headedness, drowsiness, nausea, and eye and respiratory irritation. Long-term exposure to high levels of some VOCs has caused cancer and has affected the liver, kidney and nervous system.

Key Points

  • Of the eight oxides of nitrogen, only N2O, NO and NO2 are important in the atmosphere.
  • NO is colourless and odourless; NO2 is reddish-brown with a pungent, suffocating odour.
  • NOx comes mainly from combustion of coal, oil, natural gas and gasoline, and from bacterial activity.
  • NO stays in the atmosphere about 4 days and NO2 about 3 days.
  • NOx irritates airways and lungs and can cause asthma; it also forms fine particles, ground-level ozone and PAN.
  • VOCs are gases from fuels, solvents, paints and many household products; examples are benzene, formaldehyde and toluene.
  • Short-term VOC exposure causes headache and irritation; long-term exposure can cause cancer and damage the liver, kidney and nervous system.
lessons.title: Air Pollutants: Oxides of Nitrogen and Volatile Organic Compounds

lessons.notes_html:
Oxides of Sulphur (SOx)

Sulphur dioxide and small amounts of sulphur trioxide are formed during the combustion of sulphur-containing materials such as fossil fuels. The most important and predominant form of sulphur oxides present in the lower atmosphere is SO2. It is a colourless gas and has a pungent odour. It is moderately soluble in water, forming weakly acidic sulphurous acid, and tends to form aerosols. It is heavier than air. SO3 is a colourless solid and has low melting and boiling points. It reacts quickly with water to form sulphuric acid, tending to form aerosols. These acidic aerosols are eventually precipitated as acid rain, snow, sleet or fog, but only when they encounter the right meteorological conditions.

Harmful effects of oxides of sulphur: SO2 causes irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, and premature mortality. Sulphur dioxide also causes damage to vegetation, including forests and agricultural crops.

Ozone (O3)

Ozone is an allotrope of oxygen. It is fairly soluble in water. It occurs both in the earth's upper atmosphere and at ground level. Ozone affects life on earth in either good or bad ways, depending on where it is found: it acts as a pollutant in the biosphere and as a protector in the stratosphere.

Harmful effects of ozone: ozone is a familiar component of photochemical smog. It causes various health problems: eye irritation, throat irritation, coughing and asthma. It is harmful to plants, and it reduces the durability and appearance of paint and fabrics.

Peroxyacetyl Nitrate (PAN)

The peroxyacetyl nitrates (PANs) are photochemical oxidants and are the major component of photochemical smog. PANs are both toxic and irritating, as they dissolve more readily in water than ozone.

Harmful effects of PANs: at lower concentration they cause eye irritation, and at higher concentration they cause extensive damage to vegetation.

Key Points

  • SO2 is the main sulphur oxide of the lower atmosphere; it forms sulphurous acid and aerosols in water.
  • SO3 reacts quickly with water to form sulphuric acid; acidic aerosols fall as acid rain, snow, sleet or fog.
  • SO2 irritates the eyes, nose and throat and damages forests and crops.
  • Ozone is an allotrope of oxygen: a pollutant at ground level, a protector in the stratosphere.
  • Ground-level ozone causes eye and throat irritation, coughing and asthma, and harms plants, paint and fabrics.
  • PANs are photochemical oxidants, the major component of photochemical smog; they irritate eyes and damage vegetation.
lessons.title: Air Pollutants: Oxides of Sulphur, Ozone and Peroxyacetyl Nitrate

lessons.notes_html:
Complete combustion in the petrol (or diesel) engine of an automobile produces carbon dioxide and water vapours. Incomplete combustion leads to emissions of the poisonous carbon monoxide gas and a wide range of unburnt volatile organic compounds (VOCs), including hydrocarbons, aromatics and oxygenated species. Automobiles also generate oxides of nitrogen, NO and NO2. Nitric oxide is produced when atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen combine at the high temperatures present in an automobile engine. The NO released into the atmosphere further reacts with O2 to form NO2. The unburnt hydrocarbons produce photochemical smog, and nitrogen dioxide forms photochemical smog and acid rain.

The pollution that all the cars produced together can cause lung cancer, respiratory problems, urban smog and acid rain. To reduce air pollution, modern automobiles are equipped with a device called a catalytic converter, which reduces emissions of harmful compounds such as CO, NO2 and VOCs. These compounds are converted into less harmful compounds such as carbon dioxide, water, nitrogen and oxygen before leaving the car's exhaust system. Catalytic converters can also be found in generators, buses, trucks and trains; almost everything with an internal combustion engine has a form of catalytic converter attached to its exhaust system.

The Three-Way Catalytic Converter

An efficient catalytic converter (a three-way catalytic converter) performs three functions: (i) it oxidizes CO and unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2 and H2O; (ii) it reduces NO and NO2 to N2 and O2; and (iii) it oxidizes hydrocarbons (VOCs) to carbon dioxide and water. Catalytic converters contain porous honeycomb structures made of ceramic materials coated with the catalysts. The catalyst used is a combination of platinum (Pt), palladium (Pd) and rhodium (Rh). A converter contains two types of catalyst: a reduction catalyst, which uses platinum and rhodium to reduce nitrogen oxides in the exhaust, and an oxidation catalyst, which uses platinum and palladium to reduce carbon monoxide (CO) and VOCs in the exhaust of automobiles.

Note: catalytic converters are effective at removing hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide and nitrous oxides from car exhaust, but they do not reduce the emission of carbon dioxide (CO2), which is one of the most common greenhouse gases.

Key Reactions

ReactionProcess in the Converter
2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g)Oxidation of carbon monoxide
2NO(g) → N2(g) + O2(g)Reduction of nitric oxide
VOCs + O2(g) → CO2(g) + H2O(g)Oxidation of unburnt hydrocarbons

Key Points

  • Complete combustion in an engine gives CO2 and water; incomplete combustion gives poisonous CO and unburnt VOCs.
  • NO forms when N2 and O2 combine at engine temperatures; NO then reacts with O2 to form NO2.
  • Car pollution together causes lung cancer, respiratory problems, urban smog and acid rain.
  • A catalytic converter converts CO, NOx and VOCs into CO2, water, N2 and O2 before the exhaust leaves.
  • Its catalysts are platinum, palladium and rhodium on a ceramic honeycomb.
  • The reduction catalyst (Pt, Rh) removes NOx; the oxidation catalyst (Pt, Pd) removes CO and VOCs.
  • Catalytic converters do not reduce CO2 emissions.
lessons.title: Automobile Pollutants and the Catalytic Converter

lessons.notes_html:
The word smog is a combination of smoke and fog. There are two types of smog: industrial smog and photochemical smog.

Industrial smog, sometimes known as London smog or gray smog, is created when SO2 (from the combustion of coal and oil) and particulate matter combine with the moisture in fog at suitable conditions. The particulate matter consists of larger solid particles such as metal oxides, soil particles, sea salts, fly ash, elemental carbon and small metal particles in the atmosphere. Industrial smog produces a yellow-brown colour near ground level. It is a mixture of fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs.

One of the worst cases of industrial smog was the Great Smog of 1952 in London, where the smog was so thick it killed thousands of people (about 4000 people). Industrial smog is common in many cities of the world where heavy industry and power plants are found; examples of such countries are India, China and European countries. It is formed in cities where the weather is cold and wet, and in many urban areas of developing countries industrial smog is still a major problem.

Effects: this smog has serious negative effects on people, plants and animals. Various human health problems such as emphysema, asthma, chronic bronchitis, lung infections and cancers are caused by the effects of smog.

Key Points

  • Smog = smoke + fog; its two types are industrial smog and photochemical smog.
  • Industrial (London or gray) smog forms when SO2 and particulates mix with fog moisture.
  • It is a yellow-brown mixture of fly ash, soot, SO2, smoke and some VOCs.
  • It forms in cold, wet weather in cities with heavy industry and power plants.
  • The Great Smog of London (1952) killed about 4000 people.
  • Industrial smog causes emphysema, asthma, chronic bronchitis, lung infections and cancers.
lessons.title: Industrial Smog

lessons.notes_html:
Photochemical smog, sometimes known as Los Angeles smog or brown smog, is created when oxides of nitrogen react with volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight. This reaction produces a mixture of hundreds of dangerous secondary pollutants, such as ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), aldehydes and peroxybenzoyl nitrate (PBZN). It appears as a yellow-brown haze.

Photochemical smog is common in cities that have a lot of automobiles along with a sunny, warm and dry climate. Examples of such cities are Los Angeles (California, USA), New York (USA), Sydney (Australia), Jakarta (Indonesia), Shanghai (China), Bangkok (Thailand), Rome (Italy) and Vancouver (Canada).

Effects: photochemical smog has serious negative effects on people, plants and animals. It causes health hazards such as headache, eye irritation, asthma, lung tissue damage, bronchial infections and pulmonary edema (collection of fluids in the lungs).

Key Points

  • Photochemical (Los Angeles or brown) smog forms when NOx and VOCs react in sunlight.
  • It contains hundreds of secondary pollutants: ozone, PAN, aldehydes and PBZN.
  • It appears as a yellow-brown haze.
  • It is common in sunny, warm, dry cities with many automobiles.
  • It causes headache, eye irritation, asthma, lung damage, bronchial infections and pulmonary edema.
lessons.title: Photochemical Smog

lessons.notes_html:
The greenhouse effect is the process during which radiation (thermal infrared radiation) from the sun is trapped by gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapours, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone, and these gases prevent the heat from escaping back into space. Although some of the energy passes back into space, most of it remains trapped in the atmosphere, which causes the earth to heat up. This natural process of maintaining the average temperature of our earth, and keeping it warm, is known as the greenhouse effect.

Global warming (scientists often use the term climate change instead) is the gradual increase in the overall temperature of the earth's atmosphere, caused by gases that are collecting in the air around the earth and stopping heat escaping into space. The gases responsible for causing the greenhouse effect are known as greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, water vapours, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone. Mainly carbon dioxide and water vapours keep the earth warm and thus sustain life on it. Average global temperatures are maintained at about 15°C due to the natural greenhouse effect; without this phenomenon, average global temperatures might have been around -17°C, and at such a low temperature life would not have been able to exist.

Consequences of Global Warming

If the amount of energy from the sun and the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere remain the same, the average temperature on earth will also be constant. If the greenhouse gases are very few or totally absent, the earth would be far colder and life would not be possible. But if the amounts of these gases exceed a certain limit, the earth becomes hotter. If global warming continues unchecked, by the turn of the century the temperature may rise by 5°C. Scientists believe that this rise in temperature will lead to deleterious changes in the environment, resulting in a rise in sea levels, increasing ocean acidification, extreme weather events and other severe natural and societal impacts.

Contribution of Greenhouse Gases to Global Warming

Greenhouse GasContribution
CO276%
CH416%
N2O6%
Fluorinated gases2%

The concentrations of methane and fluorinated gases are much lower than that of carbon dioxide, but they absorb heat much more effectively than carbon dioxide, so they make significant contributions to warming the earth. Carbon dioxide is the only greenhouse gas whose contribution is rising rapidly. It can be removed from the atmosphere when it is absorbed by plants; removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere reduces the greenhouse effect and global warming.

Key Points

  • In the greenhouse effect, gases such as CO2, water vapour, CH4, N2O and O3 trap infrared radiation and keep the earth warm.
  • Global warming is the gradual rise in the earth's overall temperature caused by these collecting gases.
  • The natural greenhouse effect keeps the earth at about 15°C; without it the temperature would be about -17°C and life impossible.
  • Unchecked warming may raise the temperature by 5°C by the turn of the century.
  • Consequences: rising sea levels, ocean acidification, extreme weather and severe natural and societal impacts.
  • Contributions: CO2 76%, CH4 16%, N2O 6%, fluorinated gases 2%.
  • Plants absorb CO2, so removing CO2 from the air reduces the greenhouse effect.
lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming

lessons.notes_html:
Acid rain, or more accurately acid precipitation, is created when SO2, NO2 and CO2 combine with water molecules in the atmosphere and produce mild solutions of sulphuric acid (H2SO4), nitric acid (HNO3) and carbonic acid (H2CO3). It can also occur in the form of snow, sleet, fog, dew, hail and tiny bits of dry material that settle to earth.

Normal rain water is slightly acidic, with a pH range of 5.3 to 6.0, because CO2 and H2O present in the atmosphere combine together to produce carbonic acid, which is a weak acid. When the pH level of rain water drops below this range, it becomes acidic rain.

Harmful Effects of Acid Rain

  • It increases the acidity of rivers, dams, streams, lakes and oceans and significantly affects aquatic life.
  • It increases the acidity of the soil, water and shallow groundwater, which results in the killing of plants and animals; acidity may cause the death of fish populations and other aquatic species including frogs, snails and crayfish.
  • It makes water acidic and causes it to absorb aluminium that makes its way from soil into lakes and streams; this combination makes waters toxic to crayfish, clams, fish and other aquatic animals.
  • It affects trees: they lose their leaves, their bark is damaged and their growth is stunted. Acid falling on a forest's soil disrupts soil nutrients, kills microorganisms in the soil and can sometimes cause a calcium deficiency.
  • It erodes buildings, monuments and stone statues, and corrodes steel structures such as bridges and towers. It also corrodes ceramics, textiles, plastics and paints.
  • It adversely affects human health by creating particles in the air that can cause respiratory problems to humans and animals. Children and those who already have respiratory conditions such as asthma are badly affected. Headaches and irritations of the nose, throat and eyes are some of the minor effects; intensified levels of acidic depositions are linked to risks of developing heart and lung problems such as asthma and bronchitis, and even cancer. Drinking tap water contaminated with acid rain can damage our brains.

The harmful effects of acid rain may be minimized by minimizing the emissions of nitrogen oxides, sulphur oxides and other harmful gases from power plants, industries and automobile exhausts.

Key Points

  • Acid rain forms when SO2, NO2 and CO2 combine with water to give H2SO4, HNO3 and H2CO3.
  • It can fall as rain, snow, sleet, fog, dew, hail or dry material.
  • Normal rain has pH 5.3-6.0 due to weak carbonic acid; rain below this range is acid rain.
  • Acid rain acidifies lakes and soils, kills fish and other aquatic life, and mobilizes toxic aluminium.
  • It damages trees and soil nutrients, and erodes buildings, monuments and steel structures.
  • It harms human health, especially the lungs of children and asthma patients.
  • Its effects are minimized by cutting NOx, SOx and other harmful emissions from power plants, industries and vehicles.
lessons.title: Acid Rain

lessons.notes_html:
The stratosphere is the region (the second region) from 12 km to 50 km (approximately) above the earth's surface. It consists of nitrogen, oxygen and ozone. No weather takes place in the stratosphere. The stratosphere has over 15% of the total mass of the atmosphere, and it is where the ozone layer is located. This layer is about 38 kilometres thick.

The ozone layer is present about 20-40 km above the earth's surface. Ozone (O3) is a hazardous pollutant at low altitudes, but it is significantly important in the upper atmosphere because it helps protect us from hazardous ultraviolet radiation (UV) from the sun; life on earth would not be possible without the protection of this layer. If more ultraviolet radiation reaches the earth's surface, it can cause health problems such as skin cancer, affect the immune system and may cause blindness.

Air temperature slowly increases with height in the stratosphere, in contrast with the troposphere, where the temperature quickly decreases with height. This unusual temperature structure is caused by the absorption of sunlight by ozone.

Production and Destruction of Ozone

Ozone is produced by photochemical reactions in the stratosphere when the rays of the sun split oxygen molecules into single atoms. These atoms combine with nearby oxygen to form a tri-oxygen molecule, called ozone. The ozone molecules, in turn, absorb ultraviolet rays between 220 to 330 nm, and thus prevent these harmful radiations from entering the earth's atmosphere. Ultraviolet radiation at a wavelength longer than 220 nm cannot be absorbed by O2, and it cannot break the oxygen molecule into two oxygen atoms. Thus, the total amount of ozone is maintained by this continuous process of destruction and regeneration.

Key Reactions

ReactionProcess
O2(g) →(UV, 220 nm) O(g) + O(g)Sunlight splits oxygen molecules into atoms
O2(g) + O(g) → O3(g)Formation of ozone
O3(g) →(UV, 220 to 330 nm) O2(g) + O(g)Ozone absorbs UV and breaks down; the cycle maintains the ozone amount
O2(g) →(UV, longer than 220 nm) No actionLonger-wavelength UV cannot split O2

Key Points

  • The stratosphere extends from about 12 km to 50 km and holds over 15% of the atmospheric mass.
  • No weather takes place in the stratosphere.
  • The ozone layer lies about 20-40 km up and is about 38 km thick.
  • Ozone protects life by absorbing harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun.
  • Temperature increases with height in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs sunlight.
  • Ozone is continuously produced from O2 by UV light and destroyed by absorbing UV (220-330 nm), so its total amount stays balanced.
lessons.title: Chemistry of the Stratosphere

lessons.notes_html:
The ozone layer protects the earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation by absorbing these radiations. As the layer is reduced, the amount of harmful ultraviolet radiation that reaches the earth increases. The ozone depletion (reduction) in the stratosphere is caused by ozone-depleting chemicals. Examples of these chemicals are CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl bromide, hydrobromofluorocarbons (HCFCs) and bromochloromethane (BCM).

Chemicals that are produced or influenced by human activities are known as anthropogenic (man-made) compounds. For example, chlorofluorocarbons are anthropogenic compounds in the atmosphere that are produced by aerosol propellants, refrigerator coolants and air conditioners. Many organic compounds produced by human activities, such as CO2 and CH4, also occur naturally and in sufficient quantities. Some anthropogenic organic compounds, such as DDT (insecticide), do not have a natural source. Anthropogenic compounds can have harmful effects on human health and the environment.

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are anthropogenic compounds containing atoms of carbon, chlorine and fluorine. CFCs are also called Freons. They can be readily converted from a liquid to a gas and vice versa. Examples are trichlorofluoromethane and dichlorodifluoromethane.

Halons

Halons are also anthropogenic compounds, containing atoms of carbon, bromine, chlorine and/or fluorine.

The CFCs and halons are very stable compounds; they are inert. The chlorofluorocarbons take 50 to 1700 years to break down, whereas halons take 65 years to break down. CFCs are very important compounds and are prepared on a large scale in the world. They are non-toxic, non-flammable and non-corrosive. CFCs are used as coolants in refrigerators and air-conditioners, and as propellants in aerosol sprays. Halons are also used as fire-extinguishing agents.

CFCs contain chlorine atoms, while halons contain bromine atoms. The chlorine and bromine atoms of these compounds cause chemical reactions that break down ozone molecules and, in turn, reduce the ozone's ultraviolet radiation-absorbing capacity. Bromine is many times more effective at destroying ozone than chlorine. These compounds have been banned since 1996 in advanced countries.

Key Points

  • Ozone depletion is the reduction of stratospheric ozone by ozone-depleting chemicals.
  • Depleting chemicals include CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl bromide, HCFCs and bromochloromethane.
  • Man-made chemicals are called anthropogenic compounds.
  • CFCs (Freons) contain carbon, chlorine and fluorine; halons contain carbon, bromine, chlorine and/or fluorine.
  • CFCs take 50 to 1700 years to break down; halons take about 65 years.
  • CFCs are used as coolants and aerosol propellants; halons as fire-extinguishing agents.
