  • Chlorine and bromine atoms from these compounds destroy ozone; bromine is many times more effective than chlorine.
  • These compounds have been banned since 1996 in advanced countries.
lessons.title: Ozone Depletion

lessons.notes_html:
Chlorofluorocarbons, halons and methyl bromide are ozone depleting substances (ODS). When these gases are carried to the stratosphere layer of the atmosphere, ultraviolet radiations from the sun break them to release chlorine (from CFCs) and bromine (from methyl bromide and halons). The chlorine and bromine react with the oxygen atoms in ozone and rip apart the ozone molecule. The ozone layer acts as a filter for highly hazardous ultraviolet radiation from the sun, protecting life on earth from its potentially harmful effects.

The protection of the ozone layer is only possible by developing alternatives to ozone-depleting chemicals. Scientists developed three primary substitutes for CFCs: (i) HCFCs, (ii) HFCs and (iii) HCs.

Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs)

They contain hydrogen, chlorine and fluorine atoms. They are just like CFCs, except that hydrogen atoms have replaced some chlorine atoms. They were the first substances used as replacements for CFCs. HCFCs are less stable in the lower atmosphere, enabling them to break down before reaching the ozone layer. However, they still diffuse into the stratosphere and cause significant ozone destruction. They have a shorter lifetime (2-25 years) in the lower atmosphere than CFCs (more than 100 years). But the problem is that they still contain chlorine that can attack the ozone layer. HCFCs can contribute to global warming and are more expensive to make than CFCs.

Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs)

They contain hydrogen and fluorine atoms. They are chlorine-free: they are like CFCs, except that hydrogen atoms have replaced the chlorine atoms. Due to the absence of chlorine, they have no ozone depletion potential. They are now widely used as replacements for CFCs. They have a shorter lifetime (2-25 years) in the lower atmosphere than CFCs (more than 100 years). But the problem is that HFCs can contribute to global warming and are more expensive to make than CFCs.

The HCFC and HFC substitutes are six to fifteen times more expensive than CFCs. It is better to use HFCs as compared to HCFCs, because HFCs have no ozone depletion potential.

Hydrocarbons (HCs)

They contain hydrogen and carbon atoms and are free from halogens. They (a propane/isobutane blend) replaced CFCs and are extensively used in mobile air-conditioning systems as refrigerants in many countries. They are also used in domestic and commercial refrigeration applications worldwide, and as propellants in spray cans.

Key Points

  • In the stratosphere, UV light releases chlorine from CFCs and bromine from halons and methyl bromide, and these atoms tear ozone molecules apart.
  • The three primary substitutes for CFCs are HCFCs, HFCs and HCs.
  • HCFCs contain H, Cl and F; they break down sooner (2-25 years) but still contain chlorine, so they still damage ozone.
  • HFCs contain H and F only; with no chlorine, they have no ozone depletion potential.
  • Both HCFCs and HFCs can contribute to global warming and cost six to fifteen times more than CFCs.
  • Hydrocarbons (propane/isobutane blend) are halogen-free refrigerants and spray-can propellants.
  • HFCs are preferred over HCFCs because they do not deplete ozone.
lessons.title: Substitutes of CFCs

lessons.notes_html:
Any physical, chemical and biological change in the quality of water by the addition of other substances that badly affect living organisms is called water pollution.

Water is essential for life on earth. We use water for drinking, washing, cooking, agriculture, industry, transport and recreation. Marine life is also impossible without water. Hence water must be free from deadly chemicals and bacteria in order to be drinkable.

The method in which raw water is made fit for drinking and other domestic purposes by removing foreign materials is called water treatment. The goal of water treatment is to remove contaminants and organisms through a combination of biological, chemical and physical processes, to make it safe for drinking. Contaminated water is the main source of infectious diseases such as amoebiasis, dysentery, cholera, typhoid, jaundice, malaria and paratyphoid fever.

Key Points

  • Water pollution is any physical, chemical or biological change in water quality that badly affects living organisms.
  • Water is essential for drinking, washing, cooking, agriculture, industry, transport and recreation.
  • Drinking water must be free from deadly chemicals and bacteria.
  • Water treatment makes raw water fit for drinking by removing foreign materials and organisms.
  • Treatment uses a combination of biological, chemical and physical processes.
  • Contaminated water spreads diseases such as cholera, typhoid, dysentery, jaundice and amoebiasis.
lessons.title: Water Pollution and Water Treatment

lessons.notes_html:
There are three major types of water pollutants: (i) suspended solids and sediments, (ii) dissolved solids and (iii) thermal pollution.

Suspended Solids and Sediments

The small solid particles that remain suspended in water and act as colloids are known as suspended solids. They include silt, coal dust, plankton and industrial wastes. The loose sand, clay, silt and other soil particles that settle to the bottom of a liquid are called sediments.

The process of natural erosion of soil and the decomposition of plants and animals gives rise to sediments and suspended solids in water. Sediment is subsequently transported by the action of winds, water or ice. Sediment is the most common pollutant in rivers, lakes, streams and other water reservoirs. The suspended particles and sediments produce turbidity in water and consequently reduce the amount of sunlight available to aquatic life, which is required for photosynthesis by bottom vegetation. They also reduce the storage capacities of reservoirs.

Dissolved Solids

Dissolved solids are a mixture of different organic and inorganic compounds contained in water. These solids are mostly minerals, salts, organic matter, metals, cations or anions dissolved in water. The major components of dissolved solids are cations such as calcium, magnesium, sodium and potassium, and anions such as bicarbonate, carbonate, sulphate and chloride. Dissolved solids may come from organic sources such as leaves, silt, plankton, industrial waste and sewage. Other sources are runoff from urban areas, road salts and/or fertilizers and pesticides. Dissolved solids may also come from runoff rain water and inorganic materials such as rocks.

A constant level of minerals is essential for aquatic life in the water. Changes in the quantities of dissolved solids can be damaging: amounts that are too low or too high limit the growth and lead to the death of aquatic life.

Thermal Pollution

Thermal pollution is the increase or decrease in the temperature of a natural body of water caused by human influence. The rates of biological and chemical processes depend on temperature. Thermal power plants, nuclear power plants and industries use large amounts of water for cooling purposes. The coolant water they use, which is hot, is usually discharged directly into water bodies. As a result of this hot water discharge, the temperature of the water body increases, which reduces the dissolved oxygen content of the water and adversely affects aquatic life.

Key Points

  • The three types of water pollutants are suspended solids and sediments, dissolved solids, and thermal pollution.
  • Suspended solids are small particles (silt, coal dust, plankton, industrial waste) that stay suspended like colloids.
  • Sediments are sand, clay and silt particles that settle at the bottom; sediment is the most common pollutant of rivers and lakes.
  • Suspended matter makes water turbid, cuts sunlight for photosynthesis, and reduces reservoir storage capacity.
  • Dissolved solids are dissolved minerals, salts, metals and ions from soil, sewage, industry, farm runoff and rocks.
  • Too much or too little dissolved solid harms aquatic life; a constant mineral level is essential.
  • Thermal pollution is a human-caused change in water temperature; hot cooling water from power plants lowers dissolved oxygen and harms aquatic life.
lessons.title: Types of Water Pollutants

lessons.notes_html:
There are six major categories of parameters of water analysis:

  • Physical tests: colour, turbidity, total solids, dissolved solids, suspended solids, odour and taste are estimated.
  • Chemical tests: the pH, hardness, presence of a selected group of chemical parameters, biocides, highly toxic chemicals, and BOD are estimated.
  • Toxic element tests: toxic elements such as iron, calcium, copper, chromium, manganese, magnesium, mercury, cadmium, molybdenum, selenium, arsenic, lead, zinc, aluminium, nickel, boron, etc. are estimated.
  • Bacteriological tests: the presence of harmful bacteria such as E. coli bacteria and total coliform bacteria is checked.
  • Pesticides tests: pesticides such as alachlor, atrazine, aldrin/dieldrin, alpha HCH, beta HCH, butachlor, chlorpyrifos, delta HCH, DDT, endosulfan, etc. are estimated.
  • Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) tests: benzene, toluene, xylenes, bromobenzene, butylbenzene, chlorotoluenes, dichlorobenzenes, phenolic compounds, polyaromatic hydrocarbons, etc. are estimated.

The physical, biological and chemical properties of drinking water have great importance, because a minor variation in these parameters affects human health. The defined standards of drinking water in Pakistan have been developed by the Pakistan Standards Quality Control Authority. The permissible limits, as laid down by the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the Pakistan Standards Quality Control Authority (PSQCA), are listed for comparison.

Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) and Dissolved Oxygen (DO)

Biological oxygen demand (BOD), also known as biochemical oxygen demand, is a measure of the amount of dissolved oxygen (DO) used by microorganisms (e.g. aerobic bacteria) in the oxidation of organic matter when dissolved into a body of water. BOD is measured experimentally by calculating the amount of oxygen at the beginning and at the end of a five days period at 20°C. A small amount of oxygen, up to 10 ppm, is actually dissolved in water. This dissolved oxygen is required by fish and other aquatic life to survive, and it is an important indicator of the quality of water. If water has 4 ppm or less dissolved oxygen, some fish and other organisms may not be able to survive. Dissolved oxygen is used by bacteria when large amounts of organic matter are present in the water.

Selected Water Quality Standards (Table 23.2)

ParameterWHO StandardPSQCA Standard
Colour15 TCU or less15 TCU or less
TurbidityLess than 5 NTULess than 5
Hardness as CaCO3—Less than 500 mg/L
Total dissolved solidsLess than 1000 mg/LLess than 1000 mg/L
pH6.5-8.56.5-8.5
Arsenic0.01 mg/L0.05 mg/L or less
Fluoride1.5 mg/L1.5 mg/L or less
Lead0.01 mg/L0.05 mg/L or less
Mercury0.001 mg/L0.001 mg/L or less
Nitrate50 mg/L50 mg/L or less

Key Points

  • Water is analysed under six categories: physical, chemical, toxic element, bacteriological, pesticides and VOCs tests.
  • Physical tests cover colour, turbidity, total, dissolved and suspended solids, odour and taste.
  • Bacteriological tests check for E. coli and total coliform bacteria.
  • BOD is the oxygen used by microorganisms to oxidize organic matter, measured over five days at 20°C.
  • Water holds up to 10 ppm dissolved oxygen; at 4 ppm or less, fish and other organisms may not survive.
  • Drinking water standards are set by WHO and, in Pakistan, by PSQCA; for example pH 6.5-8.5 and total dissolved solids less than 1000 mg/L.
lessons.title: Various Parameters of Water Analysis

lessons.notes_html:
Waste water (or sewage) is the mixture of wastes from the human body and used water. It includes domestic waste water (or domestic sewage), industrial waste water (or industrial sewage) and storm waste water (or storm sewage). The waste water that comes from sinks, showers, bathtubs, toilets, washing machines, kitchens and bathrooms is called domestic waste water; it is also called sanitary sewage. Industrial waste water is produced from industrial activities such as manufacturing or chemical processes. Storm waste water is rainfall runoff and other drainage that is collected in a system of pipes or open channels. The sewage is carried away from buildings by pipes under the ground, called a sewerage system. The waste water that flows into a treatment plant, basin or reservoir is called influent.

Waste water treatment (or sewage treatment) is the process of removing contaminants from waste water. Its major aim is to remove the contaminants to acceptable levels, to make the water safe for discharge back into the environment. Waste water treatment consists mainly of three steps: primary, secondary and tertiary treatments.

Primary Treatment

Primary treatment is also called physical treatment, because it is a mechanical process by which large suspended and floating material such as sand, silt and large lumps of organic matter are removed. Primary treatment removes around 40-60% of suspended solids and about 35% of BOD (biochemical oxygen demand or biological oxygen demand). Dissolved substances and pathogens cannot be removed by this process.

Secondary Treatment

Secondary treatment is also known as biological treatment, because it involves the use of bacteria and other microbes. These processes may be aerobic or anaerobic. Aerobic waste water treatment is a process where bacteria utilize oxygen to degrade organic matter (generally quantified as BOD) and other pollutants. Anaerobic treatment is a process where waste water or material is broken down by microorganisms without the aid of dissolved oxygen; however, anaerobic bacteria can use oxygen found in the oxides introduced into the system, or obtain it from organic material within the waste water. Anaerobic systems are used in many industrial systems, including food production and municipal sewage treatment systems. Secondary treatment may require a separation process to remove the microorganisms from the treated water prior to discharge or tertiary treatment. It removes around more than 85% of suspended solids and BOD. The sludge left after decomposition of sewage by aerobic and anaerobic bacteria is rich in phosphorus, nitrogen and minerals; after drying, it is used as manure.

Tertiary Treatment

This is the third and last step of waste water treatment. Tertiary treatment consists of advanced physical, chemical and biological processes. It is used when particular waste water components which cannot be removed by secondary treatment must be removed. Its major objectives are the removal of bacteria, dissolved inorganic solids, fine suspended solids and final traces of organic compounds, if needed. The water at this stage is almost free from harmful substances and chemicals. The water is allowed to flow over a wall, where it is filtered through a bed of sand to remove any additional particles. The filtered water is then used for the irrigation of a golf course, green way or park, or released into a stream, river, bay, lagoon or wetland.

Disinfection

There are still some microorganisms and pathogen contaminants in the remaining treated waste water. To kill them, the waste water must be disinfected for at least 20-25 minutes in tanks that contain a mixture of chlorine and sodium hypochlorite. Chlorination is done during tertiary treatment.

Key Points

  • Waste water (sewage) is the mixture of human-body wastes and used water: domestic, industrial and storm waste water.
  • Waste water treatment removes contaminants so the water is safe to discharge into the environment.
  • Primary (physical) treatment removes large suspended and floating matter: 40-60% of suspended solids and about 35% of BOD, but not dissolved substances or pathogens.
  • Secondary (biological) treatment uses aerobic or anaerobic bacteria and removes more than 85% of suspended solids and BOD.
  • Dried sludge from secondary treatment is rich in phosphorus, nitrogen and minerals and is used as manure.
  • Tertiary treatment removes bacteria, dissolved inorganic solids, fine solids and traces of organics; the water is sand-filtered and reused or released.
  • Disinfection with chlorine and sodium hypochlorite for 20-25 minutes kills the remaining pathogens.
lessons.title: Waste Water Treatment (or Sewage Treatment)

lessons.notes_html:
Green chemistry, also called sustainable chemistry, is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances. Green chemistry is based on a set of twelve principles that can be used to design or re-design molecules, materials and chemical transformations to be safer for human health and the environment.

Goals of Green Chemistry

  • To choose the most efficient ways to synthesize chemicals.
  • To make safe, sustainable and non-polluting chemicals that consume the minimum amount of materials and energy while generating little or no waste material.
  • To prevent and minimize the production and use of hazardous chemicals.

The Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry

In 1998, two US chemists, Paul Anastas and John Warner, sketched the Twelve Principles of Green Chemistry:

  • Prevention: it is better to prevent the generation of waste than to treat or clean up waste after it has been produced.
  • Atom Economy: synthetic methods should be planned to maximize the incorporation of all materials used in the synthesis into the desired product.
  • Design Less Hazardous Chemical Syntheses: synthetic methods should be designed to use and generate substances with little or no toxicity to either humans or the environment.
  • Designing Safer Chemicals: chemical products should be developed to affect their desired function while considerably reducing their toxicity.
  • Safer Solvents and Auxiliaries: the use of auxiliary substances such as solvents and separation agents should be avoided wherever possible; if these chemicals must be used, use harmless auxiliaries.
  • Design for Energy Efficiency: chemical synthesis should be performed at ambient temperature and pressure, if possible.
  • Use Renewable Feedstocks: a raw material or feedstock should be renewable rather than depleting, whenever feasible in technological and economic terms.
  • Reduce Chemical Derivatives: minimize or avoid unnecessary derivatization (e.g. protection/deprotection, use of blocking groups, temporary modification of physical/chemical processes) if possible, because such steps require additional reagents and can generate waste.
  • Use Catalysts: catalytic reagents are superior to stoichiometric reagents. Catalysts are effective in small amounts and can carry out a single reaction many times, so waste is minimized by using catalytic reactions.
  • Design for Degradation: chemical products should be designed so that at the end of their function they break down into harmless degradation products and do not persist in the biosphere.
  • Real-time Analysis for Pollution Prevention: advanced analytical methods have to be developed to allow real-time, in-line process monitoring and control prior to the generation of hazardous substances.
  • Accident Prevention: reagents and solvents used in a chemical process should be chosen to minimize the risk of chemical accidents, including explosions, fires and releases.

Key Points

  • Green chemistry (sustainable chemistry) designs products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances.
  • Its goals: efficient synthesis, safe and non-polluting chemicals, minimum materials and energy, little or no waste.
  • The twelve principles were sketched by Paul Anastas and John Warner in 1998.
  • Prevention comes first: stop waste being made instead of cleaning it up afterwards.
  • Other key principles: atom economy, safer chemicals and solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, catalysts, design for degradation, and accident prevention.
lessons.title: Green Chemistry
Classification of Chemical Analysis
lessons.notes_html:
Analytical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the analysis of matter. Analysis means finding the chemical composition of matter: what type of atoms constitute the matter and how many atoms form it. It involves the separation, identification and quantification of the components of a sample. The word analysis comes from a Latin word meaning to unloose a thing into its parts.

Branches of Chemical Analysis

  • Inorganic qualitative analysis: identification of inorganic compounds.
  • Organic qualitative analysis: identification of organic compounds.
  • Quantitative analysis: measurement of the amount of each component.

Qualitative analysis tells what is present in a sample and how many types of atoms or elements it contains. Quantitative analysis tells how much of a component is present. It has two main types: volumetric analysis, which measures the volume of a solution, and gravimetric analysis, which works by weighing.

Scale of Analysis

TypeSample size
Macro analysis0.1 g of substance, or more than 20 mL of solution
Semi-micro analysisAbout 0.01 g of substance
Micro analysis0.001 g of substance, or 0.001 to 0.1 mL of solution

Steps in Chemical Analysis

  • Preliminary investigation: collect information about the sample and decide the type of analysis and the method.
  • Sampling: take a small representative quantity of the material; a sampling plan is made first.
  • Preservation of sample: preserve the sample so that its composition does not change before analysis.
  • Sample preparation: physical methods (grinding, sieving, filtering) change only the physical state; chemical methods (for example precipitation from solution) are also used.
  • Measurements and data analysis: measure the required property and analyse the data to get the result.

Key Points

  • Analytical chemistry = separation, identification and quantification of the components of a sample.
  • Qualitative analysis tells what is present; quantitative analysis tells how much is present.
  • Quantitative analysis is volumetric (volume) or gravimetric (weighing).
  • Macro analysis uses 0.1 g or more; semi-micro about 0.01 g; micro about 0.001 g.
  • The steps are: preliminary investigation, sampling, preservation, sample preparation, measurement and data analysis.

lessons.title: Classical Method of Analysis
lessons.notes_html:
The classical methods are the traditional methods of analysis. They are based on chemical reactions and were the only methods available before the 1900s. They are time consuming and need a lot of expertise.

Salt Analysis (Qualitative Analysis)

The qualitative analysis of inorganic compounds is called salt analysis. It is used to identify the radicals present in an inorganic salt.

  • Cations (basic radicals): Na+, K+, NH4+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Al3+, Fe3+, Cu2+ and Zn2+ are identified by dry and wet tests.
  • Anions (acid radicals): CO3^2-, SO4^2-, NO3-, Cl-, Br- and CH3COO- are identified by wet tests.

Quantitative Classical Methods

  • Volumetric analysis: the concentration of a solution is found from the volume of a solution of known concentration that reacts with a measured volume of the unknown solution. Example: the concentration of an HCl solution is found by titrating it with NaOH solution of known concentration.
  • Gravimetric analysis: the substance to be estimated is converted into an insoluble compound of definite composition, which is separated and weighed. Example: estimation of sulphate ions in a solution as BaSO4, and the analysis of nickel in steel.

Key Points

  • Classical methods are traditional, reaction-based, slow and need much expertise.
  • Salt analysis is the qualitative analysis of inorganic salts: cations by dry and wet tests, anions by wet tests.
  • Volumetric analysis measures a reacting volume; the result is a concentration.
  • Gravimetric analysis weighs a pure insoluble compound of definite composition, e.g. sulphate as BaSO4.

lessons.title: The Combustion Analysis
lessons.notes_html:
Combustion analysis is a classical quantitative method used to find the amounts of carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound. A known mass of the compound is burnt completely in excess oxygen in a combustion tube. All the carbon changes into CO2 and all the hydrogen into H2O.

Procedure

  • The weighed sample is placed in a boat inside the combustion tube, which also contains an oxidising agent such as copper oxide (CuO), and is heated in a stream of oxygen.
  • The water formed passes into a weighed tube of magnesium perchlorate, which absorbs it; the increase in mass gives the mass of water.
  • The carbon dioxide then passes into a tube of 50% KOH solution, which absorbs it; the increase in mass gives the mass of CO2.
  • From the masses of CO2 and H2O, the masses and percentages of carbon and hydrogen are calculated. Oxygen, if present, is found by difference.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Mass of C = (12/44) x Mass of CO2Carbon in the sample
Mass of H = (2/18) x Mass of H2OHydrogen in the sample
% of element = (Mass of element / Mass of sample) x 100Percentage composition
n = Molecular mass / Empirical formula massLink between empirical and molecular formula
Molecular formula = (Empirical formula)nActual formula of the compound

Empirical and Molecular Formula

The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. From the percentage composition, divide each percentage by the atomic mass to get the mole ratio, then divide by the smallest value. Example from the book: C = 85.63% and H = 14.37% give mole ratio 7.14 : 14.37 = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH2. The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms. Example: empirical formula CH2O (mass 30) with molecular mass 180 gives n = 180/30 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6.

Key Points

  • Combustion analysis finds carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound by complete burning in oxygen.
  • Carbon is weighed as CO2 (absorbed in 50% KOH) and hydrogen as H2O (absorbed in magnesium perchlorate).
  • Mass of C = (12/44) x mass of CO2; mass of H = (2/18) x mass of H2O.
  • Empirical formula = simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, found from percentage composition.
  • Molecular formula = (empirical formula)n, where n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass.

lessons.title: Modern Methods of Analysis
lessons.notes_html:
Before modern instruments, chemists depended on chemical tests. Functional groups in organic compounds were found by chemical tests, halogens and sulphur by the sodium fusion test, aromaticity by the flame test, and molecular masses by using colligative properties.

Today, sophisticated instruments have revolutionised organic chemistry. Spectroscopic methods are used for analysis and for structure determination, and they use electromagnetic radiations as the basic tool.

What Modern Instruments Can Do

  • Determine the unsaturation in a compound by UV spectroscopy.
  • Determine the presence of functional groups in organic compounds by IR spectroscopy.
  • Detect halogens or sulphur in organic compounds by mass spectroscopy.
  • Measure aromaticity by NMR spectroscopy.
  • Determine molecular masses by mass spectroscopy.

Key Points

  • Classical chemical tests have largely been replaced by fast instrumental (modern) methods.
  • Modern methods are spectroscopic methods based on electromagnetic radiations.
  • UV gives unsaturation, IR gives functional groups, NMR gives aromaticity, and mass spectroscopy gives molecular masses and detects halogens and sulphur.
  • Modern methods need only a small amount of substance and give more accurate results.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Radiations
lessons.notes_html:
Electromagnetic radiation (EMR) is a form of energy. It consists of an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles to each other and to the direction in which the wave is moving. Because it carries energy through space, it is also called radiant energy.

EMR is all around us: the heat (infrared) from a burning fire, light from a bulb, the sun or a television, X-rays used by doctors, the energy that cooks food in a microwave, and the radio waves that carry music are all electromagnetic radiations. The family includes gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet (UV), visible light, infrared (IR), microwaves and radio waves.

Properties

  • All electromagnetic radiations show wavelike properties, like waves moving through water.
  • All travel through vacuum with the velocity of light, 2.998 x 10^8 m/s, and travel in straight lines.
  • They are not affected by electric or magnetic fields.
  • They can be reflected, refracted and diffracted, just like light waves.
  • Visible light is only a small portion of the full EM spectrum.

Wavelength, Frequency and Energy

Every radiation is characterised by its wavelength, frequency and energy. The energy of radiation increases with increasing frequency and decreases with increasing wavelength.

QuantityMeaningSymbol and unit
WavelengthDistance between two adjacent crests or troughs of a waveλ (lambda); m, nm or Å
FrequencyNumber of waves passing through a point in one secondν (nu); hertz or cycles/sec
WavenumberNumber of waves present in one centimetre; the inverse of wavelengthν bar; cm-1

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
E = hν = hc/λEnergy of radiation (h = Planck constant, c = velocity of light)
ν = c/λFrequency from wavelength; frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength
Wavenumber = 1/λWaves per centimetre

Key Points

  • EMR has electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel.
  • All EMR travels at 2.998 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum, in straight lines, and is not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
  • Energy increases with frequency and decreases with wavelength: E = hν = hc/λ.
  • Wavelength λ is the distance between adjacent crests; frequency ν is waves per second; wavenumber is 1/λ in cm-1.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.notes_html:
When the different types of electromagnetic radiations are arranged in order of increasing wavelength (or decreasing frequency), the complete arrangement is called the electromagnetic spectrum. Visible light lies between infrared and ultraviolet, with wavelengths of about 400 nm to 800 nm. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays lie towards the lower wavelength end; infrared, microwaves and radio waves lie towards the higher wavelength end. In organic chemistry we are mainly concerned with the ultraviolet-visible, infrared, microwave and radio wave regions.

Regions in Increasing Order of Wavelength

  • Gamma rays: the energy change involves nuclear excitation.
  • X-rays: the energy changes involve the inner electrons of an atom or molecule.
  • UV-Visible: the energy changes involve valence electrons of molecules.
  • Infrared: the energy changes involve transitions between vibrational levels of molecules.
  • Microwave: the energy changes involve transitions to higher rotational levels of molecules.
  • Radio wave: the energy changes involve the reversal of spin of a nucleus or electron.

Electromagnetic Radiations and their Sources (Table 24.1)

RadiationWavelength range (nm)SourceUses
Gamma rays10^-3 to 10^-1Sun, stars, unstable atomic nucleiKill cancer cells; imaging
X-rays10^-1 to 10^1Heavy metal anodeImage internal bones and organs
UV light10 to 400SunlightSterilise food, medicine and surgical equipment; body produces vitamin D
Visible light400 to 800Sun, light bulbEnables us to see
IR light800 to 10^6Hot objectsWarms objects; night vision technology
Microwave10^6 to 10^7Oven, radarRadar; warming food in microwave oven
Radio wave10^7 to 10^9Radio, TVAM and FM radio, TV, mobile phone

Key Points

  • The electromagnetic spectrum is the arrangement of all radiations by increasing wavelength.
  • Visible light is only 400-800 nm of the whole spectrum.
  • Gamma rays affect the nucleus, X-rays the inner electrons, UV-Visible the valence electrons, IR the vibrational levels, microwaves the rotational levels and radio waves the nuclear or electron spin.
  • Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher energy.

lessons.title: Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
Spectroscopy is the branch of science which deals with the study of the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter. It is one of the most important experimental techniques used to determine the electronic structure of atoms and molecules.

Uses of Spectroscopy

  • To determine the structure and functional groups in organic compounds.
  • To study the properties of molecules.
  • To monitor the progress of chemical processes.
  • To measure the purity of products.
  • To determine the chemical composition and physical properties of astronomical objects, such as their temperature and velocity.

Spectroscopic Methods

The spectroscopic methods most often used by organic chemists are: ultraviolet (UV) and visible spectroscopy, infrared (IR) spectroscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and mass spectroscopy (MS).

Key Points

  • Spectroscopy studies how electromagnetic radiation interacts with matter.
  • It reveals electronic structure, molecular structure and functional groups.
  • It is also used to follow reactions, check purity and study stars and other astronomical objects.
  • The four methods most used by organic chemists are UV-Visible, IR, NMR and mass spectroscopy.

lessons.title: Ultraviolet-visible Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The spectroscopy which deals with the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter in the ultraviolet region (200-400 nm) and the visible region (400-800 nm) is called ultraviolet-visible (UV/Vis) spectroscopy. The energy of this radiation is enough to promote loosely held electrons (non-bonding electrons or electrons in a π-bond) to higher energy levels. Because it involves electronic transitions, it is also known as electronic spectroscopy. The energy levels of an atom are quantised, so only light with a specific amount of energy can cause a transition from one level to another.

Principle of UV Spectroscopy

Molecules containing π-electrons or non-bonding electrons can absorb UV-Visible light and these electrons are excited to higher anti-bonding molecular orbitals. The more easily the electrons are excited from a lower to a higher energy level, the longer the wavelength of light absorbed. The greater the number of molecules able to absorb light at a certain wavelength, the greater the extent of absorption.

Types of Electrons Present in Compounds

  • Sigma electrons (σ-electrons): present in sigma orbitals. σ-Bonds are strong, so high energy is needed to promote these electrons. They are found in alkanes.
  • Pi-electrons (π-electrons): present in π-orbitals, in molecules with double or triple bonds, e.g. alkenes, alkynes and aromatic compounds.
  • Non-bonding electrons (n-electrons): not involved in bonding; found in compounds with heteroatoms such as N, O and S.

Types of Electronic Transitions

Four types are possible: (i) σ → σ* (ii) π → π* (iii) n → σ* (iv) n → π*. The σ → π* transition is not allowed by selection rules. The order of energy for the transitions is: n → π* < π → π* < n → σ* << σ → σ*.

Key Points

  • UV/Vis spectroscopy covers 200-400 nm (UV) and 400-800 nm (visible); it is electronic spectroscopy.
  • π-electrons and non-bonding electrons absorb the light and jump to anti-bonding orbitals.
  • Three kinds of electrons take part: σ, π and n (non-bonding) electrons.
  • Energy order of transitions: n → π* is lowest and σ → σ* is highest.

lessons.title: Types of Electronic Transitions
lessons.notes_html:
Each type of electronic transition needs a different amount of energy and so absorbs at a different wavelength.

(i) Sigma to Sigma Star (σ → σ*) Transitions

Promotion of an electron from a bonding sigma orbital to the high energy anti-bonding sigma orbital needs the highest energy, because sigma bonds are strong. It usually involves absorption of ultraviolet radiation below 150 nm and is the only transition available in alkanes. Methane, which has only carbon-hydrogen bonds, shows an absorbance maximum at 125 nm. These transitions are not available in the normal UV-Visible region (200-800 nm).

(ii) Pi to Pi Star (π → π*) Transitions

Promotion from a bonding pi orbital to the anti-bonding pi orbital needs less energy than n → σ* and σ → σ* transitions. Unconjugated alkenes absorb around 170-190 nm, and non-conjugated carbonyl compounds around 200-300 nm. This transition is available in conjugated alkenes, alkynes, carbonyls, nitriles and aromatic compounds.

(iii) n to Sigma Star (n → σ*) Transitions

Promotion of an electron from a non-bonding orbital to the anti-bonding sigma orbital needs less energy than σ → σ* and usually involves absorption of 150-250 nm. It is shown by saturated compounds containing atoms with lone pairs, such as N, O, S and halogens. The maximum absorption for water (H2O) is 167 nm and for methyl alcohol (CH3OH) is 183 nm.

(iv) n to Pi Star (n → π*) Transitions

Promotion from a non-bonding orbital to the anti-bonding pi orbital needs the least energy of all the transitions and absorbs at longer wavelengths, around 300 nm. It is shown by unsaturated molecules containing heteroatoms such as N, O and S. Saturated aliphatic ketones show absorption around 280 nm; acetone shows an absorption maximum at 279 nm.

Key Points

  • σ → σ*: highest energy, below 150 nm; the only transition in alkanes (methane 125 nm).
  • π → π*: alkenes 170-190 nm; found in alkenes, alkynes, carbonyls, nitriles and aromatics.
  • n → σ*: 150-250 nm; compounds with lone pairs (N, O, S, halogens); water 167 nm, methanol 183 nm.
  • n → π*: lowest energy, about 300 nm; acetone absorbs at 279 nm.

lessons.title: Instrumentation and Working of UV/Visible Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The modern UV spectrometer is a double beam spectrophotometer. It consists of: (i) light source, (ii) monochromator, (iii) beam chopper, (iv) sample and reference cells, (v) detectors, (vi) amplifier and (vii) recording device.

Parts and Their Functions

  • Light source: tungsten filament lamps and hydrogen-deuterium lamps are most widely used.
  • Monochromator: radiation from the source enters through an entrance slit and is dispersed into different wavelengths. It is also called the wavelength selector and is generally composed of prisms and slits.
  • Beam chopper (beam splitter): a circular disc device that splits the monochromatic beam into two beams of equal intensity.
  • Sample and reference cells: made of silica or quartz. One beam passes through the sample solution and the second through the reference solution.
  • Detectors: they have photocells. One detector receives the beam from the sample cell and the other from the reference; each generates a voltage proportional to the radiation energy striking it.
  • Amplifier: the voltage from the photocells is very weak, so the amplifier amplifies the signals many times to give clear, recordable signals.
  • Recording device: generally a computer system. It stores and records the data and generates the spectrum as a plot of wavelength of absorbed radiation against absorbance.

UV/Vis Spectrum of Acetone

In the spectrum of acetone, the π → π* band has λmax = 195 nm (shorter wavelength, stronger absorption), while the n → π* band has λmax = 274 nm (longer wavelength, weaker absorption).

Applications of UV-Visible Spectroscopy

  • Determination of equilibrium and dissociation constants.
  • Determination of the rate of a chemical reaction.
  • Detection of the structure of organic compounds, the presence or absence of unsaturation, the presence of heteroatoms, and impurities in samples of organic compounds.

Key Points

  • A double beam spectrophotometer has a light source, monochromator, beam chopper, sample and reference cells, detectors, amplifier and recorder.
  • The monochromator selects one wavelength at a time; the chopper splits the beam into two equal beams.
  • Detectors turn radiation energy into voltage, which is amplified and recorded as wavelength against absorbance.
  • Acetone shows π → π* at 195 nm (strong) and n → π* at 274 nm (weak).
  • UV-Vis is used for equilibrium and dissociation constants, reaction rates and detecting unsaturation, heteroatoms and impurities.

lessons.title: Infrared Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The spectroscopy which deals with the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter in the infrared region, from 0.8 μm to 1000 μm (800-1000000 nm), is called infrared (IR) spectroscopy. It is concerned with the absorption of infrared radiation, which causes vibrational transitions in the molecule, so it is also known as vibrational spectroscopy.

Not all molecules can absorb IR radiation. A molecule absorbs radiation when a bond in it vibrates at the same frequency as the incident radiant energy. After absorbing energy, the molecules have more energy and vibrate at increased amplitude.

The Three IR Regions

RegionWavelengthWavenumber
Near IR0.8 μm to 2.5 μm (800-2500 nm)12500-4000 cm-1
Middle IR2.5 μm to 25 μm (2500-25000 nm)4000-400 cm-1
Far IR25 μm to 1000 μm (25000-1000000 nm)400-10 cm-1

Pure vibrational transitions occur in the region 2.5-15 μm (4000-667 cm-1), so most organic chemists are interested in this region. Both wavelength and wavenumber units are used for IR spectra, but most chemists use wavenumber because it is directly proportional to energy, unlike wavelength, which is inversely proportional to energy; wavenumber is therefore more comparable to frequency.

Principle of IR Spectroscopy

Molecules are made of atoms linked by chemical bonds. The movement of the atoms and bonds is like springs and balls (vibration). This characteristic vibration is called the natural frequency vibration. If a bond is stretched or compressed and then released, the atoms vibrate. When IR radiation is applied, it causes vibration between the atoms of the molecule, IR radiation is absorbed, and a peak is observed. In daily life, infrared radiations from the sun, a heater or a fire vibrate our skin molecules; the vibration increases their kinetic energy, so we feel warmth.

Key Points

  • IR spectroscopy covers 0.8-1000 μm and causes vibrational transitions, so it is vibrational spectroscopy.
  • A bond absorbs IR only when it vibrates at the same frequency as the incoming radiation.
  • The IR region is divided into near, middle and far IR; organic chemists mainly use 4000-667 cm-1.
  • Wavenumber is preferred in IR because it is directly proportional to energy.
  • Bonds behave like springs joining balls; absorbed IR energy increases the amplitude of vibration.

lessons.title: Molecular Vibrations (Vibrational Modes) of IR Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
Atoms in a molecule do not remain at fixed positions. They vibrate back and forth about an average value of the interatomic distance. A molecular vibration occurs when atoms in a molecule are in periodic motion while the molecule as a whole has constant translational and rotational motion. The frequency of this periodic motion is the vibration frequency. There are two main types: stretching and bending vibrations.

(i) Stretching Vibrations

Stretching involves a change in bond length, resulting in a change in interatomic distance.

  • Symmetric stretching: two or more bonds vibrate in and out together.
  • Asymmetric stretching: some bonds get shorter while the others get longer at the same time, with respect to the central atom.

(ii) Bending Vibrations

Bending vibrations involve a change in bond angle, or a change in the position of a group of atoms with respect to the rest of the molecule. Bond lengths remain constant. There are four types:

  • Scissoring: two atoms move toward and away from each other, like the movement of scissors.
  • Rocking: atoms move in the same direction within a plane, like the pendulum of a clock.
  • Wagging: two atoms move up and down the plane together with respect to the central atom, like bending the fingers of a V sign back and forth from the wrist.
  • Twisting: one atom moves up the plane and the other atom moves down the plane with respect to the central atom.

Factors Affecting Vibrational Frequency

The frequency absorbed depends on: (i) the masses of the atoms in the bond, (ii) the strength of the bond, (iii) the geometry of the molecule and (iv) several other factors. Heavier atoms give a lower vibration frequency; a stronger bond gives a higher vibration frequency.

Key Points

  • Molecular vibrations are periodic motions of atoms about their average positions.
  • Stretching changes bond length: symmetric (together) or asymmetric (opposite).
  • Bending changes bond angle: scissoring, rocking, wagging and twisting; bond length stays constant.
  • Vibrational frequency falls when atoms are heavier and rises when the bond is stronger.

lessons.title: Instrumentation of IR Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The instrument used to determine the absorption spectrum of a compound is called an infrared spectrometer (more accurately, an infrared spectrophotometer). The most common type is the double beam spectrophotometer, similar to the UV spectrophotometer. Its main components are: (i) radiation source, (ii) fore optics, (iii) monochromator, (iv) sample cell, (v) detector and (vi) recorder.

Components

  • Radiation source: the commonly used sources are the Nernst glower and the globar. The Nernst glower is a hollow rod of rare earth oxides (zirconium, thorium and cerium) and is used for shorter wavelengths. The globar is a silicon carbide rod and is used for longer wavelengths.
  • Optics: mirrors and a rotating mirror divide the light from the source into two beams of equal intensity. One beam passes through the sample and the second through the reference (solvent). The rotating mirrors alternately allow light from each beam to enter the monochromator.
  • Chopper: it recombines the light before it enters the monochromator, passing the two beams alternately to a prism (or diffraction grating).
  • Monochromator: prisms and gratings produce single wavelength radiations.
  • Detector: detectors convert thermal energy into electrical energy.
  • Amplifier: the detector signals are amplified many times to generate clear and recordable signals.
  • Recorder: it automatically records all the data on a computer and plots the IR spectrum of the sample, usually as transmittance or absorbance against wavenumber. The spectrum is plotted as transmitted light, not light absorbed.

Applications of IR Spectroscopy

  • Structural determination of organic compounds.
  • Detection of the presence or absence of a particular functional group in a compound.
  • Identification of the structure of complex molecules in space.
  • Detection and measurement of even minute quantities of chemical compounds; widely applied in environment analysis, forensic analysis, industries and research.
  • Semiconductor microelectronics: applied to semiconductors such as silicon, gallium arsenide, gallium nitride, zinc selenide, amorphous silicon and silicon nitride.

Key Points

  • The IR spectrophotometer is a double beam instrument: source, optics, monochromator, sample cell, detector and recorder.
  • Nernst glower (rare earth oxides) serves shorter wavelengths; globar (silicon carbide) serves longer wavelengths.
  • The detector converts thermal energy into electrical energy; the recorder plots transmittance or absorbance against wavenumber.
  • IR spectroscopy is mainly used to detect functional groups and determine structures of organic compounds.

lessons.title: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The spectroscopy which deals with the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter in the radiofrequency region is called nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Its range is from 7.5 x 10^10 nm to 4.0 x 10^8 nm (75 m to 0.4 m, or 4 MHz to 750 MHz).

Many nuclei can be studied by NMR, but hydrogen (proton, 1H NMR) and carbon-13 (13C NMR) are the most commonly used. Proton NMR gives information about the number and type of hydrogen atoms in a molecule, and carbon-13 NMR is an important tool for structure determination in organic chemistry.

Theory of NMR Spectroscopy

Nuclei have many properties like those of electrons: a nucleus has a total charge and some nuclei also spin about their axes. The spin quantum number of a nucleus is determined by the number and pairing of its individual particles. The rules for the net spin are:

  • The nucleus has no spin when the number of protons and the number of neutrons are both even.
  • The nucleus has a half-integer spin (1/2, 3/2, 5/2) when the sum of protons and neutrons (mass number) is odd.
  • The nucleus has an integer spin (1, 2, 3) when the sum of protons and neutrons is even but both protons and neutrons are odd in number.
ProtonsNeutronsMass numberSpinExamples
EvenEvenEvenZero4He (0), 12C (0), 16O (0)
Even or oddEven or oddOddHalf-integer1H (1/2), 7Li (3/2), 13C (1/2), 17O (5/2)
OddOddEvenInteger2H (1), 6Li (1), 10B (3), 14N (1)

Nuclei with an odd mass number or odd atomic number have nuclear spins and magnetic fields; they are called NMR active nuclei, e.g. 1H and 13C. Nuclei with even numbers of protons and neutrons, such as 12C and 16O, have no overall magnetic field because their fields cancel out; they are NMR inactive.

Key Points

  • NMR spectroscopy uses radiofrequency radiation (about 4 MHz to 750 MHz).
  • 1H NMR gives the number and type of hydrogen atoms; 13C NMR helps determine structure.
  • Even protons + even neutrons = zero spin; odd mass number = half-integer spin; odd protons + odd neutrons = integer spin.
  • 1H and 13C are NMR active; 12C and 16O are NMR inactive.

lessons.title: Principles of NMR Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
All nuclei with non-zero spin have magnetic moments, so a nucleus can be considered as a tiny bar magnet. The magnetic moment is generated by the charge and spin of the nucleus.

Without an external magnetic field, the nuclear spins point in random directions. When an external magnetic field is applied, the nuclei align themselves either with or against the field.

Spin States

  • In an external field, two spin states exist: +1/2 and -1/2.
  • The +1/2 state is the lower energy state; its magnetic moment is aligned with the external field. It contains slightly more nuclei than the higher level.
  • The -1/2 state is the higher energy state; its magnetic moment is opposed to the external field.
  • Radiation whose frequency matches the energy difference can excite nuclei from the lower to the higher level. This is resonance.
  • The stronger the magnetic field, the larger the energy difference between the spin states and the higher the frequency needed for resonance.

The amount of energy absorbed is recorded as the NMR spectrum. In practice, either the magnetic field is held constant and the radio frequency is varied, or, more commonly, the radio frequency is held constant and the magnetic field is varied.

What NMR Tells Us

The main purpose of NMR is to distinguish between protons in different chemical environments in a molecule. The number of signals on the NMR chart shows the number of different types of protons, and the position of a peak gives information about the structure near that proton. Equivalent protons are chemically indistinguishable; non-equivalent protons are chemically distinguishable. For example, in CH3-CH2-Cl the CH3 protons (a) are equivalent to each other but different from the CH2 protons (b).

Key Points

  • A spinning nucleus acts as a tiny bar magnet with a magnetic moment.
  • In a magnetic field, nuclei align with (+1/2, lower energy) or against (-1/2, higher energy) the field.
  • Absorption of radiofrequency energy equal to the spin-state gap causes resonance.
  • The number of NMR signals equals the number of different proton environments in the molecule.

lessons.title: Instrumentation and Working of NMR Spectrometer
lessons.notes_html:
The instruments used to obtain NMR spectra are called NMR spectrometers. They contain a complex collection of electronic equipment and use very powerful magnets to create a small but measurable energy difference between the two possible spin states. The main parts shown in the book are the sample tube, the magnet, a radiofrequency generator, a detector and amplifier, and a recorder.

Working

  • The sample is dissolved in a solvent, usually CDCl3 (deutero-chloroform), and placed in the magnetic field.
  • A radiofrequency generator irradiates the sample with a short pulse of radiation, causing resonance.
  • When the nuclei fall back to their lower energy state, the detector measures the energy released and a spectrum is recorded.

NMR Spectrum

The NMR spectrum is a plot of the intensity of NMR signals against magnetic field (frequency), measured with reference to TMS (tetramethylsilane). The NMR signal is plotted on the y-axis and frequency on the x-axis. The frequency value increases from right to left. In an NMR spectrum the unit used is parts per million (ppm), not Hertz.

Applications of NMR Spectroscopy

  • Structure determination of biopolymers such as proteins and nucleic acids; in medicine it is used for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
  • In biology, to study biofluids and biomacromolecules such as nucleic acids (DNA, RNA), carbohydrates, proteins and peptides.
  • In physics and physical chemistry, to study high pressure diffusion, liquid crystals, liquid crystal solutions, membranes and rigid solids.
  • In food industries, food science, chemical analysis of different products and pharmaceutical work. Analysing the carbon-hydrogen framework of a molecule is the basic work of the NMR technique.

Key Points

  • An NMR spectrometer uses a powerful magnet, a radiofrequency generator, a detector-amplifier and a recorder.
  • The sample is usually dissolved in CDCl3 and irradiated with a short radiofrequency pulse.
  • The detector measures the energy released as nuclei fall back to the lower state.
  • The spectrum is plotted against TMS in ppm, with frequency increasing from right to left.
  • NMR is used for structure determination, MRI, biology, physics and food and pharmaceutical analysis.

lessons.title: Atomic Absorption and Emission Spectra
lessons.notes_html:
Atoms in which no electron is in a higher vacant level are in the ground state, the most stable electronic state. Atoms with an electron in a higher level are in an excited state. The movement of an electron from one energy level to another is an electronic transition. An atom absorbs light only when the light energy is exactly equal to the energy difference between the two levels.

Atomic Absorption Spectrum

The absorption spectrum of an atom is the spectrum of wavelengths or frequencies of photons absorbed when an electron jumps from a lower energy level to a higher energy level. The absorbed wavelengths appear as dark lines on a bright background, and absorption occurs when radiation is supplied. Sodium gives two dark lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm; hydrogen gives four dark lines at 410 nm, 434 nm, 486 nm and 656 nm.

Atomic Emission Spectrum

The emission spectrum of an atom is the spectrum of wavelengths or frequencies of photons emitted when an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower energy level. The emitted wavelengths appear as bright lines on a dark background, and emission occurs even without a radiation source. Sodium gives two bright golden yellow lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm; hydrogen gives four bright lines: 410 nm (violet), 434 nm (blue), 486 nm (bluish-green) and 656 nm (red). The positions of the bright lines in emission are exactly the same as the dark lines in absorption, because the energies emitted by excited atoms are the same as the energies absorbed.

Elements can be identified by their spectral lines, because the lines are different for every element. In flame tests, strontium gives red, barium green, potassium violet and copper blue lines; in a discharge tube helium glows pink and neon glows orange-red.

Difference between Emission and Absorption Spectra (Table 24.3)

Emission SpectrumAbsorption Spectrum
Formed at high temperatureFormed at low temperature
Formed when the substance is in the gaseous state (vapours)Formed even when the substance is in the liquid or solution state
Bright (coloured) lines on a dark backgroundDark lines on a bright background
It has bright lines of definite colourIt has dark black lines
Formed when an electron jumps from a higher to a lower energy levelFormed when an electron jumps from a lower to a higher energy level
Energy is releasedEnergy is absorbed

Key Points

  • Ground state is the most stable state; an excited atom has an electron in a higher level.
  • Absorption: electron jumps up, energy absorbed, dark lines on bright background.
  • Emission: electron falls down, energy released, bright lines on dark background.
  • Absorption and emission lines of an element are at the same wavelengths, e.g. sodium 589.0 and 589.6 nm.
  • Every element has its own line pattern, so elements are identified by their spectral lines.

lessons.title: Mass Spectrometry (MS)
lessons.notes_html:
Mass spectrometry is a technique used to measure molecular masses, to analyse the composition of a sample and to find the structures of molecules and other compounds, by the separation of gaseous ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).

Mass spectrometry is not a true spectroscopic technique, because no absorption of electromagnetic radiation is involved. It has very high sensitivity, low detection limits, and can ionise very small sample volumes.

Principle of Mass Spectrometry

Mass spectrometry does not directly determine mass; it determines the mass-to-charge ratio. It carries out three main functions:

  • (i) Ionisation of molecules.
  • (ii) Separation of the ions according to their mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio.
  • (iii) Determination of the relative abundance of each ion produced.

Components of a Mass Spectrometer

  • (i) Sample inlet system (vapouriser)
  • (ii) Ion source (ionisation chamber)
  • (iii) Accelerating plates and slits
  • (iv) Analyser (ion separation system)
  • (v) Detector (ion collector)
  • (vi) Amplifier
  • (vii) Recorder

Key Points

  • Mass spectrometry separates gaseous ions by their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).
  • It measures molecular masses, analyses composition and helps find molecular structures.
  • It is not true spectroscopy: no electromagnetic radiation is absorbed.
  • Its three functions are ionisation, separation by m/z, and measuring the abundance of each ion.
  • It is highly sensitive and works with very small samples.

lessons.title: Instrumentation and Working of Mass Spectrometry
lessons.notes_html:
How the Mass Spectrometer Works

  • Sample inlet: the material to be analysed is introduced into an inlet chamber and converted into vapour, which enters the ionisation chamber.
  • Ion source: sample molecules pass through a beam of very high energy electrons emitted from an electrically heated filament (usually tungsten). The collisions give energy to the molecules, which emit electrons and produce positively charged ions. Ions have different masses according to the isotopes present in them.
  • Vacuum system: an essential part of every mass spectrometer. The pressure is kept very low so that the ions move freely without resistance from air molecules.
  • Acceleration: a repeller plate with a positive potential directs the new positive ions towards a series of accelerating plates. A large potential difference of 1 to 10 kilovolts (kV) produces a beam of fast moving positive ions, which passes through focusing slits to form a uniform beam.
  • Analyser: it separates the fast moving ions by their m/z ratios. If all ions have a single positive charge and the same velocity, the deflection is inversely proportional to the mass: lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions.
  • Detector: the ions reach the ion collector and are detected. The electronic signal is amplified and recorded; data often go directly to a computer, which generates the mass spectrum.

The Mass Spectrum

The mass spectrum is a plot of ion intensity (relative abundance) against the mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio. The highest peak, called the base peak, is the standard against which other peaks are measured and is arbitrarily given a relative intensity of 100. The position of a peak shows the relative atomic mass and the height of a peak shows the relative abundance of the ion.

Worked Example: Iron

Iron has four isotopes: 54Fe (5.8%), 56Fe (91.7%), 57Fe (2.2%) and 58Fe (0.3%). Average mass of 100 atoms = (54 x 5.8) + (56 x 91.7) + (57 x 2.2) + (58 x 0.3) = 5591.2, so the average mass of 1 atom of Fe = 5591.2/100 = 55.91 amu.

Worked Example: Chlorine

Chlorine has two isotopes: 35Cl (75.77%) and 37Cl (24.23%). Average mass of 100 atoms = (35 x 75.77) + (37 x 24.23) = 3548.46, so the average mass of 1 atom of chlorine = 3548.46/100 = 35.48 amu.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Average atomic mass = Sum of (isotope mass x % abundance) / 100Relative atomic mass from a mass spectrum

Key Points

  • Working order: vapourisation, ionisation by electron beam, acceleration (1-10 kV), separation by m/z, detection.
  • Lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions in the analyser.
  • A vacuum is essential so ions move freely without hitting air molecules.
  • The mass spectrum plots relative abundance against m/z; the tallest peak is the base peak (intensity 100).
  • Peak position gives isotopic mass and peak height gives relative abundance, e.g. Fe = 55.91 amu and Cl = 35.48 amu.

lessons.title: Applications of Mass Spectrometry
lessons.notes_html:
Mass spectrometry is one of the most important analytical techniques, used in chemistry, biochemistry, medicine, pharmacy, agriculture, material science, food science and many related fields.

Applications

  • To determine the molecular mass of compounds by separating molecular ions on the basis of their mass-to-charge ratio.
  • To determine the molecular masses of peptides, proteins and oligonucleotides.
  • For the characterisation and sequencing of proteins.
  • In materials science, to identify the precise chemical composition of samples, which can help explain why buildings or bridges collapse unexpectedly or why engineering components suddenly fail.
  • In forensic science, to identify unusual substances found at a crime scene and match them precisely with similar substances found elsewhere.
  • To identify chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and explosive threats.
  • To understand the environment, for example to measure how quickly air and water pollution travels.
  • Mass spectrometers are increasingly used for drug testing and discovery, food contamination detection, virus and bacteria identification, pesticide residue analysis, isotope ratio determination, protein identification and carbon dating.

Key Points

  • Mass spectrometry finds molecular masses of compounds, peptides, proteins and oligonucleotides.
  • It is used to sequence proteins and to find the exact composition of materials.
  • Forensic scientists use it to identify and match substances from crime scenes.
  • It detects threats, pollution movement, food contamination, pesticide residues and disease-causing viruses and bacteria.
  • It is also used for isotope ratio determination and carbon dating.
